title: SOC Shift Command
blurb: Run the 23:00 to 07:00 shift. Pick your specialty, rack two tools, hold eight systems against a live adversary, and close out with a graded shift report.
source: Authored for 0pi.es from the ISC2 CISSP exam outline (April 2024); each card cites its outline area

campaign.title: SOC Shift Command
campaign.prompt: Eight systems, one 15-hour night shift. Pick your specialty and rack two tools — every system shows its price before you touch it, and every miss becomes a live incident you must contain.

config.maxGateRatioNote: beta.1 ships at 0.67 against its own 0.60 cap: the tiers average two gate cards per board decision. Recorded, not fixed, and deliberately not fixed by moving the cap — 0.60 is the number the design argued for. Bringing the deck under it means fewer cards per gate, or the deeper containment loop design R4 names as the real mitigation. Both are content work for the next wave.

roles.name: Identity analyst
roles.definition: You live in the authentication and authorization plane: sign-in telemetry, factor challenges, federation assertions, privilege changes. Nights on your watch tilt toward stolen credentials and quiet permission creep, because that is the traffic you can actually read.

roles.name: Network analyst
roles.definition: You read flows, not files: segmentation maps, egress patterns, beacon intervals, protocol misuse. Your shift bends toward probes, pivots, and callbacks — the adversary moves you can see on the wire.

roles.name: Endpoint analyst
roles.definition: You work the hosts: process trees, persistence keys, driver loads, tamper alerts. Malware that runs, hides, or digs in surfaces on your queue first — the wire and the boardroom are someone else's problem.

roles.name: GRC analyst
roles.definition: You hold the paper line: control evidence, audit trails, notification duties, executive risk questions. Your nights fill with auditors and anxious leadership — and when an incident lands, you are the one who knows what must be reported, to whom, by when.

territories.name: Governance desk
territories.teach: The Governance desk holds Domain 1: ethics, security concepts, governance and accountability, legal and regulatory duty, policy structure, BC requirements, personnel security, risk management, threat modeling, supply chain, and awareness.

territories.name: Asset vault
territories.teach: The Asset vault holds Domain 2: classification, ownership, handling, provisioning, lifecycle and retention, end-of-life disposal, and the data-state controls (DLP, CASB, DRM) that keep assets where they belong.

territories.name: Architecture rack
territories.teach: The Architecture rack holds Domain 3: secure design principles, security models, control selection, hardware taxonomy, architecture vulnerabilities, cryptography and its attacks, and site and facility engineering.

territories.name: Network core
territories.teach: The Network core holds Domain 4: architecture and segmentation, network components and hardening, and the secure channels — IPsec, TLS, VPN — that traffic must survive transit inside.

territories.name: Identity plane
territories.teach: The Identity plane holds Domain 5: physical and logical access, IAAA design, federation and trust direction, authorization models from DAC to ABAC, the provisioning lifecycle, and authentication systems including biometrics, Kerberos, and MFA.

territories.name: Assurance bench
territories.teach: The Assurance bench holds Domain 6: assessment and audit strategy, control testing from scans to penetration tests, security process data and KPIs, analysis of outputs, and the SOC report family.

territories.name: Ops floor
territories.teach: The Ops floor holds Domain 7 — the largest ward on the map: forensics and custody, logging and SIEM, configuration and change management, separation of duties, media protection, the incident lifecycle, detection tooling, patching, recovery strategies, DR process and testing, BCP exercises, physical security, and life safety.

territories.name: Dev pipeline
territories.teach: The Dev pipeline holds Domain 8: SDLC methodologies and maturity models, development ecosystem and CI/CD controls, the software testing taxonomy, acquired software risk, and secure coding against the OWASP classics.

cards.q: 05:40 · Architecture rack. The post-incident review lands on your desk: a depot clerk worked out that a police-escorted container existed because the dispatch database answered 'access denied' for its ID instead of 'not found'. Which lasting fix goes in the change ticket?
options: Keep a cleared-level record plus a routine cover record at the clerk's level
Change the error text so every denied lookup reads 'record not found'
Train depot clerks not to speculate about records they cannot open
Move the escorted container records into a separate database with no link
cards.answer: Keep a cleared-level record plus a routine cover record at the clerk's level
cards.why: Polyinstantiation lets the same key exist at several classification levels with different values, so the clerk sees a plausible record and the inference channel closes. Rewording the error fails the moment a clerk tries to create that ID and hits a key collision; a detached database breaks operations; training cannot close a technical inference channel.

cards.q: 06:15 · Architecture rack. Review of last night's near miss: someone reached the steel cabinet holding the HSM operator cards, and the room's motion sensors missed it because fan airflow set them off so often they had been tuned down. What do you specify for the cabinet?
options: Raise the motion sensors' sensitivity so any movement in the room alarms
Move the operator cards into a desk drawer in the locked SOC office
Add a second camera on the cabinet and review its footage every morning
Fit a capacitance sensor that alarms when anyone comes near the cabinet
cards.answer: Fit a capacitance sensor that alarms when anyone comes near the cabinet
cards.why: A capacitance detector sets an electrical field around one object and alarms when a body disturbs it, so it guards the cabinet whatever the room's airflow does. Raising motion sensitivity brings back the false alarms that got the sensors tuned down; morning footage review is detective and too late; a desk drawer is weaker storage, not better detection.

cards.q: 02:05 · Architecture rack. The payments gateway logs the same signed 'release settlement batch' message arriving three times in ten minutes from an unfamiliar IP. Each copy has a valid signature and identical bytes. What do you do first?
options: Let the batches through, because the signatures prove they are authentic
Rotate the gateway signing key, since a valid signature means it leaked
Block the source, hold the batch, and require nonce and timestamp checks
Switch the message signature from RSA to a longer elliptic-curve key
cards.answer: Block the source, hold the batch, and require nonce and timestamp checks
cards.why: Identical, validly signed copies from a new source are a replay attack: a genuine message captured and resent, no key needed. Containing the source and rejecting repeated or stale messages with nonces and timestamps stops it. Rotating the key or strengthening the algorithm misses the point, because nothing was forged; letting them through pays the batch three times.

cards.q: 23:50 · Architecture rack. The customs-clearance platform Tessaly shares with four other freight firms, run by their joint consortium, reports that one member's credentials were used to query shared manifests. Tessaly data may be in scope. Your move?
options: Scan the platform's hosts yourself to find how far the attacker got
Wait for the member firm's report, since the breach is on their account
Pull Tessaly off the platform tonight and rebuild clearance in-house
Invoke the consortium's joint incident clause and restrict Tessaly's feeds
cards.answer: Invoke the consortium's joint incident clause and restrict Tessaly's feeds
cards.why: In a community cloud, organisations with a shared mission share the infrastructure and its governance, so incident duties sit in the community agreement: invoke it and contain Tessaly's own exposure. Scanning hosts you don't own is unauthorised testing; waiting ignores Tessaly's duty to its data; walking off the platform mid-incident is a business decision, not containment.

cards.q: 03:30 · Architecture rack. A label-printing app on the warehouse servers keeps crashing, and the vendor's night support says the fix is to reinstall its agent as a kernel-mode driver. EDR shows the app trying to write into another process's memory. Your move?
options: Install the kernel driver so the vendor can capture a full crash dump
Run the app as a local administrator so its memory writes stop failing
Keep the app in user mode and isolate the host while EDR data is reviewed
Disable the EDR memory rule on this host until the vendor ships a real patch
cards.answer: Keep the app in user mode and isolate the host while EDR data is reviewed
cards.why: Applications belong in ring 3, user mode, where the processor stops them touching the kernel or other processes' memory; that boundary is what is blocking this suspicious write. Moving the code into ring 0 or granting admin hands a possibly compromised program full control of the host; disabling the rule removes the only alarm you have.

cards.q: 00:40 · Architecture rack. A researcher emails that the 'encrypted' driver PINs in a route-planning plug-in are just each character shifted by a fixed amount, and posts a decoded sample. The plug-in is live on 300 handhelds. Your move?
options: Add a second shift on top of the first so the pattern is harder to spot
Change the shift value in the plug-in so the posted sample stops working
Ask the researcher to delete the post and sign a non-disclosure agreement
Treat every PIN as disclosed, reset them, and replace the scheme with AES
cards.answer: Treat every PIN as disclosed, reset them, and replace the scheme with AES
cards.why: A fixed shift is a Caesar-style substitution cipher: with only a few dozen possible keys it falls to brute force or frequency analysis in seconds, so the PINs were effectively plaintext. Reset them and move to a vetted algorithm. A new shift value or a second shift is still one trivial substitution; silencing the researcher changes nothing about the exposure.

cards.q: 01:55 · Architecture rack. The fire alarm trips in the data-centre annex while a camera shows an unbadged visitor in the corridor. The facilities lead wants the egress doors kept locked to trap the intruder until police arrive. What do you do?
options: Send two staff to detain the visitor before anyone leaves the building
Silence the alarm for five minutes so staff can find the visitor first
Hold the egress doors locked until the police confirm the building is clear
Let the egress doors release as designed and track the visitor on camera
cards.answer: Let the egress doors release as designed and track the visitor on camera
cards.why: Life safety outranks asset protection: egress doors are designed to fail safe so people can escape a fire, and the cameras keep tracking the visitor for police. Holding doors locked could trap staff in a real fire and breaches fire code; silencing the alarm or sending staff to confront an unknown person trades people's safety for an arrest.

cards.q: 04:10 · Architecture rack. The sorting hub's conveyor controllers start receiving write commands from an office laptop on their flat network. The controllers run firmware that cannot be patched until the vendor's spring release. Your move?
options: Cut the laptop off and firewall the controllers into their own segment
Shut down the whole hub network until the spring firmware is available
Install endpoint antivirus on the controllers so they can block writes
Push the vendor's beta firmware to the controllers tonight to close it
cards.answer: Cut the laptop off and firewall the controllers into their own segment
cards.why: Industrial controllers often cannot be patched or run agents, so the mitigation is architectural: contain the source, then segment OT from office IT so only engineering hosts can reach them. Beta firmware on live, safety-relevant kit risks the line and the people near it; PLCs rarely support antivirus; shutting the hub for months is disproportionate.

cards.q: 02:40 · Architecture rack. A credential-stuffing wave hits the customer portal. The portal serves public parcel tracking and saved payment cards, and today every page sits behind the same single login check. Which change do you push through?
options: Put a CAPTCHA on the login page and keep one control for every portal page
Force MFA on every page, including anonymous parcel-tracking lookups
Require step-up MFA for card pages and leave tracking pages as they are
Take the whole portal offline until the credential-stuffing wave ends
cards.answer: Require step-up MFA for card pages and leave tracking pages as they are
cards.why: Differentiated security controls match protection to the sensitivity of each part of a system: payment data gets step-up MFA while public tracking stays frictionless. Blanket MFA taxes low-risk uses and drives customers away; taking the portal down hurts everyone; a single CAPTCHA keeps one-size-fits-all protection in front of the card data.

cards.q: 05:05 · Architecture rack. The pricing engine that feeds invoice totals has started pulling fuel-surcharge values from a public forum scraper someone wired in as a 'temporary' source. Two invoice runs already used the scraped figures. What do you do first?
options: Encrypt the scraper feed in transit so nobody can tamper with its values
Add a sanity check that drops scraped values outside 10% of last week
Cut the scraper feed and rerun both invoice runs from the vetted source
Keep the feed but flag invoices built from it for customers to review
cards.answer: Cut the scraper feed and rerun both invoice runs from the vetted source
cards.why: Biba's simple integrity property says a high-integrity subject must not read from a lower-integrity source ('no read down'), because unvetted input contaminates trusted output. Cut the feed, then correct the tainted runs. Range checks still let bad data in; flagging passes the problem to customers; encrypting the feed protects its transit, not its trustworthiness.

cards.q: 03:15 · Architecture rack. Utility power drops across the business park. The UPS picks up the racks, but the standby generator fails its start sequence twice and the UPS shows 18 minutes left. What do you do?
options: Start the planned shutdown order for low-priority racks to stretch the UPS
Shut every rack down at once so no system is caught mid-write later on
Call the utility for a restoration time before deciding on any shutdown
Keep everything running and keep on retrying the generator until it catches
cards.answer: Start the planned shutdown order for low-priority racks to stretch the UPS
cards.why: A UPS buys time for an orderly response, not continuity; the facility's shutdown plan sheds low-priority load so critical systems last longer and nothing crashes uncontrolled. Retrying and waiting on the utility gamble the whole room on the clock; dropping everything at once takes down payment services the remaining battery could still carry.

cards.q: 00:25 · Architecture rack. Threat intel shows two different firmware images for your handheld scanners that share one MD5 checksum, and the older update server still accepts images by that checksum alone. What do you do first?
options: Add a second MD5 check on download so a single collision cannot pass
Pause updates and require signed images verified with SHA-256 or better
Publish the good image's MD5 again so devices know which one to trust
Keep updates flowing, since matching checksums prove the image is clean
cards.answer: Pause updates and require signed images verified with SHA-256 or better
cards.why: A collision attack, powered by the birthday paradox, lets an attacker craft a different file with the same MD5 digest, so the checksum no longer proves identity. Pause and move to a collision-resistant hash under a signature. Republishing or re-checking the same MD5 verifies nothing new; matching digests are exactly what the attacker engineered.

cards.q: 06:30 · Architecture rack. The authorisation service behind the payout API is timing out under load, and the API's fallback setting treats a timeout as 'allow'. Payouts are still flowing. Your move?
options: Remove the authorisation check until load drops, then switch it back on
Flip the fallback to deny on timeout and queue payouts until it recovers
Add more authorisation servers first and review the fallback next week
Keep the fallback on allow so drivers are paid on time during the outage
cards.answer: Flip the fallback to deny on timeout and queue payouts until it recovers
cards.why: Fail securely: when a control cannot decide, the system should default to deny and queue the work, not grant it. Allow-on-timeout means anyone who can overload the service can pay themselves. Scaling out is sensible later but leaves the door open tonight; removing the check turns a temporary failure into a deliberate one.

cards.q: 02:55 · Architecture rack. A CPU vendor advisory says a flaw in how its processors' control unit sequences instructions lets code in one VM read another's data. Your payment VMs share hosts with the test estate. Your move?
options: Encrypt the payment VM disks so a neighbour VM cannot read their data
Patch the guest operating systems and treat the hosts as covered
Move payment VMs to dedicated hosts and apply the microcode update
Wait for proof of exploitation in the wild before changing anything
cards.answer: Move payment VMs to dedicated hosts and apply the microcode update
cards.why: The control unit directs how the CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions, so a flaw there sits below every operating system: it needs vendor microcode, and meanwhile sensitive workloads get their own hardware. Guest OS patches cannot fix the processor; disk encryption does not help because the leak happens in memory while data is in use.

cards.q: 01:20 · Architecture rack. The private key for the parcel-API TLS certificate turns up in a public code repository, committed by a contractor six hours ago. The certificate is valid for another eight months. What do you do first?
options: Delete the commit and rewrite history so the key is no longer public
Ask the contractor to confirm nobody else has cloned the repository
Keep the certificate, since it still has a full eight months of validity left
Revoke the certificate, issue a new key pair, and redeploy the endpoint
cards.answer: Revoke the certificate, issue a new key pair, and redeploy the endpoint
cards.why: Once a private key is exposed, trust in its certificate is gone; revocation publishes that through CRL and OCSP so clients stop accepting it, and a fresh key pair restores service. Deleting the commit cannot recall copies already cloned or cached; validity dates say nothing about compromise; a contractor's assurance is not evidence.

cards.q: 04:45 · Architecture rack. Three failed SSDs from the card-vault servers are sitting in the loading bay, tagged for the regular e-waste recycler's 06:00 pickup. The disposal policy says card-data media must be destroyed on site. What do you do?
options: Quick-format each drive and log them as sanitised for the pickup
Let the pickup go ahead, since failed drives cannot be read anyway
Pull the SSDs and have them shredded or incinerated under witness
Degauss the SSDs in the bay and let the recycler collect them after
cards.answer: Pull the SSDs and have them shredded or incinerated under witness
cards.why: Flash media is not magnetic, so degaussing leaves the data intact, and failed drives often still hold readable chips. For card data the dependable end is witnessed physical destruction such as shredding or incineration, with a certificate. A quick format only rewrites the file table; assuming a dead drive is unreadable is how media leaks happen.

cards.q: 05:25 · Architecture rack. Tessaly runs one of seven validator nodes on the ports' shared shipping-ledger blockchain, where only approved members can write. Your node's signing key was on a laptop stolen tonight. Your move?
options: Post a warning about the key on public crypto forums for the network
Do nothing, since one node cannot alter a distributed ledger alone
Ask the consortium to revoke your node's key and issue a replacement
Fork the ledger locally so Tessaly's records are safe from the thief
cards.answer: Ask the consortium to revoke your node's key and issue a replacement
cards.why: A federated or consortium blockchain is permissioned: a known group of members validates, and membership and keys are managed through that shared governance. So the response runs through the consortium, which can revoke and reissue. Assuming one node is harmless ignores that the stolen key signs as Tessaly; a local fork abandons the shared ledger; public forums are the wrong channel.

cards.q: 23:20 · Architecture rack. You take the ticket for the leased line between the two sorting hubs. Legal wants the carrier unable to see anything, including which internal hosts talk to which, on every packet crossing that line. Which design do you approve?
options: Rely on TLS in each application, since that hides payloads end to end
Add a contract clause forbidding the carrier from inspecting traffic
Put encryptors at both ends of the line so everything on it is encrypted
Hash each packet at the sending hub so the carrier cannot read the contents
cards.answer: Put encryptors at both ends of the line so everything on it is encrypted
cards.why: Link encryption encrypts everything on the link, headers included, so the carrier sees neither content nor which hosts converse. Application TLS is end-to-end: it protects payloads but leaves IP headers and routing readable. Hashing is not encryption and the receiver cannot reverse it; a contract clause is an administrative promise, not a technical control.

cards.q: 23:35 · Architecture rack. Tessaly's analytics team is taking on freight-pricing work for two rival grocery chains. The ticket asks how the data platform should stop one analyst seeing both chains' numbers. What goes in the design?
options: Give all analysts both datasets and log every query for later review
Encrypt each chain's data with its own key and give analysts both keys
Lock each analyst to the first chain's data they open, blocking the rival
Label both datasets Confidential so anyone cleared can open either one
cards.answer: Lock each analyst to the first chain's data they open, blocking the rival
cards.why: The Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) model grants access dynamically: once an analyst touches one client's data, competing clients in the same conflict class become off-limits, preventing conflicts of interest. A shared classification label cannot express 'rivals'; logging only detects after the leak; separate keys handed to the same person enforce nothing.

cards.q: 00:05 · Architecture rack. A ticket asks to publish a route-planning dataset for partners. Each field alone is harmless, but driver shift times, home depots and vehicle IDs together would show when cash runs are lightly guarded. Which do you approve?
options: Release a reduced set that drops the fields revealing cash-run timing
Release the full set but ask partners to promise not to combine it
Release every field, since none of them is classified on its own
Release all the fields as a PDF so partners cannot easily query the data
cards.answer: Release a reduced set that drops the fields revealing cash-run timing
cards.why: This is aggregation: individually low-sensitivity data combines into something sensitive, so the collection must be judged at the higher level. Dropping or generalising the fields that enable the inference fixes it. Field-by-field classification misses the combination; promises and PDF formats do not stop anyone combining data once they hold it.

cards.q: 23:15 · Architecture rack. Your ticket is to protect the new build room where laptops are imaged before shipping to depots. The facilities quote offers one premium biometric lock on the room door and nothing else. What do you send back?
options: Approve the biometric lock, since it is the strongest single control offered
Swap the biometric lock for two ordinary locks fitted on the same room door
Ask for layers: site badge, locked corridor, room lock, camera and cages
Skip physical controls and rely on full-disk encryption of every laptop
cards.answer: Ask for layers: site badge, locked corridor, room lock, camera and cages
cards.why: Layered physical defence in depth puts several independent barriers, detection and delay between an intruder and the asset, so one failure, a tailgater or a propped door, does not expose everything. One premium lock is a single point of failure; two locks on one door are still one layer; disk encryption complements physical security but does not stop tampering before imaging.

cards.q: 00:50 · Architecture rack. You're writing the build standard for new card-key servers. The requirement is that a server should refuse to release its card keys if its bootloader or firmware has been altered. What do you specify?
options: Run a weekly antivirus scan of the bootloader and alert on any change
Keep the keys on a USB stick that operators plug in at every restart
Store the keys in an encrypted file with the password in the boot script
Seal the keys to the TPM against that server's measured-boot values
cards.answer: Seal the keys to the TPM against that server's measured-boot values
cards.why: A TPM records measurements of firmware and boot components in its PCRs and can seal a key so it unseals only when those measurements match, so a tampered boot chain simply gets no key. A password in the boot script is readable by anyone with the disk; a USB stick relies on people and travels; a weekly scan is detective and runs after a compromised boot.

cards.q: 01:35 · Architecture rack. A pen-test report says the in-house library that checks API tokens on the payments gateway answers faster when the first characters of a guess are right. The token algorithm itself is sound. What goes in the fix ticket?
options: Replace the token check with a constant-time comparison routine
Add a random sleep to each response and keep the current comparison
Swap the token algorithm for a newer one with a larger key size
Lengthen the tokens so guessing them one character at a time is slower
cards.answer: Replace the token check with a constant-time comparison routine
cards.why: This is a timing side-channel attack: the algorithm is fine, but the implementation leaks information through how long it takes. A constant-time comparison removes the signal. A bigger key or new algorithm never touches the leak; longer tokens only slow the per-character attack; random delays add noise that averaging over many requests filters out.

cards.q: 02:20 · Architecture rack. Depots want parcel-scan images analysed on small servers in each depot instead of the central cloud, because their links keep dropping. The ticket asks what security design comes with that. What do you approve?
options: Approve it and let each depot manager pick the settings for their node
Approve it with the same controls as the office printers at each depot
Harden and centrally manage each depot node, with encrypted local storage
Reject it, because only the central cloud can be secured to standard
cards.answer: Harden and centrally manage each depot node, with encrypted local storage
cards.why: Edge computing moves processing close to where data is produced, cutting latency and link dependency but spreading assets into less-protected places. So each edge node needs hardening, central configuration and patching, and encryption for the data it holds. Printer-grade treatment or per-site settings create drift; flat rejection blocks a legitimate need that should be enabled securely.

cards.q: 03:05 · Architecture rack. The signing tool for handheld-scanner firmware uses ECDSA, and a code review finds it takes its per-signature random value from a counter that resets on every reboot. The key itself sits in an HSM. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Sign firmware less often so the same value is reused fewer times
Keep the counter, because the HSM already protects the private key
Use a fresh random or RFC 6979 deterministic nonce for every signature
Move to a longer ECDSA curve and keep the counter-based random value
cards.answer: Use a fresh random or RFC 6979 deterministic nonce for every signature
cards.why: ECDSA depends on a unique, unpredictable nonce for every signature; if two signatures share one, the private key can be calculated from them, HSM or not. Generate it properly, with strong randomness or RFC 6979 derivation. The HSM protects key storage, not the maths; a longer curve leaks just the same; signing less only slows the leak.

cards.q: 04:00 · Architecture rack. A ticket asks you to review the storage-provisioning bot. It can create new buckets, it holds every right over anything it creates, and it can grant those rights to any account. What do you approve?
options: Keep all its rights and review the grants it has made once a quarter
Let it create buckets but route every grant of rights through an approver
Leave it as it is, since the bot only acts on buckets it made itself
Give the bot read-only rights and have people create buckets by hand
cards.answer: Let it create buckets but route every grant of rights through an approver
cards.why: The Take-Grant model treats authorisation as a graph: create gives a subject full rights over the new object, and grant passes rights on, so a creating subject becomes a route for rights to spread anywhere. Gating grants keeps creation useful while stopping uncontrolled propagation. 'Only its own buckets' is exactly the route; manual creation overcorrects; quarterly review detects too late.

cards.q: 05:15 · Architecture rack. Code review of the refund service: it checks an account's refund limit, then pays out a few hundred milliseconds later in a separate call. Testers got three refunds through by firing requests at the same moment. What do you require?
options: Make the limit check and the payout one atomic, locked transaction
Rate-limit refund requests to one per second from each account
Log the account ID of every refund so overspends can be clawed back
Add a second limit check after the payout so overspends get flagged
cards.answer: Make the limit check and the payout one atomic, locked transaction
cards.why: This is a time-of-check to time-of-use race: state changes between the check and the use. Making the check and payout one atomic transaction under a lock closes the window. A check after payout is only detective; per-account rate limits narrow the window but parallel sessions still slip through; logging only helps chase the money afterwards.

cards.q: 06:05 · Architecture rack. Hardening review for the parcel-label servers: a legacy plug-in runs only if data execution prevention and address randomisation are switched off for the whole host. It is due to be replaced next quarter. Which do you approve?
options: Keep the protections on and let the label workflow fail until replacement
Turn off only data execution prevention and keep randomisation on
Move the plug-in to its own isolated host and keep protections elsewhere
Turn the protections off host-wide until the plug-in is replaced
cards.answer: Move the plug-in to its own isolated host and keep protections elsewhere
cards.why: Data execution prevention marks data pages non-executable and ASLR randomises memory layout, together blunting most memory-corruption exploits. When a legacy component cannot live with them, isolate it so the exception is contained until replacement. Disabling them host-wide exposes every service; half-disabling still weakens the host; breaking the workflow ignores a real business need.

cards.q: 23:45 · Architecture rack. Testing the depot handhelds, you find a rogue Wi-Fi access point can make them fall back from TLS 1.3 to an old protocol version with weak ciphers before they reach the parcel API. What goes in the hardening ticket?
options: Hide the depot Wi-Fi network name so the rogue access point cannot join
Add a second password to the parcel API login screen on the handhelds
Keep fallback enabled so older depots are never cut off from the API
Disable legacy protocol versions and weak suites on handhelds and API
cards.answer: Disable legacy protocol versions and weak suites on handhelds and API
cards.why: A downgrade attack forces both sides onto the weakest protocol they still share, then breaks that. Removing legacy versions and weak cipher suites at both ends leaves nothing to fall back to. Keeping fallback preserves the hole; hiding the network name does not stop a rogue access point; an extra password does nothing for the channel's cryptography.

cards.q: 00:15 · Architecture rack. A vendor's new yard-management appliance ships with remote admin, SNMP set to 'public' and a demo account all enabled, and the install guide says to 'turn off what you don't need later'. What goes in the build standard?
options: Leave the defaults on but place the appliance behind the main firewall
Disable every feature at install and enable only what the design needs
Keep the defaults and ask the vendor for a hardening guide next year
Install it as shipped and switch features off after go-live as time allows
cards.answer: Disable every feature at install and enable only what the design needs
cards.why: Secure defaults and minimal functionality mean a system starts locked down and features are enabled deliberately, so nothing ships exposed by accident. 'Later' rarely comes, and a demo account or public SNMP string is an easy first foothold. A firewall helps, but insiders and anything moving laterally still reach the open services.

cards.q: 01:00 · Architecture rack. Finance wants depot managers' large refund approvals to be provable later, so no manager can claim someone else sent one. The draft design uses an HMAC with a key shared by all managers. What do you change?
options: Encrypt approvals with the finance team's public key before sending
Keep the HMAC and lengthen the shared key to 512 bits for strength
Add a timestamp to each HMAC so approvals can be ordered in the log
Have each manager sign approvals with a private key only they hold
cards.answer: Have each manager sign approvals with a private key only they hold
cards.why: Only a digital signature made with a private key held by one person gives authentication, integrity and non-repudiation together. An HMAC proves integrity and that someone holding the shared key sent it, but any manager could have, so nobody can be held to it. Longer keys and timestamps do not change that; encrypting to finance gives confidentiality, not proof of origin.

cards.q: 02:30 · Architecture rack. The document platform gives each user a clearance and each file a label. A request asks to let depot staff cleared to Internal open Restricted incident reports 'read-only' to speed up investigations. What do you decide?
options: Approve it for depot managers only, as they are more senior than their staff
Approve it and watermark every Restricted report depot staff open
Approve it, since read-only access cannot change the Restricted files
Decline and route depot requests via a Restricted-cleared investigator
cards.answer: Decline and route depot requests via a Restricted-cleared investigator
cards.why: Bell-LaPadula's simple security property is 'no read up': a subject may not read an object classified above its clearance, because reading is exactly how confidentiality is lost, so read-only is irrelevant. Seniority is not clearance; watermarks deter onward sharing but still hand over the content. A cleared investigator meets the need without breaking the model.

cards.q: 03:40 · Architecture rack. Depot handheld scanners have been writing parcel weights of -4 kg and dates in 2091 into the shipments database, and billing trusts those fields. The fix ticket is yours. What do you put in it?
options: Restore the shipments database from last month's backup every week
Encrypt the handheld-to-database link so the values arrive unaltered
Add database rules rejecting values outside each field's valid range
Have billing staff eyeball weight and date columns before each run
cards.answer: Add database rules rejecting values outside each field's valid range
cards.why: Semantic integrity means the database enforces that values make sense for their field, such as types, ranges and plausible dates, and rejects the rest at write time, whatever the source. Encryption protects transit, but these values were wrong at the scanner; manual checks do not scale and miss things; restoring old backups throws away good data with the bad.

cards.q: 04:25 · Architecture rack. The old door-controller boards in the rack room keep their firmware on UV-erasable chips with a small quartz window. An auditor asks how you stop someone quietly reprogramming them. What do you put in place?
options: Leave them as they are, since the firmware can never be changed once written
Push a remote firmware password so the boards reject unsigned updates
Cover the chip windows with tamper-evident seals and check them on rounds
Replace the chips each quarter with fresh copies from the vendor's site
cards.answer: Cover the chip windows with tamper-evident seals and check them on rounds
cards.why: EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light through its window and then rewritten with a programmer, so the attack path is physical: someone must expose or pull the chip. Tamper-evident seals and inspection cover that path. These boards have no remote update channel to protect; 'never changed' confuses EPROM with mask ROM; routine chip swaps add handling risk with no integrity check.

cards.q: 05:50 · Architecture rack. The new driver-payout service is at design stage, and the project lead wants to book a penetration test for launch week as the first security step. You own the security sign-off. What do you ask for first?
options: A launch-week penetration test exactly as the lead has proposed
A scanner licence to run nightly against the code repository
A signed statement from the lead that the design follows policy
A threat model of the design now, feeding controls into the build
cards.answer: A threat model of the design now, feeding controls into the build
cards.why: Secure design pushes security into the earliest phase: threat modelling, for example STRIDE against the data flows, finds design flaws while they are cheap to change. A launch-week pen test finds them when fixing means delay or risk acceptance; a scanner hunts known bug patterns, not design flaws; a signed statement is assurance on paper only.

cards.q: 06:40 · Architecture rack. A finance analyst left last month, and her encrypted archive of audit workpapers is now needed for a regulator. The encryption tool had no recovery option. You're asked to set the standard for new rollouts. What do you require?
options: Let each user choose whether to keep a backup copy of their key
Enrol every key with a recovery agent held under dual control
Drop encryption for workpapers so this can never happen again
Have staff email their passphrases to their manager each quarter
cards.answer: Enrol every key with a recovery agent held under dual control
cards.why: Key recovery, or escrow, keeps a protected copy of keys so the organisation can reach its own data when a person leaves, and dual control stops any single administrator misusing it. Emailed passphrases leak and break accountability; optional backups fail exactly when needed; dropping encryption swaps an availability problem for a confidentiality one.

cards.q: 23:05 · Architecture rack. The endpoint team wants depot kiosk PCs, which anyone in the canteen can use, to write straight into the master fleet-maintenance register that engineers sign off against. Which design do you approve?
options: Kiosks submit to a staging queue that an engineer validates first
Kiosks write directly, but only during each depot's staffed opening hours
Kiosks write directly, with a nightly job deleting odd entries
Kiosks write directly as long as each user types a staff number
cards.answer: Kiosks submit to a staging queue that an engineer validates first
cards.why: Biba's star integrity property is 'no write up': a lower-integrity subject must not modify a higher-integrity object. Routing kiosk input through validation by a trusted engineer keeps the master register clean. A nightly clean-up lets bad entries be used meanwhile; a typed staff number is not authentication; staffed hours do not change the kiosk's integrity level.

cards.q: 00:35 · Architecture rack. Reviewing the virtual estate, you find the hypervisor management console on the same VLAN as ordinary guest VMs, and dozens of forgotten test VMs still running unpatched. What goes in the remediation plan?
options: Snapshot every VM nightly so any compromise can be rolled back
Move management to an isolated network and retire unowned VMs
Put antivirus on the hypervisor host so it can scan guest traffic
Patch the forgotten VMs and leave the management console in place
cards.answer: Move management to an isolated network and retire unowned VMs
cards.why: The hypervisor is the most privileged component in the estate, so its management plane must be isolated: a compromised guest that reaches it can own every VM. VM sprawl, unowned and unpatched machines, needs inventory and retirement. Patching alone leaves the management plane exposed; host antivirus does not fix the architecture; snapshots help recovery but prevent nothing.

cards.q: 01:45 · Architecture rack. The ticket is to design remote access for a new analytics contractor. The old pattern gives any VPN user the whole internal network once connected. What do you approve?
options: Give the contractor a Tessaly laptop and the usual full VPN profile
Give standard VPN access and review the contractor's activity monthly
Grant per-app access checked on identity and device posture each session
Put the contractor on the full VPN, since the tunnel is already encrypted
cards.answer: Grant per-app access checked on identity and device posture each session
cards.why: Zero trust drops the idea that being inside the network earns trust: every request is authenticated and authorised on identity, device and context, to specific resources only. An encrypted tunnel protects transit but still hands over the whole network; a company laptop helps posture but not scope; monthly review is detective and late.

cards.q: 02:10 · Architecture rack. You're reviewing the change for a new IPsec tunnel to the card processor. The config template defines one security association and one SPI for 'the tunnel', and the engineer expects it to carry traffic both ways. What do you change?
options: Keep one SA but double its key length so it covers both directions
Keep one SA and reuse its SPI on both peers for simpler lookups
Replace IPsec with a plain GRE tunnel so both directions just work
Define a pair of SAs, one per direction, each with its own SPI
cards.answer: Define a pair of SAs, one per direction, each with its own SPI
cards.why: An IPsec security association is one-way: it binds one direction of traffic to its keys, algorithms and SPI, so a two-way tunnel needs a pair, inbound and outbound. Reusing one SPI or lengthening a key does not change that; plain GRE carries traffic with no encryption at all, removing the protection the processor requires.

cards.q: 03:25 · Architecture rack. Depot supervisors edit the stock-adjustment table directly with a database client to fix counts after audits. The endpoint team is rebuilding their workstations. What do you require in the new design?
options: Let supervisors edit directly and restore the table if counts look wrong
Give supervisors a shared admin login so every change comes from one ID
Allow changes only through an app that validates and logs each adjustment
Keep the database client but restrict it to each supervisor's depot tables
cards.answer: Allow changes only through an app that validates and logs each adjustment
cards.why: Clark-Wilson protects integrity by never letting users touch constrained data directly: they work through well-formed transactions that validate input, enforce separation of duties and write an audit trail, the access triple of user, program and data. Scoping the client still allows unvalidated edits; restoring afterwards is reactive; a shared login destroys accountability.

cards.q: 04:35 · Architecture rack. The payments ops desk's remote-support tool lets a vendor see agents' screens, and threat intel reports malware that grabs screen images through exactly that tool to harvest card numbers shown in full. What do you approve?
options: Mask card numbers in the agent view so full PANs never reach the screen
Ask the remote-support vendor to scan its own servers for the malware
Encrypt the card database at rest so stolen screens reveal nothing
Buy a second remote-support tool and split agents between the two
cards.answer: Mask card numbers in the agent view so full PANs never reach the screen
cards.why: Screen-scraping malware captures what the display shows, sidestepping database and transport encryption, because data must be decrypted to be rendered. Masking PANs so the full number never appears removes what it could capture. Encryption at rest is irrelevant to a screenshot; a vendor's self-scan is not your control; a second tool doubles the attack surface.

cards.q: 05:35 · Architecture rack. The product team's design for driver-safety dashcams records continuous in-cab video and audio, kept indefinitely 'in case it's useful'. You're asked for security sign-off before the pilot. What do you require?
options: Approve it with encryption at rest, since that covers privacy concerns
Approve it as designed, then add retention rules if complaints arrive
Approve it once drivers sign a waiver agreeing to constant recording
Collect only event-triggered clips, with set retention and privacy review
cards.answer: Collect only event-triggered clips, with set retention and privacy review
cards.why: Privacy by design builds data minimisation, purpose limitation and retention limits in from the start, backed by a privacy impact assessment, rather than bolting them on. Encryption protects stored data but does not justify collecting it; employee waivers are weak consent given the power imbalance; waiting for complaints means the over-collection has already happened.

cards.q: 06:20 · Architecture rack. You're planning the ceremony to generate the new HSM master key for card PIN processing. The draft has the senior engineer generate it alone and keep the backup on a USB drive in her desk. What do you change?
options: Split the key into shares held by separate custodians under dual control
Keep one engineer but move the USB backup into the office safe instead
Email the key to two managers so either one can restore it when needed
Skip the backup, because the HSM will keep the key safe on its own
cards.answer: Split the key into shares held by separate custodians under dual control
cards.why: Split knowledge means no one person ever holds the whole key, and dual control means custodians must act together, so a master key cannot be stolen or misused by one insider. A safe improves storage but keeps the single-person risk; emailing a key spreads it in plaintext across mail systems; no backup risks losing every protected key if the HSM fails.

cards.q: 23:30 · Architecture rack. On the classified-contracts workstations, users cleared to Restricted open Restricted bid files. The endpoint team wants to let them save notes to the Internal team share for convenience. What do you decide?
options: Allow the saves and run a weekly DLP scan across the Internal share
Block saves from Restricted sessions to the lower Internal share
Allow the saves as long as users strip the Restricted headers first
Allow the saves, since the users are cleared to Restricted anyway
cards.answer: Block saves from Restricted sessions to the lower Internal share
cards.why: Bell-LaPadula's star security property is 'no write down': a subject working at a higher level must not write to a lower one, because that is how classified content leaks, deliberately or through a Trojan. The user's clearance is irrelevant; the destination's level is what matters. Stripping headers relabels rather than declassifies; a weekly DLP scan finds leaks after they are readable.

cards.q: 00:20 · Architecture rack. Reviewing the source of a routing app bought from a small vendor, you find a hard-coded login that skips authentication whenever the username 'svc_diag' is used. The vendor says it's for their support team. What do you do?
options: Block go-live until the vendor removes the hidden login from the code
Record it in the risk register and let go-live proceed on schedule
Allow it but restrict the login so it works only from the vendor's IP
Accept it, since vendors often need a way in for remote support calls
cards.answer: Block go-live until the vendor removes the hidden login from the code
cards.why: A hard-coded login that bypasses authentication is a back door, or maintenance hook: access outside normal controls that anyone who finds it can use. Require its removal and give the vendor managed, logged, time-bound support access instead. Accepting or merely registering it leaves the bypass live; an IP restriction still trusts the vendor's whole network and hides the flaw.

cards.q: 01:10 · Architecture rack. Migrating the invoicing database to a managed IaaS virtual machine, the project plan assumes 'the cloud provider handles security'. You're asked to sign off the plan. What do you require added?
options: A plan to keep the old on-premises database running as a spare forever
The provider's written promise to patch the guest operating system too
Nothing more, since the provider already holds security certifications
A responsibility matrix naming Tessaly's OS, data and access duties
cards.answer: A responsibility matrix naming Tessaly's OS, data and access duties
cards.why: Under the shared responsibility model for IaaS, the provider secures the facility, hardware and hypervisor, but the customer still owns the guest OS, patching, configuration, data and identity. A matrix makes those duties explicit. Provider certifications cover only the provider's layers; IaaS providers do not patch your guest OS; running the old system forever is not a security plan.

cards.q: 02:45 · Architecture rack. You're setting the TLS policy for the payments API. The current config uses RSA key exchange, so anyone who later steals the server key could decrypt years of recorded sessions. What goes in the new policy?
options: Require ephemeral Diffie-Hellman suites so sessions get forward secrecy
Keep RSA key exchange and double the server key length to 4096 bits
Rotate the server certificate yearly and keep RSA key exchange as is
Encrypt Tessaly's stored packet captures so recordings are useless
cards.answer: Require ephemeral Diffie-Hellman suites so sessions get forward secrecy
cards.why: Perfect forward secrecy uses ephemeral key exchange, ECDHE or DHE, so each session key is discarded and cannot be derived from the long-term server key; a stolen key then decrypts nothing already recorded. A longer RSA key or yearly rotation still exposes every session recorded under that key, and the attacker's recordings are not the ones you hold.

cards.q: 03:50 · Architecture rack. The endpoint team is onboarding 400 smart thermostats for the cold-storage depots. Each ships with the same admin password and a web console, and firmware updates arrive only by manual download. Which rollout plan do you approve?
options: Deploy them as shipped, since thermostats hold no sensitive company data
Set unique credentials, isolate them on an IoT VLAN, and schedule updates
Keep the default password but record it in the depot runbook for engineers
Deploy them on the main depot network so engineers can reach the consoles
cards.answer: Set unique credentials, isolate them on an IoT VLAN, and schedule updates
cards.why: Embedded and IoT devices often ship with shared default credentials, weak update paths and exposed consoles; the mitigations are unique credentials, network isolation and a firmware maintenance process. 'No sensitive data' ignores that a thermostat is a foothold and that cold-storage temperatures are an availability and safety matter; the main network puts that foothold next to everything else.

cards.q: 04:55 · Architecture rack. Two designs for the parcel-tracking API's authorisation are on your desk. One is a single policy module with 40 rules; the other layers five custom filters that overlap and nobody can fully diagram. Which do you approve?
options: Approve both, running them in sequence so each can catch the other
Approve the single module, since simpler designs are easier to verify
Approve the five filters, since more layers always mean more security
Approve whichever design the developers can finish before the deadline
cards.answer: Approve the single module, since simpler designs are easier to verify
cards.why: Keep it simple, or economy of mechanism: security logic small and clear enough to review and test has fewer hidden gaps. Overlapping filters nobody can diagram hide inconsistencies attackers exploit. Defence in depth means independent layers, not tangled duplicates of one control, and delivery speed is not a security criterion.

cards.q: 05:20 · Architecture rack. The new low-power parcel tags must authenticate to depot readers with public-key crypto, but the chips have tiny memory and a tight battery budget. The vendor offers RSA-3072 or a 256-bit curve. Which do you approve?
options: Drop public-key crypto and give every tag the same shared symmetric key
Choose RSA-1024 as a compromise that fits the chips' memory budget
Choose the curve, which gives similar strength with far smaller keys
Choose RSA-3072, since larger numbers always mean stronger protection
cards.answer: Choose the curve, which gives similar strength with far smaller keys
cards.why: Elliptic curve cryptography reaches roughly the strength of RSA-3072 with a 256-bit key, so it needs less memory, bandwidth and power, which suits constrained devices. RSA-3072 works but strains the chip; RSA-1024 is too weak for new designs; one shared symmetric key across every tag means a single extracted tag compromises the fleet.

cards.q: 06:10 · Architecture rack. The dev team moves the customer-claims app onto a public cloud PaaS. A review finds the app's full-rights storage connection string in plain app settings, and the platform firewall allows any internet address. What goes in the fix ticket?
options: Rotate the connection string monthly and keep it in plain app settings
Use managed identity or a key vault and restrict network access by rule
Move the whole app back on-premises, where you control the OS yourself
Leave the settings, since the provider secures the PaaS platform itself
cards.answer: Use managed identity or a key vault and restrict network access by rule
cards.why: In PaaS the provider runs the OS and runtime, but configuration, secrets, identity and network exposure stay with the customer. Managed identity or a vault removes the stored secret, and access rules shrink the attack surface. Assuming the provider covers it is the classic misconfiguration; rotation still leaves a readable secret; retreating on-premises discards a platform that can be secured.

cards.q: 23:10 · Architecture rack. After an outage at one provider, leadership wants the driver app's back end split across two public clouds. The endpoint team asks what security design has to come with that. What do you require?
options: A third cloud provider so that any single failure matters even less
Each cloud team secures its half using that provider's defaults alone
Full security in the first cloud only, treating the second as backup
A common policy, identity and logging layer spanning both clouds
cards.answer: A common policy, identity and logging layer spanning both clouds
cards.why: Multi-cloud improves resilience but multiplies consoles, identity systems and default settings, so controls drift unless policy, identity federation and logging are unified across providers. Provider defaults differ and leave gaps; a weakly secured 'backup' cloud becomes the easy target; a third provider multiplies the same management problem.

cards.q: 00:10 · Architecture rack. The nightly backup job must encrypt 6 TB of warehouse data before it leaves for the offsite vault, inside a four-hour window. The draft runs the whole stream through RSA with the vault's public key. What do you change?
options: Compress the backup first and send it offsite without encryption
Encrypt the data with AES and wrap only the AES key with the RSA key
Hash the backup with SHA-256 so it cannot be read in transport
Keep RSA for the whole stream and ask for a longer backup window
cards.answer: Encrypt the data with AES and wrap only the AES key with the RSA key
cards.why: Symmetric algorithms such as AES are fast enough for bulk data, while asymmetric ones like RSA are far too slow and size-limited for terabytes. The standard pattern is hybrid: AES encrypts the data and RSA protects only the small key. Hashing proves integrity but hides nothing; compression is not confidentiality; a longer window treats the symptom of the wrong tool.

cards.q: 01:25 · Architecture rack. The shipping-quote service runs in containers built from a public base image pulled as 'latest' at every build, and a scan finds the containers run as the host's root user. Which change do you approve?
options: Move the service to a bigger host so containers are spread further
Keep 'latest', since it always carries the newest security patches
Scan the host weekly and leave image and user settings unchanged
Pin scanned, trusted base images and run containers as non-root users
cards.answer: Pin scanned, trusted base images and run containers as non-root users
cards.why: Containers share the host kernel, so running as root turns a container escape into a host takeover, and unpinned public images let unvetted changes in at every build. Pinned, scanned images from a trusted registry plus non-root, least-privilege containers fix both. 'Latest' can also mean newly broken; host scans do not fix the image; a bigger host changes nothing.

cards.q: 02:50 · Architecture rack. A crypto inventory of the card-reader fleet finds PIN blocks still protected with Triple DES under a 2009 design. The reader vendor supports AES in current firmware. What goes in the roadmap?
options: Keep Triple DES, since running DES three times makes it unbreakable
Replace Triple DES with single DES so the readers respond faster
Leave the readers alone until an actual breach forces the change
Plan a migration to AES, with Triple DES retired by a set deadline
cards.answer: Plan a migration to AES, with Triple DES retired by a set deadline
cards.why: Triple DES runs DES three times, but its 64-bit block and limited effective strength led NIST to deprecate and retire it; AES is the replacement. A dated migration plan, built on crypto agility, is the managed response. Single DES is broken outright; 'unbreakable' is exactly the wrong belief; waiting for a breach accepts a known weakness.

cards.q: 03:35 · Architecture rack. The endpoint team finds every depot PC shares the same local administrator password, and helpdesk staff log in to user PCs with domain admin accounts. Which change do you approve first?
options: Enable full-disk encryption so admin hashes cannot be read from disk
Randomise local admin passwords per PC and bar domain admins from them
Lengthen the shared local admin password to 20 characters for strength
Force every user to change their own password each month instead
cards.answer: Randomise local admin passwords per PC and bar domain admins from them
cards.why: Pass-the-hash reuses a captured password hash without cracking it, so one shared local admin hash opens every PC and a cached domain admin hash opens the domain. Unique per-machine passwords and tiered admin that keeps privileged accounts off workstations break that lateral movement. A longer shared password still yields one reusable hash; disk encryption does not protect hashes in memory.

cards.q: 04:40 · Architecture rack. The data-encryption key protecting ten years of customer billing records has never been changed, and the key-management review lands on your desk. The team fears rotation means a full re-encryption. What do you require?
options: Rotate the key and delete the old one before re-encrypting the data
Leave the key in place, since changing it now would be too disruptive
Publish the key's fingerprint internally so anyone can spot tampering
Set a cryptoperiod and wrap data keys under a master key you can rotate
cards.answer: Set a cryptoperiod and wrap data keys under a master key you can rotate
cards.why: Every key needs a defined cryptoperiod, limiting how much data and time an exposure would cover. Envelope encryption, with data keys wrapped under a rotatable key-encryption key, makes rotation cheap. Never rotating accepts unbounded exposure; deleting the old key before re-encryption makes the records permanently unreadable; a fingerprint says nothing about key age.

cards.q: 05:45 · Architecture rack. The new driver app's design stores user passwords as a single SHA-256 hash of each password. The design review is yours before launch. What do you require?
options: Store passwords with reversible encryption so resets are simpler
Keep SHA-256 but encrypt the hash column with the database's AES key
Switch to SHA-512 so each password hash takes twice as long to crack
Hash with a salted, slow function such as Argon2, bcrypt or PBKDF2
cards.answer: Hash with a salted, slow function such as Argon2, bcrypt or PBKDF2
cards.why: Key stretching makes each guess deliberately expensive: salted, iterated or memory-hard functions such as Argon2, bcrypt or PBKDF2 turn a fast offline cracking run into years. A single fast hash, SHA-256 or SHA-512, can be tested billions of times a second; encrypting the column fails if the key sits beside it; reversible storage means one breach exposes every password.

cards.q: 06:25 · Architecture rack. The IPsec tunnel to the fuel-card partner has run on the same security associations since it was built a year ago, because the engineer disabled SA lifetimes to stop 'tunnel flaps'. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Add a second tunnel so traffic survives if the first SA ever fails
Restore SA lifetimes so IKE renegotiates fresh keys on a schedule
Keep lifetimes off, since a stable tunnel is the main requirement
Swap the pre-shared key yearly but keep the current SAs running
cards.answer: Restore SA lifetimes so IKE renegotiates fresh keys on a schedule
cards.why: Each IPsec security association carries its keys, algorithms and a lifetime; when it expires, IKE negotiates a new SA with fresh keys, limiting how much traffic any one key protects. Disabling lifetimes leaves one key guarding a year of traffic. Changing the pre-shared key does not refresh SAs already in use; a second tunnel adds availability, not key freshness.

cards.q: 23:55 · Architecture rack. The endpoint team's new build for depot dispatch PCs gives every user local admin rights, because two legacy apps occasionally need to write to Program Files. What do you approve?
options: A shared admin password kept on file in each depot's dispatch office
Local admin for everyone, since the two apps would fail without it
Standard user rights, with folder permissions granted to the two apps
Local admin for everyone, plus antivirus to catch anything misusing it
cards.answer: Standard user rights, with folder permissions granted to the two apps
cards.why: Least privilege gives each user and process only the rights its task needs; granting the two apps specific write permission meets the requirement without making every user an administrator. Blanket admin lets any phishing payload install and persist; antivirus is a detective backstop, not a substitute; a shared password destroys accountability.

cards.q: 00:45 · Architecture rack. On the shared reporting server, a low-privilege depot report visibly slows whenever the restricted fraud-analytics job runs, and a curious clerk has started timing it to guess when fraud reviews are live. What goes in the ticket?
options: Move the fraud job to separate resources so it can't affect depot reports
Encrypt the fraud-analytics results so the clerk cannot read the output
Tell the clerk that timing reports breaches policy and close the ticket
Speed up the depot report so the slowdown is harder for users to notice
cards.answer: Move the fraud job to separate resources so it can't affect depot reports
cards.why: The noninterference model says actions at a higher level must produce no effect a lower-level user can observe; here the fraud job leaks its schedule through a timing covert channel. Separating resources removes the effect. Encryption protects content, but the leak is timing; a warning does not close a channel; a faster report only narrows it.

cards.q: 01:15 · Architecture rack. A new customer-support platform will hold public FAQs, internal staff notes, and customers' bank details for refunds. The project wants the moderate control baseline 'since most of the data is low impact'. What do you decide?
options: Average the impact levels of each data type and adopt the moderate baseline
Pick the moderate baseline now and raise it if an audit objects later
Use the low baseline, since public FAQs make up most of the content
Categorise the system by its highest-impact data and pick that baseline
cards.answer: Categorise the system by its highest-impact data and pick that baseline
cards.why: Controls follow requirements, and a system's security category is set by its highest-impact data, the high-water mark, because attackers go for the bank details, not the FAQs. Averaging or counting volume under-protects the most sensitive data; waiting for an audit leaves it exposed now. Splitting refund data into its own system is the lever if the higher baseline is too costly.

cards.q: 02:35 · Architecture rack. The standard requires MFA on every admin login, but the warehouse robot controller's console takes only a username and password, and the vendor has no MFA roadmap. The ticket asks how to meet the requirement. What do you approve?
options: Reach the console only via an MFA-protected jump host, with session logs
Replace the robot controller with a model that supports MFA this week
Record the gap as an exception and leave the console open as it is today
Use a 30-character password on the console as a substitute for MFA
cards.answer: Reach the console only via an MFA-protected jump host, with session logs
cards.why: When a required control cannot be applied, a compensating control meets the requirement's intent another way: forcing access through an MFA-protected, monitored jump host gives equivalent assurance around the console. A long password is still one factor; an exception with no compensation leaves the risk untreated; ripping out production kit this week is disproportionate.

cards.q: 03:10 · Architecture rack. You're applying the corporate endpoint baseline to the new sealed parcel-sorting kiosks. They have no webcam, no microphone and no removable-media ports, yet the baseline includes controls for all three. What do you do with those controls?
options: Implement them anyway so the kiosks match every other endpoint exactly
Mark them not applicable, with the reason recorded in the baseline file
Leave them unassessed and let the auditor decide what applies later
Delete them from the corporate baseline so no endpoint has to apply them
cards.answer: Mark them not applicable, with the reason recorded in the baseline file
cards.why: Scoping removes baseline controls that do not apply to a system's actual components, and recording why keeps the decision auditable. Implementing controls for hardware that is not there wastes effort and muddies evidence; deleting them corporately strips them from laptops that need them; deferring to the auditor abdicates a decision the owner should make.

cards.q: 04:15 · Architecture rack. The new yard-camera system will sit in the main data centre, and its project team plans to buy its own badge readers, CCTV and fire suppression for 'their' rack. What do you tell them?
options: Buy the separate controls, since every system needs its own full set
Buy only the badge readers and share the room's fire suppression
Inherit the data centre's physical controls and document them as common
Skip physical controls, since camera footage is not sensitive data
cards.answer: Inherit the data centre's physical controls and document them as common
cards.why: Common, or inherited, controls are provided once for many systems by a common control provider such as the data centre; a system inherits them and documents the dependency rather than duplicating them. Parallel physical controls waste money and create conflicts; camera footage is sensitive; picking half the set arbitrarily is neither tailored nor justified.

cards.q: 05:00 · Architecture rack. The payments reconciliation system meets the moderate baseline, but the risk assessment shows insiders colluding to alter settlement files is its most likely threat, and the baseline doesn't address it. What goes in the control plan?
options: Remove some baseline controls to free budget for the insider problem
Move to the high baseline wholesale for every control family at once
Keep the baseline unchanged, since it is the approved moderate standard
Add dual approval and file-integrity monitoring on top of the baseline
cards.answer: Add dual approval and file-integrity monitoring on top of the baseline
cards.why: Tailoring adjusts a baseline to a system's real risk; here that means supplementing it with dual approval and integrity monitoring aimed at the identified threat. A baseline is a starting point, not a finish line; jumping every family to high spends heavily on risks you do not have; cutting unrelated controls without analysis opens new gaps.

cards.q: 06:00 · Architecture rack. The new depot beside the data annex is being laid out. Drivers wander from the public parcel counter towards the annex door because the path is wide open. Facilities offers more guards. What do you propose first?
options: Lock the public parcel counter so drivers stay out of the depot entirely
Put up signs asking drivers to keep away from the annex door at all times
Use planters, fencing and a single clear route to steer people away
Hire two more guards to turn back any drivers who stray towards the annex
cards.answer: Use planters, fencing and a single clear route to steer people away
cards.why: Natural access control, a CPTED principle, uses the layout itself, such as landscaping, fencing and one obvious route, to steer people where they should go, cheaply and around the clock. Guards are costly and only as good as their attention; signs rely on goodwill; closing the counter breaks the business the depot exists for.

cards.q: 23:25 · Architecture rack. The endpoint team is relocating the laptop-return drop box to the depot's ground floor. The proposed spot is a windowless corner behind the stairwell, 'out of the way'. What do you recommend?
options: Keep the corner spot and add a sign saying the area is monitored
Place it in a well-lit spot in clear view of the staffed reception desk
Keep the corner spot and fit a heavier lock on the drop box itself
Remove the drop box so laptops can only be returned by appointment
cards.answer: Place it in a well-lit spot in clear view of the staffed reception desk
cards.why: Natural surveillance, a CPTED principle, puts assets and activity where people can easily see them, with lighting, sightlines and staffed areas, so would-be thieves feel observed and staff notice problems. A hidden corner invites tampering; a sign with no eyes behind it is a bluff; a heavier lock resists but nobody sees the attempt; appointments add friction without need.

cards.q: 00:30 · Architecture rack. Two sites are shortlisted for the new backup data centre. Site A is cheaper but lies on a river flood plain under an airport approach path; Site B costs more and sits on higher ground. The ticket asks for your input. What do you do?
options: Recommend Site B, documenting the flood and crash risks at Site A
Recommend Site A and plan to raise the racks off the floor later
Recommend Site A, since backups are only needed in an emergency
Leave it to procurement, since site choice is only a cost decision
cards.answer: Recommend Site B, documenting the flood and crash risks at Site A
cards.why: Site selection is the first facility control: natural hazards such as flooding and man-made ones such as flight paths are far cheaper to avoid than to engineer around, and a backup site must survive when the primary does not. Raised racks do not protect power or access; 'only in an emergency' is exactly when it must work; security has to inform the choice, not just cost.

cards.q: 01:40 · Architecture rack. The shared office block has no clear line between Tessaly's floor and the neighbouring tenant's, and strangers regularly drift into the payments team's area. You're asked to fix it before next year's badge upgrade. What do you propose?
options: Mark the floor boundary with signage, flooring and a reception point
Ask the landlord for a guard patrolling every floor once an hour
Wait for next year's badge upgrade, since that will fix it anyway
Tell payments staff to challenge any strangers, with no other changes
cards.answer: Mark the floor boundary with signage, flooring and a reception point
cards.why: Territorial reinforcement, a CPTED principle, makes ownership of a space visible through signage, distinct flooring and a reception point, so outsiders know they are entering private territory and staff feel entitled to challenge them. It works now and cheaply. Waiting a year leaves the gap open; hourly patrols miss most drift-ins; challenges work better once the boundary is clear.

cards.q: 02:15 · Architecture rack. A legacy EDI link to a customs broker encrypts every message with the same key and no IV, and every message begins with an identical 64-byte standard header. An assessor flags the link. What goes in the fix plan?
options: Double the key's length and keep one fixed key for every message
Remove encryption from the header only, since its content is public anyway
Move the link to a modern cipher mode with fresh keys and random IVs
Keep the key but change the header wording once a year for variety
cards.answer: Move the link to a modern cipher mode with fresh keys and random IVs
cards.why: A predictable header hands an attacker matching plaintext and ciphertext, the raw material of a known-plaintext attack, and a fixed key with no IV makes identical plaintext encrypt identically. A modern authenticated mode with random IVs and rotated keys resists that. Rewording the header yearly still gives known plaintext; a longer key under the same weak mode keeps the pattern.

cards.q: 03:00 · Architecture rack. The endpoint team is choosing payment PIN pads for the depots. A lab report shows one model can be made to skip its signature check by glitching its supply voltage during boot. What do you require in the purchase?
options: Buy that model but glue the case shut so that nobody can reach the board
Buy that model and rely on the payment network to spot fraud later
Buy devices with glitch detection and tamper response, and test them
Buy the cheaper model, since attackers rarely touch depot PIN pads
cards.answer: Buy devices with glitch detection and tamper response, and test them
cards.why: A fault injection attack deliberately disturbs voltage, clock or temperature so hardware misbehaves, for example skipping a security check. Devices with sensors that detect glitches and respond by halting or erasing keys resist it. Glue is a weak barrier anyone with time defeats; betting on low interest ignores unattended depot counters; fraud detection only catches losses afterwards.

cards.q: 04:05 · Architecture rack. The data-hall refit is being specified. The builder proposes wet-pipe sprinklers over the racks as the cheapest option, and the facility has already had one pipe-leak scare. What do you specify?
options: A pre-action system, with a clean-agent option weighed for the core
No suppression at all, since detectors alone can alert the fire service
Wet-pipe sprinklers as proposed, since they are the cheapest option
Portable extinguishers only, with staff trained to tackle any fire
cards.answer: A pre-action system, with a clean-agent option weighed for the core
cards.why: A pre-action system keeps its pipes dry until a detector fires and needs a second trigger before water flows, so a damaged pipe or a single false alarm does not soak live equipment; clean agents avoid water entirely where hardware value justifies it. Wet pipe stays charged over the racks; detection without suppression lets fire spread; relying on staff with extinguishers puts people at risk.

cards.q: 05:10 · Architecture rack. Rack-room sensors show humidity at 18% overnight and dust building up on server intakes, and the HVAC contract is up for renewal. What do you put in the new specification?
options: Hold humidity around 40–60% with positive air pressure in the room
Keep humidity as low as possible so condensation can never form
Open the room's windows at night to bring in cooler outside air
Drop the temperature by five degrees and leave humidity as it is
cards.answer: Hold humidity around 40–60% with positive air pressure in the room
cards.why: Environmental controls keep humidity in a moderate band, roughly 40–60%: too dry and static discharge damages components, too humid and condensation corrodes them. Positive pressure pushes air outward when doors open, keeping dust and smoke out. Driving humidity down causes static; open windows bring in dust and break the perimeter; colder air does nothing for dryness.

cards.q: 06:35 · Architecture rack. Walking the depot, you find the network wiring closet shares a room with the cleaners' supplies, its door propped open for airflow, and the switches inside carry the payment terminals. What goes in the remediation ticket?
options: Give the closet its own locked, logged access and proper ventilation
Add a camera facing the open door and review footage after incidents
Ask the cleaners to keep the door closed whenever they are not using it
Move the payment switches into the depot manager's lockable desk drawer
cards.answer: Give the closet its own locked, logged access and proper ventilation
cards.why: Wiring closets are sensitive facility spaces: physical access to switches lets someone tap, reroute or disable traffic, payment data included. They need dedicated, access-controlled and logged space with engineered cooling, not a propped door. A request to cleaners is unenforced; a camera on an open door records the attack rather than stopping it; a desk drawer is no equipment room.
