cards.q: 23:40 · Architecture rack. The endpoint team wants to run the card-payment app and general web browsing on the same checkout PCs, separated only by two user accounts. PCI scope is at stake. Which design do you approve?
options: Keep the two user accounts, since separate logins already isolate them
Run both in one account but clear the browser cache at each shift end
Run payments in a hardware-isolated partition, apart from the browser
Install stronger antivirus so the browser cannot infect the payments
cards.answer: Run payments in a hardware-isolated partition, apart from the browser
cards.why: Hardware segmentation uses processor and memory hardware, such as MMU-enforced partitions or hardware-assisted virtualisation, to keep workloads' memory apart, so a compromised browser cannot reach payment memory. Separate user accounts are software separation that a kernel exploit crosses; clearing the cache is housekeeping; antivirus detects known threats but creates no isolation.

cards.q: 06:40 · Asset vault. Last week three failed SSDs from the settlement array went back to the vendor under warranty swap, still holding card batch files. The vendor confirms they were refurbished and resold. You are writing the control that stops this happening again. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Keep failed drives on site and shred them, with a logged destruction certificate
Require the vendor to promise in writing that it wipes every returned drive
Stop warranty claims entirely and buy spare drives in bulk for the array
Run a quick format on each failed drive before it leaves for the warranty swap
cards.answer: Keep failed drives on site and shred them, with a logged destruction certificate
cards.why: Failed SSDs often cannot be overwritten or verified, so physical destruction on site (with a keep-your-drive clause and a certificate) is the only disposal that guarantees the data is gone. A vendor promise shifts the risk without controlling it, and a format on a dead drive does nothing; dropping warranties treats cost, not the data exposure.

cards.q: 02:15 · Asset vault. A route-pricing deck marked Confidential surfaced on a freight forum yesterday, and five partners had received copies. Nobody can tell which copy leaked. You are closing the after-action with a lasting control. Which do you approve?
options: Embed a unique digital watermark per recipient in every copy sent outside
Send future decks only as locked PDFs so recipients find them harder to edit
Stop sharing pricing decks with partners and read them aloud on calls
Ask all five partners to sign a fresh non-disclosure agreement this week
cards.answer: Embed a unique digital watermark per recipient in every copy sent outside
cards.why: A per-recipient digital watermark ties each leaked copy back to its source, which deters leaks and makes attribution possible next time. A PDF is still trivially copied, a new NDA adds no way to prove who breached it, and halting all sharing breaks the business process instead of protecting the asset inside it.

cards.q: 23:35 · Asset vault. Legal emails at 23:30: a customer lawsuit has been filed and all shipment records for that account must be kept. The nightly lifecycle job that purges seven-year-old shipment records runs at midnight and will sweep that account's oldest files. What do you do first?
options: Suspend the purge for that account and apply a legal hold to its records
Let the purge run, since the seven-year schedule is the approved policy
Copy the account's records to your own laptop so nothing is lost tonight
Delete the account's records now so there is less for the lawsuit to find
cards.answer: Suspend the purge for that account and apply a legal hold to its records
cards.why: A legal hold overrides the normal destruction stage of the data lifecycle: once litigation is reasonably expected, deleting relevant records is spoliation. Letting the scheduled purge run ignores that duty, a personal copy breaks custody and handling rules, and deliberate deletion is obstruction, the worst outcome for the company.

cards.q: 03:05 · Asset vault. Cloud posture alerts show a storage bucket provisioned this afternoon for a carrier integration is set to public read. It holds customer delivery manifests, and access logs show two unknown IPs listing it in the last hour. Your move?
options: Blocklist the two IPs at the firewall and leave the bucket settings alone
Delete the bucket and its contents so the manifests are no longer exposed
Block public access now, keep the access logs, and raise it with the data owner
Email the engineer who built it and ask them to fix it in the morning
cards.answer: Block public access now, keep the access logs, and raise it with the data owner
cards.why: Containing the exposure while preserving the access logs lets you judge what was taken and whether breach notification applies; the data owner decides next steps. Deleting the bucket destroys the evidence of exposure, waiting until morning leaves customer data public, and blocking two IPs does nothing about the rest of the internet.

cards.q: 01:50 · Asset vault. EDR on a payment authorisation server flags an unknown process reading another process's memory. The disks are encrypted and all traffic uses TLS, so the platform owner says card data cannot be exposed. Your move?
options: Reboot the server to clear memory and remove the suspicious process quickly
Isolate the host, capture memory, and treat card data in use as exposed
Rotate the TLS certificate so any captured network sessions become useless
Accept the owner's view, since encryption covers data at rest and in transit
cards.answer: Isolate the host, capture memory, and treat card data in use as exposed
cards.why: Card data is decrypted in RAM while it is processed, so disk and transport encryption do nothing against memory scraping: data in use needs its own protection. Isolating and capturing memory contains the attack and keeps evidence. Rebooting wipes that volatile evidence, and rotating a certificate protects the wrong data state.

cards.q: 00:45 · Asset vault. A folder of merger due-diligence files classified Secret has been found copied to a team share whose permissions allow every staff member to read it. Access logs show forty users opened it tonight. What do you do first?
options: Reclassify the folder as Internal, since so many staff can already see it anyway
Restrict the share to cleared staff and notify the owner of the Secret data
Move the folder to a new share and keep the access logs to yourself
Send an all-staff email telling everyone to forget what they saw in it
cards.answer: Restrict the share to cleared staff and notify the owner of the Secret data
cards.why: Secret marks information whose disclosure would do serious damage, so containment comes first: restore need-to-know and alert the owner, who judges the impact. Classification reflects value, not current exposure, so downgrading it hides the incident. A mass email advertises the leak, and withholding logs from the owner undermines the response.

cards.q: 05:10 · Asset vault. Ransomware has encrypted the freight booking database. Forensics puts the attacker's first access twelve days ago, but online backups are kept only seven days, so every one of them may hold the implant. Operations wants it back by 07:00. Your move?
options: Rebuild the database empty and ask customers to re-enter their bookings
Restore from the offline monthly archive that predates the intrusion
Restore last night's backup now, since it is the most recent good copy
Pay the ransom, since no backup inside the retention window is clean
cards.answer: Restore from the offline monthly archive that predates the intrusion
cards.why: Backup retention must outlast the likely dwell time; here only the offline monthly archive predates the intrusion, so it is the clean recovery point, then you replay newer data after checks. Last night's backup probably carries the implant, paying funds crime without a guarantee, and an empty rebuild throws away recoverable records.

cards.q: 04:25 · Asset vault. A developer copied the full customer table into a test environment to debug a billing fault, and that test server is now showing beaconing to an unknown host. The table includes names, addresses and bank details. After containing the server, what do you require for the fix?
options: Allow real data in test only when the developer files a ticket first
Encrypt the test server disk so the next copied table is stored there safely
Rebuild test data from de-identified copies so no real customer is exposed
Keep using production copies, but delete them when debugging is done
cards.answer: Rebuild test data from de-identified copies so no real customer is exposed
cards.why: Test environments are rarely hardened, so the lasting fix is de-identification: masked or synthetic records keep the data useful for debugging while removing the link to real people. Disk encryption does not help once the host is compromised and running, a ticket leaves live data in test, and deleting afterwards still exposes it during use.

cards.q: 02:40 · Asset vault. A new replication rule, pushed without review, is copying EU customer records from the Frankfurt region to a US analytics region. Contracts with EU customers require their data to stay in the EU. About ten percent has copied so far. What do you do first?
options: Delete the replication logs so the transfer does not show up in an audit
Encrypt the US copy so no one there can read the EU records in the meantime
Pause the replication, record what copied, and escalate to the privacy lead
Let it finish and move the data back in the morning to avoid a partial set
cards.answer: Pause the replication, record what copied, and escalate to the privacy lead
cards.why: Data location is a lifecycle control: storing records outside the agreed jurisdiction breaches residency commitments. Pause first to stop the spread, preserve a record of what moved, and let the privacy lead decide on remediation and notification. Letting it finish widens the breach, encryption does not change where it sits, and deleting logs destroys evidence.

cards.q: 23:20 · Asset vault. An attacker has taken a copy of the loyalty database files from a compromised backup server. The card fields were encrypted with keys held in a separate HSM cluster that the attacker never reached. Leadership is drafting a breach statement. Your move?
options: Tell leadership nothing was lost, since the files were encrypted anyway
Confirm the HSM was untouched, rotate keys, and brief legal on the encryption
Decrypt the stolen copy yourself to confirm exactly what the attacker holds
Wipe the backup server immediately so the attacker cannot return to it
cards.answer: Confirm the HSM was untouched, rotate keys, and brief legal on the encryption
cards.why: Encryption with keys kept apart from the data can turn a stolen file into unreadable ciphertext, which legal can weigh against notification rules; but that holds only if the keys were not exposed, so verify and rotate. Saying nothing was lost ignores the unencrypted fields, and wiping the server destroys the forensic trail.

cards.q: 06:05 · Asset vault. Two incidents are open and you have one responder free. A dev wiki server has an active webshell; a file server holding the signed contracts for your largest carrier deals is showing mass file renames. What do you do first?
options: Send the responder to the contracts server, the asset of higher value
Send the responder to the wiki server, since the webshell came in first
Split the responder's time evenly so both incidents make steady progress
Wait for the day shift so that both incidents can get a full team at once
cards.answer: Send the responder to the contracts server, the asset of higher value
cards.why: Asset value, recorded in the inventory and classification, drives protection and response priority: the signed contracts carry far more business impact than a dev wiki, and mass renames suggest active encryption. First-come order ignores impact, splitting one responder slows both, and waiting lets the damage grow.

cards.q: 05:30 · Asset vault. A recycler's van is due at 06:00 for forty old warehouse laptops. You find the helpdesk only formatted the drives, and a quick check recovers driver schedules and customer addresses from one. Your move?
options: Hold the pickup, then purge or destroy each drive with a signed record
Format the drives a second time so the recovery tool can no longer read them
Pull the one drive that failed the check and release the other thirty-nine
Let the van go, since the recycler's contract says it wipes all drives
cards.answer: Hold the pickup, then purge or destroy each drive with a signed record
cards.why: Formatting rebuilds the file system tables but leaves the data blocks, so the drives are not sanitised. Holding the pickup and purging or destroying each drive, with a record, meets disposal requirements. A contract clause is not verification, a second format has the same flaw, and one sample proves the whole batch is exposed.

cards.q: 03:55 · Asset vault. Your ticket: courier twelve encrypted backup tapes to the offsite vault. The vault's usual courier is ill and the shift lead suggests a taxi. The data on the tapes is classified Confidential. What do you do?
options: Send the tapes by taxi, since they are encrypted and the data is unreadable
Follow the tape handling procedure: approved courier, sealed case, logged custody
Keep the tapes on site until the regular courier returns next week
Carry the tapes to the vault yourself during your break to save the fee
cards.answer: Follow the tape handling procedure: approved courier, sealed case, logged custody
cards.why: Handling requirements set how classified media is moved: approved carriers, tamper-evident packaging and a custody log, so loss can be detected and traced. Encryption reduces impact but does not waive handling rules, an unlogged personal trip breaks custody, and holding the tapes on site defeats the point of offsite backup.

cards.q: 01:20 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a retired customer file server is being repurposed as a lab box. The admin plans to delete the customer folders and empty the recycle bin before handing it over. The disks are spinning HDDs. What do you require?
options: Delete the folders and also rename the server so no one links it to customers
Leave the data in place, since the lab team signed the acceptable use policy
Overwrite the disks with a verified sanitisation tool before any reuse
Accept the plan, since emptying the recycle bin removes the files for good
cards.answer: Overwrite the disks with a verified sanitisation tool before any reuse
cards.why: Deleting files only removes the pointers to them; the data stays on the disk and is easily recovered, which is data remanence. Overwriting with a verified tool clears the media for reuse within the company. Emptying the bin changes nothing on disk, renaming is cosmetic, and an AUP does not grant lab staff need-to-know.

cards.q: 00:30 · Asset vault. Your ticket: review the nightly rate-card feed to a regional partner. You find it runs over plain FTP across the internet, with a shared password in the script. The partner says it has worked fine for years. What do you put in the change ticket?
options: Zip the files with a password before sending them over the same FTP link
Keep FTP but change the shared password every quarter as a safeguard
Accept the risk, since the rate cards were never breached in all those years
Move the feed to SFTP with key authentication and retire the FTP account
cards.answer: Move the feed to SFTP with key authentication and retire the FTP account
cards.why: Data in transit over plain FTP exposes both the files and the credentials to anyone on the path; SFTP encrypts the channel and key authentication removes the shared password. Rotating a password that still crosses in cleartext solves nothing, legacy zip passwords are weak, and a quiet history is not a risk assessment.

cards.q: 02:00 · Asset vault. Your ticket asks the SOC to set the classification for a new driver-telematics dataset so the storage team can build controls. The storage team leader wants you to pick Internal so it goes live quickly. What do you do?
options: Let the storage team choose the level, since they will build the controls
Route it to the telematics data owner, who sets the classification
Pick Secret, since choosing the highest level is always the safe move
Pick Internal as asked, since the storage team manages the dataset
cards.answer: Route it to the telematics data owner, who sets the classification
cards.why: The data owner, a business leader accountable for the data, sets its classification; custodians such as the storage team and the SOC implement the controls that follow. Picking a level yourself takes a decision that is not yours, over-classifying wastes budget and slows use, and letting the custodian choose inverts accountability.

cards.q: 04:50 · Asset vault. Your ticket: thirty HDDs from dispatch PCs are being reissued to the finance team, inside Tessaly, at the same sensitivity level. The asset manager proposes shredding them and buying new ones. What do you approve?
options: Overwrite each drive with a verified pass and reissue it to finance
Shred all thirty drives and buy new ones, as the asset manager proposes
Quick-format the drives so finance gets a clean file system for the new build
Degauss the drives before reissue so the magnetic data is scrambled for good
cards.answer: Overwrite each drive with a verified pass and reissue it to finance
cards.why: For reuse inside the organisation at the same sensitivity, overwriting (clearing) is proportionate: it defeats ordinary recovery and keeps the drives in service. Shredding is for media leaving control or failing verification, a quick format leaves data behind, and degaussing a modern HDD wipes its servo tracks, so the drive is useless.

cards.q: 23:50 · Asset vault. On a night walk-through of the loading dock office you find an unlocked drawer holding six unlabelled USB sticks. One opens to a spreadsheet of customer bank details. The dock supervisor shrugs: that is where the handover files always go. Your move?
options: Secure the sticks, log it as a handling incident, and fix the handover process
Throw the sticks in the confidential waste bin and say nothing to the dock team
Wipe all six sticks on the spot so the bank details can no longer be read
Put the sticks back and lock the drawer, since the supervisor knows the process
cards.answer: Secure the sticks, log it as a handling incident, and fix the handover process
cards.why: This is improper asset handling: sensitive data on unmarked, unencrypted media in an open drawer. Secure the media, record it as an incident so the owner can judge exposure, and replace the habit with an approved transfer method. Wiping destroys evidence, relocking keeps the broken process, and silent disposal fixes nothing that caused it.

cards.q: 00:10 · Asset vault. Your ticket: security review of a new driver onboarding form before launch. It asks for date of birth, marital status, religion and next of kin, although payroll only needs name, licence and bank details. Product says extra fields may be useful one day. What do you approve?
options: Cut the form to the fields payroll needs and record the purpose of each one
Approve it as designed and schedule a privacy review in a year's time
Keep every field as optional so drivers can decide what they share with us
Approve the form as it stands, but encrypt the extra fields so they are stored safely
cards.answer: Cut the form to the fields payroll needs and record the purpose of each one
cards.why: Data minimisation starts at collection, the first stage of the lifecycle: gather only what a stated purpose needs, so there is less to protect, retain and lose. Encrypting unneeded data still means holding it, optional fields still invite sensitive data you have no reason to keep, and a review a year later is after the harm.

cards.q: 03:20 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a data science team wants to add GPS traces from delivery vans to its routing model. The traces carry van IDs, and the roster maps each van to a named driver per shift. They classed the data as non-personal operational data. What do you do?
options: Accept the non-personal label, since the traces never contain driver names
Approve it, provided the team deletes the roster from its own project share
Treat the traces as personal data and require a privacy impact assessment
Block the project, since location data can never be used for any analytics
cards.answer: Treat the traces as personal data and require a privacy impact assessment
cards.why: Personal information includes any data that can identify a person directly or indirectly; van ID plus the roster pins a trace to a driver's movements. That triggers privacy obligations, so a privacy impact assessment decides the lawful basis and safeguards. The roster still exists elsewhere, and a blanket ban ignores legitimate, controlled use.

cards.q: 04:05 · Asset vault. A routine network sweep finds a database server at the Leeds depot that is in no asset inventory, has no owner, and holds what look like old customer invoices. Your ticket is to deal with it. What do you do first?
options: Leave it running, since it has been fine so far and nobody has complained
Shut it down and wipe it tonight, since nobody has claimed it as their own
Add it to the inventory and find its business owner to classify the data
Install the EDR agent and treat it as fully protected from now on
cards.answer: Add it to the inventory and find its business owner to classify the data
cards.why: You cannot protect what you have not inventoried: recording the asset and assigning an owner is what lets its data be classified and given proper controls and retention. Wiping an unowned server may destroy records the business must keep, ignoring it leaves an unmanaged risk, and an agent alone does not settle ownership or classification.

cards.q: 01:40 · Asset vault. Your ticket: set retention for customs declaration records. Finance wants them kept forever just in case; IT wants 90 days to save storage. Customs law in your main markets requires them to be kept for a set number of years. What goes in the retention schedule?
options: Keep them for 90 days, as IT wants, and archive a summary for customs
Let each depot manager decide locally how long its own declarations last
Keep them for the legal period, then destroy them securely on schedule
Keep them forever, as finance wants, so no record is ever lost in future
cards.answer: Keep them for the legal period, then destroy them securely on schedule
cards.why: Record retention is set by legal and regulatory duty plus business need: keep for the mandated period, then destroy on schedule. Keeping forever grows storage cost, breach impact and discovery exposure; 90 days breaks customs law; and local choice makes the schedule unenforceable and inconsistent across depots.

cards.q: 02:30 · Asset vault. Your ticket: backup tapes from the payments platform and the marketing file shares are stored in the same offsite crate. None carry any marking, so vault staff treat them all alike. What do you require?
options: Store the payments tapes in a crate of their own and leave both unlabelled
Label each tape with its classification so handling matches its data
Mark every tape Public so vault staff never have to think about any of them
Encrypt all tapes the same way so their labels no longer matter at all
cards.answer: Label each tape with its classification so handling matches its data
cards.why: Labelling media with its classification tells every handler, including third parties, what care it needs: payment tapes get stricter storage, transport and destruction than marketing ones. Encryption does not tell anyone how to handle or dispose of the tape, separation without labels depends on memory, and a false Public marking invites mishandling.

cards.q: 05:45 · Asset vault. Your ticket: procurement is about to sign a cloud payroll provider that will hold driver pay and bank data. The draft contract says nothing about how the provider may use the data or about sub-processors. Signing is set for 09:00. What do you do?
options: Sign it now, since the provider is responsible for the data it will hold
Sign it and ask the provider to send its security policy after go-live
Advise payroll to keep running on spreadsheets and skip the provider
Hold signing until a processing agreement fixes use, sub-processors and deletion
cards.answer: Hold signing until a processing agreement fixes use, sub-processors and deletion
cards.why: Tessaly stays the data controller; the provider is a processor that may act only on documented instructions. The agreement must limit use, govern sub-processors and fix deletion at contract end. Signing first hands away the leverage, assuming the processor carries the duty is wrong, and a policy after go-live is too late.

cards.q: 06:20 · Asset vault. Your ticket: review a new driver app's encryption. You find the developer wrote a custom cipher that XORs data with a fixed key compiled into the app. The developer says it is secret, so it is secure. What goes in your review?
options: Accept it, since keeping the design secret is what makes the cipher strong
Accept it, but move the fixed key into a separate config file on the phone
Replace it with a vetted algorithm such as AES-GCM and managed keys
Keep the cipher and run it twice over each record so it is harder to break
cards.answer: Replace it with a vetted algorithm such as AES-GCM and managed keys
cards.why: Proper data encryption uses vetted, public algorithms with keys managed outside the code; a secret design with a hardcoded key is broken the moment anyone reverses the app. Moving the key to a config file on the same device changes nothing, XOR twice with one key undoes itself, and secrecy of the design is not strength.

cards.q: 03:40 · Asset vault. Your ticket: an analyst wants to merge three Internal datasets into one dashboard: depot addresses, nightly cash-in-transit schedules, and guard rotas. Each alone is classed Internal. What do you do?
options: Reject it, since datasets must never be combined across different owners
Approve it at Internal, since every source dataset is already rated Internal
Escalate for a higher classification of the combined set before it is built
Approve it, provided the dashboard is only viewed on company-owned laptops
cards.answer: Escalate for a higher classification of the combined set before it is built
cards.why: Aggregation can make combined data more sensitive than any part: addresses plus cash schedules plus guard rotas is a robbery plan. The combined set needs its own, higher classification and tighter access, decided by the owners. Inheriting the lowest label ignores that, device limits do not fix the label, and a blanket ban blocks legitimate analysis.

cards.q: 00:55 · Asset vault. Your ticket: the quarterly asset review. You find four warehouse servers whose OS reached end of support last month, and the inventory has no field for support dates, so nobody was warned. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Buy extended vendor support for every server in the estate, whatever its age
Add end-of-support dates to the inventory and alert owners well in advance
Note the four servers in the review and look again at the next quarter
Patch the four servers from an unofficial source until they are replaced
cards.answer: Add end-of-support dates to the inventory and alert owners well in advance
cards.why: Asset retention includes tracking end-of-life and end-of-support dates so owners can budget and replace before vendor patches stop. Recording the dates with advance alerts turns a surprise into a planned decision. Unofficial patches add supply chain risk, waiting a quarter leaves them unpatched, and blanket extended support wastes money.

cards.q: 04:40 · Asset vault. Your ticket: IT asks the SOC to set how long to keep proof-of-delivery photos. Legal says no statute applies. Customer service uses them to settle disputes, which are almost all raised within 18 months. What do you recommend?
options: Let the storage vendor set the period that suits its pricing tiers
Delete the photos after a week, since no law says they must be kept
Keep the photos forever, since no law caps how long they may be kept at all
Have the data owner set retention from that dispute window, then delete
cards.answer: Have the data owner set retention from that dispute window, then delete
cards.why: Where no law sets a period, retention follows business requirements, decided by the data owner: here the dispute window plus a margin. Keeping photos forever adds cost and exposure with no benefit, a week breaks the dispute process, and a vendor's pricing is not a business requirement.

cards.q: 23:10 · Asset vault. Your ticket: the settlement team keeps its archive drives in a cardboard box under a desk in an open-plan office. The drives are encrypted, but the recovery keys are printed and taped inside the box lid. What do you require?
options: Leave the drives in the box, since encrypted drives are safe anywhere
Move the box to the manager's desk so fewer people walk past each day
Move the drives to a locked safe and hold the keys in the key vault
Remove the printed keys and throw them out, since the drives are encrypted
cards.answer: Move the drives to a locked safe and hold the keys in the key vault
cards.why: Secure storage separates the media from the keys and puts each under access control: drives in a locked safe, recovery keys in the managed key vault. Keys beside the ciphertext cancel the encryption, discarding the only recovery keys risks losing the archive, and a different desk is still open-plan.

cards.q: 06:50 · Asset vault. Your ticket: marketing wants to publish last year's quarterly volume figures, still classed Confidential. They were released in the annual report months ago. Marketing asks you to just lift the label. What do you do?
options: Ask the data owner to formally declassify the figures and record the change
Lift the label yourself, since the figures are public in the annual report
Keep the label, since data can never move down once it is classed Confidential
Tell marketing to publish anyway and fix the classification record later
cards.answer: Ask the data owner to formally declassify the figures and record the change
cards.why: Classification should change as value and sensitivity change, but declassification is the owner's decision and must be recorded so handling rules update everywhere. The SOC is not the owner, never downgrading wastes effort protecting public data, and publishing before the record changes breaks the handling policy.

cards.q: 01:05 · Asset vault. Your ticket: forty new laptops arrive for the night dispatch team at 06:00. The team lead wants them unboxed and handed straight over, with setup done later. What do you require first?
options: Hand them over now and enrol them in device management within the week
Enrol each in inventory and device management with the hardened image
Hand them over with local admin rights so the team can install its tools
Hand them over now and ask each user to report the serial number later
cards.answer: Enrol each in inventory and device management with the hardened image
cards.why: Secure provisioning means an asset is recorded, owned and hardened before it touches data: inventory, device management and a baseline image give you patching, encryption and remote wipe from day one. Setup later leaves unmanaged devices on live data, local admin undermines the baseline, and self-reported serials make inventory unreliable.

cards.q: 05:20 · Asset vault. Your ticket: Tessaly has adopted a control baseline catalogue. The kiosk team says several controls cannot apply to its locked-down, offline parcel kiosks and wants to skip the whole baseline. What do you do?
options: Apply every control as written, even where it cannot work on a kiosk
Write a new baseline just for kiosks with no link to the adopted catalogue
Tailor the baseline, recording why each control is dropped or swapped
Let the kiosk team skip the baseline, since the kiosks are offline anyway
cards.answer: Tailor the baseline, recording why each control is dropped or swapped
cards.why: Scoping and tailoring adapt a baseline to a system: drop controls that do not apply, add or substitute where needed, and document the rationale so assessors can follow it. Forcing unworkable controls wastes effort, skipping the whole baseline leaves the kiosks ungoverned, and a separate unlinked baseline breaks traceability.

cards.q: 02:50 · Asset vault. Your ticket: an audit finds nine copies of the carrier contracts register: the official system, three spreadsheets, and five email exports, each slightly different. One spreadsheet has banking changes not in the official system. What do you recommend?
options: Encrypt the spreadsheets and email exports but leave them where they are
Keep all nine copies, since more copies mean the data is less likely lost
Delete every copy except the official one tonight, without reconciling it
Name one system of record, reconcile into it, and retire the other copies
cards.answer: Name one system of record, reconcile into it, and retire the other copies
cards.why: Uncontrolled copies break the data lifecycle: each needs protecting, retention and disposal, and conflicting versions damage integrity. One system of record, reconciled then enforced, fixes both. Keeping them multiplies exposure (backups are for loss), encryption leaves the integrity mess, and deleting without reconciling throws away the banking changes.

cards.q: 00:20 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a regional director left yesterday amid a disputed dismissal. The helpdesk wants to reimage her laptop tonight for a new starter. The asset retention policy says leavers' devices under dispute are held for 90 days. What do you do?
options: Reimage it tonight, since the new starter needs a laptop in the morning
Let the director's old team decide whether the laptop should be kept
Copy her email to a share, then reimage the laptop for the new starter
Seal and store the laptop under the policy and give the new starter a spare
cards.answer: Seal and store the laptop under the policy and give the new starter a spare
cards.why: The asset retention policy exists so devices that may hold evidence are kept intact for the set period; sealing and storing preserves it for any legal claim. Reimaging destroys evidence, a partial copy misses local files and metadata and breaks custody, and the former team has neither authority nor independence.

cards.q: 04:15 · Asset vault. Your ticket: night payroll reports, classed Confidential, print to a shared printer by the canteen, and copies sit in the tray until the morning. Two pages were found on a canteen table last week. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Stop printing payroll reports and read them only on screen from now on
Put a sign on the printer asking staff not to read what others have printed
Require secure print release, so pages print only when the owner badges in
Move the printer into the payroll office and leave the print settings alone
cards.answer: Require secure print release, so pages print only when the owner badges in
cards.why: Handling requirements cover output as well as storage: secure print release holds the job until the authorised person is present, so Confidential pages never sit unattended. Moving the printer still leaves overnight piles for cleaners and visitors, a sign is not a control, and banning print ignores why the team needs paper.

cards.q: 03:30 · Asset vault. Your ticket: categorise a new shared platform that will host both the public parcel tracker and the settlement ledger for card payments. The platform team wants the tracker's Low impact rating so it stays cheap. What do you record?
options: Give each web page its own rating and skip rating the platform as a whole
Rate the platform Medium as a fair average of the tracker and the ledger
Rate the platform at the ledger's High impact, the highest of its data
Rate the platform Low, since most of its traffic is the public tracker
cards.answer: Rate the platform at the ledger's High impact, the highest of its data
cards.why: A system is categorised by the high-water mark: the most sensitive data it holds sets the protection level, because a breach of the platform exposes everything on it. Rating by traffic volume or averaging understates the ledger's impact, and per-page ratings ignore the shared infrastructure an attacker would actually compromise.

cards.q: 23:45 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a manager admits a spreadsheet of customer card numbers was once emailed to a personal account 'to work from home'. There is no control today that would catch it happening again. What do you approve?
options: Send an all-staff reminder that customer card data must never leave the company
Fire the manager so staff understand that the rule is taken seriously
Block every personal webmail domain at the proxy and leave outbound mail alone
Deploy DLP rules that detect card numbers in outbound mail and block them
cards.answer: Deploy DLP rules that detect card numbers in outbound mail and block them
cards.why: Data loss prevention inspects content leaving the organisation and can block or quarantine card numbers in outbound email, addressing the channel that failed. A reminder helps awareness but enforces nothing, blocking webmail at the proxy does not stop company mail sent to outside addresses, and punishment does not create a control.

cards.q: 05:55 · Asset vault. Your ticket: 200 leased laptops with self-encrypting SSDs go back to the lessor at the end of the month. Overwriting SSDs is unreliable, and the lease forbids destroying the drives. What do you approve?
options: Pull and shred the SSDs and pay the lessor the penalty for each one
Run a multi-pass overwrite on every SSD, as you would on older HDDs
Crypto-erase each drive by destroying its key, and log each serial
Quick-format each laptop and reinstall a fresh OS before return
cards.answer: Crypto-erase each drive by destroying its key, and log each serial
cards.why: Cryptographic erase destroys the media encryption key on a self-encrypting drive, making the data unrecoverable while leaving the drive usable: the right end-of-life move when drives must be returned. Overwrites are unreliable on SSDs because of wear levelling, a format leaves data, and shredding breaches the lease at needless cost.

cards.q: 02:10 · Asset vault. Your ticket: the billing, CRM and dispatch systems all store full card numbers for repeat customers, so all three are in scope for the card-industry standard. Billing needs to charge the card again; the other two only need to recognise it. What do you approve?
options: Swap stored card numbers for tokens and keep the real ones in a vault
Encrypt the card numbers in all three systems with one shared master key
Keep the full numbers and put all three systems behind one firewall
Store only the card expiry date in all three systems from now on
cards.answer: Swap stored card numbers for tokens and keep the real ones in a vault
cards.why: Tokenisation replaces card numbers with tokens that are useless if stolen, so CRM and dispatch drop out of scope and billing charges via the vault. Encryption with a shared key keeps all three in scope, since each can decrypt; an expiry date alone cannot recognise or charge a card; and a firewall does not shrink the data footprint.

cards.q: 06:30 · Asset vault. Your ticket: Tessaly launches in two EU countries next quarter. The project plan copies the UK controls unchanged, and nobody has mapped which new laws apply to the customer data involved. What do you do?
options: Copy the UK controls as planned, since the EU rules are broadly the same
Wait for the first regulator enquiry and then learn what rules apply
Buy a compliance tool that promises to cover every EU privacy law
Map the data flows and identify which laws and standards apply before launch
cards.answer: Map the data flows and identify which laws and standards apply before launch
cards.why: Compliance requirements follow the data: you must know what personal data flows where, and which laws, regulators and standards apply, before choosing controls. Assuming parity misses local rules, waiting for a regulator is non-compliance by design, and a tool cannot tell you what your obligations are without that mapping.

cards.q: 01:30 · Asset vault. Your ticket: proxy logs show staff uploading shipping manifests to five unapproved file-sharing services each week. You have no view of what is uploaded or where it ends up. What do you approve?
options: Buy a bigger internal file share and hope staff stop using the others
Deploy a CASB to find the cloud apps in use and enforce data policy
Block every cloud service at the proxy, including the approved ones
Ask each team to list which cloud services it uses and trust that list
cards.answer: Deploy a CASB to find the cloud apps in use and enforce data policy
cards.why: A cloud access security broker gives visibility of shadow SaaS use and applies data policy (allow, block, or protect uploads) between users and cloud services. Blocking everything breaks approved work and drives workarounds, self-reported lists miss the problem, and a bigger share without enforcement changes nothing.

cards.q: 00:35 · Asset vault. Your ticket: Tessaly must send tender pricing to three carriers. Legal wants the files unreadable after the tender closes and not printable or forwardable meanwhile, even once they are on the carriers' machines. What do you approve?
options: Protect the files with DRM that sets expiry, print and forward rights
Mark the files Confidential and add a legal notice about forwarding
Share the files through a password-protected link that expires on closing
Send the files by encrypted email and ask the carriers to delete them later
cards.answer: Protect the files with DRM that sets expiry, print and forward rights
cards.why: Digital rights management keeps the controls attached to the file wherever it goes, enforcing view, print, forward and expiry rights on the recipient's device. Encrypted email protects transit only, an expiring link does nothing once the file is downloaded, and a marking relies on goodwill instead of enforcement.

cards.q: 05:05 · Asset vault. Your ticket: delivery drivers carry laptops holding route plans and customer contacts, and two were stolen from vans last year. What do you approve for the fleet?
options: Encrypt the customer contacts folder only and leave the rest as it is
Enforce full disk encryption with pre-boot unlock, managed centrally
Require a strong Windows login password on every laptop in the fleet
Chain every laptop to its van so it cannot be taken from the vehicle
cards.answer: Enforce full disk encryption with pre-boot unlock, managed centrally
cards.why: Full disk encryption protects every file at rest on a lost or stolen device, including temp files and swap, and with pre-boot unlock and central key escrow the data is unreadable when powered off. A login password is bypassed by pulling the drive, folder encryption misses copies elsewhere, and a cable lock only slows a thief.

cards.q: 04:30 · Asset vault. Your ticket: every admin builds warehouse servers their own way, so no two match and audits keep finding the same gaps. What do you propose to the change board?
options: Let each admin keep their approach but review it once a year with them
Write down how each admin builds servers now and accept those as standards
Adopt a published hardening benchmark as the server baseline and audit to it
Buy a vulnerability scanner and fix whatever it reports on each server
cards.answer: Adopt a published hardening benchmark as the server baseline and audit to it
cards.why: A security baseline, drawn from a published benchmark and tailored where needed, sets one minimum configuration that can be deployed and audited consistently. Documenting current habits bakes in the gaps, annual reviews leave drift unmanaged, and a scanner finds problems but gives no standard for how servers should be built.

cards.q: 03:15 · Asset vault. Your ticket: customer service agents see full bank account numbers on every screen, although they only confirm the last four digits with callers. What do you approve?
options: Leave the numbers visible but log every time an agent views a customer
Mask the account numbers on screen, showing only the last four digits
Remove bank details from the service screens and have agents call finance
Ask agents to sign a confidentiality pledge about the account numbers
cards.answer: Mask the account numbers on screen, showing only the last four digits
cards.why: Data masking shows each role only what it needs: agents confirm the last four digits while the full number stays hidden, applying least privilege to the data itself. Logging detects misuse after the fact, removing the field entirely breaks the verification task, and a pledge is not a technical control.

cards.q: 23:25 · Asset vault. Your ticket: review the invoices database. Its encryption keys sit in a config file on the same server, readable by the same admins who run the database. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Move the keys to a managed key service with access split from DBA rights
Rotate the keys every month but keep storing them in the same config file
Rename the config file so an attacker is less likely to find the keys
Encrypt the config file with a second key kept in the same directory
cards.answer: Move the keys to a managed key service with access split from DBA rights
cards.why: Encryption is only as strong as its key management: keys stored beside the data, readable by the same people, give an attacker or insider both at once. A managed key service with separation of duties keeps keys out of DBA reach and logs their use. Another local key repeats the flaw, renaming is obscurity, and rotation leaves them exposed.

cards.q: 06:10 · Asset vault. Your ticket: each night a batch of supplier payment instructions is exported to a shared folder and the bank's uploader collects it at 06:00. Anyone with folder access could change a bank account number in between. What do you approve?
options: Digitally sign each batch and have the uploader reject any unsigned file
Check the file's timestamp before upload to confirm nobody has edited it
Encrypt the folder's disk so the payment files are protected at rest
Email the batch total to finance so that they can spot anything unusual
cards.answer: Digitally sign each batch and have the uploader reject any unsigned file
cards.why: This is an integrity risk: a digital signature proves the file came from the payments system and has not been altered, and the uploader can refuse any file that fails verification. Disk encryption protects confidentiality, not changes by authorised folder users, timestamps are easily forged, and a matching total misses a swapped account number.

cards.q: 01:55 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a sorting-hub controller cannot run endpoint protection, which the card-industry standard requires for in-scope systems, and the vendor will not support it until 2028. What do you do?
options: Record the controller as compliant, since the vendor forbids the agent
Document a compensating control, such as isolation plus allowlisting, for the owner
Install endpoint protection anyway and accept the risk of voiding the support
Remove the controller from the asset inventory so it falls out of scope
cards.answer: Document a compensating control, such as isolation plus allowlisting, for the owner
cards.why: When a required control cannot be met, a compensating control that meets the intent (network isolation and application allowlisting here) is documented, risk-assessed and accepted by the owner. Forcing the agent risks outage and lost support, recording false compliance is misrepresentation, and hiding the asset leaves the risk and adds dishonesty.

cards.q: 02:25 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a fraud analyst asks for read access to the whole customer database to study refund patterns. The study needs refund amounts, dates and postcodes, but no names or bank details. What do you provision?
options: Deny the request, since analysts should never see any customer data
Export the full table to a spreadsheet so the analyst works on a copy
Grant access to a view with only the fields the study needs, time-boxed
Grant read access to the full database, since the analyst will not change it
cards.answer: Grant access to a view with only the fields the study needs, time-boxed
cards.why: Secure provisioning applies need-to-know and least privilege to data: a restricted view gives exactly the fields the study needs, and a time limit removes access when it ends. Read-only still exposes every field, an export creates an unmanaged copy outside the database's controls, and refusing blocks legitimate fraud work.

cards.q: 05:40 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a quarterly review shows an analyst who moved from payroll to logistics six months ago still has access to the payroll share, and has opened it twice since the move. What do you do?
options: Leave it in place, since the analyst may need to help the old team one day
Suspend the analyst's account until HR has finished its investigation
Remove the payroll access, ask the owner to review the use, and fix the mover step
Remove the access quietly and close the ticket without telling anyone at all
cards.answer: Remove the payroll access, ask the owner to review the use, and fix the mover step
cards.why: When someone changes role, provisioning must revoke what the old role needed, or privileges accumulate. Remove the access, let the payroll owner judge whether the two opens were legitimate, and fix the mover process that missed it. Keeping it just in case is privilege creep, silent removal hides a process failure, and suspension presumes guilt.

cards.q: 00:50 · Asset vault. Your ticket: HR reports that a contractor's engagement ended last Friday. The contractor was issued a laptop, a hardware token and a depot door badge, and HR's checklist covers only the laptop. What do you do?
options: Disable the laptop remotely and wait for the contractor to post it all back
Ask the contractor to destroy the token and badge and confirm by email
Collect the laptop as HR's checklist says and let the other items lapse
Revoke every account and collect all three assets against the issue record
cards.answer: Revoke every account and collect all three assets against the issue record
cards.why: Provisioning is a full lifecycle: each asset issued is recorded against the person, so deprovisioning can revoke every access and recover every item. The badge and token still open doors and accounts. Collecting only the laptop leaves them live, waiting leaves the badge working, and self-destruction gives no proof and no recovery.

cards.q: 03:50 · Asset vault. Your ticket: a customs broker partner wants direct access tomorrow to Tessaly's shipment database to speed up clearance. No agreement yet says what it may do with the data or how long it may keep it. What do you do?
options: Email the broker a nightly export of the database instead of any access
Grant access tomorrow, since the broker is a long-standing trusted partner
Hold access until a data sharing agreement sets use, safeguards and deletion
Grant full database access now and draft the agreement afterwards
cards.answer: Hold access until a data sharing agreement sets use, safeguards and deletion
cards.why: Provisioning data to a third party needs agreed terms first: permitted use, security and handling requirements, retention and deletion, and audit rights, so obligations follow the data. Trust is not a control, access before terms gives up leverage, and a nightly export creates uncontrolled copies with even less oversight.

cards.q: 07:00 · Assurance bench. In the shift debrief you learn why last quarter's penetration test changed nothing: the network team commissioned it alone, and no one with budget ever saw the findings. What lasting fix do you propose?
options: Buy a continuous scanning platform so findings no longer depend on sponsorship
Keep the reports inside the SOC so weaknesses are not leaked to wider management
Have senior management approve the assessment charter, scope and result owners
Let the network team commission tests directly so findings reach engineers fast
cards.answer: Have senior management approve the assessment charter, scope and result owners
cards.why: An assessment strategy needs senior management sponsorship: they approve scope and frequency, own the risk, and fund remediation, so results reach someone accountable. Letting a single team commission tests repeats the orphaned-findings failure, a tool changes nothing about ownership, and hiding reports from management defeats the purpose of assurance.

cards.q: 06:50 · Assurance bench. After-action on last week's failed file-server restore: the backup dashboard showed 100% job success all month, and the storage vendor quotes eleven-nines durability. What becomes the backup metric?
options: Track scheduled restore-test results as the backup metric, not job success
Rely on the vendor's eleven-nines durability figure as proof of recoverability
Add a second backup job each night so one success is always on the dashboard
Report backup job completion rate to the board since it is already at 100%
cards.answer: Track scheduled restore-test results as the backup metric, not job success
cards.why: Backup verification data must prove recoverability. Durability only says stored bytes will not be lost, and job success only says a job ended; neither shows the data can be restored intact and on time. Collecting restore-test results measures what matters. Leaning on the durability figure is the tempting error that let this failure go unseen.

cards.q: 02:40 · Assurance bench. An authorised penetration test against the payments API is running overnight. Twenty minutes after the testers began fuzzing the settlement endpoint, merchants start seeing declined transactions. Your move?
options: Block the testers' IPs at the firewall without telling them or the system owner
Roll back the payments API release in case the errors are caused by new code
Invoke the rules-of-engagement stop clause and pause the test with the owner
Let the testers carry on, since production was in scope and the contract is paid
cards.answer: Invoke the rules-of-engagement stop clause and pause the test with the owner
cards.why: Rules of engagement define stop conditions and contacts for exactly this: when testing harms production, you halt through the agreed channel, involve the system owner, and resume under revised conditions. Carrying on because it was in scope puts the test above the business. Silently blocking the testers leaves them confused and the record incomplete; a rollback guesses at a cause you already know.

cards.q: 03:05 · Assurance bench. The overnight scan rates an information-disclosure flaw on the internet-facing payment gateway as Medium. Threat intel says criminals are chaining that exact flaw with another bug this week. What do you do with the finding?
options: Raise its priority for this asset given exposure and active exploitation
Queue it with the other Mediums for the standard ninety-day remediation cycle
Change the CVSS base score in the scanner so the dashboard shows it as Critical
Close it as accepted, since Medium findings do not need an owner's sign-off
cards.answer: Raise its priority for this asset given exposure and active exploitation
cards.why: A scanner's Medium is a generic base severity. Analysing test output means adjusting priority for asset criticality, exposure and live threat, which is what environmental and temporal context is for. Queuing it by label ignores active exploitation; editing the base score falsifies the record instead of documenting the context; closing it skips the risk owner.

cards.q: 03:15 · Assurance bench. The external auditors were given a service account for fieldwork. Tonight the SIEM shows it browsing HR and payroll shares that sit outside the agreed audit scope. What do you do first?
options: Grant it domain admin so the auditors stop hunting for evidence share by share
Restrict the account to the agreed scope and alert the audit liaison and owner
Leave it running, because auditors are independent and must not be obstructed
Delete the account and the auditors' extracted files before anyone is told
cards.answer: Restrict the account to the agreed scope and alert the audit liaison and owner
cards.why: Auditors get read-only access limited to the agreed scope, and deviations go through the audit liaison and management. Restricting the account contains the exposure while keeping the record. Independence covers auditors' judgement, not unscoped access to personal data. Deleting files destroys evidence of what happened, and domain admin rewards the overreach.

cards.q: 23:50 · Assurance bench. A contractor assessing the benefits platform has asked for a full export of employees' medical records 'to test the access controls', and a job to produce it is queued for midnight. What do you do?
options: Let the export run, as the assessor signed an NDA and needs complete data
Send the full export encrypted, since encryption makes any disclosure safe
Cancel the assessment of the benefits platform so no health data is exposed
Hold the job and agree a masked sample that proves the controls with the owner
cards.answer: Hold the job and agree a masked sample that proves the controls with the owner
cards.why: A sound assessment strategy defines what data testers may handle. Access controls can be tested with masked or sampled records, so data minimisation lets the test proceed without exposing health data. An NDA does not make the disclosure necessary, encryption protects transit but not the over-collection itself, and cancelling leaves the controls untested.

cards.q: 01:25 · Assurance bench. Domain-controller logs stopped reaching the SIEM three hours ago, just after an unusual admin logon. The coverage KPI still reads 100% because it counts configured sources, not received events. Your move?
options: Reset the KPI threshold so a three-hour gap no longer raises the dashboard
Open an incident for possible log tampering and restore the collection path
Wait for the morning report, since the coverage KPI is still showing green
Restart the SIEM service and close the ticket if events start flowing again
cards.answer: Open an incident for possible log tampering and restore the collection path
cards.why: Log data is security process data, and a gap right after a suspicious admin logon may be an attacker impairing defences. Treat it as an incident and restore collection. The green KPI shows why metrics must measure received events, not configured sources. Restarting and closing loses the question of why logs stopped; waiting trusts a metric that is already wrong.

cards.q: 04:05 · Assurance bench. A red-team exercise is running this week. The SOC flags credential dumping on a warehouse server, and the red-team lead confirms over the agreed channel that it is not theirs. What do you do?
options: Let the exercise continue and log the event for review in the final report
Ask the red team to investigate it, since they already have access in place
Wipe the warehouse server now so the exercise results are not contaminated
Pause the exercise and run the event as a live incident through the IR plan
cards.answer: Pause the exercise and run the event as a live incident through the IR plan
cards.why: A confirmed non-exercise event is a real attack; the exercise's deconfliction channel has done its job, and now the IR plan takes over. Pausing the exercise removes noise and frees the defenders. Logging it for the report lets a real adversary operate for days, testers are not your incident responders, and wiping destroys evidence.

cards.q: 05:10 · Assurance bench. A new scanner plugin has just flagged a critical remote-code flaw on forty Linux hosts. The ops lead wants an emergency change to rebuild them all before 07:00, but the distro backports fixes without changing version banners. Your move?
options: Validate the finding on a sample against installed packages before acting
Approve the emergency rebuild of all forty hosts before the day shift arrives
Suppress the plugin across the estate since banner checks are always wrong
Take the forty hosts offline until the scanner vendor issues a statement
cards.answer: Validate the finding on a sample against installed packages before acting
cards.why: Analysing test output means confirming findings before acting on them: banner-based checks often produce false positives on distributions that backport fixes. A quick check of installed packages on a sample shows whether the risk is real. An estate-wide emergency rebuild on an unverified finding causes its own outage; blanket suppression risks false negatives.

cards.q: 02:55 · Assurance bench. An engineer hot-fixed a failing log collector at 02:00 with no change ticket. Auditors test the ITIL-based change process at 09:00, and the engineer asks you to backdate a normal change record. What do you do?
options: Roll back the fix tonight so no unapproved change exists when auditors arrive
Leave it unrecorded, since the change fixed an outage and did no real harm
Log it as an emergency change and route it for retrospective CAB review
Backdate a normal change record so the auditors find a clean approval trail
cards.answer: Log it as an emergency change and route it for retrospective CAB review
cards.why: ITIL-style change management has an emergency change path: act now, record it truthfully, and have the CAB review it afterwards. That is the evidence auditors want to see. Backdating falsifies audit evidence, an integrity failure far worse than the missing ticket. Rolling back reopens the outage to hide a process gap, and leaving it unrecorded breaks the configuration baseline.

cards.q: 00:35 · Assurance bench. Tonight's external scan has hit an address range that belongs to Tessaly's SaaS ticketing provider, and their abuse desk is threatening to block all Tessaly traffic. Your move?
options: Keep scanning, since the provider hosts Tessaly data and so it is in scope
Switch the scan to a new source address so the abuse desk loses track of it
Tell the abuse desk it was a false alarm and resume the sweep after an hour
Stop scanning that range and rescope under the provider's testing policy
cards.answer: Stop scanning that range and rescope under the provider's testing policy
cards.why: Test strategy must cover location: you may test only what you are authorised to test, and a third party's infrastructure needs its permission. Cloud and SaaS providers usually set a testing policy or offer attestations instead. Hosting Tessaly data does not make their systems yours to scan; evading or misleading the abuse desk turns an error into unauthorised access.

cards.q: 03:40 · Assurance bench. You are compiling account-management metrics and find 31 enabled accounts belonging to leavers. One of them authenticated over VPN forty minutes ago. What do you do first?
options: Email the former employee to ask whether the VPN logon was really them
Disable that account, preserve its session logs and open an incident
Add all 31 accounts to the metrics report and flag them for HR next week
Delete all 31 accounts at once so the leaver metric drops to zero tonight
cards.answer: Disable that account, preserve its session logs and open an incident
cards.why: Account-management data exists to surface exactly this, but an active leaver session is now an incident, not a metric. Disabling the account contains it, the logs preserve evidence, and the remaining 30 then go through the deprovisioning fix. Reporting next week leaves the door open; deleting destroys the audit trail; emailing the leaver may tip off whoever holds the credentials.

cards.q: 06:15 · Assurance bench. A dynamic scan of the customer portal, meant for staging, was pointed at production by mistake and has created 9,000 junk orders that the warehouse will pick at 07:00. Your move?
options: Let the scan finish so the results are complete, then delete the orders
Let the warehouse pick the orders and reverse them once the day shift starts
Delete the orders straight from the database before anyone else notices
Stop the scan, hold the junk orders with the owner, and rerun it on staging
cards.answer: Stop the scan, hold the junk orders with the owner, and rerun it on staging
cards.why: Dynamic testing that writes data belongs in a test environment that mirrors production. Stopping the scan limits the harm, the business owner decides how to hold the bad orders, and rerunning on staging still gives you the results. Finishing the scan multiplies the damage; deleting records directly bypasses the owner and leaves no trace of what happened.

cards.q: 00:10 · Assurance bench. Reviewing tonight's penetration test output, you see the testers found a web shell on the partner portal dated months before the engagement began. What do you do?
options: Ask the testers whether they planted it and close the matter if they did not
Escalate it to incident response now and preserve the host for forensics
List it as a critical finding in the report due to management next week
Have the testers delete the web shell so the portal is clean by morning
cards.answer: Escalate it to incident response now and preserve the host for forensics
cards.why: Test output can reveal a real compromise, and that stops being a report finding: it goes to incident response at once, with the host preserved. A months-old web shell means a live adversary may still be inside. Waiting for the report gives them a week, and having testers delete it destroys evidence and tips off the attacker.

cards.q: 23:20 · Assurance bench. Procurement's ticket asks you to sign off a new cloud host for customer shipment data. The vendor has offered its marketing-site trust seal and a one-page summary. What do you ask for before sign-off?
options: Request its SOC 2 Type II report covering a recent twelve-month period
Accept the trust seal, since it shows an independent firm reviewed them
Request a SOC 2 Type I report as proof controls worked across the year
Request its SOC 1 report, since that covers the security of customer data
cards.answer: Request its SOC 2 Type II report covering a recent twelve-month period
cards.why: A SOC 2 Type II report gives an auditor's opinion on security controls operating effectively over a period, which is what vendor due diligence needs. A seal or SOC 3 summary is for the public and lacks detail. Type I covers design at a single point in time, not operation over a year, and SOC 1 addresses controls over financial reporting.

cards.q: 01:45 · Assurance bench. The ticket asks you to plan the annual assessment of the payments segmentation controls. The network team who designed and run them volunteer to do it, since they know it best. Your move?
options: Skip the assessment this year, as segmentation has not changed since last year
Let the network team assess it and have their own manager sign the report off
Assign an assessor independent of the team and share their design notes
Accept the network team's offer, since nobody knows the segmentation better
cards.answer: Assign an assessor independent of the team and share their design notes
cards.why: Assessment strategy needs independence: the people who build and operate a control should not be the ones attesting it works. An independent assessor, internal or third party, can still use the team's knowledge through design notes and interviews. Self-assessment invites blind spots and bias, and a sign-off inside the same chain of command does not fix that.

cards.q: 04:30 · Assurance bench. Your ticket: fix the monthly endpoint vulnerability scan. It runs unauthenticated and keeps reporting a clean fleet while the patch console shows hundreds of missing updates. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Run authenticated scans with a dedicated, monitored, least-privilege account
Keep unauthenticated scans, as they show only what an attacker would see
Run the scans under a domain admin account so no patch check can be blocked
Replace the scans with a yearly penetration test that covers the whole fleet
cards.answer: Run authenticated scans with a dedicated, monitored, least-privilege account
cards.why: Credentialed scans read installed software and configuration directly, so they find missing patches that unauthenticated scans cannot see. A dedicated, monitored account with only the rights needed keeps the scanner from becoming an attacker's best credential. The outside view has its place but explains the false clean; domain admin over-privileges; an annual test cannot replace monthly coverage.

cards.q: 05:35 · Assurance bench. A high-risk finding on the legacy freight scheduler cannot be fixed until the vendor ships an upgrade in six months. The remediation tracker needs a status for it. What do you record?
options: An exception approved by the SOC lead, since the SOC watches that host most
Removed from the report, as there is nothing the team can do for six months
A time-bound exception with compensating controls, signed by the risk owner
Remediated, since the vendor has already committed to shipping a fix upgrade
cards.answer: A time-bound exception with compensating controls, signed by the risk owner
cards.why: When a finding cannot be fixed yet, exception handling makes the residual risk visible: compensating controls reduce it, the risk owner formally accepts it, and an expiry forces a revisit. Marking it remediated is false reporting. The SOC lead does not own the business risk, and deleting the finding hides exposure from the people who must decide on it.

cards.q: 02:20 · Assurance bench. You are reviewing the test plan for a new customer refund feature before release. Every test case describes a legitimate customer getting a correct refund. What do you add?
options: A sign-off that user acceptance testing will catch any abuse after the release
Misuse cases, such as negative amounts, replayed requests and wrong payees
More legitimate refund cases across every currency the platform supports today
A load test proving the refund service survives double the peak-day volume
cards.answer: Misuse cases, such as negative amounts, replayed requests and wrong payees
cards.why: Misuse case testing asks what an abuser would try, so the tests prove that the feature refuses bad input and fraudulent flows as well as handling good ones. Refunds are a classic fraud target. More happy-path cases only confirm what already works, a load test answers a different question, and user acceptance testing is not designed to find abuse.

cards.q: 06:40 · Assurance bench. The CFO wants this quarter's 140-page penetration test report for the board pack by 09:00. What do you send?
options: The full 140-page report unedited, so the board sees every technical detail
A list of the raw CVE identifiers found, sorted by their CVSS base scores
A one-line note that testing is complete and all findings are in hand
An executive summary of business risk and priorities, with the full report attached
cards.answer: An executive summary of business risk and priorities, with the full report attached
cards.why: Reporting fits the audience: the board needs findings in business-risk terms, with priorities and remediation owners, so it can decide and fund. The full report stays attached for traceability. An unedited technical report buries the decision, raw CVE lists mean nothing to directors, and a one-line reassurance withholds risk the board is accountable for.

cards.q: 00:50 · Assurance bench. The ticket asks you to set next year's testing calendar. The draft tests all 300 systems once a year in alphabetical order, the payments stack included. What goes in the plan?
options: Frequency set by each system's risk, plus retests after significant changes
The alphabetical rota as drafted, since equal coverage is the fairest approach
Testing only the payments stack, because it is the one regulators ask about
One big test of all 300 systems in a single week to cut the vendor's day rate
cards.answer: Frequency set by each system's risk, plus retests after significant changes
cards.why: Assessment frequency should follow risk: critical, exposed or fast-changing systems are tested more often, and significant changes trigger a retest. That spends effort where loss is likeliest. An equal rota treats payments like a print server, testing only payments leaves the rest unassessed, and a single cram week optimises cost rather than assurance.

cards.q: 05:55 · Assurance bench. Internal audit's report on third-party access landed with six findings, and management responses are due at 09:00. The access owner says the fixes are 'obviously in hand'. What do you draft?
options: A note that fixes are in hand, leaving owners and dates for the next review
No reply at all, and fix the six issues quietly before the next audit visit
A response per finding naming an owner, an action and a target date to track
A single reply disputing all six findings to protect the team's audit rating
cards.answer: A response per finding naming an owner, an action and a target date to track
cards.why: An audit closes the loop through management's action plan: each finding gets an accountable owner, a concrete action and a date that audit can follow up. 'In hand' with no owner or date is the usual way findings reappear next year. Disputing everything by reflex damages credibility, and silent fixes leave no evidence the risk was treated.

cards.q: 01:05 · Assurance bench. The awareness programme reports 98% course completion, yet two real phishing emails last month were reported by nobody. Your ticket is to redesign the awareness metrics. What do you collect?
options: Report rate and time-to-report from phishing simulations, alongside completion
Completion alone, now tracked weekly instead of monthly for faster visibility
Quiz scores from the end of each course, since they prove staff understood it
The number of staff who clicked, so the worst offenders can be named publicly
cards.answer: Report rate and time-to-report from phishing simulations, alongside completion
cards.why: Training and awareness data should measure behaviour, not attendance. How often and how fast staff report a simulated phish shows whether the programme changes what people do. Completion and quiz scores measure activity. Counting clicks has value, but naming people publicly punishes them and discourages the reporting you actually want.

cards.q: 03:30 · Assurance bench. A new SIEM rule for encoded PowerShell went live yesterday and has not fired once. The ticket asks you to confirm the control works. Your move?
options: Lower the rule's threshold until it produces a few alerts every single day
Wait for a real attacker to use the technique and check whether it fires then
Simulate the technique on a test host, with approval, and trace the alert
Mark it working, since zero alerts means nobody is using encoded PowerShell
cards.answer: Simulate the technique on a test host, with approval, and trace the alert
cards.why: A detective control is proven by testing it: run the technique in a controlled, authorised way, as breach-and-attack simulation or purple teaming does, and follow the alert from endpoint to SIEM to analyst. Silence is not evidence of either safety or failure. Tuning for noise hides the question, and waiting for a real attacker makes the adversary your test.

cards.q: 02:05 · Assurance bench. While testing the warehouse handheld app, your team found a flaw in the vendor's firmware that affects every customer of that vendor, not just Tessaly. What do you do with it?
options: Publish the details tonight so every affected customer can protect itself
Keep it internal, since the flaw is the vendor's problem and not Tessaly's
Sell the details to a bug broker to fund the rest of this year's test budget
Report it privately to the vendor under a coordinated disclosure timeline
cards.answer: Report it privately to the vendor under a coordinated disclosure timeline
cards.why: Coordinated or responsible disclosure gives the vendor time to fix before details go public, protecting other customers without arming attackers first. It also fits the ISC2 ethics duty to protect society. Publishing tonight exposes everyone before a patch exists, keeping quiet leaves other customers at risk indefinitely, and selling it is plainly unethical.

cards.q: 06:20 · Assurance bench. A director files a ticket: 'Book a pen test for the customer portal.' Nobody can say what question the test should answer or which requirement drives it. What do you do first?
options: Book a red-team exercise instead, since it tests more than a pen test does
Agree objectives, scope and pass criteria with the owner, then pick the tests
Book the pen test as asked, since the director has already approved the budget
Run a cheap automated scan instead and file it as the pen test requested
cards.answer: Agree objectives, scope and pass criteria with the owner, then pick the tests
cards.why: Assessment design starts from objectives: what the organisation needs to know, against which requirement, and what counts as a pass. Only then do you choose the method. Booking whatever was named buys an answer to no question, a relabelled scan misleads the director, and a red team is a different tool for a different objective.

cards.q: 04:45 · Assurance bench. The ticket proposes hiring the consultancy that designed and built Tessaly's access-control framework last year to audit that same framework for the board. Your move?
options: Approve the consultancy, since it already understands the framework in depth
Approve it, provided the consultancy uses a different partner on the audit
Replace the audit with the consultancy's own assurance memo on its design
Select an audit firm with no role in building the controls it will assess
cards.answer: Select an audit firm with no role in building the controls it will assess
cards.why: Audit value rests on independence: a firm auditing its own work has a self-review threat, and the board cannot rely on the result. Pick an auditor with no stake in the design. Familiarity is exactly the conflict, a different partner at the same firm does not remove it, and a memo from the designer is not an audit at all.

cards.q: 23:40 · Assurance bench. A contractor has delivered source code for a new card-tokenisation module that goes live next week. The only testing so far is a demo that it tokenises cards. What do you add to the release gate?
options: A penetration test of the portal next year once the module is running live
Static analysis and peer code review against secure coding rules
A second demo with a wider range of card types from different card schemes
A signed statement from the contractor that the code follows secure practice
cards.answer: Static analysis and peer code review against secure coding rules
cards.why: With source code in hand, code review and static analysis find flaws such as injection, weak cryptography and secrets in code before they reach production, when fixing them is cheapest. A demo proves function, not security. A contractor's attestation is not evidence, and testing next year leaves card data exposed for months.
