cards.q: 01:35 · Assurance bench. Half of Tessaly's routing engine moved to a public cloud IaaS this year, but the assessment plan still covers only the on-premises data centre. What do you add to the plan?
options: A full penetration test of the provider's hypervisors and physical sites
A copy of the on-premises plan, applied unchanged to the cloud workloads
Tests of the cloud layers Tessaly controls, plus the provider's attestations
Nothing, since the cloud provider is responsible for securing its platform
cards.answer: Tests of the cloud layers Tessaly controls, plus the provider's attestations
cards.why: Assessment strategy must cover every location, and in IaaS the shared responsibility model splits the work: Tessaly tests what it configures, such as identities, network rules, images and storage, and relies on the provider's attestations for the rest. Leaving the cloud out ignores the half Tessaly controls. Testing the provider's hypervisors is unauthorised, and an on-premises plan misses cloud-specific risks.

cards.q: 05:05 · Assurance bench. A key payroll vendor's SOC 1 Type II report ends at 31 March. Tessaly's financial year ends at 30 June, and the external auditors want assurance for the whole year. What do you request?
options: A bridge letter from the vendor covering April to June, then assess the gap
Nothing more, since a Type II report stays valid for the following year
The vendor's SOC 3 report, since it is public and covers the same controls
A Type I report dated 30 June to prove the controls operated all quarter
cards.answer: A bridge letter from the vendor covering April to June, then assess the gap
cards.why: A bridge (gap) letter is management's statement that there have been no material changes since the report period ended. It covers the months until the next report, and you still weigh that residual risk. A Type II covers only its stated period. SOC 3 is a general-use summary, and a Type I speaks to design at one date, not operation over the quarter.

cards.q: 03:55 · Assurance bench. The EDI parser that ingests partner shipping files crashed twice last month on malformed files. The ticket asks for a test that finds more of these before an attacker does. What do you run?
options: Ask partners to validate their files more carefully before they send them
Fuzz the parser with mutated and malformed files in a test environment
Replay last month's two bad files to confirm the parser now accepts them
Run the network vulnerability scanner against the host the parser runs on
cards.answer: Fuzz the parser with mutated and malformed files in a test environment
cards.why: Fuzz testing feeds large volumes of mutated or malformed input to find crashes and memory-handling bugs that ordinary tests miss. It suits file parsers exactly, and a test environment keeps the crashes harmless. Replaying two known files only checks those two cases, a network scan does not exercise parsing logic, and relying on partners gives up on input validation.

cards.q: 00:20 · Assurance bench. Your ticket is to validate the scanning strategy. The scanner covers 1,840 hosts; the CMDB lists 2,310, and DHCP leases show about 2,600 devices on the network. Your move?
options: Trust the scanner count, since it finds anything that answers on the network
Scan only the 1,840 hosts until the CMDB team resolves its own backlog
Raise the scan rate so all 1,840 hosts are covered twice each week
Reconcile the three sources and bring every unscanned asset into scope
cards.answer: Reconcile the three sources and bring every unscanned asset into scope
cards.why: To validate a test strategy, check its coverage against reality. Reconciling scanner, CMDB and network data exposes the unknown assets that attackers find first, and brings them into scope. The scanner sees only what it is pointed at. Waiting on the CMDB leaves the gap open, and scanning the same 1,840 more often only deepens coverage you already have.

cards.q: 06:05 · Assurance bench. The vendor's SOC 2 report for the tracking platform has a clean opinion, but lists controls Tessaly must operate itself, such as reviewing its own user list quarterly. What goes in the ticket?
options: Wait until the next audit and see whether anyone asks about those controls
Assign owners for those user-side controls and gather evidence they operate
File the report as it stands, since the opinion is clean and nothing is due
Ask the vendor to perform those controls on Tessaly's behalf from now on
cards.answer: Assign owners for those user-side controls and gather evidence they operate
cards.why: Complementary user entity controls (CUECs) are the customer's share: the vendor's clean opinion assumes Tessaly operates them. Assign owners and keep evidence, or the assurance chain breaks on Tessaly's side. Filing the report ignores that assumption, the vendor cannot review Tessaly's own users on its behalf, and waiting for an auditor is not operating a control.

cards.q: 04:15 · Assurance bench. The release report for the billing upgrade says '1,200 tests passed'. Nobody can tell you which of the 40 security requirements those tests actually exercise. What do you ask for?
options: Another 1,200 tests, so the release has twice the testing behind it
A statement from the test lead that coverage is sufficient for release
The raw test logs, so you can count the number of assertions yourself
A traceability matrix mapping each security requirement to the tests run
cards.answer: A traceability matrix mapping each security requirement to the tests run
cards.why: Test coverage analysis asks what was tested, not how much. Tracing each security requirement to its tests shows which requirements were never exercised. Doubling the test count may just repeat the same paths, a lead's assurance is opinion, and counting assertions measures volume rather than coverage of the requirements.

cards.q: 02:35 · Assurance bench. Next week's scheduled pen test of the depot network overlaps the peak-season cut-off, and the depot managers and SOC have not been told it is happening. What do you do?
options: Cancel this year's test, since peak season always makes testing unsafe
Keep the date and tell only the testers, so the scope stays confidential
Move the window off peak and brief the owners and SOC on the test schedule
Keep the date and say nothing, so the SOC's reaction is tested as well
cards.answer: Move the window off peak and brief the owners and SOC on the test schedule
cards.why: Test strategy covers timing and communication: intrusive testing avoids critical business periods, and system owners and the SOC know when it runs so real alerts are not dismissed as the test. Testing the SOC blind is a separate exercise that needs management approval and a trusted agent, not an accident of poor planning. Cancelling gives up assurance that rescheduling keeps.

cards.q: 23:05 · Assurance bench. The vendor's SOC 2 Type II report for the fleet telematics platform uses the carve-out method for its hosting provider. The hosting layer is where the customer data sits. What do you do?
options: Obtain and review the hosting provider's own report for those controls
Accept the vendor's report as covering the hosting layer by reference
Ask the vendor's auditor to re-issue the report without the carve-out
Drop the vendor, because any carve-out means the report is worthless
cards.answer: Obtain and review the hosting provider's own report for those controls
cards.why: Under the carve-out method, the subservice organisation's controls are excluded from the auditor's opinion, so assurance over the hosting layer must come from that provider's own report. Assuming the vendor's report covers it leaves the data layer unassessed. The auditor cannot simply redraw scope, and a carve-out is common, not disqualifying.

cards.q: 01:15 · Assurance bench. The new customs-broker integration exchanges files and API calls between Tessaly's routing engine and an outside broker. Each side's software passed its own tests. What do you test next?
options: Load on the routing engine alone, since that is the side Tessaly owns
Nothing further, because two passed components make a passing system
The interface itself: auth, input handling and errors across both sides
Each side's software again, since the earlier tests may have missed bugs
cards.answer: The interface itself: auth, input handling and errors across both sides
cards.why: Interface testing checks where systems meet: authentication between them, how each handles the other's malformed or unexpected data, and how errors propagate. Integration flaws live there, and component tests cannot see them. Retesting the parts repeats known ground, and a load test on one side answers a different question.

cards.q: 03:10 · Assurance bench. Legal sends the draft contract for a new last-mile courier that will handle customer addresses. The vendor offers no SOC report. What do you ask Legal to add?
options: A right-to-audit clause, security duties and breach notice terms
A higher contract price so the courier can afford to get a SOC report
A clause making the courier liable, in place of any assurance rights
Nothing, since couriers only see addresses and not payment card data
cards.answer: A right-to-audit clause, security duties and breach notice terms
cards.why: Without third-party attestation, a right-to-audit clause gives Tessaly a way to verify the courier's controls, backed by contractual security duties and breach notification. Liability shifts some cost after the fact but gives no assurance beforehand. Addresses are personal data under privacy law, and paying more does not by itself produce evidence.

cards.q: 05:25 · Assurance bench. The board wants to know how much damage a disgruntled warehouse supervisor could do with their normal access. You are scoping the test. What do you give the testers?
options: No accounts or information, so they start as a true outside attacker
Domain admin rights, so they can map every system the supervisor could reach
Full source code and network diagrams of every system Tessaly operates
A supervisor-level account and the internal knowledge that role would hold
cards.answer: A supervisor-level account and the internal knowledge that role would hold
cards.why: Match the tester's starting knowledge and access to the threat you want to model. An insider scenario calls for a grey-box test with that role's account and knowledge. A zero-knowledge external test answers a different question, domain admin grossly overstates the threat, and full white-box detail models someone with far more insight than a supervisor.

cards.q: 00:45 · Assurance bench. External auditors are testing access-removal controls and ask for evidence. A colleague suggests sending them the ten cleanest leaver tickets from the year. What do you send?
options: Every ticket except the late ones, which are being handled separately
The complete leaver population, so the auditors draw their own sample
The ten cleanest tickets, since auditors only need to see a handful
A summary saying access removal is automated and always works correctly
cards.answer: The complete leaver population, so the auditors draw their own sample
cards.why: Audit evidence is only reliable if the auditor controls the sample. Provide the complete population and let them select, so the test reflects how the control really operates. Handpicking clean tickets or leaving out late ones misleads the auditor, which is an integrity breach, and an assertion that the process always works is not evidence.

cards.q: 04:50 · Assurance bench. HR asks you to run a phishing simulation next week that impersonates the CEO announcing bonus cuts, to see who clicks. Nothing is in writing yet. What do you do?
options: Run it without telling anyone in HR, so nobody can leak it to the staff
Use a real CEO email account for the lure so the test is fully convincing
Get written management sign-off and pick a lure that avoids real distress
Run it as described, since realistic lures produce the most honest results
cards.answer: Get written management sign-off and pick a lure that avoids real distress
cards.why: Social engineering tests are real attacks on people, so they need written authorisation, agreed rules and a lure that tests judgement without causing genuine harm or eroding trust. Fake bonus cuts can distress staff and trigger employee-relations fallout. Skipping approval removes accountability, and a real executive mailbox blurs the line between test and actual compromise.

cards.q: 06:30 · Assurance bench. A bank partner's contract renewal requires independent evidence that Tessaly's payment controls meet an agreed standard. The CIO suggests sending the SOC's self-assessment spreadsheet. What do you recommend?
options: Commission a formal, independent audit of the controls against that standard
Send the self-assessment, since the SOC knows the payment controls best of all
Send the latest vulnerability scan report, which shows no critical findings
Invite the bank's engineers to browse the payment systems for an afternoon
cards.answer: Commission a formal, independent audit of the controls against that standard
cards.why: When a third party needs reliance, a formal security audit is the tool: qualified, independent auditors test controls against defined criteria and issue an opinion others can trust. A self-assessment lacks independence, a scan covers technical flaws rather than the control set, and open browsing by outsiders is neither an audit nor safe.

cards.q: 23:30 · Assurance bench. Tessaly has just acquired a regional haulier with about 400 servers nobody has examined. The ticket asks for a first view of their known weaknesses within a week, without disrupting operations. Your move?
options: Wait for the haulier's own IT team to send a list of what needs patching
Connect the haulier straight to the Tessaly network and let the EDR decide
Run a broad vulnerability assessment to find and rank known weaknesses
Commission a full penetration test to exploit every server over the week
cards.answer: Run a broad vulnerability assessment to find and rank known weaknesses
cards.why: A vulnerability assessment identifies and prioritises known weaknesses across many systems quickly and with low disruption, which is exactly the brief. A penetration test goes deep on exploitation, is slower and riskier, and fits later on the highest-risk findings. Waiting relies on the people who never looked, and connecting unassessed estates imports their risk.

cards.q: 02:10 · Assurance bench. A reorganisation ticket proposes moving internal audit's IT team under the CIO 'to cut overhead'. The same CIO owns most of the systems they audit. What do you advise?
options: Keep internal audit reporting to the audit committee, not the CIO
Accept the move, since the CIO understands the systems better than anyone
Accept it, provided the CIO agrees never to edit audit reports himself
Disband internal IT audit and rely on the SOC's own monthly control checks
cards.answer: Keep internal audit reporting to the audit committee, not the CIO
cards.why: Internal audit's value depends on organisational independence: it reports to the audit committee or board so findings about management's systems cannot be softened by that management. Putting it under the CIO creates a conflict of interest that a promise does not remove. Replacing it with SOC self-checks swaps assurance for self-assessment.

cards.q: 03:25 · Assurance bench. Testers start a physical intrusion test of the Leeds depot tonight. The contract is signed, but the testers carry nothing to show a guard or police officer who stops them. What do you do before they go?
options: Give the testers staff badges so they can walk in without being challenged
Give each tester a signed letter of authority with a contact to verify it
Tell the testers to run if they are caught so the test is not compromised
Brief every guard at the depot tonight so nobody raises a false alarm
cards.answer: Give each tester a signed letter of authority with a contact to verify it
cards.why: Physical testers carry a signed authorisation letter with a reachable contact, so a stopped tester can be verified quickly and safely. It protects the testers, the guards and Tessaly. Running from security or police is dangerous, briefing every guard removes what the test is meant to measure, and real badges bypass the controls under test.

cards.q: 01:55 · Assurance bench. The ISO/IEC 27001 surveillance audit raised a major nonconformity: risk assessments were not updated after two acquisitions. The certification body wants a response. What goes in it?
options: An updated risk assessment for the two acquisitions, and no further change
An appeal arguing the acquisitions were too recent to be in the audit scope
A request to change certification bodies before the next surveillance visit
Root-cause analysis and a corrective action plan with owners and dates
cards.answer: Root-cause analysis and a corrective action plan with owners and dates
cards.why: A nonconformity calls for corrective action: find why the process failed, here the lack of any trigger to reassess after a major change, and fix that with owners and dates, not just the symptom. Updating two assessments corrects the instance but invites recurrence. Appealing on timing or shopping for a new auditor avoids the finding instead of treating it.

cards.q: 05:45 · Assurance bench. Customers sometimes report that shipment tracking fails before 06:00, when traffic is too low for real-user monitoring to show anything. The ticket asks how to catch it first. What do you set up?
options: A customer survey asking early users to report failures through a web form
Scripted synthetic tests that walk the tracking journey every five minutes
More real-user monitoring, so the few overnight users are tracked in detail
A monthly penetration test of the tracking site to find the failing component
cards.answer: Scripted synthetic tests that walk the tracking journey every five minutes
cards.why: Scripted synthetic transactions run a known journey on a schedule, so they detect failures even when no real users are present, and they give consistent baselines. Real-user monitoring needs traffic that is not there at night, a pen test looks for security flaws rather than availability, and a survey makes customers your monitoring.

cards.q: 00:15 · Assurance bench. A storage clean-up ticket would delete last year's firewall change logs tonight. The annual PCI assessment starts next month and covers that period. Your move?
options: Approve the clean-up, since the logs are over a year old and use costly disk
Approve it, but keep a summary report of the changes for the assessor
Move the logs to a personal drive so they are out of the clean-up's reach
Hold the deletion and keep the logs for the period the assessment covers
cards.answer: Hold the deletion and keep the logs for the period the assessment covers
cards.why: Audit evidence must be retained for the period under review and as the retention schedule requires. Deleting it just before an assessment destroys the evidence the auditor needs and looks like concealment. A summary is not the original records, and a personal drive breaks custody and data handling rules.

cards.q: 02:50 · Assurance bench. A hotfix for an authentication bypass in the driver app is ready. Two releases ago, a similar fix quietly broke session timeout. What do you require before release?
options: Retest the fix plus a regression suite covering existing security features
Test only the bypass itself, since the rest of the app has not been changed
Release it tonight and let the monitoring team watch for any side effects
Delay the fix until the next quarterly release so it gets full UAT cycles
cards.answer: Retest the fix plus a regression suite covering existing security features
cards.why: Regression testing confirms a change fixed its target without breaking what already worked. Security features such as session handling are exactly what fixes to authentication code tend to disturb. Testing only the bypass repeats the earlier failure, releasing untested makes production the test, and a quarterly delay leaves a known bypass open.

cards.q: 06:55 · Assurance bench. A payments vendor's SOC 2 Type II report carries a qualified opinion, with exceptions noted in change management during four of twelve months. Procurement wants to renew today. What do you do?
options: Renew, and ask the vendor to reissue the report without the exceptions
Terminate the vendor at once, since any qualified opinion is disqualifying
Weigh the exceptions' impact and agree remediation before renewal
Renew as planned, since any SOC 2 report counts as a pass for procurement
cards.answer: Weigh the exceptions' impact and agree remediation before renewal
cards.why: A qualified opinion means some controls did not operate as described. Read the exceptions, judge their impact on the services Tessaly uses, and get remediation or compensating controls before renewal. Treating any report as a pass ignores its content, reports cannot be edited on request, and automatic termination is a risk decision taken without analysis.

cards.q: 04:25 · Assurance bench. The server hardening baseline was approved in spring, but nobody has checked whether the 600 Windows servers still match it. The ticket asks for a repeatable test. What do you set up?
options: A yearly manual spot-check of five servers chosen by each server owner
A policy memo reminding admins to keep their servers on the baseline
A new baseline, since the spring version is probably out of date now
Automated configuration compliance scans against the approved baseline
cards.answer: Automated configuration compliance scans against the approved baseline
cards.why: Compliance checks test systems against an approved baseline automatically and repeatably, for example with SCAP-based content, and they show drift on every server. A yearly spot-check picked by the owners is too thin and too easy to steer, a memo is not a test, and rewriting the baseline skips the question of whether servers meet the current one.

cards.q: 01:40 · Assurance bench. The sorting-hall conveyor controllers are in scope for this month's scanning. Their vendor warns that an aggressive scan once froze a line for six hours. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Run the full scan overnight tonight, as few people work in the hall then
Passive discovery first, then gentle scans in an agreed maintenance window
Exclude the controllers from testing for good, since the vendor warned you
Run the full standard scan profile at noon, when staff can restart the line
cards.answer: Passive discovery first, then gentle scans in an agreed maintenance window
cards.why: Fragile operational technology needs a tailored test approach: passive discovery, gentle, rate-limited scans and an agreed window with the owner, so you gain visibility without stopping the line. Permanent exclusion leaves a blind spot attackers favour. The standard profile is what froze the line before, and the time of day does not change that.

cards.q: 03:50 · Assurance bench. An auditor asks for evidence of last year's quarterly privileged-access reviews. The reviews happened in meetings, but nothing was recorded. A colleague offers to write up minutes tonight. What do you do?
options: Let the colleague write minutes tonight and date them to the meetings
Send the auditor this quarter's review and describe it as last year's
Refuse the request, since the reviews did happen and auditors must trust us
Tell the auditor no records exist and set up signed, recorded reviews now
cards.answer: Tell the auditor no records exist and set up signed, recorded reviews now
cards.why: A control without evidence cannot be shown to have operated, so the honest answer is that no records exist, followed by a fix: documented, signed reviews from now on. Back-dated minutes or relabelled reviews fabricate audit evidence, breaching the ISC2 code's honesty requirement. Refusing the request obstructs the audit.

cards.q: 00:05 · Assurance bench. You are contracting an outside firm for the annual penetration test. Their proposal says, 'We start Monday; we'll let you know what we hit.' What do you require before they start?
options: An upfront list of every vulnerability they expect to find at Tessaly
Signed rules of engagement: scope, timing, methods, contacts and data handling
Nothing more, since a firm that starts fast shows it is confident in its skill
A verbal promise from their lead that production systems will be avoided
cards.answer: Signed rules of engagement: scope, timing, methods, contacts and data handling
cards.why: Testing without written authorisation and agreed rules of engagement is indistinguishable from an attack, legally and operationally. The rules of engagement set scope, windows, permitted techniques, emergency contacts and how captured data is handled and destroyed. Speed is not a control, a verbal promise leaves no record, and predicting findings is not a test plan.

cards.q: 05:15 · Assurance bench. The ticket asks you to test whether any unauthorised wireless access points are bridging into the head-office network. The wired scanner sees nothing unusual. What do you run?
options: A wireless survey of the site, matched against the authorised AP inventory
Another wired scan with a faster timing profile to catch devices sooner
A staff questionnaire asking whether anyone has plugged in a router
A firewall rule change that blocks all wireless traffic at the perimeter
cards.answer: A wireless survey of the site, matched against the authorised AP inventory
cards.why: Rogue access points are found where they operate: a wireless survey detects every broadcasting AP, and matching it against the approved inventory shows which are unauthorised. A wired scan may miss a bridging device, a questionnaire relies on people admitting it, and a perimeter rule does nothing about an AP bridging inside the network.

cards.q: 23:15 · Assurance bench. The ticket asks you to test the control 'admin activity on the finance database is reviewed weekly'. The review lead says she checks the logs every Monday. What do you do?
options: Check that database logging is switched on and mark the control effective
Review the finance admin logs yourself tonight and call that the test
Pick sampled weeks, and trace each admin action to a recorded review
Accept her statement, since she is the named owner of the weekly review
cards.answer: Pick sampled weeks, and trace each admin action to a recorded review
cards.why: Testing a log-review control means finding evidence that reviews happened and caught what they should: sample weeks and match admin actions to recorded reviews and follow-ups. An owner's statement is an assertion, not evidence. Logging being on shows the data exists, not that anyone reviews it, and doing the review yourself tests nothing about the control.

cards.q: 06:10 · Assurance bench. Mid-test, the testers phone to say they have a foothold on the web tier and can pivot into the HR subnet, which is out of scope. They want to push on tonight. Your move?
options: Hold at the boundary until the owner approves a written scope change
Tell them to push on, since it shows how far a real attacker could get
Approve it verbally over the phone so no testing time is lost tonight
End the engagement, since any out-of-scope suggestion breaks the contract
cards.answer: Hold at the boundary until the owner approves a written scope change
cards.why: Scope is part of the authorisation; testing beyond it is unauthorised access, however instructive. The HR data owner must approve a written change first, and the foothold itself is already a finding worth reporting. A verbal nod at 06:00 leaves no record and bypasses the owner, and ending the test punishes testers who did the right thing by asking.

cards.q: 02:25 · Assurance bench. You are testing the control 'every firewall change is approved before it is made'. The owner walks you through the approval workflow and it looks sound. What do you do next?
options: Ask the owner to confirm in writing that no change skipped the workflow
Test one change made today while the owner is watching the process run
Sample the period's changes and check each was approved beforehand
Mark the control effective, since the workflow design is plainly sound
cards.answer: Sample the period's changes and check each was approved beforehand
cards.why: A walkthrough shows design; operating effectiveness needs evidence over time. Sample changes across the period and check approval came before implementation. A sound design can still be bypassed in practice, a written assurance from the owner is not independent evidence, and one observed change today says nothing about the other months.

cards.q: 04:40 · Assurance bench. The risk committee's security dashboard shows only lagging figures: incidents closed, tickets resolved, patches applied. The ticket asks for early warning of rising risk. What do you add?
options: A traffic-light rating set each month by the SOC lead's overall feel
The total count of alerts the SIEM raised, since more alerts means more risk
Key risk indicators with thresholds, such as unpatched critical assets
More closed-incident figures, broken down by business unit and by month
cards.answer: Key risk indicators with thresholds, such as unpatched critical assets
cards.why: Key risk indicators are forward-looking measures tied to risk appetite, and thresholds make them trigger action before losses occur. Trends in unpatched critical assets, overdue access reviews or privileged-account growth are typical. Closed-incident counts are lagging performance measures, a gut-feel rating is not data, and raw alert volume tracks tool noise more than risk.

cards.q: 03:00 · Assurance bench. Last weekend's DR test of the order platform is marked 'successful' in the tracker. The only record is that systems came back. The ticket asks what the test report must capture. What do you add?
options: A pass flag and the tester's name, which is enough for the audit trail
Screenshots of the systems running, taken on Monday morning after the test
Nothing, since systems coming back online proves the DR plan works fine
Actual recovery times and data loss against RTO and RPO, plus issues found
cards.answer: Actual recovery times and data loss against RTO and RPO, plus issues found
cards.why: DR and BC test data must show whether recovery met its objectives: measured recovery time and data loss against the RTO and RPO, and the problems found, so management can judge and improve the plan. Coming back eventually is not success if it took three days. A pass flag or screenshots record the outcome without the measures that matter.

cards.q: 06:10 · Dev pipeline. Last week the hosted code-signing service Tessaly buys turned out to have written key-use logs to a bucket anyone could read, and the vendor told you nine days late. The renewal lands on your desk this morning. What goes into the renewal?
options: Renew the contract as it stands, since the vendor has now fixed the bucket
Replace the service with an in-house signing platform built by next spring
Add a breach-notice deadline, a right to audit and a yearly SOC 2 Type II report
Ask the vendor for a discount that covers the cost of the nine-day delay
cards.answer: Add a breach-notice deadline, a right to audit and a yearly SOC 2 Type II report
cards.why: Acquired services are governed through the contract: a notification deadline, a right to audit and an independent SOC 2 Type II report turn vendor promises into evidence Tessaly can check. Renewing unchanged accepts the same blind spot; a discount compensates without reducing risk; rebuilding in-house is a large decision this lesson alone does not justify.

cards.q: 05:40 · Dev pipeline. Yesterday's incident traced back to a cloud access key a developer pasted into a config file and pushed to the shared repository. The key is revoked and the logs are clean. What lasting control do you put in place?
options: Move secrets to a vault injected at build and scan every commit for keys
Make the repository private so that only staff can see anything pushed to it
Email every developer a reminder that keys must never be committed to code
Rewrite the repository history to purge the key, then carry on exactly as before
cards.answer: Move secrets to a vault injected at build and scan every commit for keys
cards.why: A secrets manager takes credentials out of source entirely, and secret scanning in pre-commit hooks and the pipeline catches the next slip before it spreads. A private repo still exposes keys to every insider and every clone; a reminder is awareness without a control; purging history cleans this one leak but prevents none.

cards.q: 02:15 · Dev pipeline. After a dependency update, the payments API's token-check call keeps timing out, and its catch block returns 'allowed' so checkout keeps working. Logs now show unauthenticated calls succeeding. Your move?
options: Leave the handler alone so that checkout revenue keeps flowing until morning
Raise the token-check timeout from two seconds to thirty to cut the exceptions
Add an alert on the exception count and review the trend at the stand-up
Change the handler to deny on any exception and hotfix it through the pipeline
cards.answer: Change the handler to deny on any exception and hotfix it through the pipeline
cards.why: Error paths must fail secure: when the check cannot complete, the answer is deny. Hotfixing the catch block closes the open door now; the timeout's root cause is fixed next. Keeping it open trades revenue for fraud exposure nobody accepted; a longer timeout still fails open when it trips; an alert only watches the breach continue.

cards.q: 23:50 · Dev pipeline. Threat intel flags heavy scraping of an old rate-quote API. Your records say the app was retired last spring, but its server was never switched off and it still reads the live customer database. What do you do first?
options: Patch the old server so it is at least as current as the live systems
Shut the old API down, revoke its database account and preserve its logs
Block the scraping IP ranges at the firewall and keep watching the traffic closely
Ticket the original project team to review it after the holiday break
cards.answer: Shut the old API down, revoke its database account and preserve its logs
cards.why: Disposal is an SDLC phase: retiring software means removing the service, its access and its data paths, and keeping the evidence. Shutting it down and revoking its credentials contains the exposure; preserved logs show what was taken. Patching sustains a system nobody owns; IP blocks are easily dodged; waiting on a disbanded team leaves customer data open.

cards.q: 03:05 · Dev pipeline. A customer is applying the same refund code dozens of times through the merchant portal, draining a promotion budget. Last month's automated scan of the portal came back clean. What do you do?
options: Run the automated scanner again tonight with its most aggressive profile
Switch off the refund feature flag, then have testers probe the portal's logic
Ban the customer's account and leave the refund feature running as normal
Accept the loss as fraud and pass it to finance for the regular monthly write-off
cards.answer: Switch off the refund feature flag, then have testers probe the portal's logic
cards.why: Contain first by disabling the abused function, then close the gap: automated scanners find known technical flaw patterns, not business-logic abuse such as repeat redemption, so manual business-logic testing is needed. Rescanning repeats a test blind to this class; banning one account leaves the flaw for the next; writing it off accepts a risk nobody assessed.

cards.q: 00:40 · Dev pipeline. A critical remote-code flaw is published in a widely used open-source logging library. Developers are unsure which of Tessaly's forty services bundle it, directly or pulled in by other packages. What do you do first?
options: Ask each team lead to reply by morning if they think their service uses the library
Block outbound traffic from every service until someone is certain
Wait for the maintainers to publish a patched release, then start planning
Query the SBOMs and composition scans to list every service with the library
cards.answer: Query the SBOMs and composition scans to list every service with the library
cards.why: Open-source components arrive transitively, so only an inventory answers exposure: a software bill of materials and software composition analysis show every direct and nested copy, letting you prioritise mitigation. Asking leads relies on memory that misses transitive use; blocking everything is an outage with no scope; waiting for the patch wastes the hours you need to mitigate.

cards.q: 01:25 · Dev pipeline. Attackers are probing a path-traversal flaw in the document service. The fix exists, but only inside a feature branch that has not been merged for six weeks and carries 300 other changes. Your move?
options: Commit the small fix to main on its own and ship it through the pipeline
Merge the whole six-week feature branch tonight, since it already contains the fix
Hold the fix until the feature branch is done so it ships in one release
Patch the production servers by hand and backport it to the branch later
cards.answer: Commit the small fix to main on its own and ship it through the pipeline
cards.why: Small, frequently integrated commits keep main shippable, so a fix isolated in its own change can pass the pipeline tonight. The habit of avoiding frequent commits is what built a six-week branch whose merge would drag untested code into production mid-incident. Holding the fix leaves the flaw exploitable; hand-patching creates drift the next deploy overwrites.

cards.q: 04:05 · Dev pipeline. A clean-up script deleted closed merchant accounts, but their rows in the payouts table survived. The nightly payout job is now matching those orphaned rows to recycled merchant IDs and paying the wrong accounts. What do you do?
options: Delete the orphaned payout rows by hand and let the job run on schedule
Stop reusing merchant IDs and leave the payouts table schema unchanged
Stop the payout job, reverse the bad runs and enforce foreign keys on payouts
Let the job finish, then ask finance to reclaim the misdirected payments
cards.answer: Stop the payout job, reverse the bad runs and enforce foreign keys on payouts
cards.why: Stopping the job contains the loss. The root cause is missing referential integrity: a foreign-key constraint makes the database refuse child rows without a valid parent, or cascade the delete. Hand-deleting today's orphans lets the next script create more; ending ID reuse hides the symptom; finishing the run multiplies the payments you must claw back.

cards.q: 05:15 · Dev pipeline. A hotfix for an actively exploited flaw is ready, but the engineer who normally cuts releases is on a flight. His release checklist and tagged build scripts are in the repo, yet two developers propose improvising from memory. What do you direct?
options: Let the two developers improvise the build, since the flaw is being exploited
Wait for the release engineer to land so the build is done the usual way
Build from the written release checklist and the tagged scripts in the repo
Copy the fixed file onto the production servers and skip the build step
cards.answer: Build from the written release checklist and the tagged scripts in the repo
cards.why: A documented, reusable release process is what the Capability Maturity Model calls Repeatable: success no longer depends on one person, so the team can reproduce it under pressure. Improvising risks a broken or untraceable build; waiting leaves the exploit open for hours; copying files into production bypasses testing and change control and creates drift.

cards.q: 02:50 · Dev pipeline. A stored XSS fixed in March is firing again in the customer help centre and stealing sessions. Tonight's diff shows a template refactor removed the encoding call. You have rolled back. What do you require now?
options: Turn the March exploit into an automated regression test that gates builds
Ask the reviewer who approved the refactor to be much more careful in the future
Book a full penetration test of the help centre for next quarter
Freeze the template files so nobody edits them without a VP's approval
cards.answer: Turn the March exploit into an automated regression test that gates builds
cards.why: Regression testing re-runs known-fixed cases against every change, so an old bug cannot silently return; making the March exploit a pipeline gate makes the fix permanent. Asking for care is not a control; a quarterly pen test is far too infrequent for weekly changes; a freeze blocks legitimate work and protects only these files.

cards.q: 03:30 · Dev pipeline. EDR flags the vendor build-agent software on every CI runner beaconing to an unknown host after last night's auto-update. The vendor has not answered your call. What do you do first?
options: Uninstall the agent on every runner and reinstall the previous version in place
Keep builds running while you wait for the vendor to explain the traffic
Post the indicators publicly so other customers can check their runners
Isolate the CI runners, pause auto-updates and preserve the update package
cards.answer: Isolate the CI runners, pause auto-updates and preserve the update package
cards.why: A tampered vendor update is a software supply-chain compromise: contain by isolating what runs it and stopping further updates, and keep the package and runners as evidence. Reinstalling in place destroys evidence and trusts an unverified channel; running on lets a compromised runner poison releases; disclosure goes through coordinated channels once facts are known.

cards.q: 00:15 · Dev pipeline. The partner shipping-rate API is taking 4,000 calls a minute on one partner's key, walking through every customer address in sequence. The partner says the key was never meant to leave their server. What do you do?
options: Block the source IP addresses and leave the partner's key working as before
Revoke that key, issue a new one and enforce per-key rate limits at the gateway
Turn the whole API off until the partner completes its own investigation
Ask the partner to rotate the key themselves during their business hours
cards.answer: Revoke that key, issue a new one and enforce per-key rate limits at the gateway
cards.why: API keys are credentials: a leaked one is revoked and reissued, and per-key throttling at the API gateway caps what any key can harvest next time. IP blocks are evaded by rotating addresses while the stolen key keeps working; switching the API off punishes every partner for one leak; waiting for business hours leaves customer data flowing out.

cards.q: 23:20 · Dev pipeline. A pull request to the card-terminal firmware adds a hand-written assembly routine to speed up PIN-block formatting. The usual reviewer only reads C, and the ticket is now yours. Your move?
options: Approve it, since it passed the functional tests and is only forty lines
Route it to a reviewer fluent in the assembly, focused on bounds and memory
Run the C static analyser over the routine and accept a clean result
Merge it now and ask the author to add comments explaining the routine next sprint
cards.answer: Route it to a reviewer fluent in the assembly, focused on bounds and memory
cards.why: Assembly has no type safety, bounds checking or compiler guardrails, so memory bugs hide easily and ordinary tools cannot see them. Secure coding standards call for a reviewer competent in the language, focused on buffers near PIN data. Functional tests say nothing about overflow; a C analyser cannot parse assembly; comments after merge do not make it reviewed.

cards.q: 01:45 · Dev pipeline. The loyalty-app team works in two-week sprints and wants security to 'do a review at the end' of the six-month build. The ticket to agree the plan is yours. Your move?
options: Agree to the end review and book two weeks for it before the launch date
Ask the team to switch to waterfall so security gets a formal phase gate
Attend the launch meeting and sign off on the team's own checklist
Add security stories and acceptance criteria to every sprint's backlog
cards.answer: Add security stories and acceptance criteria to every sprint's backlog
cards.why: In Agile, security belongs in every iteration: security user stories and definition-of-done criteria are built and tested each sprint while fixes are cheap. A single end review finds six months of flaws when they cost most; forcing waterfall fights the team's delivery model instead of joining it; signing off a self-assessment is no assessment at all.

cards.q: 06:30 · Dev pipeline. The first code-scanning run on the billing service returns 1,200 findings from four tools, each using its own labels. The team lead asks where to start. What do you hand them?
options: Map the findings to CWE IDs and fix those in the CWE Top 25 first
Fix the findings in file order so that no part of the code is missed
Suppress anything the tools label low and ship the rest unchanged
Buy a fifth tool that promises fewer false positives than the four
cards.answer: Map the findings to CWE IDs and fix those in the CWE Top 25 first
cards.why: The Common Weakness Enumeration gives every tool's finding one shared name, so duplicates collapse, and the CWE Top 25 points effort at the weakness types most often exploited. File order ignores risk; suppressing by each tool's own label hides what nobody assessed; a fifth tool adds another vocabulary to the same pile.

cards.q: 04:40 · Dev pipeline. You find three versions of the warehouse scanner app across the handhelds, and nobody can say which source commit built the one on the loading dock. The ticket is yours. Your move?
options: Reinstall the newest version on every handheld tonight and close the ticket
Ask the dock supervisor which version works best and standardise on that
Put builds under configuration control: tagged commits, stored artifacts
Collect the handhelds and lock them away until the vendor can audit them
cards.answer: Put builds under configuration control: tagged commits, stored artifacts
cards.why: Software configuration management ties every deployed build to a tagged commit and a versioned, stored artifact, so you always know what is running and can rebuild or roll back. Reinstalling the newest fixes today but not the cause; choosing by preference skips any security check; confiscating devices halts operations without fixing untracked builds.

cards.q: 02:05 · Dev pipeline. A form on the driver-onboarding site checks the licence-number format in the browser only. The developer says that is enough because the field is never shown to anyone. What goes in the ticket?
options: Tighten the browser check with a stricter regular expression
Hide the field from the page source so that attackers cannot find it at all
Validate the field on the server against an allow-list of formats
Log each submission so any bad input can be traced afterwards
cards.answer: Validate the field on the server against an allow-list of formats
cards.why: Client-side checks are a convenience; an attacker posts straight to the server. Secure coding requires server-side input validation, and an allow-list of what is valid beats trying to block what is bad. A stricter browser check is still bypassed; hiding the field is obscurity; logging records the attack without stopping it.

cards.q: 23:35 · Dev pipeline. Developers started a secure-coding guild on their own, but managers keep pulling its members onto feature work and no standard ever gets adopted. The guild asks you for help. What do you do?
options: Take a proposal to leadership to sponsor and mandate the coding standard
Tell the guild to keep going and publish its standard on the wiki anyway
Write the standard yourself and email it to all developers as policy
Ask the guild to meet out of hours so managers cannot keep pulling them away
cards.answer: Take a proposal to leadership to sponsor and mandate the coding standard
cards.why: A bottom-up security effort lacks authority and budget, which is why it stalls; a top-down approach, with senior management sponsoring and mandating the standard, gives it force. Publishing without backing produces a document nobody follows; issuing policy yourself exceeds your authority; unpaid out-of-hours work is unsustainable and still unenforced.

cards.q: 03:55 · Dev pipeline. A developer wants a free code-formatting plugin from an unknown publisher installed on the build servers. There is no source code for it. Before anyone approves it, what do you do?
options: Install it on one production build server and monitor it for a whole week
Check its star rating and download count in the plugin marketplace
Approve it, since formatting tools cannot change what the code does
Run it in an isolated sandbox and watch its file, network and process use
cards.answer: Run it in an isolated sandbox and watch its file, network and process use
cards.why: Sandboxing runs untrusted code in a contained environment, so you can observe what it really does without risking real systems or secrets. Trialling it on a production build server exposes signing keys and pipelines; popularity is not a security assessment; a formatter rewrites source, so it can change exactly what the code does.

cards.q: 05:05 · Dev pipeline. The mobile team is adding an endpoint, GET /orders/{id}, for the courier app. Their design covers login but not what happens if a courier changes the ID in the request. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Make order IDs long random strings so that they are harder to guess
Require a server-side check that the order is assigned to the caller
Leave the endpoint out of the public API documentation for this release
Rely on the app's login, since only couriers can install the courier app
cards.answer: Require a server-side check that the order is assigned to the caller
cards.why: Every API endpoint must authorise access to each object, not just authenticate the caller; without that, changing the ID reads other customers' orders (broken object-level authorization, top of the OWASP API list). Random IDs slow guessing but leaked IDs still work; undocumented endpoints are found by watching traffic; login proves who called, not what they may read.

cards.q: 00:55 · Dev pipeline. Code review finds the parcel-tracking search building its SQL by joining the user's search text into the query string. The author has added a filter that strips quote marks. Which fix do you approve?
options: Extend the filter to strip semicolons, dashes and SQL keywords as well
Rewrite the query with bound parameters so input is never parsed as SQL
Put a web application firewall in front and keep the query as written
HTML-encode the search text before it is placed into the query string
cards.answer: Rewrite the query with bound parameters so input is never parsed as SQL
cards.why: Parameterized queries keep code and data apart: the database treats input strictly as a value, which defeats SQL injection at its root. Deny-list filters are bypassed with encodings and dialect tricks; a WAF is a useful extra layer but leaves the flaw in the code; HTML encoding protects browsers, not SQL parsers.

cards.q: 06:45 · Dev pipeline. Tessaly is starting a new payments-routing engine: requirements are unclear, the risk is high, and the board wants risk reviewed before each round of building. The PM asks which development method security should back. What do you recommend?
options: Back waterfall, since fixing requirements up front makes audits simpler
Back code-and-fix, so the team can respond to each risk as it emerges
Back whichever method the routing library's vendor happens to recommend
Back the spiral model, which runs a risk analysis at the start of each loop
cards.answer: Back the spiral model, which runs a risk analysis at the start of each loop
cards.why: The spiral model is risk-driven: each loop starts by identifying and resolving the biggest risks before prototyping and building, which suits high-risk work with unclear requirements. Waterfall assumes requirements nobody knows yet; code-and-fix has no planned risk review at all; a vendor's preference is not a decision based on Tessaly's risk.

cards.q: 23:05 · Dev pipeline. A new parser reads customs manifests uploaded by thousands of freight agents. Its unit tests pass with the twelve sample files the team wrote. Before release, what testing do you add?
options: Fuzz the parser with large volumes of malformed and random input files
Add twelve more hand-written sample files to the existing unit tests
Ask three freight agents to upload real manifests during a pilot week
Review the parser's documentation to confirm the format is followed
cards.answer: Fuzz the parser with large volumes of malformed and random input files
cards.why: Fuzz testing throws huge volumes of unexpected, malformed input at a program to expose crashes, hangs and memory errors that hand-picked samples never trigger, which is the real risk for a parser facing untrusted uploads. More hand-written samples still test only what the team imagined; a pilot sends friendly input; documentation review executes nothing.

cards.q: 01:35 · Dev pipeline. The warehouse tablets pull app updates from an internal file share. Anyone with write access to the share could swap the installer, and the tablets would install it silently. What do you require?
options: Rename the share to something obscure and remove it from drive maps
Publish a checksum on the same share next to each new installer file
Sign releases in the pipeline and have tablets verify the signature
Ask warehouse staff to report any update that looks unusual to them
cards.answer: Sign releases in the pipeline and have tablets verify the signature
cards.why: Code signing binds each release to Tessaly's key, and verification on the device rejects anything altered or unsigned, whoever can write to the share. Renaming is obscurity; a checksum on the same share is swapped along with the installer; silent installs give staff nothing to notice.

cards.q: 04:20 · Dev pipeline. Reviewing the refund service, you find many 'catch (Exception e) {}' blocks that swallow every error and carry on. The author says they stop the service from crashing. What goes in your review?
options: Keep the empty blocks, since a running service beats a crashed one
Remove every try/catch block and let the runtime report each error
Catch specific exceptions, handle each one and roll back on failure
Replace the empty blocks with a full stack-trace print to the console
cards.answer: Catch specific exceptions, handle each one and roll back on failure
cards.why: Sound exception handling catches the errors you expect, deals with each deliberately and leaves no half-finished transaction, while unexpected ones stop the operation safely. Swallowing everything hides failures and can leave refunds half-applied; removing handling crashes users and may leak internals; console stack traces go unmonitored and risk leaking detail.

cards.q: 02:35 · Dev pipeline. A kickoff invite arrives for a new customer-identity portal. No code exists yet; the project charter lists features and budget but says nothing about the data the portal will hold. What do you bring to the kickoff?
options: Classify the data and write security requirements into the charter
Offer to run a penetration test once the portal reaches its beta
Decline the invite until there is a design document worth reviewing
Send the team the corporate password policy and ask them to follow it
cards.answer: Classify the data and write security requirements into the charter
cards.why: Initiation is where security is cheapest: establishing data sensitivity and writing security requirements into the charter shapes budget, design and tests from day one. A beta pen test finds requirement gaps when they are costly to fix; waiting for a design means it is built without requirements; a password policy covers one control, not the portal's needs.

cards.q: 06:05 · Dev pipeline. The authentication module's test suite passes and the team wants that as release evidence. The coverage report shows the tests execute only 30% of the module, missing the lockout and reset paths. What do you require?
options: Accept the passing suite, since every test that exists is green
Delete the untested lockout and reset code to lift the coverage figure
Release now and schedule the extra tests into next quarter's sprints
Extend tests to the lockout and reset paths before release sign-off
cards.answer: Extend tests to the lockout and reset paths before release sign-off
cards.why: Code coverage analysis shows how much code the tests actually exercise; a green suite that never runs the lockout and reset paths proves nothing about them, and those paths are prime attack surface. Passing tests are not evidence for untested code; deleting security features games the metric; deferring ships unverified authentication.

cards.q: 00:25 · Dev pipeline. A developer asks for standing admin access to production so he can debug the route planner faster. He already holds admin in the dev and test environments. Your move?
options: Grant it, since he already holds admin rights in both dev and test
Deny standing access; offer logged, time-limited access through change
Let him copy production data into dev so he can debug the issue there
Share the ops team's admin login with him for the duration of the fix
cards.answer: Deny standing access; offer logged, time-limited access through change
cards.why: Separating development, test and production environments, and the people working in each, stops untested changes and unaccountable access reaching production; genuine needs are met with approved, time-bound, logged access. Rights in dev do not justify production; copying live data into dev spreads it to weaker controls; a shared login destroys accountability.

cards.q: 03:15 · Dev pipeline. The legacy label-printer driver is written in assembly, and a new feature needs a string parser added to it. The author proposes another 400 lines of assembly. Which approach do you approve?
options: Approve the 400 lines of assembly so the driver stays in one language
Build the parser in a memory-safe language and call it from the driver
Approve the assembly once the author adds a long explanatory comment block
Copy an assembly parser from an online forum to save the author's time
cards.answer: Build the parser in a memory-safe language and call it from the driver
cards.why: Assembly offers no bounds checks or type safety, so a new string parser there invites buffer overflows; secure coding guidance is to put new input-handling logic in a memory-safe language and keep the low-level surface small. One-language consistency is not a security argument; comments do not prevent overflows; forum code adds unknown provenance to the riskiest part.

cards.q: 05:35 · Dev pipeline. The new customer portal passed static analysis, but nobody has tested how it behaves while running, with real sessions, cookies and headers. Staging is ready. What do you schedule?
options: Run the same static analysis again with a stricter rule set on
Scan the portal in production at peak hours to see real traffic
Skip further testing, since static analysis read all of the code
Run an authenticated dynamic scan against the portal in staging
cards.answer: Run an authenticated dynamic scan against the portal in staging
cards.why: Dynamic application security testing exercises the running application from outside, finding session, header, configuration and runtime flaws static analysis cannot see; authenticating the scan reaches pages behind login. Rerunning SAST repeats the same blind spot; scanning production at peak risks outages and data changes; reading code is not testing its runtime behaviour.

cards.q: 23:10 · Dev pipeline. The delivery-notes feature shows text that couriers type to customers on a public tracking page. The code inserts the notes into the HTML exactly as they arrive. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Encode the notes for the HTML context each time they are rendered
Limit the notes field to 200 characters so that scripts cannot fit
Trust the notes, since only Tessaly's own couriers are able to write them
Scan stored notes weekly and delete any that contain script tags
cards.answer: Encode the notes for the HTML context each time they are rendered
cards.why: Context-aware output encoding makes the browser treat user text as text, not markup, which prevents stored cross-site scripting whatever slipped past input checks. Short payloads still fit in 200 characters; courier accounts can be phished or misused; a weekly scan leaves days of exposure and misses scripts written without script tags.

cards.q: 04:50 · Dev pipeline. The new endpoint agent has passed testing, and the security assessment lists two medium risks with no fix before launch. The project manager asks you to sign off go-live. Your move?
options: Sign off yourself, since testing is complete and the risks are medium
Block the launch until both medium risks are fully remediated
Send the assessment to the system's business owner to accept the risk
Launch it quietly and add the two risks to next year's audit plan
cards.answer: Send the assessment to the system's business owner to accept the risk
cards.why: Certification is the technical assessment; accreditation is management's formal decision to operate the system and accept its residual risk, and that authority sits with the accountable owner, not the analyst. Signing yourself exceeds your authority; blocking outright substitutes your risk appetite for the business's; launching quietly hides risk from the people accountable for it.

cards.q: 01:05 · Dev pipeline. Procurement is about to sign with a five-person startup for customs-declaration software Tessaly will depend on for years. The source code stays with the vendor. What do you add before signing?
options: Ask for a discount to offset the risk that the startup might fold
Require the startup to hand Tessaly all of its source code on day one
Add a source code escrow clause with release if the vendor fails
Sign now and look for another supplier if problems start to appear
cards.answer: Add a source code escrow clause with release if the vendor fails
cards.why: Source code escrow lodges the code with a neutral third party and releases it to Tessaly if the vendor goes under or abandons the product, protecting continuity without taking the vendor's IP. A discount does not keep the software running; outright source transfer is rarely agreed; signing with no plan leaves a critical dependency without an exit.

cards.q: 02:25 · Dev pipeline. The QA lead wants a copy of last month's production card-payment records to load-test the new settlement engine, because 'synthetic data is never realistic'. Your move?
options: Supply masked or synthetic data matching production's shape and volume
Copy the production records into QA, since the test is purely internal
Copy production data but restrict the QA environment to the QA lead
Refuse load testing until the settlement engine is live in production
cards.answer: Supply masked or synthetic data matching production's shape and volume
cards.why: Test environments rarely carry production controls, so live cardholder data there multiplies exposure and breaks data-protection duties; masked or synthetic data with realistic distributions and volume gives valid results. Internal is not the same as safe; restricting access still puts real card data in a weaker environment; refusing tests pushes performance risk into production.

cards.q: 06:20 · Dev pipeline. Review of the merchant-portal login shows the session ID given to an anonymous visitor is kept unchanged after sign-in, and the cookie lacks the Secure and HttpOnly flags. Which fix do you approve?
options: Keep the session ID but cut the cookie's lifetime to one hour
Base64-encode the session ID before placing it in the cookie
Add a CAPTCHA to the login page so that bots cannot open sessions
Issue a new session ID at login and set Secure and HttpOnly flags
cards.answer: Issue a new session ID at login and set Secure and HttpOnly flags
cards.why: Regenerating the session identifier at authentication prevents session fixation, where an attacker plants a known ID before login; Secure and HttpOnly keep the cookie off plain HTTP and away from scripts. A shorter lifetime still lets a fixed ID be hijacked; base64 is encoding, not protection; a CAPTCHA does nothing for the session itself.

cards.q: 03:40 · Dev pipeline. Security scans of the endpoint agent run once a month over a big batch of changes, so findings arrive weeks late and releases pile up waiting for them. The release manager asks you for a fix. What do you propose?
options: Move the monthly scan to weekly and keep batching the changes up for it
Run fast scans on each small change in the pipeline as it moves to release
Add a second security reviewer to clear each monthly batch more quickly
Drop the scans from the release path and run them after each deployment
cards.answer: Run fast scans on each small change in the pipeline as it moves to release
cards.why: The DevOps principle of flow favours small batches moving steadily from commit to release; fast automated checks on each change remove the security queue instead of feeding it. Weekly batches only shrink the pile; more reviewers speed up a bottleneck without removing it; scanning after deployment ships the very flaws the scan exists to catch.

cards.q: 00:35 · Dev pipeline. The payments API and the ledger service each pass their own tests, but nobody has tested what the ledger does when the API sends it a malformed or duplicated message. Release is Friday. What do you add?
options: Rely on the two passing suites, since each side is already fully tested
Add interface tests of the API-to-ledger messages, including bad cases
Ask each team to add more unit tests inside its own service only
Monitor the ledger after release and fix any mismatches that appear
cards.answer: Add interface tests of the API-to-ledger messages, including bad cases
cards.why: Interface testing checks the exchanges between components, including malformed, duplicated and out-of-order messages, which is where two individually correct systems fail together. Separate passing suites never exercise the seam; more unit tests stay on either side of it; watching production after release turns the live ledger into the test environment.

cards.q: 05:50 · Dev pipeline. The courier sign-in page shows a full database error, with table names and server paths, when a login fails oddly. The developer wants to keep it because it speeds up support calls. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Keep the detailed errors, since couriers are trusted Tessaly staff
Move the detail into an HTML comment so users do not see it on the page
Remove every error message so the page simply reloads when sign-in fails
Show a generic message with a reference ID and log the detail server-side
cards.answer: Show a generic message with a reference ID and log the detail server-side
cards.why: Secure error handling gives users a generic message and a correlation ID while full detail goes to protected server logs, so support can still trace the fault without handing attackers schema and path details. Staff accounts get phished; an HTML comment is visible in page source; silent reloads confuse users and help nobody diagnose anything.

cards.q: 23:45 · Dev pipeline. The CISO wants to know whether Tessaly's secure development practices are improving year on year, and asks you for a baseline this month. What do you propose?
options: Score the practices against OWASP SAMM and set target levels per area
Use the count of findings in last year's pen test report as the baseline
Survey developers on how secure they feel their own code is today
Buy a new code scanner and use its dashboard score as the measure
cards.answer: Score the practices against OWASP SAMM and set target levels per area
cards.why: A software assurance maturity model such as OWASP SAMM measures the practices themselves across governance, design, implementation, verification and operations, giving a repeatable baseline and targets to track. One pen test's count reflects its scope and timing more than practice; self-rating is opinion; a scanner score measures one activity through one tool's rules.

cards.q: 02:55 · Dev pipeline. The new laptop-encryption agent enters user acceptance testing tomorrow. The UAT plan checks install time and battery drain but none of the security requirements the project agreed. What do you do?
options: Let UAT go ahead as planned, since the vendor has tested security itself
Replace UAT with a vulnerability scan of one laptop running the agent
Add a test for each agreed security requirement to the acceptance plan
Sign off security now and test the requirements after the rollout
cards.answer: Add a test for each agreed security requirement to the acceptance plan
cards.why: Acceptance testing is where the business verifies the system meets its requirements, and security requirements belong in that traceability: each gets a test and pass criteria before rollout. The vendor's testing is not Tessaly's acceptance; one scan finds known flaws, not whether encryption and recovery requirements are met; testing after rollout accepts unverified controls.

cards.q: 04:30 · Dev pipeline. Testing shows that two withdrawal requests sent milliseconds apart from the same driver wallet can both pass the balance check and both pay out. Which fix goes into the payments code?
options: Add a one-second delay between withdrawals from the same wallet
Run a nightly reconciliation job that claws back any double payout
Lock the balance row in one transaction for the check and the debit
Grey out the withdraw button for a few seconds after it is pressed
cards.answer: Lock the balance row in one transaction for the check and the debit
cards.why: This is a race condition, time of check to time of use. Concurrency control, doing the check and the debit atomically in one locked transaction, makes the second request see the reduced balance. A delay narrows the window without closing it; reconciliation recovers losses after the fact; greying out a button stops honest double-taps, not scripted requests.

cards.q: 01:15 · Dev pipeline. A test of the payroll portal shows that a hidden form on any outside website can change a logged-in employee's bank details, because the portal accepts the request on the session cookie alone. What fix do you require before retest?
options: Require an anti-CSRF token on state changes and set SameSite cookies
Move the bank-details change from POST requests over to GET requests
Tell staff not to browse other websites while logged in to payroll
Encrypt the bank-details column in the database at rest with AES-256
cards.answer: Require an anti-CSRF token on state changes and set SameSite cookies
cards.why: Cross-site request forgery works because the browser attaches the session cookie automatically; a per-request anti-CSRF token the attacker cannot read, plus SameSite cookies, lets the portal reject forged requests. Switching to GET makes forgery easier; advice to staff is not a control; encryption at rest protects stored data, not the request that changes it.

cards.q: 03:20 · Dev pipeline. The test plan for the new driver-tipping feature covers every happy path: the customer tips, the driver sees it, payout adds it. It has no cases for what an abusive user might try. What do you add?
options: Add more happy-path cases for every supported currency and device type
Rely on the payment provider's fraud engine to catch any abusive tips
Launch it and let customer complaints show where abuse is happening
Write misuse cases, such as negative tips or tipping with stolen cards
cards.answer: Write misuse cases, such as negative tips or tipping with stolen cards
cards.why: Misuse case testing models what an attacker or abuser would do, such as negative amounts, replayed tips or stolen cards, and checks the feature refuses it. More happy paths still test only intended use; the provider sees card fraud but not negative-tip logic inside Tessaly; letting complaints find abuse turns customers into the test team.

cards.q: 05:25 · Dev pipeline. The handheld scanners parse a barcode-label format from a supplier that will not share its specification. You have thousands of real label files from the dock. How do you fuzz the parser?
options: Wait for the spec, then build a generator that models the label format
Mutate the real label files at random and feed the variants to the parser
Feed the parser only the real label files, since they are known valid
Skip fuzzing, since results without a spec cannot be interpreted at all
cards.answer: Mutate the real label files at random and feed the variants to the parser
cards.why: Mutation, or dumb, fuzzing needs no specification: it flips bits and alters fields in real samples, so it suits undocumented formats and finds crashes quickly. Generation-based fuzzing needs the spec you may never get; valid files test only normal input; crashes and hangs are meaningful whether or not the format is documented.

cards.q: 00:05 · Dev pipeline. The mobile-wallet team merges about forty pull requests a day, and security findings surface only in the annual pen test. You want flaws caught while the developer still remembers the code. What do you put in the pipeline?
options: Move the annual pen test to twice a year and leave the pipeline as is
Run static source-code analysis on every pull request before merge
Scan the production app weekly with a network vulnerability scanner
Ask reviewers to check security as well as style on each pull request
cards.answer: Run static source-code analysis on every pull request before merge
cards.why: Static application security testing reads source without running it, so it can gate each pull request and flag injection, crypto misuse and similar flaws minutes after they are written. Twice-yearly pen tests still find them months later; network scanners do not examine application code; unguided reviewer checks are inconsistent at forty merges a day.

cards.q: 06:55 · Dev pipeline. The vendor of the fleet-telemetry app emails that all four critical findings from your pen test are 'fixed in v2.3' and asks you to close them. What do you do before closing anything?
options: Close all four findings, since the vendor confirmed them in writing
Ask the vendor for release notes listing the fixes, then close them
Keep all four open until next year's pen test covers them again
Retest each finding against v2.3 and close only the verified ones
cards.answer: Retest each finding against v2.3 and close only the verified ones
cards.why: A fix counts only once verified: retesting each finding against the new version is the evidence that closes it, and anything still exploitable stays open. A vendor email or release note is a claim, not proof; waiting a year leaves genuinely fixed items marked open and hides the true risk picture.

cards.q: 02:45 · Dev pipeline. A commercial dock-scheduling package arrives ready to install, with a default admin account, sample data and every optional module switched on. Go-live is next week. What goes in the deployment ticket?
options: Harden it first: change defaults, remove samples, disable unused modules
Install it as shipped, since the vendor has tested its default settings
Install it as shipped and ask the vendor to harden it at the next upgrade
Put it behind the firewall and leave the default settings in place
cards.answer: Harden it first: change defaults, remove samples, disable unused modules
cards.why: Commercial software ships for easy installation, not security, so before go-live Tessaly hardens it to a secure baseline: change default credentials, remove sample content and disable unneeded features to shrink the attack surface. Vendor defaults are not your risk decision; deferring hardening leaves defaults live; a firewall does not fix a known default admin password.

cards.q: 04:10 · Dev pipeline. The endpoint team is designing a self-update feature for the laptop agent that will run as SYSTEM and fetch packages from the internet. Coding starts Monday. What do you do this week?
options: Wait for the finished code, then run a penetration test against it
Approve the design, since the agent already runs with SYSTEM rights
Threat-model the update design with the team and add controls to it
Ask the team to add antivirus scanning of each downloaded package
cards.answer: Threat-model the update design with the team and add controls to it
cards.why: Threat modeling at design time, walking data flows and trust boundaries with a method such as STRIDE, surfaces risks like spoofed update servers and tampered packages while design changes are cheap, leading to controls such as signed packages. A pen test after coding finds design flaws at the costliest point; high privilege demands more scrutiny, not less; antivirus misses tailored payloads.

cards.q: 23:25 · Dev pipeline. A rapid prototype of a driver-payments dashboard impressed the executives, and the sponsor now wants the prototype itself live next week. It uses hard-coded test accounts and has no input checks. Your move?
options: Let it go live next week and harden it once drivers are using it
Remove the hard-coded accounts, then approve it for next week
Rebuild it through the full SDLC with security requirements first
Keep it live but only share its URL with drivers who need it
cards.answer: Rebuild it through the full SDLC with security requirements first
cards.why: Rapid-development prototypes prove an idea; they skip requirements, design review and testing, so they must be rebuilt or brought through the full SDLC before handling real payments data. Hardening after launch exposes real drivers now; removing one known flaw leaves the unknown ones; an unshared URL is obscurity, not access control.

cards.q: 01:55 · Dev pipeline. The team is moving the build system to a managed cloud CI service. The vendor's SOC 2 report is clean, and the project plan assumes the vendor now 'handles security'. What do you add to the plan?
options: Map the shared-responsibility split and assign Tessaly's controls to owners
Accept the plan as written, since the SOC 2 report covers the whole service
Ask the vendor to take over management of Tessaly's pipeline secrets
Keep the old build system running alongside so security is not reduced
cards.answer: Map the shared-responsibility split and assign Tessaly's controls to owners
cards.why: In a managed service the provider secures its platform, but Tessaly still owns its access rights, secrets, pipeline configuration and data; mapping the shared-responsibility model assigns those controls. A SOC 2 report covers the vendor's controls and lists complementary user controls you must run; handing over secrets widens trust; a parallel system doubles the attack surface.

cards.q: 23:40 · Governance desk. After-action review: a sole-trader merchant in the EU asked Tessaly Pay for the personal data she had supplied, and six weeks later got a stack of scanned PDFs. Her complaint is now with the regulator. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Keep the PDF exports, but route every future request through a legal review first
Build a self-service export in a structured, machine-readable format within a month
