Delete each merchant's records right after export so no duplicate copy stays behind
Add a contract clause where merchants waive export requests in return for lower fees
cards.answer: Build a self-service export in a structured, machine-readable format within a month
cards.why: The GDPR right to data portability entitles a person to the data they provided in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable form, normally within one month. A self-service export makes that the default. A contract cannot waive a statutory right, PDFs still fail the format test however carefully reviewed, and deletion is a different right (erasure) that she never invoked.

cards.q: 06:15 · Governance desk. After-action review: last week a USB stick found in a dock-office PC was passed between four people before anyone wrote it down, and counsel now doubts it will stand up. What becomes the standing rule?
options: Image the stick and throw the original away, since the copy is what the analysts examine later
Photograph physical items and hand them back to their owner so work is not disrupted
Let whoever finds an item keep hold of it until the investigator arrives on site
Bag, tag and log physical items at seizure, with a signed custody entry for each handover
cards.answer: Bag, tag and log physical items at seizure, with a signed custody entry for each handover
cards.why: The stick itself is real evidence: a physical object presented in its own right, so its value depends on identification and an unbroken chain of custody from seizure onward. Imaging supports analysis but never replaces the original, and discarding it loses the best evidence. Returning items or leaving them with the finder breaks custody and invites an authenticity challenge.

cards.q: 02:05 · Governance desk. HR says a payments engineer was dismissed at 18:00 for misconduct, yet his VPN session into the settlement cluster opened at 01:50 and is still live. His manager asks you to leave it until the morning exit meeting. Your move?
options: Reset his password but leave the live session up so that he is not tipped off early
Kill the session, disable his accounts now, and tell HR and his manager what you did
Wait for the morning exit meeting as asked, since HR owns every step of a termination
Watch the session quietly until morning so you capture a full record of his actions
cards.answer: Kill the session, disable his accounts now, and tell HR and his manager what you did
cards.why: Access removal must coincide with termination; a dismissed insider with a live session on the settlement cluster is an active threat. Cut the session and disable the accounts, keeping the logs, then inform HR. Waiting or watching lets harm happen for the sake of a nicer record, and a password reset does not end a session that is already authenticated.

cards.q: 00:35 · Governance desk. A lure titled 'Driver roster changes' is landing in depot inboxes. Three drivers have already typed in their credentials and more night-shift staff are opening it. Awareness training is booked for next quarter. What do you do first?
options: Discipline the three drivers so that the rest of the depot takes the lure seriously
Purge the lure, reset the three drivers' logins, and alert staff how to report it
Bring the quarterly awareness course forward and enrol every depot user tonight
Email the full phishing course to all staff and require it to be finished by 07:00
cards.answer: Purge the lure, reset the three drivers' logins, and alert staff how to report it
cards.why: Contain first: pull the message and kill the stolen credentials, then give staff a short, just-in-time alert with a clear reporting path so they become sensors for the rest of the wave. A course is education on a slow cadence and will not stop tonight's clicks. Punishing the clickers teaches people to hide mistakes, which kills the reporting you need.

cards.q: 03:20 · Governance desk. The risk register shows the CFO accepted the risk of an unsupported invoicing server last year, citing low exposure. Tonight a public exploit for it was released and outside scanning has begun. The acceptance reads 'valid until March'. Your move?
options: Record the risk as transferred, because the vendor originally sold Tessaly the server
Put a temporary block in front of it and ask the CFO to re-decide the accepted risk
Decommission the server tonight on your own authority, since it is out of support
Leave the server as it is, because the CFO's signed acceptance runs until March
cards.answer: Put a temporary block in front of it and ask the CFO to re-decide the accepted risk
cards.why: A risk acceptance holds only for the conditions that were assessed. A public exploit and active scanning change the likelihood, so the risk owner must decide again, while an interim control keeps exposure inside tolerance. Hiding behind the old signature ignores changed risk, decommissioning on your own authority oversteps the owner, and an unsupported product transfers nothing to its vendor.

cards.q: 04:40 · Governance desk. Mid-incident, a responder refuses to rotate a compromised API key because the 'Key Handling Guideline' suggests rotating only in change windows, and the next one is Friday. The key is being used from an unknown address. Your move?
options: Order the rotation now; the guideline is advice and the incident procedure governs
Raise an exception request with the policy committee and rotate once it is approved
Rewrite the guideline into a mandatory standard tonight so the responder has a rule
Wait for Friday's window, since the architecture board approved the guideline
cards.answer: Order the rotation now; the guideline is advice and the incident procedure governs
cards.why: A guideline is a recommended, non-mandatory practice: it informs judgement and yields to the incident response procedure and emergency change path when a key is being abused. Treating advice as a hard rule leaves the key live for days. Exception requests exist for departing from mandatory policy, not advice, and rewriting documents mid-incident does nothing to stop the attacker.

cards.q: 01:25 · Governance desk. A storage failure has taken down the carrier-booking portal, the internal wiki and the card-settlement batch at once. The ops lead wants the portal back first because customers are complaining loudly. What order do you give?
options: Restore all three in parallel with equal staff so that no business unit feels deprioritised
Restore the carrier-booking portal first, because customer complaints are the loudest
Restore the internal wiki first so responders can reach the recovery runbooks quickly
Restore in the BIA's order, starting with whichever process hits its downtime limit first
cards.answer: Restore in the BIA's order, starting with whichever process hits its downtime limit first
cards.why: The business impact analysis already set maximum tolerable downtimes and recovery priorities; the settlement batch, with payment cut-offs behind it, likely has the tightest one. Follow the plan rather than the noise. Loud complaints are not criticality, runbooks should be reachable offline rather than drive the order, and an equal split slows the most critical recovery.

cards.q: 05:10 · Governance desk. Someone is copying customer card data from the payments reporting share to a personal cloud account right now, and the upload volume is climbing. Which control do you reach for?
options: Email every member of staff a reminder that personal cloud storage is forbidden
Post a security guard at the reporting team's desks until investigators arrive
Add a card-data clause to next year's contracts and have all staff sign it again
Enforce a DLP block on uploads from that share and suspend the account doing it
cards.answer: Enforce a DLP block on uploads from that share and suspend the account doing it
cards.why: A technical (logical) control acts inside the system itself, so a DLP block and account suspension stop the exfiltration within minutes. The alternatives are the wrong type for a live leak: reminders and contract clauses are administrative controls that deter slowly, and a guard is a physical control that cannot stop a network upload in progress.

cards.q: 02:50 · Governance desk. The vendor of Tessaly's route-planning agent has just posted that its signed update from yesterday carried a backdoor. The agent auto-updated on 140 depot machines. What do you do first?
options: Tell the vendor's account manager Tessaly is withholding payment until it is fixed
Uninstall the agent everywhere and move to a rival planner before dispatch opens
Wait for the vendor's clean update, since the code signature proves it is genuine
Isolate hosts on the tainted build, block its callbacks, and freeze vendor updates
cards.answer: Isolate hosts on the tainted build, block its callbacks, and freeze vendor updates
cards.why: This is a software supply chain compromise: a valid signature proves where the code came from, not that it is safe. Contain the affected hosts and stop further pushes through the abused channel, then work the supplier's incident obligations. Switching vendors overnight swaps one unassessed supplier for another, waiting trusts the compromised channel, and withholding payment contains nothing.

cards.q: 03:45 · Governance desk. Containing an intrusion properly means taking Tessaly Pay offline for up to six hours, halting merchant settlements in three countries. The incident commander can isolate hosts but not whole business services. Who makes the call?
options: Take Tessaly Pay offline yourself, since security outranks revenue at night
Keep Tessaly Pay online until the board meets on Thursday to review events
Wake the crisis committee's executive on call to take the business decision
Let the payments team lead decide, because they know the platform the best
cards.answer: Wake the crisis committee's executive on call to take the business decision
cards.why: Trading enterprise revenue against risk is a governance decision reserved for the executive committee; the incident plan's escalation path should name the executive who holds it on call. Security informs the decision with the containment options and impact. Shutting the service yourself exceeds delegated authority, a team lead has no enterprise mandate, and waiting for the board leaves the intruder active.

cards.q: 00:20 · Governance desk. Attackers are abusing the parcel-tracking API's unauthenticated search to scrape customer addresses. Last spring's threat model flagged exactly this and specified rate limits and authentication, but neither was ever shipped. Your move?
options: Log the finding as proof the model was accurate and schedule a fix next sprint
Expand the threat model with more threats before anyone touches the live API
Re-run the full threat model tonight to confirm the threat still ranks the highest
Deploy the specified rate limit and auth to production under an emergency change
cards.answer: Deploy the specified rate limit and auth to production under an emergency change
cards.why: Threat modelling identifies and ranks threats and specifies mitigations, but nothing is protected until those security controls are deployed in production. The analysis is done; the gap is implementation, so an emergency change closes it now. Re-running or expanding the model is analysis while data leaks, and a next-sprint fix accepts ongoing harm nobody has approved.

cards.q: 04:05 · Governance desk. A colleague has traced the botnet hammering Tessaly Pay to a home server and wants to log into it with a leaked password to wipe the attack tools. 'It's self-defence,' he says. Your move?
options: Approve it, since the botnet is harming customers and every minute matters now
Let him do it from off the corporate network so Tessaly cannot be held liable
Approve the login, but only to collect evidence, without deleting anything on it
Refuse, block the traffic, and report the source to its host provider and police
cards.answer: Refuse, block the traffic, and report the source to its host provider and police
cards.why: Hacking back is unauthorised access: illegal, and against the ISC2 Code's canon to act honourably, justly, responsibly and legally. The server may belong to an innocent, compromised owner. Defend your own perimeter and report to parties with authority. Logging in 'just for evidence' is still unauthorised access, and doing it off the corporate network adds deceit to the offence.

cards.q: 06:30 · Governance desk. Tessaly Group's shares trade in New York, and tonight's breach of the settlement ledger may prove material. The CFO asks you to keep it out of every filing until the quarterly report in two months. Your move?
options: Hold all disclosure until the quarterly report, exactly as the CFO has asked of you
Brief the disclosure committee now so materiality is decided and filed on time
Tell the largest merchants privately so rumours cannot move the share price
Post a breach notice on the company website tonight before anyone is briefed
cards.answer: Brief the disclosure committee now so materiality is decided and filed on time
cards.why: Publicly traded companies in the US must disclose material cybersecurity incidents: SEC rules require a Form 8-K within four business days of deciding an incident is material, and executives answer for accurate reporting. Route it to the disclosure committee and legal. Sitting on it risks securities liability, an unreviewed website post pre-empts that process, and tipping selected merchants is selective disclosure.

cards.q: 01:40 · Governance desk. A former contractor is draining merchant payouts to mule accounts, and the CEO says Tessaly will press criminal charges. His Tessaly-issued laptop is still connected over VPN. What do you do first?
options: Warn the contractor that charges will follow unless the payouts stop tonight
Wipe the laptop remotely so the contractor can no longer reach Tessaly systems
Cut the VPN link, image the laptop forensically, and bring in the police early
Log in to the laptop remotely and browse it to find the list of mule accounts
cards.answer: Cut the VPN link, image the laptop forensically, and bring in the police early
cards.why: A criminal court needs proof beyond reasonable doubt, built on evidence that survives admissibility challenges. Contain the access, collect forensically sound images under chain of custody, and involve law enforcement, who carry the prosecution. Browsing the live machine alters the evidence, a remote wipe destroys it, and warning the suspect invites evidence destruction and flight.

cards.q: 23:55 · Governance desk. With the payouts clerk on her first two-week leave in three years, her stand-in has found refunds to one card number every Tuesday. The clerk still has remote access and has just logged in from home. Your move?
options: Suspend her access, preserve the refund records, and hand the case to HR and legal
Cancel her leave and bring her back in so that she can clear the anomaly herself
Reverse every Tuesday refund now and let her come back to work as normal later
Phone the clerk tonight and ask her to explain the refunds before you do anything else
cards.answer: Suspend her access, preserve the refund records, and hand the case to HR and legal
cards.why: This is mandatory vacation doing its job: fraud that needs constant tending surfaces when someone else runs the process. Now remove her access, preserve the records and let HR and legal investigate. Calling her first tips off a suspect who is logged in right now; reversing refunds disturbs the trail; recalling her from leave hands the process straight back to the person under suspicion.

cards.q: 03:05 · Governance desk. The service desk has taken three calls tonight from a 'regional director' demanding MFA resets for staff 'stuck abroad'. One reset went through before a technician grew suspicious. The caller is on hold on line two. Your move?
options: Ask for his employee number and approve the resets if it matches HR records
Keep the caller talking while more accounts are reset, to trace where he is
End the call, reverse the reset, and brief the desk on call-back checks tonight
Grant the other resets, since turning down a director will cause a formal complaint
cards.answer: End the call, reverse the reset, and brief the desk on call-back checks tonight
cards.why: This is vishing: social engineering by voice, using authority and urgency. Identity must be verified through an independently sourced channel, such as calling back the number on file, never with details a caller can research. Reverse the completed reset and review that account, then brief the desk. Employee numbers leak easily, and bowing to rank is exactly what the attacker is exploiting.

cards.q: 05:45 · Governance desk. The CEO texts the CISO: 'You own security, so you own this. Sign the risk acceptance for keeping the exposed warehouse cameras online until Monday.' The CISO forwards it to you to draft. Your move?
options: Skip the paperwork and pull the cameras offline, since nobody wants to sign it
Draft it for your own signature as the analyst who knows the cameras best
Draft it for the CISO to sign, since the CEO has handed over the decision
Draft it for the CEO's own signature, stating the exposure and interim controls
cards.answer: Draft it for the CEO's own signature, stating the exposure and interim controls
cards.why: Senior management holds ultimate responsibility for risk decisions; security advises, it does not own business risk. An acceptance must be signed by someone with authority over the business consequence, with the exposure and interim controls spelled out. A text message is not a formal delegation, an analyst has no authority to accept, and acting unilaterally sidesteps the owner entirely.

cards.q: 02:30 · Governance desk. Two responders are isolating infected warehouse scanners in different ways: one is powering them off and losing volatile memory, the other is pulling network cables. The runbook has a step-by-step scanner containment section. What do you tell them?
options: Stop work until the policy committee rewrites the policy to be much clearer
Power everything off, as one consistent method matters more than the steps
Follow the runbook's containment steps in order and log each step as you go
Keep your own methods, since both approaches stop the scanners calling out
cards.answer: Follow the runbook's containment steps in order and log each step as you go
cards.why: A procedure is the mandatory step-by-step instruction that makes results repeatable and evidence-safe, which is exactly what the runbook section is for. Improvised methods destroy volatile memory and make the containment record inconsistent. Waiting for a policy rewrite confuses the policy, which says what must happen, with the procedure, which says how.

cards.q: 23:15 · Governance desk. Your ticket: kick off Tessaly's first business continuity plan. The IT director offers to write it alone over two weeks and sign it off himself to keep things quick. What is your first step?
options: Buy BCP software so that the plan template gets filled in automatically
Let the IT director write and approve it, since IT runs most of the business systems
Get senior management to sponsor the plan, approve its scope, and name a team
Start with the backup schedule, since data recovery is most of continuity
cards.answer: Get senior management to sponsor the plan, approve its scope, and name a team
cards.why: Business continuity planning starts with senior management: they sponsor it, commit resources, approve scope and ultimately own the plan, and a cross-functional team does the work. Continuity covers business processes, not just IT, so an IT-authored, self-approved plan lacks both breadth and authority. Software does not create commitment, and backups are a recovery detail, not the plan.

cards.q: 00:50 · Governance desk. You are threat modelling the new merchant portal with STRIDE. A design note shows any logged-in merchant can call the 'set_role' endpoint, which the interface simply hides from non-admins. What do you record and require?
options: Log an elevation-of-privilege threat and require server-side role checks
Log a denial-of-service threat and require rate limits on that endpoint
Accept the design, since hiding the button stops ordinary merchants
Log a spoofing threat and require merchants to use stronger passwords
cards.answer: Log an elevation-of-privilege threat and require server-side role checks
cards.why: An ordinary user reaching an admin function is STRIDE's elevation of privilege, and the mitigation is authorisation enforced on the server for every call. Hiding the button is security through obscurity; anyone can call the endpoint directly. The caller is already authenticated, so password rules miss the flaw, and rate limiting only slows the abuse down.

cards.q: 01:05 · Governance desk. A vendor is pitching a €90,000-a-year anti-fraud module for the loyalty-points system. Your analysis puts expected yearly loss from points fraud at €20,000, and the module would cut that by 80%. What do you recommend?
options: Buy the module and accept the leftover risk, since the vendor has offered a discount
Set the numbers aside and buy it anyway, because fraud always damages the brand
Decline the module and look for cheaper controls, as it costs more than it saves
Buy the module, because any control that cuts loss by 80% is worth having in place
cards.answer: Decline the module and look for cheaper controls, as it costs more than it saves
cards.why: Safeguard value is ALE before minus ALE after minus the control's annual cost: 20,000 − 4,000 − 90,000 leaves minus €74,000. A control that costs more than the loss it prevents is not cost-justified, so look for cheaper mitigation or have the owner accept the risk. Effectiveness alone is not a business case, and brand harm should be estimated, not assumed.

cards.q: 04:25 · Governance desk. HR asks you to look into a dispatcher suspected of browsing gambling sites on a depot PC during shifts. No law appears to be broken and nobody wants the police involved. How do you run it?
options: Run an internal policy inquiry: pull that PC's proxy logs, document, report to HR
Install a hidden keylogger on the PC and record everything he does for a full month
Hand the case to the police, as any investigation needs the criminal standard
Confront the dispatcher on shift tonight and make him open his browser history
cards.answer: Run an internal policy inquiry: pull that PC's proxy logs, document, report to HR
cards.why: This is an administrative investigation: an internal policy matter whose outcome is HR action, so a lower standard of proof applies and the scope stays proportionate to the acceptable use policy. Evidence is still gathered and documented properly. The police handle crimes, a shift-floor confrontation compromises the inquiry, and covert keylogging is disproportionate and may breach privacy law.

cards.q: 05:30 · Governance desk. Ticket: carriers upload nightly rate sheets that feed Tessaly's pricing engine, and last month one sheet was altered in transit without anyone noticing. Which control do you specify?
options: Encrypt the rate sheets at rest on the pricing server using a stronger AES key size
Restrict read access to the rate sheets inside Tessaly to the pricing team alone
Require carriers to sign each sheet and verify it before the pricing engine loads it
Add a second pricing server so that the engine stays up if a single sheet fails
cards.answer: Require carriers to sign each sheet and verify it before the pricing engine loads it
cards.why: The property that failed is integrity, along with proof of origin. A digital signature verified on arrival detects any alteration and binds the sheet to the carrier that sent it. Encryption at rest protects confidentiality after the sheet has arrived, a second server serves availability, and read restrictions are confidentiality again. Match the control to the property that broke.

cards.q: 23:30 · Governance desk. Ticket: Tessaly Pay is hiring a treasury operator who will approve high-value payouts. The hiring manager wants to skip the checks to fill the seat by Monday. What goes in the hiring requirement?
options: Obtain a signed NDA on day one, which removes the need for any screening
Screen the candidate only if they come from outside the company's home country
Complete role-appropriate background screening before any access is issued
Start the hire on Monday and finish screening whenever the agency replies
cards.answer: Complete role-appropriate background screening before any access is issued
cards.why: Pre-employment screening scaled to the role's sensitivity, such as references, identity, and criminal and credit checks for someone approving payouts, must be complete before access is granted; afterwards is too late. An NDA is a different control with a different purpose. Screening by nationality is discriminatory and says nothing about the risk the role carries.

cards.q: 02:10 · Governance desk. Ticket: finance wants a recovery time objective set for the customs-declaration service. Nobody has asked the customs team what a day offline would actually cost. What do you do before any number is set?
options: Set a four-hour RTO, since that is the usual industry figure for business services
Run a business impact analysis with the process owners to find tolerable downtime
Ask IT how fast they can restore it and record that speed as the service's RTO
Set the RTO to zero so the customs service can never be offline for any length
cards.answer: Run a business impact analysis with the process owners to find tolerable downtime
cards.why: An RTO comes out of the business impact analysis: impact over time gives the maximum tolerable downtime, and the RTO must sit inside it. Only the process owners know the fines, delays and contract penalties involved. An industry default ignores Tessaly's impacts, IT's current capability is an input to strategy rather than the requirement, and a zero RTO is rarely cost-justified.

cards.q: 06:05 · Governance desk. Ticket: a reorganisation proposal moves the CISO under the CIO, whose bonus is tied to delivery speed. You are asked to comment for the board pack. What do you recommend?
options: Approve the move, since security and IT already share infrastructure budgets
Approve the move, and ask the CIO to certify the security posture every quarter
Keep the CISO reporting outside IT, with direct board access, to avoid a conflict
Split the CISO role across the IT team so every engineer owns security equally
cards.answer: Keep the CISO reporting outside IT, with direct board access, to avoid a conflict
cards.why: Good governance needs independence: a security function reporting to the executive it must sometimes challenge creates a conflict of interest, and direct board access supports oversight. Shared budgets do not remove the conflict, and self-certification by the conflicted executive is weak assurance. Spreading the role across engineers removes the single point of accountability that governance depends on.

cards.q: 00:10 · Governance desk. Ticket: the awareness dashboard shows 98% course completion, yet reported-phish numbers are flat and click rates are rising. The HR director calls the programme a success. What do you change?
options: Measure behaviour: track report and click rates and tune content to the gaps
Double the length of the annual course so staff spend more time on the topic
Make the course harder to pass so completion drops to a more believable level
Keep the course as it is, since 98% completion shows the programme working
cards.answer: Measure behaviour: track report and click rates and tune content to the gaps
cards.why: An awareness programme is judged by the behaviour it changes, not the activity it logs. Report and click rates show whether people act differently, and the gaps they reveal tell you which content to rework. Completion is a vanity metric, a longer course adds seat time rather than skill, and a harder quiz changes the dashboard without changing anyone's behaviour.

cards.q: 03:35 · Governance desk. Ticket: the policy says 'systems must be hardened', but every depot sets up its scanners differently and audits keep failing. What do you draft?
options: Draft an optional guideline suggesting settings depots may choose to adopt
Draft a reminder email asking depot managers to take hardening more seriously
Draft a new high-level policy restating that systems must be hardened properly and fully
Draft a mandatory configuration standard stating the exact baseline for scanners
cards.answer: Draft a mandatory configuration standard stating the exact baseline for scanners
cards.why: Standards turn policy intent into specific, mandatory requirements, here a configuration baseline every scanner must meet, which also gives auditors something to test against. Restating the policy adds nothing enforceable. An optional guideline recreates the inconsistency that is failing audits, and a reminder email is not a control at all.

cards.q: 01:55 · Governance desk. Ticket: IT wants to move EU driver HR records to a cheaper cloud region in a country without an EU adequacy decision. The contract has no transfer clauses. What do you require before approval?
options: Require a statement from the provider that it obeys the local laws in that country
Require nothing extra, since encryption at rest makes the data's location legally irrelevant
Require a lawful transfer mechanism, such as standard contractual clauses plus an assessment
Require consent emailed to drivers, treating silence after a week as their agreement
cards.answer: Require a lawful transfer mechanism, such as standard contractual clauses plus an assessment
cards.why: GDPR restricts transfers of personal data outside the EEA. Without an adequacy decision you need an approved mechanism such as standard contractual clauses, backed by a transfer impact assessment. Encryption helps but is not a legal basis, the provider obeying local law may itself be the risk, and silence is never valid consent, which employees can rarely give freely anyway.

cards.q: 05:00 · Governance desk. You are scoring bids for Tessaly's new SIEM contract. One bidder is the startup your brother co-founded, and it is the strongest on paper. Nobody at Tessaly knows about the connection. Your move?
options: Disclose the relationship to procurement and step back from scoring that bidder
Mark the startup down slightly so nobody could accuse you of favouritism
Leave the panel quietly without giving procurement any reason for leaving
Keep scoring, since the startup is genuinely the strongest bid on its own merits
cards.answer: Disclose the relationship to procurement and step back from scoring that bidder
cards.why: The ISC2 Code asks you to act honourably and honestly, and an undisclosed conflict of interest undermines both, however fair your scoring. Disclosure lets the organisation manage it. Genuine merit does not cure the appearance of bias, marking the bid down is dishonest in the other direction, and a silent exit hides the conflict instead of surfacing it.

cards.q: 04:50 · Governance desk. Ticket: 60 new card-payment terminals for the depots arrived tonight in resealed boxes, via a courier not named on the supplier's shipping notice. Depot managers want them deployed by 07:00. Your move?
options: Deploy them tonight and run a vulnerability scan on each one within a month
Quarantine the shipment and verify serials and seals with the supplier first
Deploy them tonight, since they are listed in the approved supplier's catalogue
Return the whole shipment to the courier and cancel the supplier's contract
cards.answer: Quarantine the shipment and verify serials and seals with the supplier first
cards.why: Supply chain risk includes delivery: hardware can be tampered with in transit, and an unexpected courier plus resealed boxes means custody cannot be trusted. Verify serial numbers, seals and firmware with the supplier before anything touches card data. An approved catalogue says nothing about this shipment, a scan will not find a hardware skimmer, and cancelling the contract acts before the facts are known.

cards.q: 23:05 · Governance desk. Ticket: the board wants to deal with a residual ransomware exposure that further controls cannot cost-effectively reduce. The loss would be large but the event is rare. What do you propose?
options: Accept it outright, since rare events do not need any treatment at all
Transfer part of it through cyber insurance sized to the residual loss
Avoid it by switching off every system that ransomware could reach
Add yet more controls until the ransomware risk reaches exactly zero
cards.answer: Transfer part of it through cyber insurance sized to the residual loss
cards.why: Rare, high-impact residual risk is the classic case for transfer: purchasing cybersecurity insurance shifts the financial impact, although accountability for the risk stays with Tessaly. Accepting a large loss outright may exceed the board's appetite, zero risk is neither possible nor economic, and avoiding the risk by switching systems off would stop the business it is meant to protect.

cards.q: 02:40 · Governance desk. Ticket: legal says a former logistics partner is suing Tessaly over a data-sharing contract. Mailboxes and shared drives for that project roll off under a 90-day retention rule. What do you put in place first?
options: Hold off for now, as civil evidence is only collected once a trial date is set
Place a legal hold that suspends deletion on the relevant mailboxes and shares
Copy the data to an analyst's laptop so it is safe from the retention rule
Purge the project data early so there is less material exposed in discovery
cards.answer: Place a legal hold that suspends deletion on the relevant mailboxes and shares
cards.why: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, Tessaly must preserve relevant electronically stored information, and a legal hold suspends routine deletion. Civil cases turn on the preponderance of evidence, which makes the record critical. Waiting lets the 90-day rule destroy it, an early purge is spoliation, and ad hoc copies on a laptop break integrity and custody.

cards.q: 06:40 · Governance desk. Ticket: the legacy customs gateway cannot support MFA, which the access standard requires, and its replacement is 18 months away. The owner asks how to stay compliant meanwhile. What do you put forward?
options: Propose stronger gateway passwords and report them as meeting the MFA rule
Propose a waiver that simply drops the MFA rule until the replacement finally arrives
Propose nothing, since legacy systems are exempt from access standards anyway
Propose MFA on a jump host, IP allowlisting and session recording in its place
cards.answer: Propose MFA on a jump host, IP allowlisting and session recording in its place
cards.why: A compensating control delivers comparable protection when the required control cannot be implemented. MFA enforced at a jump host, allowlisting and session recording bring the risk close to what gateway MFA would, documented and reviewed until replacement. A bare waiver leaves the gap open, stronger passwords are still a single factor, and there is no default exemption for legacy kit.

cards.q: 00:30 · Governance desk. Ticket: an analyst moved from merchant refunds to treasury last month. The HR move form triggered her new treasury access, but her refunds approval rights are still active. What do you do?
options: Remove the refunds rights and wait for the annual review to find any others
Remove the refunds rights and fix the move process so old access ends on transfer
Give her a second account for refunds so the two roles at least stay separate
Leave the refunds rights in place, since she may still help her old team at times
cards.answer: Remove the refunds rights and fix the move process so old access ends on transfer
cards.why: A role change must revoke old access as well as grant new, or privilege creep builds up. Here it has produced a toxic combination: refunds plus treasury. Fix this case and the process that caused it. Keeping rights 'just in case' breaks least privilege, an annual review is too slow to catch the rest, and a second account leaves the same person holding both roles.

cards.q: 03:15 · Governance desk. Ticket: Tessaly moved all parcel routing to a new cloud platform in May, but the continuity plan still lists the old data centre and its call tree names two people who have left. What do you do?
options: Update the plan for the new platform and contacts, then re-test it with the owners
Retire the plan, since the cloud provider's resilience now covers continuity
Fix only the call tree, since contact details are the part people actually use
Leave the plan alone until its scheduled review comes round again next year
cards.answer: Update the plan for the new platform and contacts, then re-test it with the owners
cards.why: A continuity plan has to be maintained through change: a major platform move should trigger an update and a fresh test with the process owners. Waiting leaves a plan that fails on the night it is needed. The provider's resilience covers its own infrastructure, not Tessaly's processes, and a contact-only fix leaves recovery steps that point at a data centre that no longer runs anything.

cards.q: 05:20 · Governance desk. Ticket: your new information security policy is finished, but depot managers are ignoring it as 'just a security team document'. What will give it force?
options: Have the CEO and executive team approve it and issue it in their own name
Have the security team sign it again and send it out with a firmer cover note
Have IT block depot logins until each manager passes a quiz on the new policy
Have each depot manager write a local version so they feel they own the policy
cards.answer: Have the CEO and executive team approve it and issue it in their own name
cards.why: A policy's authority comes from senior management. Executive approval signals commitment, allocates resources and turns compliance into a management expectation rather than a request from one department. Re-signing by security changes nothing about its authority, local rewrites fragment the rules, and blocking logins coerces people without giving the policy any legitimacy.

cards.q: 23:50 · Governance desk. Ticket: the same 20-minute general awareness module goes to every employee, including payment-app developers who keep shipping injection flaws. What do you add to the programme?
options: Add a second viewing of the general module for the developers every quarter
Add nothing, since awareness training should be identical for all staff
Add role-based secure coding training for developers alongside the general module
Add a poster campaign about injection flaws in the developers' break room
cards.answer: Add role-based secure coding training for developers alongside the general module
cards.why: Awareness points everyone's attention at risks; training builds role-specific skills, and a good programme is tailored by role. Developers shipping injection flaws need hands-on secure coding training grounded in the OWASP classics. Watching the general module again teaches no new skills, posters are just more awareness, and a one-size programme ignores the people with the most technical risk.

cards.q: 04:15 · Governance desk. Ticket: the warehouse team asks to keep an old label-printer driver that breaks the patching standard. The printer maker will ship a fix in 60 days. What do you approve?
options: Approve a quiet workaround, telling nobody, since it lasts only sixty days
Approve a permanent exception, as the warehouse says the driver is essential
Approve a time-limited, documented exception with the risk owner's sign-off
Approve an edit to the patching standard so old printer drivers are allowed
cards.answer: Approve a time-limited, documented exception with the risk owner's sign-off
cards.why: An exception process keeps the standard intact while recording a justified deviation: time-bound, accepted by the risk owner, with compensating measures and a review date. A permanent exception quietly becomes the new rule, an undocumented workaround is unmanaged risk, and rewriting the standard for one printer weakens it for everyone.

cards.q: 02:20 · Governance desk. Ticket: forensics confirms last night's intrusion exposed the home addresses of 4,000 EU customers. The comms lead wants to wait until the full root cause is known. What do you set in motion?
options: Brief the DPO to notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours
Wait for the complete root cause, then decide whether to tell anyone
Notify only if the stolen addresses appear on a leak site later on
Email every customer tonight, before legal has reviewed the wording
cards.answer: Brief the DPO to notify the supervisory authority within 72 hours
cards.why: Under GDPR a personal data breach likely to put people at risk must reach the supervisory authority no later than 72 hours after Tessaly becomes aware, and details can follow in phases. Waiting for the full root cause blows the deadline, a leak-site sighting is not the legal test, and an unreviewed mass email may be inaccurate and still does not meet the duty to notify the regulator.

cards.q: 01:15 · Governance desk. Ticket: preparing for tomorrow's PCI audit, your manager asks you to backdate three access reviews that were never done, 'so we don't lose the certification'. Your move?
options: Backdate them, but keep a private note showing the real completion dates
Ask a colleague to sign the reviews instead, so you are not the one dating them
Backdate them this once, since the reviews will genuinely be done next week
Decline, record the missed reviews honestly, and escalate a remediation plan
cards.answer: Decline, record the missed reviews honestly, and escalate a remediation plan
cards.why: The ISC2 Code requires you to act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally. Backdated reviews are falsified records that mislead the assessor, whoever signs them. Report the gap truthfully with a plan to close it and escalate internally if pressure continues. A private note does not undo the falsification, and handing the pen to a colleague just spreads the misconduct.

cards.q: 06:20 · Governance desk. Ticket: procurement is about to pick a managed SOC provider and asks you to 'compare their SLAs'. Nobody has written down what response times Tessaly actually needs. What do you do first?
options: Copy the strongest provider's SLA terms and adopt them as Tessaly's own needs
Write Tessaly's service-level requirements, then test each SLA against them
Choose the provider with the longest SLA document, since it covers more cases
Accept the cheapest provider's standard SLA and negotiate it after go-live
cards.answer: Write Tessaly's service-level requirements, then test each SLA against them
cards.why: A service-level requirement (SLR) states what the customer needs, such as detection and response times, coverage hours and reporting, and it drives the SLA that is negotiated. Without SLRs you are ranking vendors against each other, not against Tessaly's need. Document length is not coverage, post-go-live negotiation has no leverage, and copying a vendor's terms lets the market set your requirement.

cards.q: 23:20 · Governance desk. Ticket: rank the risk of drone surveillance of the Rotterdam yard. There is no loss history and no reliable probability data, but the CFO wants a euro figure. How do you assess it?
options: Invent a probability and a loss figure so that the CFO gets the euro-based answer
Borrow the ALE of another yard's theft risk and apply it to drone surveillance
Use a qualitative likelihood-impact rating from expert input and note its limits
Skip it, as risks without historical loss data cannot be assessed in any way
cards.answer: Use a qualitative likelihood-impact rating from expert input and note its limits
cards.why: When hard data is missing, a qualitative assessment built on informed judgement gives a defensible ranking, and stating its limits keeps the decision honest. A made-up euro figure offers false precision the CFO might act on. No loss history does not mean no risk, and a figure borrowed from a different threat at a different site describes neither.

cards.q: 05:35 · Governance desk. Ticket: the national payments regulator has opened an inquiry into last quarter's settlement outage and wants logs and incident reports within ten days. An engineer suggests sending only the flattering ones. What do you do?
options: Send only the reports that show Tessaly handling the outage well, as the engineer suggested
Refuse the request until the regulator produces a court order for the material
Ask for a longer deadline and pause all collection until the regulator replies
Work with legal to gather the full requested set and respond before the deadline
cards.answer: Work with legal to gather the full requested set and respond before the deadline
cards.why: A regulatory investigation is run by a government body under its own authority, and the organisation must comply fully and on time, coordinated through legal. Selective disclosure risks being treated as obstruction. Regulators generally do not need a court order to request records within their remit, and asking for more time does not suspend the obligation to keep collecting.

cards.q: 00:45 · Governance desk. Ticket: the card-authorisation service must answer in under two seconds, around the clock; a failed day costs more than any leaked test record could. The team proposes adding heavy inline inspection to it. What do you advise?
options: Add the inline inspection anyway, since confidentiality always comes first
Place the inspection out of band so it protects without risking availability
Add inline inspection twice over, in series, to double the protection layers
Drop all inspection from the service so the two-second response is guaranteed
cards.answer: Place the inspection out of band so it protects without risking availability
cards.why: The CIA triad is balanced by business priority, and for card authorisation availability dominates, so a control must not become the outage. Out-of-band inspection still watches the traffic without sitting in its path. Confidentiality does not automatically come first, removing all inspection overcorrects, and stacking inline devices multiplies exactly the latency and failure risk you are trying to avoid.

cards.q: 03:50 · Governance desk. Ticket: a cleaning contractor's staff will get badge access to the Tessaly Pay server room at night. The facilities contract says nothing about screening or conduct. What do you add before badges are issued?
options: Add nothing, since the cleaners are employed by the contractor, not Tessaly
Add unescorted access for all cleaners, with CCTV reviewed once a year
Add terms requiring screening, NDAs, escort rules and prompt leaver notice
Add a single master badge shared by all cleaners to limit the badges issued
cards.answer: Add terms requiring screening, NDAs, escort rules and prompt leaver notice
cards.why: Personnel security reaches third parties through the contract: screening, confidentiality, conduct rules and prompt notice when someone leaves hold the vendor's staff to Tessaly's standard. The employer of record does not change who is exposed. A shared badge destroys accountability, and unescorted access with yearly CCTV review is far too little oversight for a server room.

cards.q: 01:30 · Governance desk. Ticket: the Leipzig hub's continuity plan covers systems and suppliers in detail, but says nothing about what night-shift staff do in a fire or chemical spill. What do you add?
options: Add a cyber incident response plan naming who isolates the hub's network links
Add an occupant emergency plan with evacuation, assembly points and headcounts
Add a disaster recovery plan for the hub's servers with failover to another site
Add a crisis comms plan with press lines ready for local media about the hub
cards.answer: Add an occupant emergency plan with evacuation, assembly points and headcounts
cards.why: An occupant emergency plan protects people during a physical threat: evacuation routes, shelter, assembly points and accounting for everyone on shift. Human safety always comes before systems. Disaster recovery, incident response and crisis communications plans all matter, but they protect technology and reputation, and none tells a night-shift picker where to go when the alarm sounds.

cards.q: 06:50 · Governance desk. Ticket: Tessaly is buying a small parcel-locker company next month. The deal team has examined its finances but not its security. What do you insist on before signing?
options: Rely on a seller clause stating nothing bad has ever happened to the company before
Check its security after closing, since until then it is the owners' problem
Carry out security due diligence on its controls, breaches, debt and contracts
Connect its network to Tessaly's straight away so you can see what it runs
cards.answer: Carry out security due diligence on its controls, breaches, debt and contracts
cards.why: Acquisitions are a governance process, and due diligence must cover security: undisclosed breaches, technical debt and inherited compliance obligations all become Tessaly's on closing. After signing, the liability is already yours. Connecting an unassessed network imports its risk, and a seller warranty may help recover losses later but does not tell you what you are buying.

cards.q: 02:45 · Governance desk. Ticket: plan the first simulated phishing exercise for depot staff. A manager wants the names of everyone who clicks pinned to the canteen noticeboard. What design do you approve?
options: Skip any follow-up, since the simulation itself is the whole of the lesson for staff
Name clickers publicly on the noticeboard to shame them into caring more
Give clickers private, instant coaching and praise anyone who reports the lure
Deduct pay from anyone who clicks, so the lesson is felt in their pocket
cards.answer: Give clickers private, instant coaching and praise anyone who reports the lure
cards.why: Simulations exist to teach and to build a reporting culture. Private, just-in-time coaching at the moment of the mistake, plus visible praise for reporting, changes behaviour. Public shaming and pay penalties teach staff to hide clicks, which is the worst outcome during a real attack, and a simulation with no follow-up measures people without improving them.

cards.q: 04:35 · Governance desk. Ticket: the 'security policy' you inherited is 90 pages of firewall rules, password lengths and product names, and it goes out of date every time a tool changes. How do you restructure it?
options: Keep everything in one document and assign someone to update it every week
Cut it to a short statement of management intent and move detail into standards
Replace it with vendor hardening guides, since vendors keep those guides up to date
Turn all 90 pages into optional guidelines so that nobody can fail an audit
cards.answer: Cut it to a short statement of management intent and move detail into standards
cards.why: A security policy is management's high-level statement of goals, scope and responsibilities, and it should rarely change. Technology-specific detail belongs in standards, baselines and procedures beneath it, which can change without re-approving the policy. Weekly edits to one giant document never end, vendor guides carry no Tessaly authority, and optional guidelines remove the mandate.

cards.q: 23:35 · Governance desk. Ticket: a software audit finds a route-optimisation library running in production under a 'non-commercial use only' licence. The team says nobody will ever notice. What do you do?
options: Keep using it but credit the author in release notes to show goodwill
Rename the library files so an outside licence audit cannot recognise it
Escalate to legal, then license it commercially or replace the library
Leave it in place, as code published online is free for any kind of use
cards.answer: Escalate to legal, then license it commercially or replace the library
cards.why: Software licences are enforceable intellectual property terms, and commercial use under a non-commercial licence is infringement. Bring in legal and either buy the right licence or replace the component. Public availability is not permission, disguising the files turns a mistake into wilful infringement, and attribution satisfies only some licences, never a commercial-use restriction.

cards.q: 05:55 · Governance desk. Ticket: while testing, you find a flaw in a widely used shipping-label printer that lets anyone on the network take it over. Thousands of firms use it. A friend who runs a blog wants the story tonight. Your move?
options: Sell the details to a broker and donate the proceeds to a security charity
Give the blogger full details tonight so every affected firm hears quickly
Keep it to yourself, since fixing the maker's products is not Tessaly's job
Report it privately to the maker under coordinated disclosure via Tessaly
cards.answer: Report it privately to the maker under coordinated disclosure via Tessaly
cards.why: The first canon of the ISC2 Code is to protect society, the common good and the infrastructure. Coordinated disclosure gets the flaw fixed before attackers learn of it, and going through Tessaly respects your employer's interests. Publishing before a fix exists arms attackers against thousands of firms, silence leaves them exposed, and selling the flaw is dishonourable whatever happens to the money.

cards.q: 00:15 · Governance desk. Ticket: onboard a new payroll processor that will hold every employee's bank details. Its security questionnaire is glowing, and it subcontracts hosting to an unnamed firm. What do you require?
options: Require a SOC 2 report, named subprocessors, and a right-to-audit clause
Require only its questionnaire, as the answers already show strong security
Require nothing more, since the risk moves to the processor once it signs
Require a lower price, since the unnamed host's risk should be priced in
cards.answer: Require a SOC 2 report, named subprocessors, and a right-to-audit clause
cards.why: Supplier risk management needs independent evidence rather than self-attestation, so ask for a SOC 2 Type II or similar. Subprocessors are fourth parties that extend the chain and must be known, and audit rights keep assurance alive after signing. A discount does not reduce exposure, and accountability for staff data stays with Tessaly whatever the contract says.

cards.q: 03:00 · Governance desk. Ticket: the risk register is refreshed once a year, and last year's top risk, unpatched depot scanners, grew worse for months without anyone noticing. What do you set up?
options: Set a bigger annual assessment with more consultants to catch everything
Set up a new register tool, since the spreadsheet let the risk go unseen
Set key risk indicators for the top risks, with thresholds that trigger review
Set the top risk aside, as it is now a known issue and needs no tracking
cards.answer: Set key risk indicators for the top risks, with thresholds that trigger review
cards.why: Risk management is continuous. Key risk indicators, such as scanner patch lag, watch for drift between assessments, and thresholds force the owner to act before the next annual cycle. A bigger yearly assessment still leaves eleven blind months, a new tool does not fix a process that never looks, and a known risk that is still growing must stay on the register.

cards.q: 01:50 · Governance desk. Ticket: threat intel says a freight forwarders' forum that Tessaly dispatchers visit daily was serving malicious scripts last week. No Tessaly alerts fired. What do you do?
options: Report the forum's owner to the police for deliberately targeting Tessaly's dispatch staff
Tell dispatchers to be careful on the forum and carry on as normal meanwhile
Hunt proxy logs for visits to the forum, check those hosts, and block it for now
Wait for an alert, since no detection fired and so nothing reached Tessaly
cards.answer: Hunt proxy logs for visits to the forum, check those hosts, and block it for now
cards.why: A watering hole attack compromises a site a target group trusts, so victims are infected just by visiting. No alerts does not mean no compromise, so hunt retrospectively through proxy logs, examine the hosts that visited, and block the site until it is clean. The forum owner is most likely a victim too, and a vague warning cannot stop scripts that run on page load.

cards.q: 06:10 · Governance desk. Ticket: a senior merchant-risk analyst has resigned on good terms and leaves on Friday. She knows Tessaly's fraud-scoring rules in detail. What goes on the offboarding checklist?
options: Plan a farewell lunch only, as friendly leavers need no formal exit steps
Remove every bit of her access today, three days ahead of her last day
Ask her to delete her own work mailbox before handing back the laptop
Hold an exit interview restating her NDA, recover assets, end access on Friday
cards.answer: Hold an exit interview restating her NDA, recover assets, end access on Friday
cards.why: Friendly departures still need formal offboarding. An exit interview reminds her of continuing confidentiality obligations, assets come back, and access ends when employment does. Good terms do not make fraud-scoring knowledge less sensitive. Cutting access days early is disproportionate without a specific risk, and having her delete her own mailbox destroys business records.

cards.q: 02:35 · Governance desk. Ticket: the BIA says depot dispatch can be down for no more than 8 hours, but the only recovery strategy on file is rebuilding servers, which takes 24. What do you do?
options: Keep the current strategy and hope a long outage never hits dispatch
Change the BIA limit to 24 hours so it matches the recovery on file
Record 24 hours as the RTO and treat the owner's 8 hours as advisory
Take the gap to the owner and fund a strategy that meets the 8-hour limit
cards.answer: Take the gap to the owner and fund a strategy that meets the 8-hour limit
cards.why: A recovery strategy must deliver an RTO inside the maximum tolerable downtime set by the business impact analysis. A 16-hour gap means the owner must choose and fund a different strategy, such as a warm standby or a manual dispatch workaround. Editing the BIA or the RTO to match current capability turns the process upside down, and hoping is not a strategy.

cards.q: 00:55 · Governance desk. Ticket: security decisions at Tessaly are made ad hoc by whichever engineer is on call, and priorities swing week to week. The board asks for structure. What do you propose?
options: Form a steering committee of business leaders to set direction and oversee it
Give the engineering team a single, larger budget for security tooling
Hand security priorities to an outsourced SOC to set on Tessaly's behalf instead
Create a rota where on-call engineers vote on security priorities weekly
cards.answer: Form a steering committee of business leaders to set direction and oversee it
cards.why: Security governance means setting strategic direction aligned to business objectives, assigning accountability and overseeing results; a steering committee of business leaders does that. An engineers' vote is operations making strategy, an outsourced provider can deliver services but cannot hold Tessaly's accountability, and budget without direction is spending, not governance.

cards.q: 04:00 · Governance desk. Ticket: new depot staff get system logins on day one, but their first awareness session can be up to six months later. What do you change?
options: Exempt depot staff from training, since they handle parcels, not data
Require a short awareness module at onboarding before logins are enabled
Keep the six-month wait so new staff settle in before training begins
Send new staff a policy link and count opening it as the training complete
cards.answer: Require a short awareness module at onboarding before logins are enabled
cards.why: Awareness starts at onboarding, before access is granted, and is refreshed at regular intervals afterwards. The first months are when new starters know the least and attackers target them the most. Anyone with a login is a phishing target whatever their job, and clicking a policy link records an event without building any awareness.

cards.q: 05:05 · Governance desk. Ticket: the remote-work policy was last reviewed in 2019 and still bans laptops from leaving the building, so staff simply ignore it. What do you set up?
options: Set out an informal note that staff may ignore any policy that seems dated
Set the policy aside and delete it, since nobody follows it any more anyway
Set stricter enforcement of the 2019 rule so staff stop taking laptops home
Set a review cycle where owners revise and reapprove policies on a schedule
cards.answer: Set a review cycle where owners revise and reapprove policies on a schedule
cards.why: Every policy needs a named owner and a periodic review so it keeps pace with how the business actually works. A stale rule breeds normalised non-compliance that spreads to other policies. Enforcing an obsolete ban fights the business, an informal licence to ignore rules erodes all of them, and deleting the policy leaves remote work with no rules at all.

cards.q: 23:25 · Governance desk. Ticket: Tessaly Pay wants full card numbers copied into the analytics warehouse 'for better fraud models'. The warehouse sits outside the PCI DSS scope today. What do you recommend?
options: Tokenise the card numbers so analytics works without widening PCI scope
Copy them in now and bring the warehouse into scope after the next audit
Copy them in encrypted, with the key stored in the same warehouse for ease
Copy them in, since PCI DSS is only an industry standard and not the law
cards.answer: Tokenise the card numbers so analytics works without widening PCI scope
cards.why: PCI DSS is an industry standard enforced by contract with the card brands, so it binds Tessaly Pay even though it is not statute. Storing full card numbers pulls the warehouse into scope. Tokenisation keeps analytic value while keeping raw card data out. Copying first and scoping later is a live violation, and a key stored beside its data protects very little.

cards.q: 02:15 · Governance desk. Ticket: during a log review you see that a fellow ISC2-certified analyst has been reading a celebrity customer's account history with no business reason. He asks you to let it go. Your move?
options: Report it through Tessaly's process and weigh a complaint to ISC2 as well
Let it go this once, as no data left the company and he is a friend
Delete the log entries so the matter cannot ever hurt the team's reputation
Post an anonymous warning in the team chat without naming the analyst
cards.answer: Report it through Tessaly's process and weigh a complaint to ISC2 as well
cards.why: Browsing a customer's records without need breaches privacy and the ISC2 Code, and members are expected to support the Code, including by reporting breaches they witness. Use Tessaly's process first; a formal ISC2 ethics complaint is available if warranted. Friendship does not change the breach, deleting logs destroys evidence and is misconduct itself, and a vague chat post fixes nothing.

cards.q: 06:45 · Governance desk. Ticket: renewal talks with the cloud host for the parcel-tracking app. It had four long outages last year and Tessaly had no remedy. The app must stay up for customers around the clock. What must the contract gain?
options: Add a best-efforts promise, since uptime is never fully in a host's control
Add a bigger discount in exchange for dropping reliability commitments
Add a clause giving the host ownership of Tessaly's whole continuity plan
Add a high uptime guarantee with service credits and exit rights on breach
cards.answer: Add a high uptime guarantee with service credits and exit rights on breach
cards.why: An SLA turns supplier performance into something measurable and enforceable. A high uptime guarantee matched to the app's need, backed by service credits and termination rights, gives Tessaly leverage it lacked last year. Best efforts means no remedy, continuity accountability cannot be handed to a supplier, and a discount does nothing to reduce the impact of the next outage.

cards.q: 01:20 · Governance desk. Ticket: a flood would cause $120,000 of damage to the Hamburg depot's IT room each time, and the insurer's data says such a flood happens about once every four years. Facilities asks how much it is worth spending each year on flood protection. What figure do you give?
options: Allow up to $120,000 a year, since that is what one flood would cost
Cap yearly flood spending at $30,000, the annualised loss expectancy
Allow $480,000 a year, covering four years of flood damage up front
Allow nothing, since a flood is only expected once every four years
cards.answer: Cap yearly flood spending at $30,000, the annualised loss expectancy
cards.why: Annualised loss expectancy is the single loss expectancy times the annual rate of occurrence: $120,000 × 0.25 = $30,000. That is the ceiling for yearly spend on the risk; paying more costs more than the loss it prevents. The single-loss figure is per event, not per year, multiplying by four inverts the rate, and an infrequent loss still carries an expected annual cost.

cards.q: 03:25 · Governance desk. Ticket: reviewing the BIA, you notice that all five 'critical' processes rely on one SMS provider for drivers' one-time codes, yet it appears nowhere in the analysis. What do you do?
options: Cancel the SMS provider so the critical processes lose the dependency
Leave it for the provider's own continuity team to cover in their plan
Ignore it, as the BIA only needs to list Tessaly's own internal systems
Add the provider as a dependency, rate its impact, and plan another channel
cards.answer: Add the provider as a dependency, rate its impact, and plan another channel
cards.why: A business impact analysis must map dependencies, including third parties, because that is where hidden single points of failure live. Once the provider is rated, continuity strategy can supply an alternate channel such as an authenticator app. Internal-only scope misses exactly this risk, cancelling the provider breaks the processes, and the supplier's plan protects the supplier, not Tessaly.

cards.q: 05:40 · Governance desk. Ticket: auditors, customers and the board each ask for different security evidence, and Tessaly answers every request from scratch. Leadership wants one structured approach. What do you propose?
options: Keep answering each request separately, since every audience differs
Adopt a recognised framework like ISO/IEC 27001 and map requests to it
Write Tessaly's own framework from scratch so it is wholly original
Buy a compliance tool and let its default checklist define our controls
cards.answer: Adopt a recognised framework like ISO/IEC 27001 and map requests to it
cards.why: A recognised control framework, such as an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS or the NIST CSF, gives governance a structure: one managed control set, mapped once to many external demands. Answering from scratch wastes effort and yields inconsistent claims. A tool's default checklist lets a vendor define your controls, and a home-grown framework is harder for auditors and customers to trust.

cards.q: 00:25 · Governance desk. Ticket: drivers use Tessaly tablets for streaming and personal messaging, and nothing in writing says they can't. HR wants to discipline one driver. What do you put in place first?
options: Lock every tablet app except dispatch without telling the drivers the reason
Discipline the driver now, since any sensible person knows streaming is wrong
Publish a guideline suggesting limited streaming and let drivers interpret it
Issue an acceptable use policy that drivers acknowledge, listing allowed uses
cards.answer: Issue an acceptable use policy that drivers acknowledge, listing allowed uses
cards.why: An acceptable use policy sets out what staff may and may not do with company equipment, and a signed acknowledgement makes it enforceable. Disciplining someone for breaking an unwritten rule is unfair and hard to defend. Locking tablets without explanation creates workarounds and resentment, and a guideline is optional by definition, so it gives HR nothing to enforce.

cards.q: 04:45 · Governance desk. Ticket: Tessaly is selling its courier-app business next month. The buyer will keep running the app, which still authenticates against Tessaly's directory and shares its databases. What do you plan?
options: Plan the separation: split the data, move identities, and cut shared access
Delete the courier app's data on the day of sale to protect Tessaly's records
Give the buyer admin rights on Tessaly's directory to smooth the transition
Leave the shared links running indefinitely as goodwill toward the buyer
cards.answer: Plan the separation: split the data, move identities, and cut shared access
cards.why: Divestitures are a governance process too: data must be split under agreed terms, identities migrated, and every shared trust path removed by an agreed date, with transitional access tightly limited. Admin rights on the directory hand another company the keys to Tessaly, open-ended shared links leave a permanent back door, and deleting data the buyer has paid for breaches the deal.

cards.q: 06:00 · Governance desk. Ticket: after new controls, the residual risk on the returns portal now sits inside the board's stated appetite. The team wants to keep adding controls 'to be safe'. What do you recommend?
options: Stop tracking the risk, since it is within appetite and needs no attention
Have the owner formally accept the residual risk and keep monitoring it
Keep adding controls until the risk score drops as low as it can go
Insure the residual risk anyway, although it is already within appetite
cards.answer: Have the owner formally accept the residual risk and keep monitoring it
cards.why: Once residual risk falls within appetite, the right move is formal acceptance by the risk owner, with monitoring in case conditions change. More controls past that point spend money beyond the value they protect. Accepted risks stay on the register and are watched, and paying to transfer a risk the board has already said it can live with is wasted premium.

cards.q: 03:40 · Governance desk. Ticket: the audit found Tessaly's refund process has strong approval steps, but nothing that would notice a fraudulent refund that slips through. What control do you add?
options: Add a third approval step so refunds are even harder to push through
Add a banner reminding approvers that fraud is a sackable offence
Add a restore-from-backup routine in case a refund record is deleted
Add a daily reconciliation flagging refunds with no matching return
cards.answer: Add a daily reconciliation flagging refunds with no matching return
cards.why: The gap is detection. Preventive controls will eventually be bypassed, so defence in depth layers a detective control behind them: a daily reconciliation catches the refund that slipped past approval. Another approver strengthens the layer that already exists, a warning banner is a deterrent, and restoring deleted records is a recovery control that never notices the fraud.

cards.q: 01:35 · Governance desk. Ticket: marketing wants to reuse drivers' GPS logs, collected for route safety, to publish a league table ranking drivers on 'speed and hustle'. What do you advise?
options: Hold the reuse until a privacy impact assessment and lawful basis back it
Approve it if the table shows drivers by first name only, not full name
Approve it, since Tessaly already holds the GPS data lawfully for route safety
Approve it and add the new purpose to the privacy notice afterwards
cards.answer: Hold the reuse until a privacy impact assessment and lawful basis back it
cards.why: Purpose limitation means personal data collected for one purpose cannot simply be reused for an incompatible one. Publicly ranking employees from location data is a new, intrusive purpose that needs its own lawful basis and a data protection impact assessment. Lawfully holding the data for safety does not cover marketing, first names still identify drivers, and a retroactive notice is too late.

cards.q: 23:45 · Governance desk. Ticket: the COO wants to launch cash-on-delivery in three new markets and asks security to 'just pick the controls'. Nothing about those markets has been analysed yet. What is your first step?
options: Copy the home market's control set straight across into the three new ones
Launch first and pick controls once the early losses show the gaps
Conduct a risk assessment of the new markets before choosing controls
Buy the controls the biggest local competitor advertises as its own
cards.answer: Conduct a risk assessment of the new markets before choosing controls
cards.why: Controls are selected to treat assessed risks, so governance starts with a risk assessment of the markets' threats, laws, fraud patterns and cash handling. Copying the home market's controls assumes identical risks, a competitor's marketing tells you nothing about Tessaly's exposure, and waiting for losses to reveal the gaps makes customers and staff pay for the analysis.

cards.q: 02:55 · Governance desk. Ticket: the sorting robots at the Lyon hub are valued at $900,000. Engineers estimate a ransomware hit would wipe out 35% of that value. The insurer wants the single-loss figure for the policy. What do you submit?
options: Submit $900,000, as the whole fleet is at risk in principle
Submit $2.57 million: the asset value over exposure factor
Submit $315,000: the asset value times the exposure factor
Submit $35,000, reading the exposure factor as a dollar sum
cards.answer: Submit $315,000: the asset value times the exposure factor
cards.why: Single loss expectancy is asset value times exposure factor: $900,000 × 0.35 = $315,000. The exposure factor is the share of value lost in one event, so the full asset value overstates the loss, and treating 35% as a dollar figure or dividing by it confuses the formula. The SLE later feeds the annualised loss expectancy once a rate of occurrence is known.

cards.q: 05:15 · Governance desk. Ticket: engineering plans to ship laptops with full-disk encryption and a custom encrypted VPN to a new Tessaly office in a country under export restrictions. Nobody has checked the rules. What do you do?
options: Ship now, since strong encryption is freely available on the internet
Route the laptops via a third country to get around the restrictions
Strip the encryption out so there is nothing to declare at customs
Have legal check export and import controls on the crypto before shipping
cards.answer: Have legal check export and import controls on the crypto before shipping
cards.why: Cryptography is subject to export and import controls, under the Wassenaar Arrangement and national law, and some destinations need licences or ban certain products. Legal must clear the shipment first. Availability online is not a licence, removing encryption leaves the office's data exposed, and routing through a third country is deliberate evasion of the law.

cards.q: 04:10 · Governance desk. Ticket: Tessaly's freight arm has been designated an essential transport entity under the EU's NIS2 directive. The incident plan has no regulatory reporting step. What do you add?
options: Add a yearly summary of all incidents, sent to the regulator each January
Add a step to report only those incidents that end up in the news
Add nothing, since NIS2 only covers energy firms and hospitals anyway
Add NIS2's staged reports: early warning in 24 hours, notification in 72
cards.answer: Add NIS2's staged reports: early warning in 24 hours, notification in 72
cards.why: NIS2 covers transport among its sectors and requires essential entities to report significant incidents in stages: an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours, and a final report within a month. Assuming the directive is limited to energy and health is wrong, media coverage is not the threshold, and a yearly summary misses every statutory deadline.

cards.q: 00:05 · Governance desk. Ticket: the card brands say a pattern of fraud traces back to Tessaly Pay and require an investigation under their rules. Your internal team is keen to start alone. What do you do?
options: Engage an approved PCI forensic investigator, as the card brands require
Clear out the old card logs first to limit what investigators find
Keep it internal, since the card brands have no legal authority here
Refuse until a court orders it, since this is not a criminal matter
cards.answer: Engage an approved PCI forensic investigator, as the card brands require
cards.why: This is an industry-standards investigation: Tessaly Pay's obligations come from its contracts with the card brands, which can require an approved PCI forensic investigator and impose fines or withdraw processing if ignored. The internal team supports that work rather than replacing it. Lack of statutory authority does not void a contract, no court order is needed, and deleting logs is evidence destruction.

cards.q: 03:10 · Governance desk. Ticket: the board wants the new instant-payouts feature threat modelled in a way that ties attacker scenarios to business impact and risk, not just a list of technical flaws. What do you plan?
options: Run a vulnerability scan on the payouts code and report counts upward
Run PASTA: start from business goals, simulate attacks, then score risk
Run a STRIDE pass over the data flows and give the board the resulting flaw list
Run a pen test after launch and treat its findings as the threat model
cards.answer: Run PASTA: start from business goals, simulate attacks, then score risk
cards.why: PASTA (attack simulation plus threat analysis, run as a process) is a seven-stage risk-centric method that starts from business objectives and ends with impact and risk analysis, which is exactly what the board wants. STRIDE is useful for categorising threats but produces a technical list, while scans and penetration tests find flaws in built code rather than modelling threats before launch.

cards.q: 06:25 · Governance desk. Ticket: threat modelling the merchant refund flow, you see merchants could later claim 'we never issued that refund', and the system logs only a shared API key per merchant. What do you require?
options: Require the refunds to travel under a stronger TLS cipher configuration
Require per-user signed requests and tamper-evident logs of each refund
Require merchants to agree in contract never to dispute their refunds
Require a longer shared API key so outsiders cannot guess it so easily
cards.answer: Require per-user signed requests and tamper-evident logs of each refund
cards.why: A plausible denial of an action is STRIDE's repudiation threat, and the counter is non-repudiation: individual identities, signed requests and tamper-evident logs that prove who did what. A longer shared key still cannot tell one merchant user from another, stronger TLS protects the channel rather than attribution, and a contract clause cannot manufacture proof the system never recorded.

cards.q: 01:00 · Governance desk. Ticket: kick off threat modelling for the warehouse IoT gateway. The team jumps straight to listing attacks they have read about in the news. What do you have them do first?
options: Test the gateway in production and model whatever threats the tests expose
