Buy a threat intelligence feed and treat its alerts as the gateway's threats
List every attack in the news this year and check each against the gateway
Draw the data flows and trust boundaries, then find threats at each crossing
cards.answer: Draw the data flows and trust boundaries, then find threats at each crossing
cards.why: Threat modelling starts by decomposing the system: a data flow diagram with its trust boundaries shows where data crosses between levels of trust, and each crossing is where threats are systematically found. Headline-driven lists miss threats specific to this design, a threat feed describes the outside world rather than the gateway, and production testing comes after design, when fixes cost the most.

cards.q: 04:30 · Governance desk. Ticket: the treasury team asks how an attacker could realistically redirect a supplier payment. You need to show every path to that goal and which paths are cheapest. What do you build?
options: Build an attack tree rooted at 'redirect payment', with costs on each branch
Build one worst-case scenario and design every control around it alone
Build a list of every CVE on the treasury servers and sort it by CVSS severity
Build a policy stating that payment redirection is forbidden at Tessaly
cards.answer: Build an attack tree rooted at 'redirect payment', with costs on each branch
cards.why: An attack tree decomposes an attacker's goal into alternative paths, such as a spoofed supplier email, a compromised approver or a changed bank file, and annotating costs or difficulty shows which branches are cheapest and need controls first. A CVE list covers only technical flaws on servers, a policy stops no attacker, and a single worst case misses the cheaper paths real attackers take.

cards.q: 02:00 · Governance desk. Ticket: a critical flaw has been announced in a common logging library, and nobody can say which of Tessaly's bought-in applications include it. What do you make a standing supplier requirement?
options: Require an up-to-date SBOM from each supplier with every product release
Require suppliers to email Tessaly whenever they happen to notice a flaw
Require suppliers to promise their products never use open-source parts
Require Tessaly staff to reverse-engineer each product after every flaw
cards.answer: Require an up-to-date SBOM from each supplier with every product release
cards.why: A software bill of materials lists the components inside each product, so when a library flaw is announced Tessaly can find its exposure in minutes rather than weeks. Making it a contract requirement builds transparency into supply chain risk management. Banning open source is unrealistic, reverse-engineering every product is slow and may breach licences, and ad hoc emails depend on supplier goodwill.

cards.q: 05:50 · Governance desk. Ticket: the CFO asks you to personally sign off Tessaly's new cloud cryptography design for a regulator. You have never worked with that key management service, and the deadline is Friday. Your move?
options: Sign it off anyway, as refusing the CFO could harm your career here
Sign it off after skimming the vendor's marketing pages about the service
Say where your expertise ends and bring in a qualified reviewer to sign
Refuse the task outright and leave the CFO to find someone on her own
cards.answer: Say where your expertise ends and bring in a qualified reviewer to sign
cards.why: The ISC2 Code asks you to provide diligent and competent service to principals, which means being honest about the limits of your expertise and making sure the work is still done well. Signing beyond your competence misleads the CFO and the regulator, marketing pages are not due diligence, and a flat refusal leaves your principal without the help the canon requires.

cards.q: 06:10 · Identity plane. The after-action review is in: a dispatcher who left in June still signed in to CargoLink, the freight partner's portal, because staff hold local accounts there. CargoLink supports SAML. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Federate CargoLink with Tessaly's IdP so a disable at home ends its access
Ask CargoLink to email a monthly list of active local accounts for review
Sync Tessaly password hashes to CargoLink so staff reuse one credential
Move the CargoLink accounts into one shared dispatch login held by the lead
cards.answer: Federate CargoLink with Tessaly's IdP so a disable at home ends its access
cards.why: Federated identity makes Tessaly's IdP the source of truth: CargoLink trusts signed assertions, so disabling the account at home ends partner access at once and no partner password is left to forget. A monthly list keeps the gap open for weeks; syncing hashes spreads credentials to a third party; a shared login ends accountability.

cards.q: 05:40 · Identity plane. The review found a picker who moved from the Leeds depot to Bristol still holding Leeds dock-scheduler rights; groups are edited by hand from HR emails. Which fix do you approve?
options: Remind depot managers to email the service desk within a week of any move
Remove all dock-scheduler rights and make staff re-request them each quarter
Drive group membership from HR attributes such as site and job code, daily
Stand up a second directory for depots so site access sits apart from HR
cards.answer: Drive group membership from HR attributes such as site and job code, daily
cards.why: Attribute-driven provisioning ties access to authoritative HR data: when the site or job-code attribute changes, the rules move the person's entitlements with it, closing the mover gap. Manager emails are the manual process that already failed; a quarterly wipe disrupts work and still lags; a second directory adds another source of truth instead of fixing the process.

cards.q: 02:15 · Identity plane. Three callers in an hour have asked the night desk to enrol a new phone for MFA, each claiming to be a newly hired depot manager with no badge yet. One name matches an HR record. How do you handle that caller?
options: Enrol the phone since the name matches HR, then confirm with HR next Monday
Hold enrolment until they show government photo ID matched to the HR record
Ask the caller to confirm a start date and employee number, then enrol
Enrol with a temporary password so the account works but expires in a day
cards.answer: Hold enrolment until they show government photo ID matched to the HR record
cards.why: Identity proofing binds a claimed identity to a real person before any credential is issued; checking a government photo ID such as a driver's licence against the HR record does that. A start date and employee number are facts a social engineer can research, and enrolling first, even temporarily, hands an attacker a working authenticator mid-campaign.

cards.q: 03:05 · Identity plane. The svc-invexport account, which only writes CSVs to one finance share, is logging on interactively to two database servers. It sits in Domain Admins 'because the vendor said so'. What do you do?
options: Rotate the password and leave its groups alone so the export keeps running
Delete the export job and account so nothing is left for the attacker to use
Alert on the account's logons and keep watching to learn the attacker's aim
Disable the account, then reissue it with write rights to that share only
cards.answer: Disable the account, then reissue it with write rights to that share only
cards.why: Disabling contains the misuse, and reissuing the account with only write rights to the export share applies least privilege, so if it is stolen again the blast radius is one folder. A rotation leaves domain-wide privilege in place; deleting destroys evidence and breaks a business process; watching lets someone holding domain admin keep moving.

cards.q: 00:50 · Identity plane. CCTV shows someone opening the payments cage by pressing a film against the fingerprint reader. The log credits a cashier who is on leave abroad, and the reader is the only factor on that door. Your move?
options: Switch the door to badge plus fingerprint and open a case for liveness checks
Lower the reader's sensitivity so fewer genuine staff are turned away
Re-enrol every user's fingerprint tonight so the copied print stops matching
Keep the reader as it is and post a guard, since spoofing takes lab skills
cards.answer: Switch the door to badge plus fingerprint and open a case for liveness checks
cards.why: Biometric authentication can be spoofed with a lifted print, so a characteristic alone is weak at a high-value door. Adding the badge makes entry multifactor tonight, and liveness detection targets the spoof itself. Re-enrolling fails because the copy is of the cashier's real finger; lowering sensitivity raises false acceptance, the very failure being exploited.

cards.q: 04:35 · Identity plane. The dock doors logged the same proximity badge twice in two minutes, at readers 400 metres apart. It belongs to a forklift driver who is at home, and the site still runs low-frequency badges. What do you do first?
options: Call the driver in to hand back the badge so the original can be examined closely
Revoke that badge ID now and add a PIN prompt at the dock doors until morning
Leave the badge live so its reader hits can guide guards to the person
Order encrypted smart cards for the site and swap them in next quarter
cards.answer: Revoke that badge ID now and add a PIN prompt at the dock doors until morning
cards.why: Two reads far apart mean the RFID credential was cloned: low-frequency proximity cards send a static ID any cheap reader can copy. Revoking the ID kills every copy, and a PIN adds a factor the clone lacks. Encrypted cards are the right long-term fix but leave the door open tonight, and recovering the original badge does nothing about the copy.

cards.q: 01:25 · Identity plane. The payroll SaaS shows admin sessions for users who never signed in at Tessaly's IdP, and an unknown process read the IdP server's key store yesterday. Which containment do you run?
options: Reset the affected users' passwords and force them to re-register MFA
Turn off federation and give everyone local payroll accounts until Monday
Block the source addresses of the payroll sessions at the perimeter
Replace the IdP signing key, update relying parties, revoke live sessions
cards.answer: Replace the IdP signing key, update relying parties, revoke live sessions
cards.why: Sessions with no IdP sign-in mean someone is forging assertions with the stolen token-signing key, and every relying party trusts them. Replacing the key and pushing new metadata removes that trust; revoking sessions evicts the attacker. Password resets fail because forged assertions never touch passwords; local accounts scatter credentials and outlast the incident; addresses are trivially changed.

cards.q: 23:40 · Identity plane. HR calls: a network engineer was dismissed on the spot two hours ago and left angry. His VPN session is still open and his admin account is active. What do you do?
options: Wait for HR's formal leaver ticket in the morning so the process is followed
Change his password only, so his mailbox stays open for his manager
Disable his accounts, end live sessions, revoke tokens, and log each step
Message him to log off, since forcing the session may lose his open work
cards.answer: Disable his accounts, end live sessions, revoke tokens, and log each step
cards.why: Deprovisioning is timed to the termination, and for a hostile leaver with admin rights that means now: disabling accounts, ending sessions and revoking tokens closes every path, and the log shows due care. Waiting for paperwork leaves a live admin session in angry hands; a password change alone leaves open sessions and refresh tokens working.

cards.q: 03:30 · Identity plane. Five executive accounts were reset overnight through the self-service portal, which asks for mother's maiden name and first school. The executives' public profiles list both. What do you change right now?
options: Suspend question-based resets and require a code from a registered device
Add a third security question so an attacker must research one more answer
Make the answers case-sensitive so guesses from public profiles miss more
Email the executives asking them to make their public profiles private
cards.answer: Suspend question-based resets and require a code from a registered device
cards.why: Security questions are a knowledge factor, and knowledge that is public is no longer secret. Adding more of the same factor, or tightening its format, only adds more researchable facts. Replacing it with something the user has, a code on a registered device, stops the resets tonight; tidying profiles helps later but not with answers already exposed.

cards.q: 02:40 · Identity plane. Directory logs show a helpdesk account pulling password data from a domain controller through replication calls, from an ordinary laptop. Someone granted it replication rights last month for a 'sync tool'. First move?
options: Reboot the domain controller so the replication session drops and stops
Strip the replication rights, isolate the laptop, treat the hashes as stolen
Move the laptop into the domain controllers OU so its replication is audited
Reset the helpdesk account's password and keep the sync tool's rights
cards.answer: Strip the replication rights, isolate the laptop, treat the hashes as stolen
cards.why: Replication rights let an account ask a domain controller for every password hash, so only domain controllers should hold them. Removing the grant and isolating the host contains it, and treating the hashes as stolen drives resets, krbtgt included. Rebooting drops one session but keeps the right; a password reset leaves the over-privileged grant for the attacker to reuse.

cards.q: 05:15 · Identity plane. The SIEM flags Kerberos tickets on three servers with ten-year lifetimes and a user ID that does not exist in the directory. The KDC never issued them. What do you do?
options: Cut the domain's ticket lifetime policy to ten hours and wait it out
Remove the unknown user ID from the three servers' local admin groups
Restart the three servers so the forged tickets drop out of memory
Reset krbtgt twice, with a gap, and hunt the host that forged them
cards.answer: Reset krbtgt twice, with a gap, and hunt the host that forged them
cards.why: Tickets the KDC never issued, with impossible lifetimes, are forged with the stolen krbtgt key. Kerberos honours any ticket signed by that key, so the key must change, twice, because the previous key is still accepted. Lifetime policy fails because forged tickets ignore it; restarts clear memory but the attacker can mint more.

cards.q: 01:55 · Identity plane. A contractor badge opened the card-operations room at 01:30, and CCTV shows the holder photographing unlocked screens of cardholder records. The contractor's work order is for the canteen. What do you do first?
options: Log it for the contractor's manager to raise at the morning stand-up
Power off the card-operations PCs so nothing more can be seen tonight
Have guards stop and escort the person, suspend the badge, lock screens
Tell guards to delete the photos from the phone before they let the person go
cards.answer: Have guards stop and escort the person, suspend the badge, lock screens
cards.why: The harm is to confidentiality: cardholder data is being disclosed to someone with no need to know. Stopping the person, suspending the over-scoped badge and locking the screens ends the exposure. Deleting the photos destroys evidence, and guards may lack authority to search a phone; powering off loses volatile data and leaves the person in the room.

cards.q: 00:20 · Identity plane. Forty staff clicked a 'shipment tracker' link and granted a third-party app permission to read their mail through Tessaly's cloud sign-in. No passwords were typed. What contains this?
options: Revoke the app's consent and tokens, block it, and require admin approval
Force password resets for the forty users and ask them to choose longer ones
Turn on MFA for the forty users so the app must pass a second factor
Warn staff by email and let the app's tokens expire on their own
cards.answer: Revoke the app's consent and tokens, block it, and require admin approval
cards.why: This is a consent grant: the third party holds delegated OAuth tokens, not passwords, so resets and MFA do nothing to access already granted. Revoking the consent and tokens and blocking the app ends it; requiring admin approval for third-party apps stops the next one. Refresh tokens can live for weeks, so waiting leaves mail flowing out.

cards.q: 03:50 · Identity plane. A contractor account unused since March just logged on to the route-planning server. The agency ended that contract in April, but nobody raised a leaver ticket. What is your move?
options: Assign the contractor's old manager as owner so someone watches it
Delete the account at once so the attacker can never sign in with it again
Reset the password and email it to the agency to confirm who used it
Disable it, keep its logs, and reconcile all contractors with the agency
cards.answer: Disable it, keep its logs, and reconcile all contractors with the agency
cards.why: An orphaned account is a lifecycle failure: access outlived the relationship because deprovisioning hung on a ticket nobody raised. Disabling contains it while keeping evidence, and reconciling against the agency's list finds the others. Deleting destroys the identifiers and audit trail an investigation needs; emailing a new password to a third party hands out a fresh credential.

cards.q: 23:15 · Identity plane. You are specifying the new server-hall door. An audit found staff lend each other badges and share the door PIN, so logs no longer prove who entered. The requirement is a factor that cannot be handed over. What do you specify?
options: Badge plus a personal PIN each person changes monthly and never writes down
Badge plus a vein or fingerprint reader enrolled per person, with liveness
Two badges per person, both required, issued by separate departments
Badge plus a paper logbook the guard checks against the badge holder
cards.answer: Badge plus a vein or fingerprint reader enrolled per person, with liveness
cards.why: A Type 3 factor, something you are, is bound to the body and cannot be lent the way a badge (Type 2) or PIN (Type 1) can, so it restores individual accountability at the door. A personal PIN is still shareable; two badges are the same factor type twice; a logbook relies on a guard and a signature, both easily defeated.

cards.q: 00:35 · Identity plane. A ticket asks you to review the access rules for the new shipment-pricing API. The draft names five groups that are blocked and lets everyone else through. What do you send back?
options: Approve it and add new groups to the blocked list as they are created
Approve it but log every call so misuse can be spotted and blocked later
Add a sixth blocked group for contractors and approve the rest as it is drafted
Rewrite it as deny by default with explicit allows for groups that need it
cards.answer: Rewrite it as deny by default with explicit allows for groups that need it
cards.why: Authorization should fail closed: implicit deny with explicit allows means a new group or account gets nothing until someone decides it should. A block list fails open, so every group created tomorrow can call the pricing API. Logging detects misuse after the fact instead of preventing it, and one more blocked group keeps the same flawed model.

cards.q: 01:40 · Identity plane. Quarterly access reviews run from spreadsheets, and last quarter 98% of lines came back 'approved' in under a minute. Tessaly's identity governance platform is used only for joiners. Which change do you raise?
options: Keep the spreadsheets but have reviewers comment on each approved line
Certify in the governance platform and revoke what owners do not sign off
Have the identity team approve every line so the review finishes faster
Move the review to yearly so reviewers can study every line more closely
cards.answer: Certify in the governance platform and revoke what owners do not sign off
cards.why: An identity governance system turns reviews into tracked certification campaigns: data owners attest to real entitlements, evidence is kept, and access nobody certifies is removed instead of left in place. Comments add effort, not assurance; the identity team cannot judge business need, which is the owner's call; reviewing less often lets privilege creep run longer.

cards.q: 02:05 · Identity plane. The draft password standard on your desk forces a change every 60 days and demands symbols, and the help desk reports staff cycling 'Summer2026!' variants. What do you recommend?
options: Shorten rotation to 30 days so any reused variant has much less time to be cracked
Add a rule that each new password differs from the last by four characters
Drop forced rotation, require length, and screen new ones against breach lists
Require two symbols and two digits so the variants become harder to guess
cards.answer: Drop forced rotation, require length, and screen new ones against breach lists
cards.why: NIST SP 800-63B favours long passwords checked against known-breached lists, changed only on evidence of compromise. Forced rotation and composition rules breed predictable patterns like seasonal variants, which is exactly what the help desk sees. Faster rotation and stricter composition make the patterns worse, and a difference rule is met by changing the year and symbol.

cards.q: 04:10 · Identity plane. Delivery drivers want the dispatch app and company mail on their own phones. Two phones lost last month held unencrypted manifests. Which design do you approve?
options: Allow any phone if drivers sign a policy promising to lock their screens
Issue a shared dispatch login so no driver's own account is ever exposed
Allow any phone and rely on the app's own password prompt for manifests
Allow access only from phones enrolled in MDM with encryption and wipe
cards.answer: Allow access only from phones enrolled in MDM with encryption and wipe
cards.why: Authenticating the device as well as the person belongs in the identity strategy: MDM enrolment gives each phone an identity the access policy can check, enforces encryption and screen lock, and allows remote wipe when one goes missing. A signed promise is not enforcement; a shared login destroys accountability; an app password does nothing for data cached on an unencrypted phone.

cards.q: 06:20 · Identity plane. The payment-switch admin console must be reachable only from the hardened jump hosts and only during approved change windows, whoever the user is. Which control do you configure?
options: A global rule on the console allowing only jump-host sessions in windows
A Switch-Admin role whose members may reach the console at any time
Owner-set permissions so each switch admin decides who else gets in
A named admin list plus an email reminder to use jump hosts in change windows
cards.answer: A global rule on the console allowing only jump-host sessions in windows
cards.why: Rule-based access control applies the same conditions, source and time, to every subject regardless of identity, which is what 'whoever the user is' requires; it layers under roles, not instead of them. A role alone grants access at any hour from anywhere; owner-set permissions are discretionary and spread access; a reminder is guidance, not a control.

cards.q: 23:55 · Identity plane. Your ticket: badge logs for the data-centre door show about 40 entries a night, but CCTV counts nearly 70 people, because staff hold the door for each other. Facilities asks what to fund. Which do you recommend?
options: Fund brighter signage telling staff not to hold the door for colleagues
Fund a one-person mantrap with anti-passback on the data-centre entrance
Fund a second badge reader on the inside so exits are logged as well
Fund more CCTV cameras so every person who enters is clearly recorded
cards.answer: Fund a one-person mantrap with anti-passback on the data-centre entrance
cards.why: Tailgating defeats the reader because it authenticates one person and admits many. A mantrap admits one person per badge read, and anti-passback stops a badge being handed back out for reuse. Signs rely on goodwill that is already failing; exit readers and extra cameras record the problem without preventing it, detection bought in place of access control.

cards.q: 00:05 · Identity plane. You are onboarding a carrier-rates SaaS to Tessaly's single sign-on. In testing it accepts an assertion you edited by hand with the signature stripped. The vendor wants go-live tomorrow. What do you do?
options: Go live and ask the vendor to fix signature checks in their next release
Go live but restrict the SaaS to users who already hold MFA at the IdP
Block go-live until it rejects unsigned assertions and checks audience
Replace SSO with a local SaaS password so the assertion flaw is avoided
cards.answer: Block go-live until it rejects unsigned assertions and checks audience
cards.why: In federation the service provider trusts the IdP only through the signature on each assertion. If it accepts edited or unsigned ones, anyone can claim to be anyone and MFA is bypassed because the IdP never sees them. Signature and audience checks are go-live criteria. Shipping now accepts a known total bypass; local passwords abandon federation instead of fixing the relying party.

cards.q: 01:20 · Identity plane. Joiner tickets for new customer-service agents say 'same access as Priya'. Priya has been here nine years and has moved teams twice, and six more tickets are queued tonight. How do you provision them?
options: Copy Priya's access as asked, then trim it at the next quarterly review
Grant nothing until each agent's manager lists every system they need
Copy the newest agent's access instead, as they carry less history
Grant the agent role defined with its owner, not Priya's personal set
cards.answer: Grant the agent role defined with its owner, not Priya's personal set
cards.why: Role-based provisioning gives each joiner the entitlement set defined for the job and agreed with its owner, so access matches function on day one. 'Same as' copying clones nine years of accumulated rights, and the newest agent may carry oddities of their own. Trimming later leaves the excess live meanwhile; listing every system from scratch is slow and error-prone.

cards.q: 02:30 · Identity plane. The network team logs in to 300 switches with a shared local 'admin' account. You are asked to centralise device logins so each engineer signs in as themselves and every command is recorded. Which do you build?
options: TACACS+ against the directory, with per-command authorization and logs
A local account per engineer on every switch, kept in sync by a script
A single strong shared password stored in the team's password manager
RADIUS with the shared account kept as the only user the switches know
cards.answer: TACACS+ against the directory, with per-command authorization and logs
cards.why: TACACS+ centralises authentication, authorization and accounting for device administration: each engineer uses their own directory identity, commands can be authorized one by one, and accounting records who ran what. Scripted local accounts sprawl across 300 boxes; a stronger shared password still leaves nobody accountable; RADIUS with one shared account keeps the anonymity the ticket is meant to end.

cards.q: 03:40 · Identity plane. The new label-printing microservice will call the shipping API. Its developers plan to bake a shared API key, the same one four other services use, into the container image. What do you require?
options: Keep the shared key but load it from an environment variable at start
Give the service its own workload identity with a short-lived credential
Generate a longer shared key and rotate it yearly for all five services
Put the shared key behind an IP allow list for the container subnet
cards.answer: Give the service its own workload identity with a short-lived credential
cards.why: Services need identities too: a distinct workload identity with short-lived, automatically issued credentials lets the shipping API know which service is calling, scope it, and revoke it without breaking four others. A shared key gives no attribution and one stolen copy works everywhere; moving or lengthening it keeps the sharing; an allow list trusts a whole subnet.

cards.q: 04:50 · Identity plane. Eight cloud engineers hold standing Owner rights on the production payments subscription, though each uses them about twice a month. The platform supports time-bound elevation with approval. What do you set up?
options: Keep standing Owner for all eight and review their sign-in logs monthly
Cut the group to the two most senior engineers with permanent Owner
Remove standing Owner and let engineers elevate for approved, timed windows
Keep standing Owner but require the engineers to use a named admin device
cards.answer: Remove standing Owner and let engineers elevate for approved, timed windows
cards.why: Just-in-time access removes standing privilege: rights exist only for the approved, time-boxed window when someone needs them, so a stolen engineer account is not an Owner account most of the time. Reviewing logs finds misuse afterwards; two permanent Owners still leave standing privilege and a bottleneck; an admin device helps but does not shrink the time privilege exists.

cards.q: 05:05 · Identity plane. A contractor's engineers visit overnight to service the parcel sorters. They sign a paper book at reception and then walk the building alone. Your ticket asks for a visitor process. What do you put in it?
options: A tablet sign-in in place of the paper book so names are easier to read
A permanent staff badge for each regular engineer so reception is skipped
A contract clause making the contractor liable for anything its staff do
Pre-booked visits, ID checks, dated visitor badges, escorts in secure areas
cards.answer: Pre-booked visits, ID checks, dated visitor badges, escorts in secure areas
cards.why: Visitor access is identified, time-limited and supervised: pre-booking ties the visit to a sponsor, an ID check proves who arrived, a dated badge marks them as a visitor, and escorts keep them out of areas they have no reason to be in. A tablet digitises the weak log; permanent badges grant standing access to non-staff; liability transfers cost, not risk.

cards.q: 06:35 · Identity plane. Harbourline, a new partner, asks for a directory trust with Tessaly. Harbourline already trusts two of its own subsidiaries, one breached last year. Only Harbourline's customs team needs one Tessaly app. What trust do you design?
options: A two-way transitive trust, since Harbourline vouches for its subsidiaries
A one-way, non-transitive trust scoped by selective auth to that one app
A two-way trust with SID filtering off so partner groups map cleanly
A one-way transitive trust so customs and the subsidiaries all get in
cards.answer: A one-way, non-transitive trust scoped by selective auth to that one app
cards.why: Transitive trust means Tessaly would also trust whoever Harbourline trusts, including the breached subsidiary. A one-way, non-transitive trust with selective authentication admits only Harbourline's users, and only to the named app, so trust stops at the partner. Turning SID filtering off invites privilege escalation across the boundary, and any transitive option inherits the subsidiary's risk.

cards.q: 23:30 · Identity plane. HR's feed shows a finance controller starting six months of parental leave tomorrow. Her account holds payment-approval rights and remote access. Which lifecycle action do you schedule?
options: Suspend sign-in and approval rights for the leave, restoring them on return
Delete the account and build a new one when she returns in six months
Leave everything active in case she needs to approve payments from home
Copy her approval rights to her deputy's account and leave hers active
cards.answer: Suspend sign-in and approval rights for the leave, restoring them on return
cards.why: The lifecycle covers more than joiners and leavers: extended absence is a state change, and suspending a dormant high-privilege login stops it being abused unnoticed. Deleting loses history and forces a full rebuild; leaving it active gives an attacker a quiet target; cover for her approvals should be a separate, approved grant to the deputy, not a copy of her rights.

cards.q: 00:45 · Identity plane. A red-team report shows they requested Kerberos service tickets for the SQL service account and cracked its eight-character password offline within hours. It has not changed since 2019. Which fix do you ticket?
options: Lock out any user who requests more than five service tickets an hour
Disable Kerberos for the SQL service and fall back to NTLM sign-in
Change it to a new eight-character password and rotate it each year
Move the service to a managed account with long, auto-rotated secrets
cards.answer: Move the service to a managed account with long, auto-rotated secrets
cards.why: Any domain user can request a service ticket, and part of it is encrypted with the service account's password, so a short password falls to offline cracking. Managed service accounts use long random secrets that rotate automatically, leaving nothing worth cracking. Lockouts do not stop a normal-looking request; NTLM is weaker still; a new eight-character password falls the same way.

cards.q: 01:50 · Identity plane. A pre-release test of the customer shipment portal shows that changing the order number in the URL displays another customer's invoice. The developers propose hiding the order number. What do you require before launch?
options: Hide order numbers from the URL and send them in a hidden form field
Make order numbers long and random so customers cannot guess others
Check on the server, per request, that the order belongs to the caller
Log invoice views and alert when one customer opens many orders
cards.answer: Check on the server, per request, that the order belongs to the caller
cards.why: Authorization belongs in the web application's server logic: every request for an object is checked against the signed-in user's rights, which fixes this insecure direct object reference. Hiding the number or moving it to a form field is obscurity any proxy defeats; random identifiers slow guessing but leaked links still work; alerting only detects abuse after invoices leak.

cards.q: 02:50 · Identity plane. A night supervisor reports losing the master key ring for every cabinet and cage in the Bristol depot, including the controlled-drug store run for a pharmacy client. Your move?
options: Wait a week for the keys to turn up before spending on locksmiths
Rekey the affected locks, drug store first, with a guard on it meanwhile
Issue the supervisor a spare master ring so the night shift keeps working
Log the loss and rekey all locks at the next planned facilities refresh
cards.answer: Rekey the affected locks, drug store first, with a guard on it meanwhile
cards.why: A lost master key compromises every lock it opens, so physical access control means rekeying, prioritised by what each door protects, with a guard on the highest-risk store until it is done. Waiting or deferring to a refresh leaves the drug store open to whoever holds the ring; a spare ring restores convenience while doubling the keys in circulation.

cards.q: 03:15 · Identity plane. Marketing bought a survey SaaS with its own logins, and 60 staff already have accounts there. Your ticket asks how it should join Tessaly's identity and access management. What do you set up?
options: Let marketing keep local logins and send you a user list each quarter
Block the SaaS at the proxy until marketing chooses another product
Create one shared marketing login and keep its password in a vault
SSO from the corporate IdP with automated provisioning, local logins off
cards.answer: SSO from the corporate IdP with automated provisioning, local logins off
cards.why: Bringing the SaaS under central identity and access management means one identity per person: SSO through the corporate IdP applies Tessaly's authentication and MFA, and automated provisioning such as SCIM creates and removes accounts as people join and leave. Quarterly lists leave leavers active for months; blocking punishes the business; a shared login destroys accountability.

cards.q: 04:25 · Identity plane. An account review shows a warehouse analyst holding rights from three past roles: stock control, returns and carrier billing. She now works only in carrier billing. What do you do with the finding?
options: Leave the old rights, since she may be asked to cover those teams again
Confirm her role with her manager and remove the two old role grants
Remove every right she holds and have her request billing access afresh
Note it for the annual audit and take no action until auditors ask
cards.answer: Confirm her role with her manager and remove the two old role grants
cards.why: Privilege creep is access that piles up as people move and nobody removes the old grants. Confirming the current role with the manager and removing what no longer matches restores least privilege; any cover should be a separate, time-bound request. Wiping everything stops her real work tonight, and deferring to an audit leaves excess rights live for months.

cards.q: 05:30 · Identity plane. The canteen fingerprint time clocks reject one in five genuine scans, queues form at every shift change, and the clocks only record attendance. The vendor offers a sensitivity setting. Which change do you approve?
options: Keep the threshold and add a second fingerprint scan to every clock-in
Raise the threshold so the clocks match the data-centre door readers
Lower the clocks' matching threshold, accepting more false accepts
Swap the clocks for the data-centre iris readers to cut the rejections
cards.answer: Lower the clocks' matching threshold, accepting more false accepts
cards.why: A biometric threshold trades false rejections against false acceptances. For attendance, a false accept costs little while false rejects stall a shift, so lowering the matching threshold is the right risk call; the same move would be wrong on a high-security door. Raising it lengthens the queues, a second scan doubles the chances of rejection, and iris readers are costly overkill.

cards.q: 06:05 · Identity plane. A defence-logistics contract requires that staff cannot share classified shipment files, even with colleagues, and that access follows clearances and file labels set by security. Which access model do you configure?
options: Mandatory controls: system-enforced labels matched to user clearance
Discretionary controls, with owners told not to share outside the team
Role groups for the contract team with sharing left on for flexibility
Discretionary controls with a DLP alert whenever a file is shared out
cards.answer: Mandatory controls: system-enforced labels matched to user clearance
cards.why: Mandatory access control is enforced by the system: security sets labels and clearances, and users, owners included, cannot pass access on, which is what the contract demands. Discretionary models let owners grant access, so a rule not to share is only a request; roles without labels ignore clearance; a DLP alert fires after the file has already moved.

cards.q: 23:05 · Identity plane. An inventory finds 140 service accounts; 55 have no named owner, no description, and passwords older than the people who set them. Which lifecycle control do you add?
options: Reset all 140 passwords tonight to one strong shared value for simplicity
Delete the 55 unowned accounts at once, since nobody claims them
Exclude service accounts from reviews, as they do not belong to people
Require a named owner and purpose for each; disable any left unclaimed
cards.answer: Require a named owner and purpose for each; disable any left unclaimed
cards.why: Non-human identities need a lifecycle too: every account has an accountable owner and documented purpose, and one nobody claims is disabled first, then removed after a quiet period, so a hidden dependency surfaces without an outage. Deleting outright can break a payment job at 03:00; one shared password is worse than the old ones; excluding them from reviews is how this happened.

cards.q: 00:55 · Identity plane. Two staff this month approved push prompts they had not started, after being sent dozens at night. The MFA platform supports number matching and showing the sign-in location. Which change do you roll out?
options: Remind staff by email never to approve a prompt they did not start
Require number matching, with location shown, on every push approval
Cap push prompts at twenty per night so staff are bothered less often
Replace push with SMS codes so users type the code into the sign-in page
cards.answer: Require number matching, with location shown, on every push approval
cards.why: Push fatigue works because a plain approve button needs no context. Number matching makes the user enter the number shown on the sign-in screen, so a prompt they did not start cannot be approved blindly, and location adds a cue. Reminders already failed; a cap still allows bombing; SMS codes are exposed to SIM swap and real-time phishing.

cards.q: 01:35 · Identity plane. Claims handlers should see claims only for their own region, only while on shift and only from managed devices. Role groups for every region, shift and device combination would top 200. What do you design?
options: Create the 200 groups and assign handlers to each combination they need
One claims-handler role with access to every region's claims at any hour
Attribute-based policies that evaluate region, shift time and device state
Let team leaders grant claim access to handlers as each case comes in
cards.answer: Attribute-based policies that evaluate region, shift time and device state
cards.why: Attribute-based access control evaluates attributes of the user, the resource and the context, here region, shift time and device compliance, in one policy at request time, avoiding role explosion. Two hundred groups become unmanageable and drift; one broad role breaks least privilege across regions; case-by-case grants by team leaders are discretionary and leave no consistent rule.

cards.q: 02:20 · Identity plane. External auditors need read access to the general ledger for three weeks from Monday. Last year's auditor accounts were still active the following March. How do you provision them?
options: Named read-only accounts, sponsored by finance, that expire with fieldwork
One shared read-only auditor login whose password finance changes later
Named accounts with full finance rights so auditors are never held up
Re-enable last year's auditor accounts, since the same firm is returning
cards.answer: Named read-only accounts, sponsored by finance, that expire with fieldwork
cards.why: Temporary access should be provisioned with its end built in: named accounts keep accountability, a finance sponsor owns the need, and an expiry date removes access without anyone having to remember, which is what failed last year. A shared login loses attribution; full finance rights exceed a read need; old accounts carry unknown history and may belong to people who left.

cards.q: 03:55 · Identity plane. A packet capture on the warehouse LAN shows the stock app binding to the directory with LDAP simple bind on port 389, sending its service password in clear text on every connection. Which change do you raise?
options: Move the directory to its own VLAN so fewer hosts can sniff the traffic
Rotate the service password monthly, since it crosses the wire daily
Switch to anonymous bind so no password ever crosses the network
Move the bind to LDAPS or StartTLS and rotate the exposed password
cards.answer: Move the bind to LDAPS or StartTLS and rotate the exposed password
cards.why: Simple bind sends credentials in clear text; protecting the channel with LDAPS or StartTLS encrypts the bind, and the password already seen on the wire must be treated as exposed and rotated. A VLAN narrows who can sniff but anyone on it still can; faster rotation leaves each new password readable; anonymous bind removes authentication and opens the directory to anyone.

cards.q: 04:05 · Identity plane. A request asks to add a payables clerk to Vendor-Master-Edit so she can fix supplier bank details. She already holds Payment-Release, and her manager has approved the request. What do you do?
options: Grant it, since her manager approved and she has years of trusted service
Decline the pairing and route bank-detail edits to someone else in AP
Grant it, and have internal audit sample her payments once a quarter
Grant it for one week only, then remove it once the backlog is cleared
cards.answer: Decline the pairing and route bank-detail edits to someone else in AP
cards.why: Editing supplier bank details and releasing payments are a toxic combination: one person could point a supplier at their own account and pay it. Separation of duties keeps the two in different hands whatever a manager approves. Quarterly sampling finds fraud after the money has gone, and a time limit still leaves a week when one person holds both halves.

cards.q: 05:20 · Identity plane. A warehouse supervisor who left in 2024 is being rehired as a driver. HR asks you to 'switch her old account back on'. It still holds her supervisor groups. How do you provision her?
options: Re-enable it as asked, since her identity and history are already there
Re-enable it with all groups and let her new manager trim what is unneeded
Provision driver access only, removing the old supervisor groups first
Create a second account for driving and keep the old one enabled too
cards.answer: Provision driver access only, removing the old supervisor groups first
cards.why: A rehire is a joiner: access is granted for the new role, not restored from the old one. Reusing the identity is fine, but the stale supervisor groups must go before sign-in is enabled, or she returns with rights she no longer needs. Handing the trim to a manager invites privilege creep, and a second enabled account doubles the attack surface for one person.

cards.q: 06:25 · Identity plane. A new depot goes live Monday with its own domain controller. The build sheet has the controller's clock set by hand and no time source for the depot's servers. What do you add before sign-off?
options: Point the controller at the domain time hierarchy and the servers at it
Nothing, since clocks set by hand drift only a few seconds each month
A monthly task for the depot lead to check the clocks against a phone
Widen Kerberos clock tolerance to an hour so drift never blocks sign-in
cards.answer: Point the controller at the domain time hierarchy and the servers at it
cards.why: Kerberos timestamps its authenticators and rejects any outside a small skew, five minutes by default, to block replay. A consistent time hierarchy keeps controllers and servers in step so sign-ins work and logs line up. Hand-set clocks drift beyond tolerance; manual checks miss it between visits; widening tolerance to an hour opens a long replay window.

cards.q: 23:20 · Identity plane. The fleet-telematics system grants 900 drivers, mechanics and planners individual permissions, one user at a time. Every change takes a ticket, and nobody can say who is able to edit routes. What do you propose?
options: Give every user the same broad permission set to end the ticket queue
Let each depot manager edit any user's permissions directly in the app
Define roles per job, grant permissions to roles, then users to roles
Export the permissions to a spreadsheet so auditors can read them yearly
cards.answer: Define roles per job, grant permissions to roles, then users to roles
cards.why: Role-based access control assigns permissions to job-function roles and people to roles, so a new mechanic gets the mechanic role in one step and 'who can edit routes' is answered by looking at one role. A single broad set breaks least privilege; manager-edited permissions are discretionary and drift; a yearly spreadsheet documents the mess without controlling it.

cards.q: 00:10 · Identity plane. A phishing kit that relays sign-ins in real time captured an IT admin's password and SMS code last week. Domain and cloud admins all use SMS today. Which authenticator do you move them to?
options: An authenticator app showing six-digit codes that change every 30 seconds
Email one-time codes sent to the admin's corporate mailbox at sign-in
Longer 20-character admin passwords, keeping SMS as the second factor
Hardware security keys using FIDO2, bound to Tessaly's sign-in domain
cards.answer: Hardware security keys using FIDO2, bound to Tessaly's sign-in domain
cards.why: A real-time relay forwards whatever code the victim types, so SMS, app and email codes all fall to it. FIDO2 security keys sign a challenge bound to the genuine site's origin, so a look-alike page gets nothing usable: they are phishing-resistant. Longer passwords do not help when the password is captured along with the code.

cards.q: 01:05 · Identity plane. A fraud investigator in payments, fully cleared, asks for read access to every customer's full card history 'to be ready for anything'. Her current case covers 12 accounts. What do you grant?
options: Read access to all histories, since her clearance already covers them
Access to the 12 accounts in her open case, widened as new cases open
Access to all histories for a month, then a review with her manager
No access, and have a colleague read the records out to her instead
cards.answer: Access to the 12 accounts in her open case, widened as new cases open
cards.why: Clearance says what someone may see in principle; need-to-know limits it to what their current work requires. Granting the 12 accounts in her case, and more as cases open, keeps exposure proportionate. Blanket access, even for a month, exposes every customer's history through one account; relaying records through a colleague just moves the disclosure and loses the audit trail.

cards.q: 02:10 · Identity plane. The customer shipping portal is taking 40,000 sign-in attempts an hour from thousands of addresses, each trying a different email and password pair, with about 2% succeeding. What do you put in place first?
options: Lock every customer account after three failed attempts for 24 hours
Block the country the largest share of the traffic appears to come from
Rate-limit and challenge risky sign-ins, and screen for breached passwords
Email all customers asking them to change their passwords this week
cards.answer: Rate-limit and challenge risky sign-ins, and screen for breached passwords
cards.why: This is credential stuffing: pairs leaked elsewhere replayed at scale. Rate limiting and challenges on risky sign-ins slow it, and screening against breached-password lists stops known pairs working, with forced resets for accounts already hit. Three-strike lockouts let the attacker lock out real customers; geo-blocks are dodged with proxies; a general email changes nothing tonight.

cards.q: 03:25 · Identity plane. On the project file share, folder owners set their own permissions. You find the M&A folder shared with 'Everyone' by its owner, who wanted a contractor to read one file. Which change do you propose?
options: Remove 'Everyone', share only that file, and limit what owners can grant
Leave it, since this model gives the owner the right to share the folder
Take ownership of every folder on the share into the identity team
Delete the contractor's account so nobody outside can use the grant
cards.answer: Remove 'Everyone', share only that file, and limit what owners can grant
cards.why: Discretionary access control lets owners grant access at will, which is how 'Everyone' landed on M&A data. Removing the grant, sharing the single file, and limiting what owners may grant, such as blocking broad groups, keeps owner flexibility without letting one click expose a folder. Taking every folder into IT kills ownership; deleting the contractor leaves 'Everyone' in place.

cards.q: 04:40 · Identity plane. The vendor of the new remote-access gateway offers a '2FA' option that asks for the user's password and then a six-digit personal PIN. Remote access reaches the payments network. Which do you approve?
options: The vendor option, since two separate secrets are checked at sign-in
A 16-character password with no second prompt of any kind
Password plus PIN, with the PIN changed every 30 days for safety
Password plus a code from a registered device or hardware token
cards.answer: Password plus a code from a registered device or hardware token
cards.why: Two-factor authentication needs factors of different types. A password and a PIN are both something you know, so one phishing page or keylogger captures both. Adding something you have, a code from a registered device or hardware token, is genuine 2FA. Changing the PIN often or lengthening the password still leaves a single factor type.

cards.q: 05:50 · Identity plane. A treasury officer's smart card for the payments workstation was stolen with her bag tonight; she still knows her PIN. The workstations check certificates only against a revocation list published weekly. What do you do?
options: Revoke the certificate and move workstations to live OCSP checking
Reset her Windows password, since the card is useless without it
Wait for next week's revocation list, since the thief lacks her PIN
Issue her a new card and leave the old certificate valid until expiry
cards.answer: Revoke the certificate and move workstations to live OCSP checking
cards.why: Certificate-based sign-in stops a stolen card only once the relying system learns the certificate is revoked. Revoking it and moving to live OCSP checking closes the week-long gap a stale list leaves. A PIN is a small keyspace and can be observed, so hoping the thief lacks it is not a control; a password reset is irrelevant to card sign-in; a new card leaves the old one working.

cards.q: 06:40 · Identity plane. Warehouse pickers share six terminals on the dock, each signing in through SSO. Audit logs show picks recorded under whoever signed in last, sometimes for hours. What do you change?
options: One shared dock login so the logs stop naming the wrong picker
Short idle timeouts, with a badge tap so each picker signs in fast
Longer SSO sessions so pickers are not slowed by frequent sign-ins
A notice asking pickers to sign out whenever they leave the terminal
cards.answer: Short idle timeouts, with a badge tap so each picker signs in fast
cards.why: On shared terminals a session that outlives its user breaks accountability: actions land on someone who has walked away. Short idle timeouts end the session, and a fast badge tap keeps re-authentication practical so pickers do not work around it. A shared login removes attribution entirely; longer sessions worsen it; a notice relies on memory at shift pace.

cards.q: 23:45 · Identity plane. Finance users sign in to the treasury portal once each morning with MFA and can release payments of any size all day. A hijacked session last quarter released a large transfer. What do you require?
options: A shorter morning session of four hours, then a full sign-in again
MFA only at the morning sign-in, but with a longer, stronger password
A daily email to finance listing every payment released the day before
Fresh MFA at the moment of releasing any payment above a set threshold
cards.answer: Fresh MFA at the moment of releasing any payment above a set threshold
cards.why: Step-up authentication demands fresh, strong proof of identity at the point of a high-risk action, so a stolen or hijacked session cannot release large payments on its own. Shorter sessions shrink the window but a hijacker can still act inside it; a stronger password protects only the morning sign-in; a next-day email detects the loss after the money has left.

cards.q: 00:30 · Identity plane. Your ticket: plan retiring NTLMv1 across the domain after a relay attack last month. Nobody knows which old systems still depend on it, and a scanner at one depot is suspected. What is the first step?
options: Block NTLMv1 domain-wide tonight and fix whatever breaks in the morning
Leave NTLMv1 on, since the depot scanner might stop working without it
Allow NTLMv1 only from the depot's subnet and block it everywhere else
Turn on NTLM auditing to find dependents, then fix them and block v1
cards.answer: Turn on NTLM auditing to find dependents, then fix them and block v1
cards.why: Retiring a legacy protocol is a change, and change starts with knowing its dependents: NTLM auditing shows which systems still use v1 so each can be upgraded or isolated before enforcement. Blocking blind risks halting depot operations overnight; leaving it on keeps the relay exposure; an allow rule for a whole subnet exempts every host there, not just the scanner.

cards.q: 01:15 · Identity plane. Dispatch planners sign in once a day and stay signed in to the routing console. Last week a session token stolen from a Leeds planner was replayed from a data centre abroad for six hours. Which design do you approve?
options: Re-check each session's location and device, re-prompting on change
Shorten planner sessions to eight hours so a stolen token dies sooner
Require a stronger password at the one daily sign-in for every planner
Block all sign-ins from outside the UK at the routing console's firewall
cards.answer: Re-check each session's location and device, re-prompting on change
cards.why: Continuous authentication re-evaluates trust through the session, not only at sign-in: when the location or device behind a token changes, the platform demands fresh proof, so a replayed token fails at once. An eight-hour session still gave the attacker six hours; the password was never used in the replay; a geo-block is dodged by an attacker renting a UK host.

cards.q: 02:35 · Identity plane. If the cloud IdP goes down, nobody can reach the admin console to fix it, because every admin signs in through that IdP. You are asked to design emergency access. What do you set up?
options: One admin keeps a local account with a known password for emergencies
No emergency path, since any bypass of the IdP is a security weakness
Two sealed break-glass accounts outside the IdP, alerting on every use
A shared admin password printed in the ops runbook for the on-call team
cards.answer: Two sealed break-glass accounts outside the IdP, alerting on every use
cards.why: Break-glass accounts give a controlled path when normal authorization fails: kept outside the IdP dependency, credentials sealed, use monitored so every sign-in raises an alert and a review. One admin's private account is standing privilege without oversight; no path at all turns an IdP outage into a lockout; a runbook password is readable by anyone holding the runbook.

cards.q: 03:45 · Identity plane. Code review for the new driver-app backend shows passwords stored as plain SHA-256 hashes, and two drivers with the same password have identical hashes. What goes in the review?
options: Encrypt the SHA-256 hashes with a key kept in the application config
Store each password with a unique salt and a slow hash such as Argon2
Hash twice with SHA-256 so each password takes two rounds to crack
Store them in a separate table only the backend service account reads
cards.answer: Store each password with a unique salt and a slow hash such as Argon2
cards.why: A unique salt per password means identical passwords produce different hashes, so precomputed tables and crack-once-use-everywhere attacks fail; a deliberately slow algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt makes each guess expensive. Encrypting with a key stored beside the data adds little once the server is breached; a second fast hash barely slows cracking; table permissions do not change what a stolen dump reveals.

cards.q: 04:15 · Identity plane. Six firewall engineers share the root password for the perimeter firewalls, kept in a spreadsheet. It has not changed since one of them left last year. Which control do you implement?
options: Change the root password now and email the new one to the five engineers
Protect the spreadsheet with a password known only to the team lead
Keep the spreadsheet but change the root password whenever someone leaves
A privileged access vault with checkout, rotation after use, and logging
cards.answer: A privileged access vault with checkout, rotation after use, and logging
cards.why: A privileged access management vault holds the root credential so nobody needs to know it: engineers check it out under their own identity, the vault logs who had it and rotates it after use, restoring individual accountability for a shared account. Emailing a new password recreates the leak; a password on a spreadsheet is a thin wrapper; rotating only on leavers leaves every use untraceable.

cards.q: 05:35 · Identity plane. After a password-spray attempt, someone proposes locking any account for an hour after three failed sign-ins. Dispatch runs around the clock, and a locked-out dispatcher delays trucks. What do you recommend instead?
options: Lock accounts permanently after three failures until the desk resets
Remove lockout so dispatchers are never locked out, and rely on alerts
Throttle failures by source, ban common passwords, and require MFA
Lock accounts for an hour after three failures, exactly as proposed
cards.answer: Throttle failures by source, ban common passwords, and require MFA
cards.why: Spraying tries one common password across many accounts, so per-account lockout barely touches it while handing the attacker a way to lock out dispatchers. Throttling by source, banning common passwords and requiring MFA defeat the spray without a denial-of-service lever. Permanent lockout makes that lever worse; removing lockout leaves unlimited guessing watched only by alerts.

cards.q: 06:15 · Identity plane. A route-optimisation partner needs to read delivery addresses from Tessaly's orders API. Its integration request asks for the 'orders.admin' scope, which also allows edits and refunds. What do you grant?
options: The requested admin scope, since the partner has signed a data NDA
A read-only scope limited to delivery addresses for that client ID
The admin scope for the pilot, trimmed if their calls look excessive
Your own admin token, so the partner needs no client of its own
cards.answer: A read-only scope limited to delivery addresses for that client ID
cards.why: An integration's authorization is expressed in the scopes its token carries. Granting only the read scope it needs applies least privilege, so a compromised partner key cannot edit orders or issue refunds. An NDA is a contractual control, not a technical limit; trimming later leaves refund rights live through the pilot; lending your own token destroys attribution and hands over everything you hold.

cards.q: 23:10 · Identity plane. Handheld scanners join the warehouse Wi-Fi with one pre-shared key every temp worker has seen, and a rogue laptop was found on it. You are asked to redesign how scanners sign in to the network. What do you choose?
options: Change the shared key monthly and give it to permanent staff only
Hide the network name so casual devices cannot see it to connect
802.1X with EAP-TLS, each scanner holding its own device certificate
Filter by MAC address so only the listed scanners can join the Wi-Fi
cards.answer: 802.1X with EAP-TLS, each scanner holding its own device certificate
cards.why: Port-based authentication with 802.1X and EAP-TLS authenticates each device by its own certificate, so a leaked shared key admits nothing and a lost scanner is revoked individually. Rotating a shared key still spreads it to everyone; hiding the network name is trivially bypassed; MAC addresses are broadcast in the clear and easily spoofed by the rogue laptop.

cards.q: 00:40 · Identity plane. A scan flags the invoicing web server as trusted for unconstrained delegation, so it caches the Kerberos tickets of every user who connects, admins included. It only needs to reach one SQL database for them. What do you change?
options: Leave delegation as is but keep admins from signing in to that server
Switch it to constrained delegation limited to that one SQL service
Remove delegation and give the web server a SQL admin account instead
Leave it and add antivirus so tickets on the server stay protected
cards.answer: Switch it to constrained delegation limited to that one SQL service
cards.why: Unconstrained delegation lets a server impersonate connecting users to any service, so compromising it yields every cached ticket. Constrained delegation limits impersonation to the one SQL service it needs, which is least privilege for delegation. Keeping admins away helps but leaves every other user's ticket reusable; a SQL admin account loses per-user authorization; antivirus does not change what the server is allowed to do.

cards.q: 01:45 · Identity plane. The payroll database server sits in a cage only three people can enter, so its admin console accepts any sign-in from the office network with the default account. Facilities says the cage makes it secure. What do you require?
options: A second lock on the cage so only two people can physically reach it
CCTV inside the cage so anyone who touches the server is recorded
Nothing more, since the cage already limits who can reach the server
Named accounts, the default login disabled, and access from admin hosts
cards.answer: Named accounts, the default login disabled, and access from admin hosts
cards.why: Physical controls protect the box, not the network path to it: anyone on the office network can reach the console, so the cage does nothing for that route. Logical access controls, named accounts, disabling the default login and restricting which hosts may connect, protect the system where it is actually exposed. More locks or cameras on the cage harden the wrong door.

cards.q: 06:40 · Network core. Last night an intruder hopped from a compromised handheld scanner in the Rotterdam depot straight to the card-settlement database, because depot devices and payment servers share one flat network. The after-action board wants one lasting control in the plan. Which do you write in?
options: Buy a network detection appliance and leave the flat addressing as it is today
Split depot devices into their own zone with default-deny rules toward payments
Reset every scanner's password and close the incident as a credential problem
Allowlist the scanners on the core firewall so tonight's alerts stop repeating
cards.answer: Split depot devices into their own zone with default-deny rules toward payments
cards.why: Segmentation with default deny is defense in depth at the network layer: a compromised depot device can no longer reach payment systems at all, shrinking the blast radius. A detection appliance only watches the same flat path being used again, and a password reset treats one symptom while the architecture that allowed the pivot stays unchanged.

cards.q: 06:10 · Network core. The overnight sweep found a consumer Wi-Fi router plugged into a wall jack in the Leeds depot break room, bridging anyone nearby onto the corporate LAN. It has been pulled. What lasting control goes in the after-action plan?
options: Hide the corporate SSID so staff are less likely to join a rogue network
Issue a memo banning personal network gear and rely on staff to comply
Lower transmit power on the company access points to stay inside the walls
Run wireless intrusion prevention and require 802.1X on every wired wall port
cards.answer: Run wireless intrusion prevention and require 802.1X on every wired wall port
cards.why: A rogue access point is a component nobody approved sitting inside the perimeter. Wireless intrusion prevention detects and contains unauthorised radios, and 802.1X port authentication stops an unknown device getting a live wired link in the first place. Hiding the SSID is not a control, since hidden networks are trivially discovered, and a memo alone relies on goodwill instead of enforcement.

cards.q: 02:15 · Network core. The TLS certificate on the partner payments API gateway expired at midnight and carrier systems are failing to connect. A partner's engineer suggests everyone simply switch off certificate validation until morning. What do you do?
options: Agree that partners disable certificate checks until the day shift arrives
Serve the API over plain HTTP behind the firewall for the rest of the night
Issue a self-signed certificate and ask partners to trust it without checks
Raise an emergency change to renew the certificate and keep validation on
cards.answer: Raise an emergency change to renew the certificate and keep validation on
cards.why: Certificate validation is what lets partners authenticate the gateway; without it the channel is open to interception. An emergency change restores a trusted certificate while keeping the change record. Turning validation off, or asking partners to blindly trust a self-signed certificate, trains every connected system to accept an impostor, and plain HTTP removes confidentiality and integrity outright.

cards.q: 03:05 · Network core. Monitoring shows an unknown autonomous system announcing Tessaly's public prefix, the block Tessaly holds from ARIN, and some card traffic is detouring through it. The prefix has no signed route origin record. What do you do first?
options: Block the rogue AS number on the perimeter firewall and wait to see
Have upstream ISPs filter the bogus route and publish ROAs through ARIN
Move every public DNS record to new addresses from a different block
Wait for the registry to notice and withdraw the rogue announcement
cards.answer: Have upstream ISPs filter the bogus route and publish ROAs through ARIN
cards.why: This is a BGP route hijack: the traffic is diverted before it ever reaches Tessaly, so only upstream providers can filter the bad route now. Publishing route origin authorisations through ARIN, the regional internet registry holding the allocation, lets networks using RPKI reject invalid origins in future. A perimeter firewall rule never sees the diverted packets, and registries do not police routing tables.

cards.q: 01:35 · Network core. An access switch in the Antwerp depot has started flooding every frame out of every port; its MAC address table is full of thousands of random entries arriving from a single wall port. What is your move?
options: Reboot the switch so the address table clears and let the depot carry on
Move the depot to a new VLAN without doing anything about the wall port
Shut the offending port and enable port security to cap learned addresses
Mirror the depot ports to the IDS and keep watching the flood develop
cards.answer: Shut the offending port and enable port security to cap learned addresses
cards.why: Flooding the MAC table makes a switch fail open and behave like a hub, so every frame can be sniffed. Shutting the port contains the source, and port security limits how many addresses a port may learn, which prevents a repeat. A reboot clears the table only until the flood refills it, and a new VLAN still carries the same port.

cards.q: 00:50 · Network core. The core routers are still managed over Telnet, and endpoint telemetry shows a packet capture tool running on a jump host that shares the management segment. What do you do?
options: Keep Telnet but change router passwords weekly from tonight onwards
Uninstall the capture tool and treat the matter as closed by morning
Rotate router passwords and move management to SSH on a separate network
Restrict Telnet to the jump host, since it is already the admin path
cards.answer: Rotate router passwords and move management to SSH on a separate network
cards.why: Telnet sends credentials in cleartext, so anyone capturing on that segment has probably eavesdropped on them already: rotation is required. SSH encrypts the session, and an isolated management network keeps admin traffic away from general hosts. Weekly rotation still sends each new password in the clear, and removing the tool ignores what it has already captured.

cards.q: 04:25 · Network core. A point-of-sale subnet is sending thousands of long, random-looking DNS queries straight to an external resolver on port 53, bypassing Tessaly's own DNS servers. What do you do first?
options: Add the external resolver's address to a watchlist and review it next week
Shut down the internal DNS servers, since the POS subnet is not using them
Increase the DNS cache lifetime so the POS hosts send fewer outbound queries
Block outbound port 53 and force every POS lookup through internal resolvers
cards.answer: Block outbound port 53 and force every POS lookup through internal resolvers
cards.why: Long random subdomains sent directly to an outside resolver are the signature of DNS tunnelling for exfiltration. Forcing all resolution through internal resolvers and denying direct outbound DNS contains the channel and gives you logs to inspect. A watchlist leaves data leaving for a week, and caching changes nothing because every tunnelled query is unique.

cards.q: 02:55 · Network core. The carrier self-service portal is being hit with malformed HTTP requests carrying SQL fragments. The only thing in front of it is a stateful packet filter, which lets the traffic through because it is valid TCP on port 443. What do you deploy?
options: Put an application-layer proxy in front that inspects the HTTP content
Raise the stateful firewall's session timeout to absorb the request load
Close port 443 at the edge and take the portal offline until the morning
Add more packet-filter rules keyed on the attackers' source port numbers
cards.answer: Put an application-layer proxy in front that inspects the HTTP content
cards.why: A stateful packet filter judges addresses, ports and session state; it cannot read what is inside an HTTP request. An application-layer proxy firewall terminates the connection and inspects the content, so injection payloads can be blocked while real carriers keep working. Closing 443 turns an attack into a self-inflicted outage, and source ports are random, so rules on them block nothing.

cards.q: 03:40 · Network core. A finance user's remote-access VPN account has logged in from two continents within ten minutes and is now browsing file shares. The user is asleep at home. What is your move?
options: Kill the VPN session, disable the account, and require MFA on the concentrator
Let the session continue so you can learn which shares the intruder wants
Email the user to ask whether they are travelling and wait for their reply
Block the second country at the edge and leave the account itself enabled
cards.answer: Kill the VPN session, disable the account, and require MFA on the concentrator
cards.why: Impossible travel on a remote-access tunnel means stolen credentials inside the network. Terminating the session and disabling the account contains it, and multi-factor authentication on the VPN concentrator stops a password alone opening the channel again. Watching lets data leave, waiting on a sleeping user wastes the window, and geo-blocking is bypassed by switching exit nodes.

cards.q: 05:15 · Network core. Laptops on the Hamburg office VLAN have picked up IPv6 addresses and a default route from a host nobody recognises. Tessaly's policy says IPv6 is not in use, so no IPv6 controls were ever configured. What do you do?
options: Ignore the alert, since Tessaly has never deployed IPv6 on this network
Add IPv4 firewall rules to block the rogue host's IPv4 address only
Disconnect the whole VLAN until IPv6 is stripped from every laptop
Isolate the host, enable RA Guard, and bring IPv6 under the same policy
cards.answer: Isolate the host, enable RA Guard, and bring IPv6 under the same policy
cards.why: Modern operating systems run IPv6 by default, so rogue router advertisements let an attacker become the gateway for all IPv6 traffic, a man-in-the-middle position. Isolating the host contains it; RA Guard on the switches blocks unauthorised advertisements, and governing IPv6 like IPv4 closes the blind spot. Ignoring it because it is officially unused is exactly how the gap arose.

cards.q: 23:40 · Network core. An unmanaged laptop has plugged into a wall port in the Lyon depot office and started scanning the subnet. Network access control has flagged it as unknown. What is your move?
options: Have NAC move the port to the quarantine VLAN and capture the device details
Disable every wall port in the building until the day shift can check them
Let the laptop keep scanning so you can observe the attacker's full toolkit
Push a remote wipe to the laptop through the corporate device management tool
cards.answer: Have NAC move the port to the quarantine VLAN and capture the device details
cards.why: Network access control exists for this: it moves an unknown device to a quarantine VLAN, containing it on that one port while you collect the details to investigate. Shutting every port punishes the whole depot for one device, letting the scan run widens exposure, and a remote wipe cannot work on a laptop that was never enrolled in device management.

cards.q: 01:20 · Network core. On the payments VLAN, a workstation is answering ARP requests for the default gateway's address, and settlement traffic is now flowing through it. What do you do first?
options: Clear the ARP caches on the payment servers and hope it does not recur
Add a static route on the gateway that points back at the payment hosts
Isolate the workstation and turn on dynamic ARP inspection for the VLAN
Restart the gateway router so it reclaims its own address from the host
cards.answer: Isolate the workstation and turn on dynamic ARP inspection for the VLAN
cards.why: Gratuitous ARP replies claiming the gateway place the workstation in the middle of the traffic, a man-in-the-middle interception. Isolating it contains the attack, and dynamic ARP inspection validates ARP against trusted bindings so the poisoning cannot recur. Clearing caches or restarting the router lasts only until the next forged reply, and a static route works at the wrong layer.

cards.q: 02:05 · Network core. Utilisation on every Ethernet link in the Madrid building just hit 100 percent and switches are close to unresponsive. The logs show the same broadcast frames circling endlessly after a contractor patched a cable between two wall ports. What do you do?
options: Reboot the core switches so the storm clears and the building recovers
Pull the looped patch cable and enforce BPDU guard on all the edge ports
Upgrade the uplinks to faster links so the storm has room to pass through
Add a firewall rule that blocks the broadcast address on the Madrid VLAN
cards.answer: Pull the looped patch cable and enforce BPDU guard on all the edge ports
cards.why: Ethernet frames carry no time-to-live, so a layer-2 loop circulates broadcasts until links saturate. Removing the loop stops the storm, and BPDU guard with spanning tree shuts any edge port that starts behaving like a switch, preventing a repeat. Rebooting brings the loop straight back, bigger links just fill faster, and a firewall never sees traffic inside one broadcast domain.

cards.q: 04:50 · Network core. One of the two power supplies in the primary core router has failed, and the second is running hot. There is no spare on site, and the device carries all of tonight's settlement traffic. What do you do?
options: Leave the router as it is, since one working power supply is still enough
Fail traffic over to the standby core per the runbook and call vendor support
