Swap in a power supply taken from the lab router in the test environment
Shut the router down for safety and let settlement wait for the day shift
cards.answer: Fail traffic over to the standby core per the runbook and call vendor support
cards.why: Securing network components includes their availability: redundant hardware, support contracts and a tested failover runbook. Moving traffic to the standby core keeps settlement running while the vendor replaces the part under contract. Running on a single hot supply risks an unplanned outage, an unapproved lab part bypasses change control, and a voluntary shutdown creates the outage you are trying to avoid.

cards.q: 23:25 · Network core. A change ticket from the network team proposes pushing switch configurations to all forty depots over TFTP across the WAN, because the old tooling already supports it. Which do you approve?
options: Approve only if configs travel over SCP or SFTP with authenticated accounts
Approve the TFTP push as written, since the WAN links are privately leased
Approve TFTP and schedule the pushes at night when fewer people are watching
Approve TFTP if the config files are renamed so they are hard to identify
cards.answer: Approve only if configs travel over SCP or SFTP with authenticated accounts
cards.why: TFTP has no authentication and no encryption, so switch configurations, which often hold credentials and community strings, cross the WAN readable and alterable by anyone on the path. SCP or SFTP gives an authenticated, encrypted channel. A private lease is not encryption, quiet hours do not stop capture, and renaming files is obscurity rather than protection.

cards.q: 00:20 · Network core. A ticket asks you to sign off a new fibre run between the Dublin warehouse and office. The only route is a riser shared with two other tenants. What goes in the approval conditions?
options: Rely on VLAN tagging to keep Tessaly's frames private inside the riser
Label the fibre clearly so the other tenants do not unplug it by accident
Run it in locked conduit and encrypt the traffic that crosses the link
Rely on switch port security at both ends to detect any physical tap
cards.answer: Run it in locked conduit and encrypt the traffic that crosses the link
cards.why: Controls at higher layers do nothing if someone can reach the cable itself: physical-layer protection means locked conduit to deter tapping, with link encryption so a successful tap yields nothing readable. VLAN tags are just labels in cleartext frames, port security watches MAC addresses rather than light on a fibre, and a clear label only helps an attacker find the run.

cards.q: 03:30 · Network core. Your ticket is the quarterly firewall rule review. You find an any-to-any allow rule added by a vendor engineer two years ago, with no ticket reference and no named owner. What do you do?
options: Delete it on the spot tonight so the attack surface shrinks straight away
Trace its traffic and owner, then replace it with narrow rules or remove it
Leave it untouched, since nothing has broken in the two years it existed
Move it to the top of the ruleset so the next auditors notice it faster
cards.answer: Trace its traffic and owner, then replace it with narrow rules or remove it
cards.why: An undocumented any-any rule defeats least privilege, but deleting it blind can break a process nobody remembers. Reviewing the logs to see what actually uses it, finding an owner, and then replacing it with specific rules through change control closes the hole safely. Leaving it tolerates known risk, and moving it to the top makes it match everything first.

cards.q: 01:50 · Network core. The warehouse Wi-Fi runs on one pre-shared key used at every depot, and it has been printed on a laminated card in at least one break room. Your ticket is to redesign authentication. Which design do you approve?
options: Keep the shared key but rotate it monthly and email it to depot leads
Hide the SSID and filter access points by each handheld's MAC address
Move to WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and EAP-TLS device certificates
Keep the shared key and put the Wi-Fi onto a VLAN of its own instead
cards.answer: Move to WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and EAP-TLS device certificates
cards.why: A shared key cannot tell devices apart or be revoked for just one of them. Enterprise mode with 802.1X authenticates each device individually, and EAP-TLS uses certificates, so there is no password to print on a card and a lost scanner is revoked alone. Monthly rotation still circulates one secret, MAC addresses are easily spoofed, and a VLAN limits reach without fixing authentication.

cards.q: 00:35 · Network core. Carrier partners want to look up live shipment status rather than phoning the night desk. The request is on your queue to design. Which option do you approve?
options: Give each carrier a VPN account that lands on the internal office LAN
Place the tracking database directly on the public website for speed
Email each carrier a nightly export of the full shipment tracking tables
Publish tracking to carriers via an authenticated extranet segment
cards.answer: Publish tracking to carriers via an authenticated extranet segment
cards.why: An extranet gives named outside partners authenticated access to specific services in a segment separate from the internal network. VPN accounts onto the internal LAN hand partners far more reach than tracking needs, a public database exposes shipment data to everyone, and nightly exports are stale and leave full copies in inboxes Tessaly does not control.

cards.q: 05:45 · Network core. Your ticket flags that the distribution switches in three depots run firmware the vendor stopped supporting last year; no further security fixes will ship. Replacement budget is not until next quarter. What do you put in the plan?
options: Keep running them as they are, since they have not been attacked so far
Apply a firmware build from an unofficial forum that claims to fix the flaws
Take the three depots offline until the new switches finally arrive on site
Record the risk with its owner and restrict their management plane until swap
cards.answer: Record the risk with its owner and restrict their management plane until swap
cards.why: End-of-support hardware is a lifecycle risk the owner must knowingly accept for a set period, with compensating controls: locking management access to an admin network and logging it reduces exposure until replacement. Doing nothing leaves unowned risk, unofficial firmware adds an untrusted supply chain into the core, and taking depots offline is a disproportionate business impact for a manageable risk.

cards.q: 04:05 · Network core. The monitoring platform polls every router and switch using SNMP version 2c with the community string 'public', and some devices also accept write access with it. Your ticket is to fix this. What goes in the change?
options: Move polling to SNMPv3 with authentication, privacy and unique users
Change the community string to a longer one and keep SNMP version 2c
Leave read access as it is and only turn off the write-enabled community
Stop monitoring the devices altogether so SNMP can be switched off entirely
cards.answer: Move polling to SNMPv3 with authentication, privacy and unique users
cards.why: SNMPv2c sends its community string in cleartext and offers no real authentication, so a longer string is just as sniffable. SNMPv3 in its auth-and-privacy mode gives per-user authentication and encrypted traffic, which keeps both monitoring and device configurations safe. Dropping only write access still leaks configuration data, and ending monitoring trades a confidentiality gap for blindness.

cards.q: 01:05 · Network core. A design ticket proposes putting 2,000 new warehouse temperature sensors on one flat /21 subnet. The pilot showed each sensor sending frequent frames to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, and the handheld scanners sharing the segment slowed down. What do you recommend?
options: Keep one flat subnet but buy faster access switches for the depot floor
Split the sensors into small VLANs routed apart from the scanners
Put the sensors on the same subnet as the servers so they respond faster
Ask the vendor to spread the sensors' broadcasts across the whole night
cards.answer: Split the sensors into small VLANs routed apart from the scanners
cards.why: Frames sent to the all-ones MAC address reach every host in the broadcast domain, so one huge layer-2 segment makes every device process every sensor's chatter. Smaller VLANs bound each broadcast domain, and routing between them adds a point of control between sensors and scanners. Faster switches still deliver every broadcast everywhere, and moving sensors beside servers widens exposure.

cards.q: 23:50 · Network core. A ticket asks for a 140-metre copper twisted-pair Ethernet run from the Rotterdam dock office to a gate camera, routed along the crane's power feed. Which cabling do you approve?
options: Approve the copper run as specified and add a second cable in case one fails
Use fibre for this run, since it ignores interference and covers the distance
Approve copper but coil the extra length at each end to reduce interference
Approve copper unshielded, since cameras tolerate a few dropped frames anyway
cards.answer: Use fibre for this run, since it ignores interference and covers the distance
cards.why: Copper twisted pair is rated to about 100 metres per segment and picks up electromagnetic interference from heavy power feeds, so this run would be unreliable and could expose signals. Fibre carries light, is immune to that interference and covers the distance easily. A second copper cable duplicates the same flaws, and coiled slack does not shorten the electrical run.

cards.q: 02:40 · Network core. A hardening ticket shows that internal services still accept TLS 1.0 because 300 older depot handhelds cannot do anything newer. The handhelds are due for replacement in the spring. Which plan do you approve?
options: Keep TLS 1.0 enabled everywhere until the last handheld is replaced
Disable TLS entirely on internal services so the handhelds all connect
Require TLS 1.2+ and fence the old handhelds in a limited segment
Turn TLS 1.0 off tonight and let the depots cope without the handhelds
cards.answer: Require TLS 1.2+ and fence the old handhelds in a limited segment
cards.why: Deprecated protocol versions have known weaknesses, so the secure channel should require current versions by design. Where a legacy device cannot comply, isolating it in a restricted segment is a compensating control until it is replaced. Keeping 1.0 everywhere weakens every client for the sake of a few, dropping TLS removes protection altogether, and an overnight cutoff halts depot work.

cards.q: 00:15 · Network core. An audit of mobile mail setup finds that the approved profile connects phones to the mail server using IMAP on port 143 with plain login, from hotel and home networks. What change do you make?
options: Allow only IMAP over TLS on port 993 and close port 143 at the edge
Keep port 143 open but tell staff to avoid using hotel Wi-Fi at night
Move IMAP to an unusual high port number so scanners do not find it
Replace IMAP with POP3 so messages leave the server more quickly
cards.answer: Allow only IMAP over TLS on port 993 and close port 143 at the edge
cards.why: Plain IMAP sends usernames, passwords and mail in cleartext over whatever network the phone sits on. IMAP over TLS on 993 encrypts the whole session, and closing 143 at the edge makes the secure path the only one. Advice to users is not enforcement, a non-standard port is obscurity, and POP3 without TLS has exactly the same cleartext problem.

cards.q: 05:20 · Network core. Servers in the settlement VLAN can reach any website directly on ports 80 and 443. Your ticket asks for an egress design that would stop malware on a server calling out to arbitrary sites. What do you propose?
options: Leave direct egress open but keep antivirus on every server up to date
Block ports 80 and 443 outbound and let servers call out on other ports
Send server egress through an application proxy with a domain allowlist
Allow direct egress but record all traffic with a full packet capture
cards.answer: Send server egress through an application proxy with a domain allowlist
cards.why: An application-level proxy firewall understands HTTP and TLS connection requests, so it can enforce which destinations servers may reach and log each request; servers that only talk to named update and partner domains leave malware with nowhere to call home. Antivirus alone misses new tools, blocking two ports pushes traffic elsewhere, and capturing everything records the breach rather than preventing it.

cards.q: 03:15 · Network core. Sales staff laptops spend most nights on hotel and airport Wi-Fi, and the endpoint baseline disables the host firewall whenever a laptop is off the corporate network. Your ticket is to fix the baseline. What do you set?
options: Enforce the host firewall on all networks, with the strictest public profile
Leave the host firewall off and rely on the VPN once staff choose to connect
Turn on the host firewall only while the laptop is inside a Tessaly office
Ask staff to switch the firewall on themselves whenever they are travelling
cards.answer: Enforce the host firewall on all networks, with the strictest public profile
cards.why: Endpoint security matters most where the network cannot protect the device. An always-on host firewall with the strictest profile on untrusted networks blocks inbound attacks from other hotel guests. Relying on the VPN leaves the laptop exposed before the tunnel is up, enabling protection only in the office inverts the risk, and optional steps for users are routinely skipped.

cards.q: 02:20 · Network core. The storage team wants to run iSCSI traffic for the new warehouse database cluster over the same office VLAN that user desktops sit on, to save switch ports. Which design do you approve?
options: Put iSCSI on a dedicated storage VLAN with CHAP and no user hosts
Share the office VLAN as proposed and rely on the database's logins
Share the office VLAN but give the storage traffic a higher QoS class
Put the storage on the guest Wi-Fi network, since it has spare capacity
cards.answer: Put iSCSI on a dedicated storage VLAN with CHAP and no user hosts
cards.why: iSCSI is a converged protocol that carries block storage over IP, and it trusts its network heavily: anyone on the segment can sniff or attempt to mount volumes. A dedicated storage VLAN with CHAP authentication keeps users off the path. Database logins do nothing at the block layer, QoS manages priority rather than access, and guest Wi-Fi is the least trusted network available.

cards.q: 06:15 · Network core. A ticket asks for a site-to-site IPsec link between the Dublin and Madrid gateways so the warehouse systems can replicate. The internal addressing of both sites must stay hidden from the carrier in between. Which configuration do you approve?
options: Use AH in transport mode, since it already authenticates packets
Use ESP in tunnel mode so each whole inner packet is encrypted
Use ESP in transport mode, since only the payload needs protection
Use plain GRE tunnels, since they already wrap the inner packets
cards.answer: Use ESP in tunnel mode so each whole inner packet is encrypted
cards.why: In tunnel mode, ESP encrypts the entire original packet, including its internal addresses, and wraps it in a new header between the two gateways, which is the standard design for site-to-site links. AH gives integrity with no confidentiality, transport mode leaves the original header readable, and GRE encapsulates without any encryption at all.

cards.q: 01:25 · Network core. A new inline intrusion prevention system is being installed in front of the payments segment. The vendor recommends turning on every blocking signature on day one. What do you approve?
options: Enable every blocking signature on day one as the vendor recommends
Leave it in detect-only mode for good so it can never block payments
Place it on a span port instead, so it can block without being inline
Run detect-only first, tune out false positives, then enable blocking
cards.answer: Run detect-only first, tune out false positives, then enable blocking
cards.why: An IPS that blocks legitimate payment traffic is a self-inflicted outage. Running in detection mode first gives a baseline to tune false positives, then blocking can be enabled with confidence. Blocking everything on day one risks halting settlement, permanent detect-only discards the prevention you bought, and a device fed from a span port sees copies of traffic, so it cannot block inline.

cards.q: 04:40 · Network core. The public shipment-tracking site sits behind a content delivery network, but a scan shows the origin server also answers requests from anyone on the internet who finds its address. What goes in the change ticket?
options: Leave the origin open, since its address is not published in public DNS
Add a second CDN provider so there are two different paths to the origin
Allow origin traffic only from the CDN and keep TLS from edge to origin
Turn off TLS between the CDN and the origin to reduce processing load
cards.answer: Allow origin traffic only from the CDN and keep TLS from edge to origin
cards.why: A CDN only protects an origin that cannot be reached around it. Restricting the origin to the CDN's address ranges, or an authenticated origin connection, forces every request through the edge's filtering and DDoS absorption, while TLS protects the hop behind it. An unpublished address is easily discovered, a second CDN adds another path, and dropping TLS exposes the back leg.

cards.q: 23:15 · Network core. The warehouse application team asks for a full packet capture on the core to debug intermittent timeouts. The traffic on that link includes payroll and card data. Which request do you approve?
options: An unfiltered capture of the whole core link kept for the next month
A capture copied to the app team's shared drive for anyone to review
Refuse any capture, since sniffing on the network is always prohibited
A time-boxed capture filtered to the app's hosts, stored as sensitive
cards.answer: A time-boxed capture filtered to the app's hosts, stored as sensitive
cards.why: Sniffing is a legitimate diagnostic tool when it is authorised, minimised and protected. Filtering to the application's hosts and a short window captures what the team needs, and handling the file as sensitive data respects the payroll and card data it may contain. Capturing everything for a month over-collects, a shared drive leaks it, and a blanket refusal blocks a legitimate operational need.

cards.q: 05:30 · Network core. A ticket proposes a point-to-point wireless bridge between two Madrid warehouse buildings across a public road, to avoid digging a trench for cable. Which condition do you attach to approval?
options: Rely on the narrow beam of the antennas to keep the link confidential
Encrypt the bridge link and authenticate both ends with certificates
Use a hidden network name so passers-by cannot find the wireless link
Approve as it is, since both buildings belong to Tessaly Group anyway
cards.answer: Encrypt the bridge link and authenticate both ends with certificates
cards.why: Radio is a transmission medium anyone in range can receive, and a directional beam still spills well beyond the far antenna. Strong link encryption keeps intercepted frames unreadable, and mutual certificate authentication stops a rogue device posing as either end. Beam width and hidden names are obscurity, and owning both buildings says nothing about who owns the road between them.

cards.q: 03:55 · Network core. In the data centre, the web, application and database tiers of the booking system all sit in one VLAN and can talk to each other on any port. A design ticket asks how to limit east-west movement. What do you propose?
options: Put a bigger firewall at the internet edge to stop attacks before entry
Micro-segment the tiers so each one reaches only its next tier's ports
Merge the tiers onto a single server so there is no traffic between them
Keep the one VLAN and review the booking system's flows once every year
cards.answer: Micro-segment the tiers so each one reaches only its next tier's ports
cards.why: Micro-segmentation enforces policy between individual workloads, so a compromised web server can reach only the application tier on the ports it needs and never the database directly. That contains lateral movement inside the data centre. An edge firewall does nothing once an attacker is inside, merging tiers removes separation entirely, and an annual review leaves the flat network in place.

cards.q: 02:30 · Network core. The network automation API that pushes configurations to every router accepts a username and password from any host that can reach it over the VPN. Your ticket is to harden access. What goes in the change?
options: Require mutual TLS with client certificates on managed admin devices
Keep passwords but force a change every thirty days for all admin users
Move the API to a non-standard port so it is harder for anyone to find
Allow the API from any VPN host but log each call it receives in full
cards.answer: Require mutual TLS with client certificates on managed admin devices
cards.why: Certificate-based client authentication ties access to a device Tessaly issued and manages, so a stolen password alone no longer opens the most powerful system on the network. Mutual TLS also authenticates the API to the client. Frequent password changes still leave a single phishable factor, a new port is obscurity, and logging records misuse rather than preventing it.

cards.q: 00:45 · Network core. The new next-generation firewall can decrypt and inspect outbound TLS. The project wants to turn it on for all staff traffic tonight, including personal banking and health sites visited on breaks. What do you approve?
options: Enable inspection for every site tonight as the project team asks
Skip TLS inspection completely, since decryption is always unlawful
Enable it silently for all sites and tell staff only if one complains
Enable inspection with privacy exemptions agreed with Legal and HR
cards.answer: Enable inspection with privacy exemptions agreed with Legal and HR
cards.why: TLS inspection restores visibility into encrypted threats, but decrypting employees' banking and health sessions carries legal and privacy obligations. Category exemptions agreed with Legal and HR, plus notice to staff, keep the control proportionate and defensible. Inspecting everything by default risks a privacy breach, a blanket refusal forfeits the visibility, and silent deployment undermines trust and possibly the law.

cards.q: 06:30 · Network core. Visitors to the Leeds office get guest Wi-Fi, which today lands them on the same subnet as the meeting-room displays and printers. A design ticket asks you to fix it. What design do you approve?
options: Keep the shared subnet but change the guest password every single week
Hide the guest network so only visitors who are told about it can join
Put guests on an internet-only segment with client isolation turned on
Remove the guest network and give visitors the staff Wi-Fi password
cards.answer: Put guests on an internet-only segment with client isolation turned on
cards.why: Guest wireless should be a separate zone that reaches the internet and nothing internal, with client isolation so guests cannot attack each other either. That keeps untrusted devices off meeting-room systems entirely. Weekly passwords still land guests on the internal subnet, a hidden network is easily found, and handing out the staff password puts visitors on the corporate network.

cards.q: 01:40 · Network core. The night desk is moving to IP phones, and agents regularly take card details read aloud by customers. The vendor's default setup sends voice as plain RTP. Which configuration do you require?
options: Accept plain RTP because voice travels only inside Tessaly's LAN
Put the phones on a voice VLAN and leave the RTP media unencrypted
Require SRTP for the voice media and TLS for all SIP signalling
Ban customers from reading card numbers out loud over the phone
cards.answer: Require SRTP for the voice media and TLS for all SIP signalling
cards.why: Plain RTP can be captured and replayed as audio by anyone on the path, which would expose spoken card numbers. The Secure Real-Time Transport Protocol encrypts and authenticates the media stream, and TLS protects the signalling that carries its keys. A voice VLAN helps quality and separation but does not encrypt, and the internal LAN is exactly where an intruder would listen.

cards.q: 04:15 · Network core. Forty new access switches arrive for the depots. The installer plans to rack them with factory settings and 'tidy up later'. What do you require before they carry traffic?
options: Rack them on factory settings now and harden each one during next audit
Apply the hardened baseline: default logins changed, unused ports off
Leave the factory settings, since the switches sit behind the firewall
Harden only the first switch and trust the rest to behave the same way
cards.answer: Apply the hardened baseline: default logins changed, unused ports off
cards.why: Network components should enter service already hardened: default credentials replaced, unused ports shut, and unneeded services disabled, applied from a secure baseline so every unit matches. Later is where hardening gets forgotten, sitting behind a firewall does nothing against an insider or a compromised depot device, and hardening one unit leaves thirty-nine others on factory defaults.

cards.q: 05:05 · Network core. Contractors use the corporate VPN, which drops them onto the internal network with reach to hundreds of systems they never need. A design ticket asks for a better model. What do you propose?
options: Keep the VPN but make contractors change their passwords every month
Give contractors their own VPN that lands on the same internal network
Grant per-app access checked on identity and device health per session
Block contractors from remote access and ask them to work from depots
cards.answer: Grant per-app access checked on identity and device health per session
cards.why: Zero trust network access replaces broad network-level trust with per-application access decided each session on who the user is and whether their device is healthy, so a contractor reaches only the apps their work needs. Password rotation keeps the same wide reach, a separate VPN into the same network changes nothing, and banning remote work solves the risk by removing the business function.

cards.q: 00:05 · Network core. Remote staff complain that video calls stutter over the always-on VPN, and a ticket asks to turn on full split tunnelling so only 'work stuff' goes through the tunnel. Which version do you approve?
options: Turn on full split tunnelling and let each laptop decide what is work
Split out only named meeting services; all other traffic stays tunnelled
Turn the VPN off for home workers, since their routers have firewalls
Keep full tunnelling and tell staff to switch their cameras off instead
cards.answer: Split out only named meeting services; all other traffic stays tunnelled
cards.why: Split tunnelling trades visibility for performance, so the design should decide the exception rather than the laptop. Sending only named, trusted meeting services direct keeps corporate and general web traffic inside the tunnel, under Tessaly's inspection. Full split tunnelling bypasses egress controls for most traffic, dropping the VPN removes the protected channel, and cameras off dodges the business need.

cards.q: 03:20 · Network core. The carrier offers an MPLS WAN to link all depots. The network team proposes dropping the existing IPsec encryption because 'MPLS is a private network'. What goes in the design decision?
options: Adopt MPLS and drop IPsec, since the carrier keeps customers apart
Reject MPLS and stay on internet VPNs, since carriers are untrusted
Adopt MPLS but keep IPsec over it, since labels are not encryption
Adopt MPLS and encrypt only the traffic of the settlement systems
cards.answer: Adopt MPLS but keep IPsec over it, since labels are not encryption
cards.why: Multiprotocol Label Switching separates customers by labels inside the carrier's network; it provides traffic engineering and isolation, not confidentiality. Traffic still crosses equipment Tessaly does not control, so encryption over the MPLS WAN keeps protection end to end. Dropping IPsec trusts the carrier with everything, rejecting MPLS discards real benefits, and encrypting one system leaves the rest in clear.

cards.q: 02:45 · Network core. The data-centre refresh moves to software-defined networking, where one controller will program every switch. The project plan puts the controller on the general server VLAN with default API settings. What do you require?
options: Isolate the controller, authenticate its APIs, and give it a standby
Accept the plan, since the switches keep working if a controller dies
Let every admin workstation reach the controller's API for flexibility
Replace SDN with manual switch configuration to avoid a single controller
cards.answer: Isolate the controller, authenticate its APIs, and give it a standby
cards.why: In software-defined networking the control plane is centralised, so whoever controls the controller controls the whole network. It belongs on an isolated management network, with authenticated and authorised APIs and a redundant standby so it is not a single point of failure. Broad API reach widens the attack surface, and abandoning SDN discards its central policy benefits.

cards.q: 01:15 · Network core. A new site-to-site tunnel to the Porto depot keeps failing. The depot sits behind the carrier's address translation, and the tunnel is configured with IPsec AH. What change do you approve?
options: Keep AH and ask the carrier to stop translating the depot's addresses
Switch to ESP with NAT traversal over UDP port 4500 for the tunnel
Drop IPsec and run the depot link as a plain GRE tunnel across the NAT
Keep AH but disable its integrity check so address rewriting passes
cards.answer: Switch to ESP with NAT traversal over UDP port 4500 for the tunnel
cards.why: AH signs the outer IP header, so Network Address Translation rewriting that header breaks the integrity check every time. ESP with NAT traversal wraps the packets in UDP so they survive translation, and it also gives confidentiality that AH never provided. Asking the carrier to stop NAT is not in Tessaly's control, GRE carries no encryption, and switching off integrity guts the protocol.

cards.q: 06:05 · Network core. Finance asks how the card-payment gateway would survive a large volumetric flood. The current plan is a bigger on-premises firewall on the 10 Gbit/s internet link. What do you recommend?
options: Buy the bigger firewall as planned, since it can drop flood traffic fast
Hide the gateway's address by changing its public IP every single week
Accept the risk, since floods are short and customers will retry later
Contract upstream scrubbing, since floods fill the link before any kit
cards.answer: Contract upstream scrubbing, since floods fill the link before any kit
cards.why: A volumetric DDoS saturates the internet link itself, so anything behind that link, however powerful, never gets the chance to help. An upstream scrubbing service or the ISP's mitigation absorbs the flood before it reaches Tessaly's pipe. A bigger firewall sits on the far side of the bottleneck, rotating addresses breaks partners, and accepting outages on payments is a business call Finance would not make.

cards.q: 04:30 · Network core. The courier-booking web server has to be reachable from the internet. The developers want to place it on the internal LAN beside the booking database and forward port 443 to it. Which placement do you approve?
options: Place it on the internal LAN and forward port 443 to it
Place it outside every firewall with no filtering at all
Put it in a screened subnet between two filtering layers
Host it on the booking database server to cut down on hops
cards.answer: Put it in a screened subnet between two filtering layers
cards.why: A screened subnet holds internet-facing systems in their own zone, filtered from the internet on one side and from the internal network on the other. If the web server is compromised, the attacker still faces a second boundary before reaching the database. Port-forwarding into the LAN puts the attacker inside, no filtering at all invites compromise, and co-hosting erases separation.

cards.q: 23:35 · Network core. Customers are reporting fake invoices that appear to come from billing@tessaly-group.example, and header checks show them sent from servers Tessaly has never used. Your ticket is to make the domain harder to spoof. What do you put in place?
options: Ask customers to phone the night desk before paying any invoice at all
Publish SPF, sign mail with DKIM, and enforce a DMARC reject policy
Move billing mail to a new domain name and abandon the current one
Add a warning footer about fraud to every legitimate invoice email
cards.answer: Publish SPF, sign mail with DKIM, and enforce a DMARC reject policy
cards.why: Sender Policy Framework lists the servers allowed to send for the domain, DKIM signs messages so receivers can verify them, and a DMARC policy tells receivers to reject mail that fails both. Together they let customers' mail systems discard the spoofed invoices automatically. Phone checks shift the burden to customers, a new domain can be spoofed just as easily, and a footer appears on the fakes too.

cards.q: 03:50 · Network core. The new network intrusion detection sensors are being placed. The draft puts one on the internet link outside the TLS-terminating load balancer and none inside the data centre. Which placement do you approve?
options: Keep the single sensor outside the load balancer to see all attacks first
Put a sensor on every desktop switch port rather than between the zones
Place sensors on inter-zone links and behind the TLS termination point
Skip network sensors, since endpoint agents already see every connection
cards.answer: Place sensors on inter-zone links and behind the TLS termination point
cards.why: A network sensor can only judge traffic it can read and that passes it. Outside the TLS terminator it sees mostly encrypted sessions, and with none internally it misses east-west movement. Sensors behind the decryption point and on links between zones see the traffic that matters. Per-port sensors are costly noise, and endpoint agents miss unmanaged devices.

cards.q: 05:55 · Network core. Delivery trucks carry cellular routers that link onboard tablets to the dispatch system. A scan shows each router has a public IP address with its web admin page reachable from the internet. What do you require?
options: Change each router's admin password and leave the public address in place
Use a private APN or tunnel back so no router is publicly reachable
Remove the admin page from the scan scope so it stops appearing in reports
Turn the routers off when trucks are parked and on again when they depart
cards.answer: Use a private APN or tunnel back so no router is publicly reachable
cards.why: Cellular links are just another untrusted network. A private access point name from the carrier, or a tunnel back to Tessaly, keeps truck routers off the public internet so there is no exposed admin page to attack. A new password leaves the interface open to brute force and exploits, dropping it from the scan hides the finding, and power schedules still expose trucks on the road.

cards.q: 00:30 · Network core. A new freight partner needs a site-to-site VPN to exchange customs files with one Tessaly server. Their engineer asks for the tunnel to allow 'any to any' so troubleshooting is easier. Which do you approve?
options: Allow any-to-any as requested and tighten the rules once it is working
Give the partner's engineer a Tessaly account on the internal network
Sign an interconnection agreement and filter the tunnel to named hosts
Let the partner post files to a public share that has an obscure name
cards.answer: Sign an interconnection agreement and filter the tunnel to named hosts
cards.why: A third-party connection needs both a governance and a technical boundary. An interconnection security agreement sets responsibilities, notification duties and permitted use, and filtering the tunnel to the named hosts and ports enforces least privilege. Any-to-any tends to stay forever, an internal account over-grants, and an obscure public share protects customs files with nothing but secrecy.

cards.q: 02:00 · Network core. A hardening ticket proposes blocking IP protocol 1, all ICMP, at the internet edge. The web team warns that some large partner uploads already stall mysteriously. Which rule do you approve?
options: Block all ICMP at the edge as proposed, since it can be used to scan
Allow every ICMP type in both directions to avoid breaking anything
Block ICMP only on weekdays, when the partner uploads are not running
Allow essential ICMP such as fragmentation-needed, rate-limit echo
cards.answer: Allow essential ICMP such as fragmentation-needed, rate-limit echo
cards.why: ICMP is IP protocol number 1, and parts of it are needed: path MTU discovery depends on fragmentation-needed messages, and blocking them causes exactly the stalled large transfers the web team describes. Allowing the essential types while rate-limiting or filtering echo balances reconnaissance risk against function. Blocking everything breaks the network, allowing everything exposes it, and a weekday schedule is not a security design.

cards.q: 06:50 · Network core. A switch audit finds user access ports set to negotiate trunking automatically, and every trunk using VLAN 1 as its native VLAN, which is also the users' VLAN. What goes in the remediation ticket?
options: Disable auto-trunking on user ports and set an unused native VLAN
Leave the settings, since VLANs already keep every user segment apart
Move all users to VLAN 1 so that the native VLAN is fully accounted for
Replace the VLANs with separate physical switches for every department
cards.answer: Disable auto-trunking on user ports and set an unused native VLAN
cards.why: Auto-negotiating trunks let a device on a user port become a trunk, and a native VLAN shared with users enables double-tagging, both routes to VLAN hopping. Hard-setting user ports to access mode and moving the native VLAN to an unused ID closes both. VLAN separation is only as good as that configuration, crowding users onto VLAN 1 worsens it, and separate hardware is overkill for a configuration fix.

cards.q: 01:55 · Network core. Network engineers currently SSH into routers directly from their own laptops, wherever those laptops happen to be. A ticket asks how admin access should work from now on. What do you approve?
options: Allow direct SSH from any engineer laptop that has antivirus running
Share one admin account among engineers so access is simpler to audit
Route admin access through a hardened, logged jump host with MFA
Open router SSH to the internet so engineers can reach devices on call
cards.answer: Route admin access through a hardened, logged jump host with MFA
cards.why: A jump host gives one hardened, monitored entry point into the management plane: it enforces multi-factor authentication, keeps a record of every session, and lets router ACLs trust a single source. Direct access from many laptops multiplies entry points, a shared account destroys individual accountability, and exposing SSH to the internet invites brute force against the core.

cards.q: 05:10 · Network core. Depot supervisors' phones pair with handheld scanners over Bluetooth and are left discoverable all shift. A threat note describes attackers in car parks taking control of unpatched phones over Bluetooth to read messages and place calls. What do you require?
options: Keep phones undiscoverable, use secure pairing, patch the Bluetooth
Let the phones stay discoverable, since Bluetooth range is only a few metres
Ban scanners from using Bluetooth and go back to cable connections only
Rename every phone to a random string so attackers cannot pick targets
cards.answer: Keep phones undiscoverable, use secure pairing, patch the Bluetooth
cards.why: Bluebugging abuses weak or unpatched Bluetooth stacks to take control of a phone, and discoverable devices are easy to find and target. Turning off discoverability after pairing, requiring secure pairing modes and patching the stack remove the entry points while the scanners keep working. Short range is no barrier with directional antennas, a cable-only ban cripples depot work, and random names are obscurity.

cards.q: 04:55 · Network core. Threat intel shows staff at several firms clicking links to newly registered look-alike domains. Tessaly's internal resolvers forward every query to the ISP with no filtering. Your ticket asks for a network-level control. What do you choose?
options: Forward internal resolvers to a protective DNS service with blocklists
Give each staff member a printed list of known malicious domain names
Have the resolvers ignore any domain registered in the last few years
Stop internal resolution and let every laptop use a public DNS server
cards.answer: Forward internal resolvers to a protective DNS service with blocklists
cards.why: A protective DNS resolver refuses to resolve known-malicious and newly registered risky domains for every device at once, which breaks many phishing and command-and-control chains before a connection is made, and it logs the attempts. Printed lists age instantly, blocking years of registrations breaks legitimate sites, and public resolvers remove both filtering and Tessaly's visibility.

cards.q: 03:10 · Network core. A failed edge firewall is going back to the vendor under warranty. It still holds the full ruleset, VPN pre-shared keys and admin hashes on its internal storage. What do you do before it ships?
options: Ship it as it is, since the vendor has signed a confidentiality clause
Wipe the config and keys, or keep the storage and rotate the secrets
Remove only the admin password and leave the VPN keys on the storage
Tape the case shut and label it confidential so couriers do not open it
cards.answer: Wipe the config and keys, or keep the storage and rotate the secrets
cards.why: Returned hardware is a data-leaving-the-building event. Sanitising the device, or keeping its storage under a keep-your-media option, protects the ruleset and keys, and rotating any secret it held removes the residual risk if the wipe fails. A confidentiality clause does not stop loss in transit or in a repair depot, partial removal leaves the VPN keys, and tape is not sanitisation.

cards.q: 06:25 · Network core. The core firewalls were installed as a high-availability pair eight months ago, but failover has never been triggered. The quarterly report lists the pair as fully resilient. What do you schedule?
options: Nothing yet, since the vendor certified the pair on the installation day
An unannounced power pull on the primary unit during daytime trading
A report edit that removes the word 'resilient' so nobody over-relies
A planned failover test in a change window, with rollback steps ready
cards.answer: A planned failover test in a change window, with rollback steps ready
cards.why: Redundancy that has never been exercised is an assumption, not a control. A planned failover in a change window, with rollback ready, proves that state sync and routing work while limiting impact if they do not. Vendor sign-off at install says nothing about eight months of config drift, an unannounced daytime pull risks a real outage, and rewording the report hides the gap instead of closing it.

cards.q: 00:55 · Network core. The platform team wants to stretch a layer-2 segment between the Dublin and Frankfurt data centres using VXLAN, sent across the public internet so failover VMs keep their addresses. What do you require?
options: Send VXLAN directly over the internet, since it already encapsulates frames
Replace the VXLAN overlay with one flat VLAN spanning both data centres
Send VXLAN in the clear but monitor the link for unexpected layer-2 frames
Carry VXLAN only inside an encrypted IPsec underlay, UDP 4789 filtered
cards.answer: Carry VXLAN only inside an encrypted IPsec underlay, UDP 4789 filtered
cards.why: Virtual eXtensible LAN wraps layer-2 frames in UDP, typically on port 4789, but it has no encryption or authentication of its own: across the internet anyone could read or inject frames into the stretched segment. Carrying it inside an IPsec underlay and filtering its port at the edge keeps the overlay private. Encapsulation is not protection, a spanned flat VLAN is worse, and monitoring only watches the exposure.

cards.q: 02:35 · Network core. During tonight's investigation you could not line up firewall, switch and VPN logs, because each device keeps its own local logs and the clocks differ by several minutes. What change do you raise?
options: Raise the local log size on each device so events are kept for longer
Ask engineers to screenshot device logs whenever an incident is opened
Adjust the timestamps by hand in the incident report after each event
Ship device logs to the central collector with all clocks on NTP
cards.answer: Ship device logs to the central collector with all clocks on NTP
cards.why: Network components are only useful as evidence if their logs survive the device and share a timeline. Central collection protects logs from local tampering and loss, and synchronised time via NTP lets events correlate across firewall, switch and VPN. Bigger local buffers still die with the device, screenshots are incomplete and hard to defend, and hand-adjusted timestamps undermine the evidence.

cards.q: 23:55 · Network core. A walk-through finds that every network jack in the Leeds reception lobby, where couriers and visitors wait, is live on the office VLAN. What do you put in the change ticket?
options: Leave the jacks live, since reception staff are always watching the lobby
Disable unused lobby jacks and enable them only on approved request
Put furniture in front of the jacks so visitors cannot easily reach them
Label each jack 'staff only' so couriers know not to plug anything in
cards.answer: Disable unused lobby jacks and enable them only on approved request
cards.why: Live wall ports in public areas hand any visitor a connection to the internal network. Administratively disabling unused jacks, and activating them only through an approved request, removes that exposure at the transmission medium itself. Receptionists get busy, furniture is moved in seconds, and a label deters only people who were never going to plug in anyway.

cards.q: 04:10 · Network core. An external scan shows port 3389 open to the internet on a warehouse control server, so a vendor can connect with Remote Desktop for support. What do you require?
options: Leave RDP open and change the local administrator password each month
Move RDP to a high random port so internet scanners stop reporting it
Allow RDP only during office hours, when the vendor usually connects
Close public RDP and broker vendor access through a gateway with MFA
cards.answer: Close public RDP and broker vendor access through a gateway with MFA
cards.why: Remote Desktop exposed to the internet is a favourite ransomware entry point. Closing it and routing the vendor through a remote access gateway or VPN with multi-factor authentication, ideally approved per session and logged, keeps support possible over a controlled channel. Rotating a password still leaves the service open to exploits, a high port is obscurity, and time windows leave it exposed for hours.

cards.q: 06:55 · Network core. An abuse report says a flood of packets with forged source addresses came from Tessaly's address space last week, launched by a compromised depot server. Your ticket asks for a network design fix. What do you propose?
options: Block all inbound traffic from the complaining network's address range
Reply to the abuse report that spoofed traffic cannot be traced to Tessaly
Filter egress so only Tessaly's own source addresses can leave
Rate-limit only the depot's uplink and leave the other sites unchanged
cards.answer: Filter egress so only Tessaly's own source addresses can leave
cards.why: Egress filtering in line with BCP 38 drops any packet leaving with a source address Tessaly does not own, so a compromised host cannot join spoofed floods or reflection attacks from inside. Blocking the reporter is backwards, denying the report ignores Tessaly's duty of care as an internet citizen, and rate-limiting one uplink leaves every other site able to spoof.

cards.q: 06:40 · Ops floor. Last week's DR test of the freight-booking platform finished late: the runbook named a storage array Tessaly retired in spring, and two restore steps ran out of order. The test lead wants to close the ticket as passed. What goes in the after-action ticket?
options: Close the test as passed, since the platform did come back up in the end
Update the DR plan with the findings and retest the corrected steps
Buy a second storage array so the old runbook reference becomes valid again
Stop DR testing the platform until the next annual audit asks to see a test
cards.answer: Update the DR plan with the findings and retest the corrected steps
cards.why: A DR test exists to find gaps in the plan, and its output is plan maintenance: correct the stale asset references and step order, then retest to prove the fix. Marking it passed hides a plan that would fail in a real disaster, and buying hardware to match an outdated document fixes the wrong thing.

cards.q: 05:15 · Ops floor. Yesterday's intruder wiped the Windows event logs on a payments jump host before logging off, and the only surviving trail came from a firewall. The ops lead asks what should change so this never blinds you again. What do you put in the change ticket?
options: Forward host logs in near real time to a central, append-only log store
Raise the local event log size so wiped entries take longer to roll over
Remove admin rights from the jump host so nobody can open Event Viewer
Email the host logs to the SOC mailbox once a night after the backup run
cards.answer: Forward host logs in near real time to a central, append-only log store
cards.why: Centralised, tamper-resistant log collection protects log integrity: once events leave the host within seconds, an attacker who clears the local log cannot erase the copy. A bigger local log is still on the compromised box and can still be cleared, and a nightly email leaves a whole day of events exposed before they leave the host.

cards.q: 02:05 · Ops floor. A warehouse-systems engineer's account is copying payroll exports from the HR share. His role never needed that share; the group granting it was added two years ago for a one-off project. The copies are still running. What do you do first?
options: Let the copies finish, then ask the engineer tomorrow why he needed payroll
Delete the HR share so no other account can reach the payroll exports again
Add the engineer to the HR team formally so the access matches the activity
Remove the stale group membership now and open an incident for the copies
cards.answer: Remove the stale group membership now and open an incident for the copies
cards.why: Need-to-know and least privilege say access should match the current job; access kept after a project ends is privilege creep. Pulling the membership stops the exposure while the incident process finds out whether the account or the person is the problem. Letting the copies finish lets the data go, and deleting the share hurts HR while destroying evidence.

cards.q: 03:25 · Ops floor. Mid-containment, the fire alarm sounds in the Ops floor building and smoke is reported on the level below. You are halfway through isolating a compromised payment server and two analysts want to stay and finish. What do you do?
options: Stay with the two analysts until the isolation completes, then leave
Send the others out and keep just one analyst behind to finish the work
Evacuate everyone and hand the isolation to the remote on-call analyst
Silence the alarm panel until someone confirms whether the smoke is real
cards.answer: Evacuate everyone and hand the isolation to the remote on-call analyst
cards.why: Human safety is always the first priority; no system, containment step or evidence outranks a life. Evacuate, account for everyone, and let a remote colleague carry on if the work can continue. Staying behind, even with one person, puts people at risk for a task that can be handed off, and silencing a fire alarm endangers the whole building.

cards.q: 23:40 · Dev pipeline. The build server raises an alert: a new outbound connection from the release-signing service to an unfamiliar cloud host. The on-call developer says it is probably a new dependency mirror. Nothing else has fired yet. What do you do first?
options: Declare a major incident and shut the pipeline down across all regions
Triage it: confirm the process and destination before declaring anything
Close the alert, since the developer on call knows the build system best
Block every outbound connection from the build network until morning
cards.answer: Triage it: confirm the process and destination before declaring anything
cards.why: Detection is followed by triage: validate the event, scope it, and decide whether it is an incident before choosing a response. A signing service talking to an unknown host deserves a fast look at the process, destination and recent changes. Closing on a guess skips the analysis, while a full shutdown or blanket block is a response sized before anyone knows what happened.

cards.q: 04:50 · Ops floor. Ransomware encrypted the shipment-tracking database at 01:00. Your newest backup is from 00:30, but the malware's first beacon on that host was logged at 22:10 yesterday. Ops wants the 00:30 copy restored immediately. Which do you approve?
options: Restore a copy from before 22:10 and replay the verified transactions
Restore the 00:30 copy right away because it loses the least order data
Restore the 00:30 copy and rely on antivirus to catch anything left over
Rebuild the database from scratch and ask customers to resend their orders
cards.answer: Restore a copy from before 22:10 and replay the verified transactions
cards.why: Recovery must restore to a known-good point, before the compromise began, or the attacker returns with the data. Restoring from before 22:10 and replaying clean transactions balances integrity against data loss. The 00:30 copy almost certainly carries the foothold, and trusting antivirus to clean it gambles on a tool that already missed the intrusion once.

cards.q: 05:30 · Ops floor. A payments outage is now two hours old and a reporter has emailed three Tessaly staff asking whether card data was stolen. One analyst has already started drafting a reply. What do you do?
options: Let the analyst reply quickly so the story does not run without Tessaly's side
Tell staff to ignore the reporter until the incident is fully closed out
Post a technical timeline on the status page so the press can see the facts
Route all outside questions to the named spokesperson in the crisis comms plan
cards.answer: Route all outside questions to the named spokesperson in the crisis comms plan
cards.why: A crisis communications plan names who speaks for the organisation and pre-approves how, so statements are accurate, legally reviewed and consistent. An analyst's quick reply can speculate about a breach or contradict legal advice, and silence with no owner lets rumour run. A raw technical timeline may disclose details that help the attacker or prejudice legal notification duties.

cards.q: 01:55 · Ops floor. Flooding has taken the primary data centre off power, and the card-authorisation service can tolerate only about an hour of downtime. Tessaly contracts a hot site kept in sync with production. Facilities thinks the power may return in three hours. What do you recommend?
options: Wait for facilities, because moving to the hot site costs money every hour
Order new servers for a cold site so the move is cheaper if power stays off
Invoke the hot site now, as the outage exceeds the tolerable downtime
Run card authorisations by phone until the primary data centre is back
cards.answer: Invoke the hot site now, as the outage exceeds the tolerable downtime
cards.why: A hot site is fully equipped and near-current, so it restores service in minutes to hours; it exists precisely for systems whose maximum tolerable downtime is short. A three-hour estimate already breaks the one-hour limit. Waiting to save cost turns a recoverable outage into a business failure, and a cold site takes days to stand up.

cards.q: 00:35 · Ops floor. An attacker is pivoting through the print-management server using a remote file-sharing service that nobody at Tessaly uses; it was enabled in the vendor's default install. The server's only job is managing warehouse label printers. Your move?
options: Leave the service on but change its password so the attacker is locked out
Disable the unused service on this server and remove it from the build image
Add a second antivirus agent to the server to watch the file-sharing service
Reinstall the server from the same vendor default image to clear the attacker
cards.answer: Disable the unused service on this server and remove it from the build image
cards.why: Least functionality means a system runs only what its role needs; a service that serves no purpose is pure attack surface. Turning it off contains this path, and fixing the build image stops it returning on the next server. A new password leaves the service exposed to its next weakness, and reinstalling from the same default image brings the hole straight back.

cards.q: 03:10 · Ops floor. The vendor of Tessaly's VPN concentrator has published a fix for a flaw now being exploited widely, and your concentrator logs show scanning against it tonight. The vendor recommends the patch go on immediately. What do you do?
options: Raise an emergency change, patch after a quick staging check, then verify
Wait for the monthly patch window so the fix goes through normal testing
Patch production now and skip testing because the vendor says it is urgent
Turn the VPN off until next month's window so nothing can be exploited
cards.answer: Raise an emergency change, patch after a quick staging check, then verify
cards.why: Patch management scales urgency to risk: an actively exploited flaw on an internet-facing device justifies the emergency change path, with a short sanity test and verification afterwards rather than none at all. Waiting a month leaves a known open door, and patching blind can break remote access for the whole company during an incident.

cards.q: 04:05 · Ops floor. An attacker's command server is active, and you need a firewall rule blocking its address at the network edge right now. The change advisory board next meets on Thursday. Your team lead says to push it and worry about paperwork later. What do you do?
options: Wait until Thursday so the board approves the rule through the normal cycle
Push the rule silently and skip the paperwork since the block is temporary
Ask the vendor to make the change so it sits outside the change process
Apply the block under the emergency change process and log it for review
cards.answer: Apply the block under the emergency change process and log it for review
cards.why: Change management includes an emergency path: urgent changes are made with the minimum authorisation available, recorded, and reviewed retroactively by the board. That keeps the fix fast and the record complete. Waiting for Thursday leaves the attacker connected, and an undocumented rule becomes configuration drift that nobody can explain or safely remove later.

cards.q: 02:40 · Ops floor. A visitor at the Ops floor lobby shows a Tessaly contractor badge to get to the server room, claiming an urgent disk swap. The guard notices the badge's embedded hologram is missing and the photo looks printed on. What do you tell the guard?
options: Let him in with an escort, since urgent disk swaps do happen overnight
Take a copy of the badge and allow entry if the name is on any vendor list
Refuse entry and verify the visit with the vendor on a known number
Ask him to come back with a better badge after the morning shift arrives
cards.answer: Refuse entry and verify the visit with the vendor on a known number
cards.why: Badge anti-counterfeiting features like an embedded hologram exist so guards can spot forgeries; a missing hologram is a red flag that must stop entry. Verifying the visit by calling the vendor on a number Tessaly already holds defeats the social-engineering pretext. An escort still puts a possible impostor beside the servers, and a name on a list does not prove the person is who the badge says.

cards.q: 06:05 · Ops floor. Two police officers arrive at reception asking to take a server tied to a fraud case involving a Tessaly customer. They show ID but no written order, and they want it before 07:00. What do you do?
options: Hand over the server now, since refusing police could be seen as obstruction
Call Tessaly's legal counsel before any handover and record every step taken
Refuse outright and ask them to leave until the day staff are on site
Copy the server's data onto a USB stick so the officers can take it with them
cards.answer: Call Tessaly's legal counsel before any handover and record every step taken
cards.why: Working with law enforcement is a legal decision: counsel confirms the authority for the request (warrant, subpoena or voluntary consent), what can be released and how custody is documented. Handing the server over without that may breach customer obligations, while a flat refusal harms cooperation. A quick USB copy breaks chain of custody and may be useless as evidence.

cards.q: 01:35 · Ops floor. The courier for tonight's off-site backup rotation reports that one box of tapes never reached the vault; its seal number is not on the delivery log. The tapes hold customer payment history. What do you do first?
options: Open a security incident and confirm whether the tapes were encrypted
Wait a day in case the box turns up at the courier's depot in the morning
Rerun the backup and send a fresh set of tapes so the vault is complete
Change the courier firm and keep the lost box out of the incident records
cards.answer: Open a security incident and confirm whether the tapes were encrypted
cards.why: Media protection covers media in transit: a missing box of customer data is a potential breach, so the incident process starts now and the first question is whether encryption protects the data. That answer drives notification. Waiting a day loses time you may owe regulators, and replacing the tapes fixes the vault while ignoring the data that may be in someone else's hands.

cards.q: 00:20 · Ops floor. A macro-laden spreadsheet is launching an unsigned binary from a temp folder on several finance PCs. Your endpoint policy blocks known malware but allows any other executable to run. The binary's hash matches nothing in threat feeds. Your move?
options: Wait for the antivirus vendor to add this hash to the next signature update
Block this one hash on finance PCs and leave the default-allow policy in place
Remove Excel from finance PCs until the attacker stops sending spreadsheets
Switch finance PCs to allowlisting so only approved applications can run
cards.answer: Switch finance PCs to allowlisting so only approved applications can run
cards.why: Application allowlisting flips the default from allow to deny: only approved software runs, so a never-seen binary is blocked without needing a signature. Finance PCs run a small, stable set of tools, which makes the policy practical. Waiting for signatures leaves the gap open, and blocking one hash fails the moment the attacker recompiles.

cards.q: 23:30 · Ops floor. During a parallel DR test for the parcel-routing system, a misconfigured script starts sending live customer traffic to the recovery site instead of production. Orders are failing. The test lead wants to keep going to finish the timings. What do you do?
options: Let the test finish so the timings are captured, then move traffic back
Switch fully to the recovery site and call it an unplanned full test
Halt the test, restore traffic to production, and log what went wrong
Keep testing but only on the orders that are not currently failing
cards.answer: Halt the test, restore traffic to production, and log what went wrong
cards.why: A parallel test is meant to run the recovery site alongside production without touching live operations; once the test starts harming the business it must stop. Restoring production comes first and the fault becomes a finding. Continuing for timings trades real orders for test data, and turning an accident into a full interruption test risks the outage the plan exists to prevent.

cards.q: 02:55 · Ops floor. A payments analyst's workstation is showing signs of a live intrusion, and the screen is still unlocked with a remote session open. HR suspects the analyst may also be involved. The desk tech wants to pull the power cord now. What do you do first?
options: Pull the power cord now so the remote attacker cannot do any more damage
Capture memory and live state, then image the disk before shutdown
Log in as admin and browse the analyst's files to see what was taken
Run a full antivirus scan on the workstation to clean it before imaging
cards.answer: Capture memory and live state, then image the disk before shutdown
cards.why: Evidence follows the order of volatility: memory, network connections and running processes vanish at power-off, so capture them first, then image the disk. Pulling the plug loses that volatile evidence. Browsing files or running a scan changes timestamps and data on the original, which weakens the evidence if HR or a court later relies on it.

cards.q: 04:35 · Ops floor. The night guard radios a code phrase that Tessaly's security guide lists as the duress signal, while saying calmly that a visiting engineer needs the loading door opened. The CCTV feed to that door has just gone dark. What do you do?
options: Keep the door shut, call police, and sound normal on the radio
Open the door as the guard asks, since he sounds calm and in control
Radio back asking the guard to confirm whether he really used the duress code
Walk down to the loading door yourself to check on the guard in person
cards.answer: Keep the door shut, call police, and sound normal on the radio
cards.why: A duress signal lets someone under threat ask for help without alerting the attacker; the response is to summon help while keeping up appearances. Asking the guard to confirm out loud could expose him, and going down alone adds a second person to danger. Opening the door gives the intruders what they want.

cards.q: 05:50 · Ops floor. The warehouse-management system will be down for at least a day after a failed storage controller. The business continuity plan has a paper-based picking process for exactly this case, but the warehouse supervisor has never used it. What do you do?
options: Tell the warehouse to stop picking until the system is back up tomorrow
Ask staff to improvise their own tracking in spreadsheets on their laptops
Buy a cloud warehouse tool tonight and migrate the stock records to it
Invoke the manual process in the BCP and brief the supervisor on the steps
cards.answer: Invoke the manual process in the BCP and brief the supervisor on the steps
cards.why: Business continuity keeps critical functions running while systems are recovered; a pre-planned manual workaround is exactly what the BCP is for. Invoking it and briefing people shows why plans need training and exercises. Stopping work turns an IT outage into a business outage, and improvised spreadsheets create uncontrolled copies of stock and customer data.

cards.q: 03:45 · Ops floor. The SIEM dashboard looks unusually calm: the domain controllers for the payments network stopped sending events 40 minutes ago, just after an admin logon from a new host. Nothing has alerted. What do you do first?
options: Wait for the event feed to resume on its own before looking any further
Restart the SIEM collectors and close the gap as a routine outage ticket
Treat the silent log source as an attack and investigate that logon
Mark the new host as trusted so its admin logons stop cluttering the view
cards.answer: Treat the silent log source as an attack and investigate that logon
cards.why: Monitoring must watch the watchers: a critical log source going quiet right after an unusual admin logon matches the attacker technique of impairing defences. The absence of data is itself an indicator. Waiting or treating it as routine gives the attacker free time, and trusting the new host removes exactly the evidence you need.

cards.q: 23:15 · Ops floor. Tonight's vulnerability scan returned 1,900 findings across the Ops floor estate. Your ticket asks for a remediation order the platform teams can start on in the morning. Which approach do you put in the ticket?
options: Fix the findings in the order the scanner lists them until the queue is empty
Rank findings by severity, exploitability and asset value, then fix
Give each platform team an equal share of the findings chosen at random
Patch only findings rated critical and accept every other one without review
cards.answer: Rank findings by severity, exploitability and asset value, then fix
cards.why: Vulnerability management is risk-based: a medium flaw on an internet-facing payment host can matter more than a critical on an isolated lab box. Weighting severity by exploitability and asset value spends limited effort where the risk is. Scanner order ignores context, and blanket-accepting everything below critical is a risk decision nobody with authority made.

cards.q: 00:50 · Ops floor. The DR coordinator wants the next test of the customer-portal recovery plan to go further than last quarter's walkthrough, but the board has ruled out touching production. Which test do you schedule?
options: Run a simulation that plays out a scripted outage with recovery steps
Run a full interruption test that shuts production down during the night
Repeat last quarter's walkthrough, since it passed without any issues
Circulate the plan by email and ask each owner to confirm it is up to date
cards.answer: Run a simulation that plays out a scripted outage with recovery steps
cards.why: A simulation test acts out a realistic disaster scenario, with teams carrying out their recovery steps against it, without disrupting production. It goes further than a walkthrough and stays within the board's constraint. A full interruption test breaks that constraint, a repeated walkthrough learns nothing new, and an emailed plan is a checklist review, the lightest test of all.

cards.q: 01:20 · Ops floor. Tessaly's nightly full backup of the settlement database now runs past 06:00 and collides with the morning batch. The business needs any restore to finish within four hours. Which backup scheme do you approve?
options: Weekly full backups with nightly incrementals, restored one day at a time
Keep the nightly full backup and ask the batch team to start later instead
Move to a monthly full backup and skip the nightly jobs to save the window
Weekly full backups with nightly differentials, so a restore needs two sets
cards.answer: Weekly full backups with nightly differentials, so a restore needs two sets
cards.why: Differential backups copy everything changed since the last full, so nightly jobs are shorter than a full yet a restore needs only the full plus the latest differential. That meets the four-hour restore target. Incrementals are faster to take but must be applied in sequence, which stretches the restore, and monthly-only backups leave weeks of settlement data unprotected.

cards.q: 02:25 · Ops floor. You are building the standard image for 300 new warehouse handheld terminals. Today each one is set up by hand, and no two have the same settings. What do you put in the build ticket?
options: Let each site's technician configure the terminals the way they prefer
Copy the settings from whichever terminal has had the fewest problems
Build one hardened, documented baseline image for every device
Ship the terminals in their factory state and harden them after rollout
cards.answer: Build one hardened, documented baseline image for every device
cards.why: Configuration management starts with a secure baseline: a documented, approved, hardened configuration applied identically everywhere, which makes drift detectable and patching predictable. Hand setup produces 300 different attack surfaces. Copying a lucky device captures its unknown quirks, and hardening after rollout puts devices on the network with default settings.

cards.q: 03:05 · Ops floor. A batch of retired payroll server drives is heading for reuse in a test lab run by a contractor. The drives held unencrypted salary and bank details. What do you require before they leave the Ops floor?
options: Delete the payroll files and empty the recycle bin on each of the drives
Purge the drives with a verified method and record the certificate
Reformat the drives with a quick format so the contractor starts clean
Label the drives confidential and trust the contractor not to look inside
cards.answer: Purge the drives with a verified method and record the certificate
cards.why: Media reused outside the original trust boundary must be sanitised to a level that defeats laboratory recovery, such as a verified purge, with the result documented. Deleting files or a quick format only removes directory entries, leaving the data easily recoverable. A label is a handling marking, not a control, and relying on trust hands salary data to a third party.

cards.q: 04:10 · Ops floor. Your ticket is to cut standing domain-admin accounts on the Ops floor from nineteen to as few as possible. The platform team says admins need those rights 'at any time' for emergencies. Which design do you approve?
options: Vault admin credentials and grant them on request, time-limited and logged
Keep all nineteen accounts but ask their owners to change passwords monthly
Share a single domain-admin login among the team to cut the account count
Give every engineer domain admin so emergencies are never held up by rights
cards.answer: Vault admin credentials and grant them on request, time-limited and logged
cards.why: Privileged account management removes standing privilege: credentials are vaulted and checked out just in time, with approval, expiry and session logging, so emergencies are still served. Password rotation alone leaves nineteen always-on targets. A shared login destroys accountability, and giving everyone admin is the opposite of least privilege.

cards.q: 05:25 · Ops floor. An engineer wants to raise the TLS version on the payments gateway tonight during a quiet period. It is a planned improvement, not an emergency, and nothing has been filed yet. The engineer says it is a two-line edit. What do you tell him?
options: Go ahead now, since a two-line change is too small to need an approval
Make the edit tonight and raise the change ticket once it is known to work
Ask the vendor to push the change remotely so Tessaly avoids the process
Raise a change request for review, with a test and backout plan
cards.answer: Raise a change request for review, with a test and backout plan
cards.why: Change management applies to planned changes regardless of size: request, impact review, approval, testing, scheduled implementation and a backout plan. A TLS change can break older partner clients, which is exactly what review catches. Small edits made outside the process cause many outages, and filing afterwards turns the ticket into a record instead of a control.

cards.q: 06:15 · Network core. The worm that spread through the warehouse VLAN is contained and the infected hosts are rebuilt. Root-cause analysis shows it entered through an exposed remote-management port on a branch router. The ops lead wants to close the incident. What do you do before closing?
options: Close the incident now, since the rebuilt hosts are all healthy again
Add more antivirus on warehouse hosts so the worm is caught next time
Close the exposed management port on every router, then close out
Monitor the branch router for a month and decide on any fix after that
cards.answer: Close the exposed management port on every router, then close out
cards.why: Remediation removes the root cause, not just the symptoms: rebuilding hosts cleans up the damage, but the router port that let the worm in is still open. Fixing it across all routers stops reinfection. Closing now invites the same incident, extra antivirus treats the symptom, and watching the router for a month leaves the door open while you wait.

cards.q: 23:55 · Ops floor. Endpoint detection on the warehouse laptops fires 400 alerts a night, nearly all from a legitimate stock-scanning tool. Analysts have started ignoring the queue entirely. What goes in your tuning ticket?
options: Turn the detection rule off across the estate so the queue quietens down
Tune a narrow exclusion for the verified tool and keep the rule live
Hire another analyst for nights so all 400 alerts can be read every shift
Exclude the whole warehouse laptop fleet from endpoint monitoring entirely
cards.answer: Tune a narrow exclusion for the verified tool and keep the rule live
cards.why: Detection tools need ongoing tuning: a precise exclusion for the verified scanning tool removes the false positives while the rule still catches real threats. Alert fatigue is itself a risk, because true alerts get missed. Disabling the rule or excluding the fleet creates blind spots, and more staff to read noise treats the symptom rather than the rule.

cards.q: 01:05 · Ops floor. You are drafting the DR procedure for Tessaly's core payments cluster. The current draft lets any on-call engineer fail over to the recovery site whenever something looks wrong. Which change do you make?
options: Name who can declare a disaster, with deputies, and the criteria for doing so
Keep the draft, since letting anyone fail over gives the fastest recovery
Require the whole board to vote before any failover is ever started
Remove failover from the plan and leave it to engineers' judgement on the night
cards.answer: Name who can declare a disaster, with deputies, and the criteria for doing so
cards.why: A DR plan must state who has authority to declare a disaster, backed by named deputies and clear criteria, because failover is costly and hard to reverse. That gives speed with accountability. Letting anyone fail over risks needless disruption, a full board vote is far too slow at 03:00, and leaving it unwritten produces exactly the confusion the plan exists to prevent.

cards.q: 02:15 · Ops floor. Door logs for the Ops floor show several badge swipes followed by two or three people entering at once. Staff say they hold the door to be polite. The ticket asks for a fix. What do you put in it?
options: Send a reminder email about tailgating and take no further measures
Replace the badge readers with newer models from a different vendor
Leave the door propped open at night so the swipe records stay accurate
Install a mantrap at the entrance and brief staff on tailgating
