cards.answer: Install a mantrap at the entrance and brief staff on tailgating
cards.why: A mantrap lets only one authenticated person through at a time, physically preventing tailgating and piggybacking; pairing it with awareness explains why. A reminder email alone rarely changes a polite habit, and new badge readers still let a second person walk through behind the first. Propping the door open removes the control entirely.

cards.q: 03:50 · Ops floor. Legal emails the SOC: Tessaly expects to be sued by a former logistics partner, and all records about that partner must be kept. The routine log purge for that period runs at 04:00. What do you do?
options: Let the purge run on schedule, since it is Tessaly's normal retention policy
Delete the partner's records early so there is less for the other side to see
Suspend the purge for the affected records and confirm the hold with legal
Copy everything to a USB drive and let the scheduled purge run as usual
cards.answer: Suspend the purge for the affected records and confirm the hold with legal
cards.why: A legal hold overrides normal retention: once litigation is reasonably expected, relevant records must be preserved for e-discovery, and destroying them can be sanctioned as spoliation. Suspending the purge for the scoped records meets that duty. Letting a routine purge run after notice is still destruction, and an uncontrolled USB copy has no custody record.

cards.q: 04:25 · Ops floor. You are correlating an intrusion across an endpoint, a proxy and a domain controller, but the events do not line up; the endpoint's clock is seven minutes fast. Your ticket asks for a lasting fix. What do you propose?
options: Adjust the timestamps by hand for this investigation and close the ticket
Sync every device to an authoritative time source and alert on clock drift
Set each device's clock manually once a month during the patch window
Record only the SIEM's receive time and ignore each device's own clock
cards.answer: Sync every device to an authoritative time source and alert on clock drift
cards.why: Log correlation depends on consistent time; synchronising every device to an authoritative source (NTP) and alerting on drift keeps timelines trustworthy across systems. Hand-fixing timestamps fixes one case and invites challenge to the evidence. Monthly manual setting drifts again within days, and SIEM receive time adds variable delays that hide the real order of events.

cards.q: 05:05 · Ops floor. A patch for the fleet-tracking server fixes a serious flaw but is known to break some third-party modules. The server runs one of those modules. The vendor calls it a must-install. What do you do?
options: Test the patch in staging with the module before it goes to production
Install it straight to production, since the vendor rates it must-install
Skip this patch permanently, because it may break the installed module
Install it on the live server and roll it back if customers report errors
cards.answer: Test the patch in staging with the module before it goes to production
cards.why: Patch management tests before deployment: a staging trial against the real configuration shows whether the module breaks and gives time to plan a fix or compensating control. Going straight to production risks an outage, and letting customers find the breakage makes them the test. Skipping the patch forever leaves a serious vulnerability without any risk decision.

cards.q: 06:25 · Ops floor. The recovery plan for the billing system was rewritten after a reorganisation. None of the new team leads has seen it. You want a first, low-risk test that catches wrong names and missing steps. Which test do you book?
options: Book a full interruption test to see if the plan works under real load
Run a parallel test that starts the recovery site next to production
Wait until a real outage to find out whether the new plan holds up
Hold a structured walkthrough where each lead talks through steps
cards.answer: Hold a structured walkthrough where each lead talks through steps
cards.why: A structured walkthrough (a tabletop review) gathers the people named in the plan to talk through each step, cheaply exposing wrong contacts, missing steps and unclear handoffs before heavier testing. A full interruption or parallel test is premature for a plan nobody has read and costs far more. Waiting for a real outage makes the disaster the test.

cards.q: 00:10 · Ops floor. The fleet database sits on a RAID 6 array, and the storage team suggests dropping separate backups because 'RAID already protects the data'. What do you put in your reply?
options: Agree to drop backups, since RAID 6 can survive two disks failing at once
Switch to RAID 1 instead, so every write is mirrored as a backup copy
Keep separate backups, because RAID cannot undo deletion or corruption
Take one snapshot a year on the same array and drop the nightly backups
cards.answer: Keep separate backups, because RAID cannot undo deletion or corruption
cards.why: RAID provides fault tolerance for disk failure, not backup: a deletion, corruption or ransomware attack is written to every disk in the array at once. Only independent backup copies let you restore a prior state. Mirroring has the same limitation, and a snapshot on the same array shares its fate when the array or its controller fails.

cards.q: 01:45 · Ops floor. A weekly scan finds that 40 of the 300 handheld terminals have drifted from their approved baseline: an extra app, a weaker screen-lock time. Nobody filed changes for them. What do you do?
options: Update the baseline to match the drifted devices so the scan comes back clean
Investigate the drift, then restore the baseline and enforce it automatically
Ignore the drift, because the terminals are still working for warehouse staff
Replace all 40 terminals with new units shipped straight from the factory
cards.answer: Investigate the drift, then restore the baseline and enforce it automatically
cards.why: Configuration monitoring compares devices against the approved baseline; unauthorised drift is both a weakness and a possible sign of compromise, so investigate it, then remediate and enforce the baseline automatically. Rewriting the baseline to match approves unreviewed changes, and ignoring drift lets it grow. New hardware does not fix the process that allowed the drift.

cards.q: 02:30 · Ops floor. A developer's change request would let the parcel-tracking API accept uploads from partner systems. It has a test plan and a rollback plan. Before the board votes, what do you add to the ticket?
options: A security impact analysis of how the new upload path changes the risk
A request that the board approve it quickly, since rollback is available
A note that security will look at the feature after it goes into production
A list of every developer who worked on the code, for accountability
cards.answer: A security impact analysis of how the new upload path changes the risk
cards.why: A security impact analysis examines how a change alters the system's security posture, here a new file-upload path with new injection and malware risks, so the board decides with full information and the right controls are added. A rollback plan limits outage risk but not a breach. Reviewing after go-live is too late, and a list of developers is not an assessment.

cards.q: 06:45 · Identity plane. The credential-stuffing attack on the customer portal is contained, compromised accounts are reset and MFA is now enforced. Service is back to normal. The team wants to go home and move on. What do you do next?
options: Close the incident now, since service is restored and the attack has stopped
Delete the incident notes so the attack details cannot leak to anyone outside
Wait until the next incident and review both of them together at that point
Book a lessons-learned review to record what happened and what should change
cards.answer: Book a lessons-learned review to record what happened and what should change
cards.why: After recovery and remediation, the incident lifecycle ends with lessons learned: a review while memories are fresh captures the timeline, what worked, what failed and which controls or processes should change. Closing without it wastes the incident's only benefit. Deleting the notes destroys records you may need for regulators, and waiting for the next incident lets the details fade.

cards.q: 03:30 · Ops floor. The IDS on the payments segment keeps catching exploit attempts, but it sits on a mirrored port and can only alert. The ops lead asks whether it can stop attacks as well. What do you propose?
options: Leave the IDS on its mirror port and turn on its blocking option there
Replace the IDS with a honeypot that draws attackers away from payments
Place an IPS inline, starting in alert mode before it blocks
Turn the IDS off, since it only alerts and cannot stop anything on its own
cards.answer: Place an IPS inline, starting in alert mode before it blocks
cards.why: An IPS sits inline and can drop malicious traffic; an IDS on a mirror port only sees copies and can only alert. Starting in alert mode lets you tune rules before blocking, so false positives do not take down payments. A mirrored sensor cannot block what it never carries, and a honeypot or turning detection off leaves the segment with no protection at all.

cards.q: 04:40 · Ops floor. Tessaly's DR plan for the sorting-centre systems says 'restore all systems at the recovery site'. It gives no order, and staff argue about what comes first. Which change do you make to the plan?
options: Restore systems alphabetically so the order is clear to everyone on the night
Set a recovery order based on each system's tolerable downtime from the BIA
Restore whatever system the loudest department head asks for first
Restore the smallest systems first so the recovery shows progress quickly
cards.answer: Set a recovery order based on each system's tolerable downtime from the BIA
cards.why: Recovery priority should follow the business impact analysis: systems with the shortest maximum tolerable downtime and recovery time objectives come back first. That puts effort where delay causes the most harm. Alphabetical order or ease of restore ignores business impact, and taking requests from whoever shouts loudest turns a plan into a negotiation mid-disaster.

cards.q: 05:40 · Ops floor. An analyst reports that his laptop was taken from his car overnight. It is a Tessaly endpoint with access to the payments VPN. Your ticket asks what should protect the next stolen laptop. What do you propose?
options: Enforce full-disk encryption and remote wipe on every Tessaly laptop
Ask staff to hide laptops under the car seat when they are away from home
Put a Tessaly asset sticker on each laptop so it can be returned if found
Buy insurance for the laptops so the cost of replacing them is covered
cards.answer: Enforce full-disk encryption and remote wipe on every Tessaly laptop
cards.why: Mobile devices will be lost or stolen; full-disk encryption makes the data unreadable without credentials, and remote wipe plus revoking VPN access close the rest. An asset sticker helps inventory, not confidentiality. Hiding advice is a weak habit, and insurance covers the hardware while doing nothing for the payment data on it.

cards.q: 23:20 · Ops floor. HR has asked you to collect a departing engineer's company laptop as evidence in a suspected theft of route-pricing data. You will take it from his desk tonight and pass it to an outside forensics firm next week. What do you do?
options: Take it home tonight for safekeeping and give it to the firm next week
Boot it up to check the data is there before handing it to the firm
Leave it on the desk with a note so the firm can collect it themselves
Seal it, start a custody log, and record every handover with signatures
cards.answer: Seal it, start a custody log, and record every handover with signatures
cards.why: Evidence collection must preserve integrity and provenance: sealing the device and keeping a chain-of-custody record of every person who handled it, when and why, lets the evidence stand up later. Taking it home or leaving it on a desk leaves gaps anyone can challenge, and booting it changes data and timestamps on the original.

cards.q: 00:45 · Ops floor. A critical flaw is announced in the warehouse label-printer firmware and the vendor says a patch is weeks away. The printers sit on the same network as the order-picking PCs. What goes in your ticket?
options: Wait for the vendor patch and take no other steps before it is released
Unplug all the printers so warehouse staff write shipping labels by hand
Isolate the printers on a restricted segment until the patch arrives
Write a firmware fix in-house and flash it onto every printer tonight
cards.answer: Isolate the printers on a restricted segment until the patch arrives
cards.why: When no patch exists, use a compensating control that reduces exposure: segmenting the vulnerable printers limits who can reach them until the fix is available. Waiting accepts the risk without anyone deciding to, and unplugging halts shipping for a threat you can contain. Home-made firmware voids support and can brick the fleet.

cards.q: 01:30 · Ops floor. The DR plan for the HR system has not been touched in eighteen months. Before anything more elaborate, you want each team to confirm its contact list, equipment and steps are still correct. Which test do you set up?
options: Run a parallel test that brings up the HR recovery site tonight
Send each team a checklist review of its section to confirm and correct
Run a full interruption test that switches HR to the recovery site
Skip testing and plan to rewrite the HR plan from scratch next year
cards.answer: Send each team a checklist review of its section to confirm and correct
cards.why: A checklist (read-through) test has each team review its part of the plan for accuracy: current contacts, equipment and steps. It is the cheapest way to catch staleness before investing in heavier tests. Parallel or full interruption tests on an unverified plan waste effort and add risk, and skipping tests leaves a plan that may fail when needed.

cards.q: 02:50 · Ops floor. Ransomware hit a logistics firm down the road through its online backups, which were encrypted along with production. Your ticket asks how Tessaly's endpoint backups should be protected. What do you propose?
options: Keep an immutable or offline copy that production credentials cannot touch
Back up endpoints more often to the same network share they use now
Rely on the endpoints' local restore points to recover after ransomware
Encrypt the backups with the same admin account that manages endpoints
cards.answer: Keep an immutable or offline copy that production credentials cannot touch
cards.why: Backups are a ransomware target, so at least one copy must be immutable or offline and out of reach of production credentials, in line with the 3-2-1 approach. More frequent copies to a reachable share are encrypted just as fast, and local restore points are commonly deleted by ransomware. Protecting backups with the same admin account leaves them exposed to the same compromise.

cards.q: 03:40 · Ops floor. Server builds at Tessaly depend on whoever is on shift: some turn off unused services, some do not. Your ticket asks for a single target configuration. What do you propose?
options: Let each engineer keep their own build habits and review them once a year
Write a new hardening guide from scratch without any outside reference
Buy a new server model that comes pre-hardened from the manufacturer
Adopt an industry benchmark, tailor it, and approve it as the standard
cards.answer: Adopt an industry benchmark, tailor it, and approve it as the standard
cards.why: Configuration standards give every build the same approved, hardened settings; starting from a recognised benchmark and tailoring it to Tessaly's needs is faster and better tested than inventing one. Individual habits create inconsistent attack surfaces. Writing from scratch duplicates effort and misses known issues, and a pre-hardened model still needs Tessaly's own standard to stay consistent.

cards.q: 04:15 · Ops floor. A change to the customs-declaration service is approved for 05:00. The plan explains how to deploy but says nothing about what happens if the new version fails. What do you add before it goes ahead?
options: Nothing, since the change was approved and approval covers any failure
A promise from the developer to fix any problem in the morning if needed
A tested rollback plan with the trigger for using it and who makes the call
A note to the service desk telling them to expect complaints from customers
cards.answer: A tested rollback plan with the trigger for using it and who makes the call
cards.why: A sound change request includes a backout plan: tested steps to restore the previous state, the conditions that trigger it and who decides. Without one, a failed change becomes an unplanned outage. Approval does not undo a failure, a morning fix leaves customs filings broken overnight, and warning the service desk plans for failure instead of preventing it.

cards.q: 03:00 · Network core. Traffic analysis shows a compromised warehouse server sending gigabytes to an unknown address. The server also runs the nightly stock sync the morning shift relies on. The ops lead wants to wait until the sync finishes at 05:30. What do you do first?
options: Let the sync finish at 05:30, then isolate the server once it is done
Isolate the server's network now, then plan around the stock sync
Wipe and reinstall the server now so the attacker is removed at once
Phone the address's hosting provider and wait to see what they report
cards.answer: Isolate the server's network now, then plan around the stock sync
cards.why: In the incident lifecycle, containment comes before convenience: active exfiltration must be stopped to limit damage, and the business impact of the sync is managed separately. Waiting two and a half hours lets more data leave. Wiping now destroys the evidence needed to understand the breach, and waiting on a hosting provider hands your response to someone else.

cards.q: 05:10 · Ops floor. Your ticket proposes a decoy server in the DMZ to learn how attackers probe Tessaly. A colleague suggests adding a banner inviting visitors to download 'free payment data'. What do you decide?
options: Build the decoy to be found, and drop the banner that lures attackers
Add the banner, since more attackers means more intelligence to collect
Place the decoy inside the payments network so it looks more convincing
Fill the decoy with real customer data so attackers find it believable
cards.answer: Build the decoy to be found, and drop the banner that lures attackers
cards.why: A honeypot works by enticement, being there to be found, not by entrapment, actively inducing someone to commit an offence they would not otherwise commit. Entrapment can undermine legal action and create liability. Placing the decoy on the real payments network or seeding it with real data turns a research tool into an actual exposure.

cards.q: 06:20 · Ops floor. Tessaly's disaster budget is tight. For the internal archive-search service, which the business can live without for two weeks, finance proposes a recovery site that is only space, power and cooling. What do you recommend?
options: Reject it and ask for a hot site so the archive service fails over instantly
Reject it and keep no recovery site at all, since the service is not critical
Accept it but also move the payments systems onto the same cold site
Accept the cold site, since this service can tolerate two weeks down
cards.answer: Accept the cold site, since this service can tolerate two weeks down
cards.why: A cold site provides the building and utilities but no equipment or data, so recovery takes days to weeks. It is the cheapest option and fits a service whose maximum tolerable downtime is two weeks. A hot site overspends on a low-priority system, having no site at all ignores the two-week limit, and payments would badly miss their downtime limits on a cold site.

cards.q: 23:35 · Ops floor. CCTV covers the Ops floor loading bay, but recordings are overwritten after 48 hours and nobody watches the feeds at night. Your ticket asks how to make the cameras useful. What do you propose?
options: Remove the cameras, since nobody is watching them anyway at night
Add more cameras to the loading bay and keep the 48-hour overwrite
Monitor feeds at night and keep recordings as long as policy requires
Post dummy cameras across the site to deter intruders at lower cost
cards.answer: Monitor feeds at night and keep recordings as long as policy requires
cards.why: CCTV deters, detects and records, but detection needs someone watching or alerting, and investigation needs recordings retained long enough to be reviewed. Removing cameras loses the deterrent and the evidence. More cameras without monitoring or retention just record more that gets overwritten, and dummy cameras can deter but never detect or record.

cards.q: 00:25 · Ops floor. A forensic image of a compromised payments server is sitting on the evidence store, with its hash recorded at collection. You are about to start analysis tonight. What do you do first?
options: Mount the original image read-write so you can search it faster tonight
Verify the hash, then analyse a working copy and keep the original sealed
Skip the hash check, since the image was hashed when it was collected
Analyse the live server directly, since it still has everything on it
cards.answer: Verify the hash, then analyse a working copy and keep the original sealed
cards.why: Evidence processing protects integrity: confirming the hash shows the image has not changed since collection, and working on a copy keeps the original pristine for verification or court. Mounting the original read-write may alter it. Skipping verification leaves integrity unproven, and working on the live server changes evidence and alerts any attacker still inside.

cards.q: 01:40 · Ops floor. Last night's external scan of the Ops floor reported almost no vulnerabilities, yet an internal audit keeps finding outdated software on the same servers. Your ticket asks why. What do you propose?
options: Add credentialed scans that log in and inspect installed software versions
Accept the external scan's results, since that is what attackers would see
Replace the scanner with a different vendor's product and scan again
Scan only once a year, because the results differ between the two methods
cards.answer: Add credentialed scans that log in and inspect installed software versions
cards.why: Unauthenticated scans see only what is exposed on the network, so they miss outdated software inside the host. Credentialed scans log in and check installed versions and configuration, giving a far more complete picture. Accepting the outside view ignores insiders and attackers who get a foothold, a new scanner has the same blind spot without credentials, and scanning less often is worse.

cards.q: 02:10 · Ops floor. Tessaly's order-entry servers run as a pair, but they are both in the same rack on the same power feed. When the rack PDU failed last month, both went down together. What do you propose?
options: Keep them in one rack, but buy a spare PDU to swap in if it fails again
Add a third server to the same rack so more nodes are in the cluster
Remove the second server, since it clearly did not help during the outage
Place the pair in separate racks on independent power and network feeds
cards.answer: Place the pair in separate racks on independent power and network feeds
cards.why: High availability depends on removing single points of failure: redundant servers must not share one rack, power feed or network path. Separating the pair makes one PDU failure survivable. A spare PDU still needs a manual swap during an outage, a third node in the same rack shares the same failure, and removing redundancy makes things worse.

cards.q: 03:20 · Ops floor. Tessaly's DR plan relies on a reciprocal agreement: a partner freight company will host Tessaly's systems if disaster strikes. The partner has since doubled its own workload on the same kit. What do you recommend?
options: Keep relying on the agreement, since it was signed in good faith by both sides
Move all Tessaly workloads into the partner's data centre permanently
Review whether the partner can still take the load and plan a firm alternative
Drop the recovery site entirely and rely on insurance to cover any disaster
cards.answer: Review whether the partner can still take the load and plan a firm alternative
cards.why: Reciprocal (mutual aid) agreements are cheap but fragile: the partner's capacity changes, the agreement is hard to enforce, and hosting may expose Tessaly's data. A doubled workload means the capacity assumption must be retested, with a contracted alternative if it no longer holds. Relying on good faith ignores the risk, and insurance pays out money but does not keep the business running.

cards.q: 04:30 · Ops floor. Every month the platform team files the same change request to rotate the payments TLS certificate, using the same steps, and it never fails. The board is tired of reviewing it. Which do you approve?
options: Stop recording the rotation in the change process, since it always works
Make it a standard pre-approved change with a fixed, documented procedure
Keep bringing it to the board every month exactly as it is done today
Let each engineer decide how to rotate the certificate each month
cards.answer: Make it a standard pre-approved change with a fixed, documented procedure
cards.why: Change management recognises standard changes: low-risk, repeatable tasks with a proven procedure are pre-approved once, then carried out and logged without a board review each time. That keeps the record and frees the board for real risk. Dropping it from the process loses the record, and letting each engineer improvise throws away the proven procedure that made it low risk.

cards.q: 05:00 · Ops floor. Legal confirms that last night's breach exposed some customer card data. Tessaly's contracts and local regulation both set notification deadlines, and the ops lead wants to wait until the investigation is fully complete. What do you do?
options: Have legal confirm the deadlines and start notifications on time
Wait until the investigation is complete so every notice is fully accurate
Notify every customer on the list tonight by email, without legal review
Hold off notifying anyone unless the story reaches the press first
cards.answer: Have legal confirm the deadlines and start notifications on time
cards.why: Incident reporting duties run on legal and contractual timelines that do not wait for a complete investigation; legal determines who must be told, by when and in what form, and notices can be updated as facts emerge. Waiting risks missed deadlines and penalties, notifying without review risks inaccurate statements, and notifying only if the press finds out breaks the obligation itself.

cards.q: 06:10 · Ops floor. Tessaly's backup reports show green for the finance laptops every night, but nobody has ever tried restoring one. Your ticket asks for evidence the backups actually work. What do you propose?
options: Rely on the green backup reports, since they show every job has finished
Double the backup frequency so there are more copies to choose from
Wait until a laptop actually fails and treat its restore as the first test
Run regular test restores of sample laptops and record the results
cards.answer: Run regular test restores of sample laptops and record the results
cards.why: A backup is only proven by a successful restore: regular test restores catch corrupt media, missing files and broken procedures before a real loss. A completed job can still hold unusable data. More frequent copies multiply an unverified process, and waiting for a real failure makes the incident the test.

cards.q: 23:05 · Ops floor. Staff keep receiving invoice attachments that pass antivirus but later turn out to be malicious. Your ticket asks for a control at the mail gateway. What do you propose?
options: Block every attachment company-wide so no invoices can arrive by email
Ask staff to check each attachment's file size before they open it
Detonate unknown attachments in a sandbox before they reach any mailbox
Rely on antivirus signatures, since they will catch up with the threat
cards.answer: Detonate unknown attachments in a sandbox before they reach any mailbox
cards.why: Sandboxing runs unknown files in an isolated environment and watches their behaviour, catching malware that signatures miss before it reaches users. Blocking every attachment breaks legitimate invoicing, and asking staff to judge file sizes offers no real protection. Waiting for signatures leaves users exposed to exactly the new threats already getting through.

cards.q: 00:40 · Ops floor. The SIEM raises a 'failed logon' alert every time any account mistypes its password once, burying the queue. Your ticket asks how to keep real brute-force attempts visible. What do you propose?
options: Turn off failed-logon alerts entirely, since they are almost always typos
Alert only when failures pass a set threshold within a short time window
Keep alerting on every single failure and add more analysts to cope
Alert on failures only for accounts belonging to senior executives
cards.answer: Alert only when failures pass a set threshold within a short time window
cards.why: A clipping level sets a baseline threshold of normal errors, so alerts fire only when failures exceed it in a set window, which is what a brute-force attempt looks like. That filters the noise without losing the signal. Turning alerts off hides real attacks, more analysts spend time on typos, and watching only executives ignores the service and admin accounts attackers prefer.

cards.q: 01:15 · Ops floor. Tessaly's incident response plan lists team members who have since left, and nobody knows who to call for legal or PR at night. Your ticket is to get the IR function ready. What do you do?
options: Update the IR plan's roles and 24/7 contacts, then brief the team on them
Wait for the next real incident, then find the right contacts on the night
Buy a new SIEM, since better tooling will make up for the missing contacts
Keep the plan as it is, since most listed people can still be reached somehow
cards.answer: Update the IR plan's roles and 24/7 contacts, then brief the team on them
cards.why: Preparation is the first phase of incident response: current roles, authority and 24/7 contacts for technical, legal and communications support must be defined and known before an incident. Hunting for contacts mid-incident wastes the hours that matter most. A new tool does not tell you who to call, and a plan full of departed staff will fail when needed.

cards.q: 02:35 · Ops floor. Tessaly has moved half its warehouse staff to new laptops and a new remote-access tool since the business continuity plan was last updated. Your ticket is to keep the plan usable. What do you do?
options: Leave the BCP as it is, since the business processes themselves have not changed
Rewrite the BCP only after the next real disruption shows what went wrong
Replace the BCP with the vendor's generic continuity guide for the tool
Update the BCP for the new tools and set a regular review after major changes
cards.answer: Update the BCP for the new tools and set a regular review after major changes
cards.why: A business continuity plan must be maintained as the organisation changes; new tools and working patterns change recovery steps, dependencies and contacts. Regular reviews triggered by major change keep the plan usable. Leaving it stale means recovery steps no longer match reality, waiting for a disruption makes the plan fail first, and a vendor's generic guide does not reflect Tessaly's processes.

cards.q: 03:15 · Ops floor. You want Tessaly's leadership to rehearse their decisions for a regional flood that closes two warehouses, without disrupting any operations or systems. Which exercise do you set up?
options: Close the two warehouses for a day to see how the business actually copes
Run a full failover of warehouse systems to the recovery site overnight
Run a tabletop exercise where leaders talk through the flood scenario
Email leaders the continuity plan and ask them each to read it this week
cards.answer: Run a tabletop exercise where leaders talk through the flood scenario
cards.why: A tabletop exercise gathers decision-makers to discuss a realistic scenario step by step, testing roles, decisions and communication without touching operations. It reveals gaps in the plan and leaders' understanding cheaply. Closing warehouses or failing over systems is disruptive and aimed at technical recovery, and reading the plan alone does not rehearse any decisions.

cards.q: 04:55 · Ops floor. The only signed copies of Tessaly's customer contracts and insurance policies are in a filing cabinet at head office. The continuity plan does not mention them. What goes in your ticket?
options: Leave them in the cabinet, since head office has not had a problem so far
Add these records to a vital records programme with protected off-site copies
Scan them to a shared folder on the head-office file server and stop there
Shred the paper copies so nobody can steal the signed contracts from the office
cards.answer: Add these records to a vital records programme with protected off-site copies
cards.why: A vital records programme identifies the records the business needs to operate and recover, such as contracts, insurance and legal documents, and keeps protected copies off-site. A single cabinet can be lost in one fire or flood. A scan on the same site's server shares the same risk, and shredding the originals destroys records Tessaly may need to prove its rights.

cards.q: 05:35 · Ops floor. Night staff at the sorting centre say they would not know what to do in a chemical spill or bomb threat; the emergency steps are buried in a 90-page continuity plan. Your ticket is to fix this. What do you propose?
options: Give staff short emergency response guidelines, posted and practised
Tell staff to read the full 90-page plan so they understand every detail
Leave emergency decisions to whoever happens to be the most senior on shift
Hire an outside firm to take over all emergency decisions at the centre
cards.answer: Give staff short emergency response guidelines, posted and practised
cards.why: Emergency response guidelines give people the immediate actions to protect life and safety: who to call, how to evacuate, what to do first. They must be short, visible and practised. A 90-page plan will not be read in a crisis, leaving it to whoever is senior produces inconsistent responses, and an outside firm cannot act in the first minutes on site.

cards.q: 06:30 · Ops floor. Endpoint engineers still apply security settings to new laptops by following a checklist by hand, and audits keep finding missed steps. Your ticket asks for a better approach. What do you propose?
options: Add more steps to the checklist so engineers remember each setting
Let each engineer choose which settings matter most for their laptops
Stop applying settings to laptops and rely on staff to be careful online
Automate the baseline with configuration tooling and report on compliance
cards.answer: Automate the baseline with configuration tooling and report on compliance
cards.why: Configuration management scales through automation: tooling applies the approved baseline identically every time and reports devices that fall out of compliance, removing human error. A longer checklist adds more steps to miss. Letting engineers pick settings creates inconsistency, and dropping hardening leaves every laptop at its insecure defaults.

cards.q: 23:45 · Ops floor. A new vulnerability affects a specific database version, and nobody can say which Tessaly servers run it. Your ticket asks how to answer questions like this in minutes next time. What do you propose?
options: Ask each team by email which database versions they happen to be running
Scan the whole network every time a new vulnerability is announced
Keep an automatically updated inventory of assets and their versions
Standardise on one database vendor so there is less to track in future
cards.answer: Keep an automatically updated inventory of assets and their versions
cards.why: Configuration management depends on knowing what you have: an accurate, automatically updated asset and configuration inventory (a CMDB) answers exposure questions quickly and underpins patching and incident response. Email surveys are slow and incomplete, ad-hoc scans take time and miss offline systems, and switching vendors still leaves you not knowing where each version runs.

cards.q: 00:55 · Ops floor. Last month's patch run on the web servers reported success, but a follow-up audit found a third of the servers still vulnerable. Your ticket asks how to close this gap. What do you propose?
options: Trust the patch tool's success report, since it covers every server
Rescan after each patch run to confirm the fix actually took effect
Patch twice each month so any missed servers are caught the next time
Replace the patch tool with a new product from a different vendor
cards.answer: Rescan after each patch run to confirm the fix actually took effect
cards.why: Vulnerability management is a cycle, and verification closes it: a follow-up scan confirms each vulnerability is actually gone, catching failed installs, pending reboots and missed hosts. A tool's success report shows the job ran, not that the fix is in place. Patching more often repeats the blind spot, and a new tool without verification has the same gap.

cards.q: 01:50 · Ops floor. The recovery site for the payments platform has been built, and you want to prove it can process real transactions while production keeps running normally. Which test do you schedule?
options: Run a parallel test that processes real workload at the recovery site too
Run a full interruption test that shuts down payments production for it
Hold a walkthrough where the team talks through the recovery steps
Do a checklist review of the recovery site's equipment inventory list
cards.answer: Run a parallel test that processes real workload at the recovery site too
cards.why: A parallel test brings the recovery site up and runs real workloads there alongside production, proving it can take the load without interrupting the live service. A full interruption test shuts production down and carries real risk. Walkthroughs and checklist reviews check the plan on paper but do not show the site can process transactions.

cards.q: 02:45 · Ops floor. A single endpoint engineer can write a new software package, approve it for the fleet, and push it to every laptop without anyone else being involved. Your ticket asks how to reduce the risk. What do you propose?
options: Keep the current process, since the engineer is trusted and experienced
Log every deployment and review the logs once a year during the audit
Give the whole endpoint team the same rights so there is no bottleneck
Split the tasks so a different person approves what the engineer deploys
cards.answer: Split the tasks so a different person approves what the engineer deploys
cards.why: Segregation of duties splits a sensitive process so no one person can complete it alone; separating build, approval and deployment means fraud or error needs collusion to succeed. Trust is not a control. Yearly log review detects misuse long after the damage, and giving everyone full rights multiplies the same risk.

cards.q: 03:35 · Ops floor. The master key for Tessaly's payment encryption hardware is currently known in full to one senior engineer. Your ticket asks how the key should be handled. What do you propose?
options: Leave the key with the senior engineer, since only he understands the system
Write the whole key on paper and lock it in the office safe as a backup
Divide the key into parts held by separate custodians, none knowing the whole
Email the key to the security team so more people can recover it if needed
cards.answer: Divide the key into parts held by separate custodians, none knowing the whole
cards.why: Split knowledge divides a secret so that no single person knows or holds all of it, with key components held by separate custodians and combined only under dual control. One person holding the whole key is a single point of failure and fraud. A single paper copy in a safe still gives one person the whole key, and email spreads it far beyond control.

cards.q: 04:20 · Ops floor. Tessaly's managed firewall provider takes up to three days to make rule changes, even during incidents. The contract says nothing about response times. Your ticket asks how to fix this. What do you propose?
options: Accept the delays, since the provider has always taken this long to act
Negotiate an SLA with agreed response times, faster for incidents
Give Tessaly staff the provider's admin password so they can make changes
Cancel the contract tonight and run the firewalls in-house from tomorrow
cards.answer: Negotiate an SLA with agreed response times, faster for incidents
cards.why: A service level agreement sets measurable commitments, such as response times by priority, with remedies if they are missed; it is how security operations hold providers to what the business needs. Accepting the delay leaves incidents unanswered for days. Sharing the provider's admin password breaks accountability, and cancelling overnight leaves nobody ready to run the firewalls.

cards.q: 05:15 · Ops floor. The same accounts-payable clerk has approved supplier payments for eight years and has never taken more than two days off. Auditors are uneasy. Your ticket asks for a control. What do you propose?
options: Rotate the approval role regularly and require an uninterrupted block of leave
Leave it as it is, since the clerk has never been caught doing anything wrong
Add a second clerk who approves exactly the same payments in the same way
Ask the clerk to sign a yearly statement saying no fraud has taken place
cards.answer: Rotate the approval role regularly and require an uninterrupted block of leave
cards.why: Job rotation and mandatory vacation bring a fresh person into a role, exposing ongoing fraud or errors the incumbent could otherwise hide. Never being caught is not evidence of no wrongdoing. A second clerk doing the same work gives no independent check, and a signed statement from the person being checked adds no assurance.

cards.q: 06:00 · Ops floor. A Tessaly executive is flying to a country known for searching devices at the border. She plans to take her everyday laptop with full access to finance systems. Your ticket asks what she should carry. What do you propose?
options: Let her take her normal laptop, since she will keep it in her bag the whole time
Tell her to leave the laptop in the hotel safe while she is out at meetings
Give her an extra laptop so she can carry both a work and a personal machine
Issue a clean loaner laptop with only what the trip needs, wiped on return
cards.answer: Issue a clean loaner laptop with only what the trip needs, wiped on return
cards.why: Travel security for high-risk destinations limits what can be lost or copied: a clean loaner holding only the data the trip needs, wiped and checked on return, protects both the traveller and Tessaly. An everyday laptop exposes all her access at a border search. A hotel safe is not secure against determined actors, and an extra laptop doubles the exposure.

cards.q: 23:25 · Ops floor. Facilities is replacing the Ops floor's emergency exit doors. The vendor offers doors that stay locked if power fails, saying this keeps intruders out during outages. What do you advise?
options: Accept the doors that stay locked, since protecting the servers comes first
Keep the old doors, since changing them now will only add to the cost
Choose doors that unlock on power failure so people can always get out
Install locked doors and give the night guard the only key to open them
cards.answer: Choose doors that unlock on power failure so people can always get out
cards.why: Emergency exits must be fail-safe, unlocking on power loss so people can escape; life safety always outranks asset protection. Fail-secure doors that stay locked can trap people during a fire that cuts power. Keeping unsuitable doors ducks the question, and relying on one guard with a key makes everyone's escape depend on one person being present.

cards.q: 00:15 · Ops floor. The server room is protected by a gas fire-suppression system. Engineers often work inside at night, and the system discharges with no warning. What goes in your ticket?
options: Switch to water sprinklers so the gas never discharges near the servers
Add a pre-discharge alarm and abort switch so people can get out first
Keep the system as it is, since the fire risk in the room is very low
Ban all night work in the server room instead of changing the system
cards.answer: Add a pre-discharge alarm and abort switch so people can get out first
cards.why: Gas suppression can displace oxygen or harm people, so life safety requires a pre-discharge alarm, time delay and abort switch to let occupants evacuate before release, plus training on what the alarm means. Sprinklers would damage the equipment the system protects, a low fire risk is no reason to accept a lethal hazard, and banning night work does not help people already inside.

cards.q: 01:25 · Ops floor. Two Tessaly engineers often work alone overnight in the remote sorting-centre plant room. Last month one slipped and lay injured for an hour before anyone noticed. Your ticket asks for a safety fix. What do you propose?
options: Set up a lone-worker check-in with automatic escalation if one is missed
Tell the engineers to be more careful when they work alone at night
Add CCTV to the plant room and review the recordings each morning
Stop all night work at the sorting centre until more staff are hired
cards.answer: Set up a lone-worker check-in with automatic escalation if one is missed
cards.why: Lone-worker safety needs a way to raise the alarm when someone cannot: regular check-ins, or a man-down device, that escalate automatically when missed. Telling people to be careful does not help after a fall. Reviewing CCTV in the morning finds an injury hours too late, and stopping all night work halts operations without addressing the risk.

cards.q: 02:20 · Ops floor. An engineer finds the Ops floor server rack left unlocked with a keyboard and monitor attached and an admin console logged in. Nobody signed out the rack. What goes in your ticket?
options: Leave the console logged in, since only staff can enter the Ops floor anyway
Remove the keyboard and monitor so nobody can use the console at all
Post a sign asking staff to lock the rack when they are finished with it
Lock racks by default, log key access, and time out idle console sessions
cards.answer: Lock racks by default, log key access, and time out idle console sessions
cards.why: Physical security works in layers: locked racks with logged key access control who reaches the hardware, and a console session that times out stops anyone walking up and using live admin rights. Relying on the room door alone ignores insiders and visitors. Removing the console hampers legitimate work, and a sign changes nothing on its own.

cards.q: 03:55 · Ops floor. Delivery drivers, cleaners and auditors all visit the Ops floor, and the sign-in book is often blank. Last week a visitor was found alone near the network cabinet. What goes in your ticket?
options: Trust visitors to sign in themselves, since most of them are regulars
Ban all visitors from the Ops floor, including auditors and contractors
Require ID checks, a sign-in log, badges and escorts in secure areas
Add a camera near the network cabinet and keep the current visitor rules
cards.answer: Require ID checks, a sign-in log, badges and escorts in secure areas
cards.why: Visitor management verifies identity, records who is on site and when, marks visitors with badges and keeps them escorted in secure areas. That prevents an unescorted person near the network cabinet. Self sign-in is not a control, banning all visitors blocks necessary work such as audits, and a camera only records what the missing escort should have prevented.

cards.q: 05:20 · Ops floor. HR asks you to pull a warehouse manager's email and browsing logs because a colleague has accused him of harassment. There is no suggestion of a crime. Nobody from legal has been involved. What do you do?
options: Pull everything about the manager now, since HR has asked for it tonight
Confirm HR and legal have authorised and scoped it before acting
Refuse, since only the police are allowed to investigate employees
Tell the manager about the request so he can explain his side first
cards.answer: Confirm HR and legal have authorised and scoped it before acting
cards.why: An administrative (internal) investigation still needs proper authority, a defined scope and respect for privacy law and policy; checking HR and legal sign-off keeps the evidence usable and protects everyone involved. Pulling everything on request risks overreach. Refusing ignores Tessaly's legitimate right to investigate internally, and tipping off the subject can lead to lost evidence.

cards.q: 06:35 · Ops floor. A file-integrity monitor shows the payments gateway's configuration changed at 01:10. There is no change ticket, and the on-call engineer says it was not him. What do you do?
options: Treat it as a potential incident and investigate before rolling back
Raise a change ticket now to cover the edit, so the records are complete
Roll the change back at once and do not look into how it was made
Ignore it, since the gateway is still processing payments without errors
cards.answer: Treat it as a potential incident and investigate before rolling back
cards.why: An unauthorised change is a change management failure and possibly a sign of compromise, so it is investigated as a potential incident: who made it, how, and why. Filing a retroactive ticket hides the question. Rolling back without looking destroys evidence and may miss the attacker's access, and a working gateway says nothing about whether it is secure.

cards.q: 04:45 · Ops floor. Staff at the sorting centre regularly copy delivery manifests with customer addresses onto personal USB sticks to work from home. Your ticket asks for a control. What do you propose?
options: Allow personal USB sticks as long as staff promise to keep them safe
Glue every USB port shut so no device of any kind can ever be used
Tell staff to delete the files from their sticks at the end of each week
Block unapproved USB storage and provide encrypted, company-issued devices
cards.answer: Block unapproved USB storage and provide encrypted, company-issued devices
cards.why: Removable media control lets only approved, encrypted devices be used, so data leaving the site stays protected and accountable, while giving staff a sanctioned way to work. Promises are not controls. Gluing ports blocks keyboards and legitimate devices too, and weekly deletion leaves customer data on lost or stolen sticks in the meantime.

cards.q: 05:45 · Ops floor. Tapes, drives and USB media in the Ops floor store room carry no markings, so nobody can tell which hold confidential payment data. Your ticket asks how to fix this. What do you propose?
options: Treat all the media as public, since nobody knows what is on it anyway
Throw all unlabelled media away tonight to clear out the store room
Label each piece of media with its classification and handling requirements
Keep the media unlabelled so a thief cannot tell which items are valuable
cards.answer: Label each piece of media with its classification and handling requirements
cards.why: Media marking shows the classification and handling rules for each item, so people store, transport and destroy it correctly. Treating unknown media as public invites exposure, and throwing it away unsanitised may leak data and destroy records. Leaving media unmarked relies on obscurity while ensuring your own staff mishandle it.

cards.q: 06:50 · Ops floor. Tessaly's backup tapes are kept in a cupboard next to the servers they back up. Your ticket asks how to protect them against a fire or flood in the Ops floor building. What do you propose?
options: Keep the tapes in the cupboard, since the Ops floor has never flooded
Store copies at a secure off-site facility well away from the building
Move the tapes into the server room so they are close when needed
Keep backups on a second disk inside each server instead of on tapes
cards.answer: Store copies at a secure off-site facility well away from the building
cards.why: Backup media must be stored off-site, securely and far enough from the primary site that one disaster cannot destroy both the systems and their backups. A cupboard next to the servers shares their fate, the server room is even closer to it, and a second disk in the same server is lost with it.

cards.q: 23:10 · Ops floor. Old backup tapes with customer data are piling up far beyond the seven years Tessaly's retention schedule requires. Nobody has ever destroyed a tape. What goes in your ticket?
options: Destroy tapes past retention with a certified method, and record each one
Keep every tape forever, since the data might be useful again one day
Put the old tapes in the normal office bins for collection this week
Overwrite the old tapes with new backups and keep them in circulation
cards.answer: Destroy tapes past retention with a certified method, and record each one
cards.why: Media management covers the full lifecycle: when retention expires, media should be securely destroyed with a verified method and a certificate, cutting the data exposed in any breach or legal demand. Keeping everything forever raises risk and discovery cost. Ordinary bins leak data, and reusing tapes past their service life risks failed backups.

cards.q: 00:30 · Ops floor. An intruder on a finance laptop ran PowerShell commands, but your logs show only that PowerShell started, not what it did. Your ticket asks for better endpoint visibility. What do you propose?
options: Block PowerShell entirely on every laptop in the finance department
Log everything on each laptop but keep the logs only on the laptop itself
Review the laptop logs by hand once a quarter during the internal audit
Turn on command-line and script logging and forward it to the SIEM
cards.answer: Turn on command-line and script logging and forward it to the SIEM
cards.why: Useful monitoring captures the events that matter: process command lines and script-block logging show what an attacker actually ran, and forwarding them centrally keeps them safe and correlated. Blocking PowerShell outright breaks administration without improving visibility. Local-only logs can be wiped by the intruder, and quarterly review finds the attack months late.

cards.q: 01:55 · Ops floor. The SIEM fires an alert for a possible credential dump on a domain controller. Two analysts handled the last one completely differently, and one of them forgot to preserve memory. Your ticket asks for consistency. What do you propose?
options: Let each analyst handle the alert the way their experience tells them to
Turn the alert off until a senior analyst is on shift to handle it
Write a runbook for the alert with steps, evidence and escalation
Buy a new SIEM product that promises to handle this type of alert
cards.answer: Write a runbook for the alert with steps, evidence and escalation
cards.why: A runbook documents the exact steps for a known alert type: triage checks, evidence to preserve, containment actions and when to escalate. It makes responses consistent and repeatable and prevents missed steps such as memory capture. Personal judgement produced the inconsistency, disabling the alert creates a blind spot, and a new SIEM does not tell analysts what to do.

cards.q: 02:40 · Ops floor. Threat intelligence reports a campaign targeting logistics firms, with known malicious domains and file hashes. Nobody at Tessaly does anything with these reports. Your ticket asks how to use them. What do you propose?
options: Read the reports and file them, since the campaign may not target Tessaly
Feed the indicators into detection tools and hunt for them in recent logs
Block every domain registered in the last year to be on the safe side
Forward the reports to all staff and ask them to watch for the domains
cards.answer: Feed the indicators into detection tools and hunt for them in recent logs
cards.why: Threat intelligence is useful only when acted on: loading the indicators into detection tools catches new activity, and hunting through recent logs shows whether the campaign already reached Tessaly. Filing reports unread wastes them. Blocking every new domain breaks legitimate business, and asking all staff to watch for domains is not a reliable control.

cards.q: 03:10 · Ops floor. The disaster is over and the primary data centre is repaired. Tessaly has been running at the recovery site for five days. The ops lead wants to move everything back tonight in one go. What do you recommend?
options: Move the least critical systems back first, then the critical ones
Move everything back tonight in one go so the recovery site can be closed
Move the most critical systems back first so they get the best hardware
Stay at the recovery site permanently to avoid the risk of moving at all
cards.answer: Move the least critical systems back first, then the critical ones
cards.why: Returning to the primary site starts with the least critical systems, proving the rebuilt site works before critical operations depend on it; the disaster is not over until everything is back and stable. Moving everything at once risks a second outage. Moving critical systems first exposes them to an unproven site, and staying at a recovery site built for short-term use is not a plan.

events.title: Reconnaissance sweep
events.text: 03:00 — A cluster of week-old lookalike domains is walking your public surface: DNS lookups, careers-page scrapes, a polite portscan that stays just under the alerting threshold. Someone is drawing a map of you.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0043, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.15 · outline 6.2

events.title: Resource development in your name
events.text: 03:10 — Intel flags fresh infrastructure staged in your name: a typosquatted package on a public registry and a signing certificate bought by a shell company. Nothing has touched you yet. It is being built to.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0042, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.2 · outline 1.11

events.title: Initial access — the lookalike portal
events.text: 03:20 — A finance analyst just entered credentials on a page that looked exactly like your SSO portal, and an inbound VPN session followed forty seconds later from an address no employee has ever used.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0001, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.2 · outline 1.12

events.title: Execution — a spreadsheet with children
events.text: 03:30 — A spreadsheet on a workstation in accounts payable just spawned a shell, and the shell spawned a script host, and the script host is pulling something down over an encrypted channel. Word documents do not usually have children.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0002, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.17 · outline 7.7

events.title: Persistence — autoruns nobody ordered
events.text: 03:40 — Change monitoring reports a new scheduled task, a fresh run key, and a service account nobody remembers creating — all in the last hour, all on machines that were clean at midnight. Someone is making sure a reboot will not evict them.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0003, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.16 · outline 7.3

events.title: Privilege escalation request
events.text: 03:50 — A helpdesk account that has never touched a server just requested a domain-admin token, citing a change window that is not on the calendar. The request is syntactically perfect. That is what worries you.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0004, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.14 · outline 5.4

events.title: Stealth — dressed as your baseline
events.text: 04:00 — Nothing is alerting, which is the problem: a review pass shows outbound traffic timed to mimic your backup jobs, binaries named one character off from system utilities, and logons that only ever occur inside business-hours noise. Somebody is dressing as your baseline.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0005, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.17 · outline 7.2

events.title: Defense impairment — eyes going dark
events.text: 04:10 — Three EDR agents went silent inside two minutes, a log-forwarding pipeline is dropping events on the floor, and someone just tried to add an exclusion path to the on-access scanner. Your eyes are being put out one by one.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0112, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.17 · outline 7.7

events.title: Credential access on the jump host
events.text: 04:20 — Memory forensics on a jump host found a credential-dumping tool parked next to lsass, and the domain controller shows a slow, patient spray against service accounts: two guesses per account per hour, forever.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0006, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.14 · outline 5.6

events.title: Discovery — a workstation gone shopping
events.text: 04:30 — A single workstation has, in the last hour, enumerated every share it can reach, queried group memberships it has no business caring about, and pinged its way across two subnets. It is not lost. It is shopping.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0007, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.17 · outline 7.2

events.title: Lateral movement across the map
events.text: 04:40 — The compromised workstation just opened admin sessions on three servers in a segment it should not be able to see, riding remote-service credentials that checked out as valid. The map you failed to defend is being walked.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0008, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.11 · outline 4.1

events.title: Collection — a suitcase in the vault
events.text: 04:50 — A staging directory is quietly filling on a file server: customer exports, key material, an HR extract — compressed, encrypted, and named to look like installer cache. Someone is packing a suitcase in your vault.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0009, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.5 · outline 2.6

events.title: Command and control heartbeat
events.text: 05:00 — Egress analytics found a heartbeat: one HTTPS request every 47 seconds to a content-delivery domain registered eleven days ago, payload sizes almost — not quite — identical. Something inside is checking in with something outside.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0011, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.12 · outline 4.2

events.title: Exfiltration at nine times normal
events.text: 05:10 — Outbound volume from the file segment is running nine times its nightly norm, chunked into polite parcels and routed through a cloud storage API your business does use — just never at 5 a.m., and never this much.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0010, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.5 · outline 2.6

events.title: Impact — the quiet part is over
events.text: 05:20 — File servers are renaming their contents with an extension you have only seen in incident reports, shadow copies are being deleted in bulk, and a text file titled HOW_TO_RECOVER just appeared in every share. The quiet part of the night is over.
events.citation: MITRE ATT&CK TA0040, attack.mitre.org · SG ch.18 · outline 7.10

events.title: Fieldwork ping — SOC 2 Type II
events.text: 03:15 — The external audit team's fieldwork portal pings: they have pulled tonight's control evidence for the service-organization report and want the operating-effectiveness samples walked through before breakfast. Type II means the whole period counts — including this shift.
events.citation: SG ch.15 · outline 6.5

events.title: Change reconciliation demand
events.text: 04:15 — Internal audit's continuous-monitoring job flagged four production changes this week with no linked approval record. They are asking the night desk to reconcile each one against the change calendar before the morning stand-up — emergency changes included.
events.citation: SG ch.16 · outline 7.9

events.title: Recertification red row
events.text: 05:30 — The quarterly access recertification came back with a red row: a departed contractor's account shows a successful logon dated three days after their exit interview. HR says leaver, the directory says active, and the reviewer wants to know which one is lying.
events.citation: SG ch.13 · outline 5.5

events.title: CISO ping — board pre-read math
events.text: 03:45 — The CISO, unable to sleep, messages the desk directly: the board pre-read is due at 08:00 and the annualized-loss figures for the top three scenarios read wrong to her. Sanity-check the exposure math before it goes to print.
events.citation: SG ch.2 · outline 1.9

events.title: Counsel joins the bridge
events.text: 04:45 — Outside counsel joins the incident bridge uninvited: if tonight's activity touched resident data from two particular jurisdictions, notification clocks may already be running, and they need the exposure scoped — what data, whose, and under which law — before advising the CEO.
events.citation: SG ch.4 · outline 1.4

events.title: The chair wants failover answers
events.text: 05:45 — A board member read about a rival's three-day outage and emailed the chair at midnight. By 05:45 it has rolled downhill to you: could we survive that, how long could finance be down, and when did we last actually test the failover rather than talk about it?
events.citation: SG ch.3 · outline 1.7
